en: The Complete Works of the Five Lamps, Volume One.
Compiled by the monk (Chao Yong), Abbot of Shenggan Chan Temple in the Capital;
proofread by the monk (Chao Kui), Abbot of Gu Huayan Temple in the Capital. Presented for Imperial Review.

The ancient Buddhas of the seven directions appeared in the world throughout an infinite succession of time; it is impossible to know them all or enumerate them exhaustively. The ancestral lamp continues to shine...
The transmission must have originated with the Buddha; therefore, from Śākyamuni upwards, we briefly enumerate the Seven Buddhas. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"By the power of the diligence of the Seven Buddhas, they emitted light to extinguish the darkness. Each sat beneath a tree and therein attained Perfect Enlightenment."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, you are the teacher of the seven Buddhas; therefore, in this present compilation, the seven Buddhas are generally cited.
Regarding Vipaśyin Buddha (the 998th of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*), the verse says: "The body receives birth from within the signless, Just like various forms produced by illusion.
The mind-consciousness of the one who perceives the illusion is fundamentally non-existent; Both sin and merit are empty, with nothing upon which to dwell."
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste, with the clan name Koliya.
His father was Bandhu and his mother was Bandhumatī; he resided in the city of Bandhumatī.

Sitting beneath a Pāpala tree, he preached the Dharma in three assemblies, delivering three hundred and forty-eight thousand people. He had two disciples of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*): the first was named Khaṇḍa.
Tea. His second name was Tiṣya. His attendant was Aśoka. His son was Fangyeng.

Śikhin Buddha (the ninth hundred and ninety-ninth Tathāgata of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*) spoke in verse: "All wholesome dharmas that arise are fundamentally illusory; The various evil karmas one creates are likewise illusory.
The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind. Illusion produces that which has no root and no real nature. From the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
The *Saṃyuktāgama* states: When the human lifespan was seventy thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste, with the clan name Kauriya.

His father was Mingxiang (Vimalaprabha) and his mother was Guangyao (Prabhāvatī). He resided in the city of Guangxiang (Prabhāsa). He sat beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree and preached the Dharma in three assemblies.
He delivered two hundred and fifty thousand people. He had two disciples with supernormal powers: the first was named Abhibhū and the second was named Vāsavu.
His attendant was Kṣāntivādin, and his son was Ananta.

Vipaśyin Buddha (the first of the thousand Buddhas of the *Kṛtayuga*/*Bhadrakalpa*) spoke in verse: "The body is provisionally constructed from the four great elements; the mind is fundamentally unborn, yet it arises due to objects.
If the external object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist. Sin and merit are like illusions—they arise and they perish.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that this Buddha appeared in the world when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years. He was of the Kṣatriya caste and the Kauṇḍinya clan.
His father was named Good Lamp; his mother was named Renowned Precept. He resided in the city of Incomparable and sat beneath a *bala* tree.

He held two assemblies for preaching the Dharma, through which he delivered thirteen hundred thousand people. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Upavaṃśa and Uttara. His attendant was Śānti, and his son was Subuddhi.
Kakusandha Buddha (the first honored one of the present Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body;
To realize the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion. Having realized that the nature of body and mind is empty, How can such a person differ from the Buddha?
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Brahmin caste and belonged to the Kāśyapa clan.
His father was named Datta; his mother was Supratiṣṭhā. He resided in the city of Saṃmodana and sat beneath a Śirīṣa tree.

In a single assembly, he taught the Dharma and delivered forty thousand people across. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Sani and Vīra. His attendant was Sujāta; his chief disciple was Jayanta.
The Buddha Kanakamuni (the second honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha;

If there were truly a knowing subject, there would be no Buddha apart from it. The wise are able to know that the nature of sin is empty; They remain composed and are not terrified by birth and death. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was thirty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the caste of Brahmins and belonged to the Kāśyapa clan.
His surname was Śāla; his father was Mahābhūti and his mother was Sujayā. He resided in the city of Viśuddha and sat beneath an Udumbara tree as a brahmin.
In one assembly he preached the Dharma, delivering thirty thousand people. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Śubhananda and Uttara.
His attendant was Saumya, and his son was Nāyaka.
Kāśyapa Buddha (the third honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure; from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished.
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was of the Brāhmaṇa caste, with the clan name Kāśyapa; his father was Brahmā.

The Buddha was named Śrī (Virtue). His maternal uncle, Dhanañjaya, resided in the city of Vārāṇasī. Seated beneath a nyagrodha tree, he preached the Dharma in a single assembly, delivering twenty thousand people across [to liberation].
He possessed two disciples with supernormal powers: first, Tiṣya, and second, Bhāradvāja. His attendant was Subhūti, and his son was Senaka.
Śākyamuni Buddha (the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) was of the Kṣatriya caste. His father was King Śuddhodana; his mother was Mahāmāyā.

Having attained the rank of the Stage of Rebirth as Successor (*upapadya-parivarta*), he was born in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he was named the Celestial Being Viśeṣacintin, also known as the Great Being Vajrapāṇi.

He delivered the various heavenly hosts, expounding the practices of a successor. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he manifested his body and preached the Dharma, universally illuminating all.
The Sūtra says: When the Buddha was first born into the family of the Kṣatriyas, he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
Golden lotuses sprang up from the earth, spontaneously supporting his two feet. He took seven steps each toward the east and west, as well as the north and south.

Pointing his fingers at heaven and earth, he let out a lion’s roar, declaring: "In the zenith and nadir, as well as in the four intermediate directions, there is none who can surpass me. Immediately...
In the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin, on the eighth day of the fourth month, he was nineteen years old.
By the eighth day of the second month of the forty-second year, desiring to leave the household life, he thought to himself, "What further encounter shall I have?
He then went out to observe the sights at the four gates and witnessed the four signs; his heart was moved by both sorrow and joy, and he reflected: "This is old age and sickness..."
Death is ultimately something to be weary of and renounced. Then, at the hour of midnight, a celestial being named Śuddhāvāsa appeared within the window and, with palms joined, said:
"The time for your renunciation has arrived; you may depart. Upon hearing this, the Prince felt great joy in his heart and immediately leaped over the city wall and departed.
He went to Mount Daṇḍaka to practice the Way, beginning his training under Ārāḍa Kālāma.

He studied under Ārāḍa Kālāma for three years, but when he realized that the state of meditative concentration was not the ultimate goal, he abandoned it. He then went to Udraka Rāmaputra and studied the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for three years;

realizing this too was not the way, he likewise abandoned it. He then went to Mount Elephant Head (Gajaśīrṣa), where he joined the various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), subsisting on hemp and wheat for six years.
Thus the Sūtra says: "By means of being without mind or intention and without the activity of sensation, he completely subdued [all adversaries]."
The various non-Buddhists first underwent trials of heterodox methods; [the Buddha] demonstrated various skillful means and inspired diverse views to lead them to Bodhi.

Thus, the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* states that on the eighth day of the second month, at the time when the morning star appeared, the Bodhisattva attained enlightenment and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans;
he was then thirty years of age. This was precisely the third year of King Mu’s reign, the year of *Guiwei*. Subsequently, at the Deer Park...
In a forest grove, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the five disciples, including Kauṇḍinya, whereby they realized the fruits of the Path.
He remained in the world preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years. Later, he addressed his disciple Mahākāśyapa:
"I entrust to you the pure Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the true mark which is markless, and the subtle, sublime, orthodox Dharma. You must protect it."

"Maintain it, and command Ānanda to act as your deputy in transmitting this transformation so that it shall never be interrupted. Then he spoke a verse, saying: "The Dharma is originally without Dharma;
The Dharma-less is also Dharma. Now, at the time of entrusting the Dharma-less, How has any dharma ever been a dharma?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he further addressed Kāśyapa: "I now take this saṃghāṭī robe of golden thread and transmit it to you..."
“You must transmit this in turn to the one who holds the place of succession, until the appearance of the Buddha Maitreya, so that it does not perish.
When Kāśyapa heard these verses, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and said, “Excellent, excellent! I shall follow your instructions out of reverent obedience to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the city of Kuśinagara and addressed the great assembly: “I now suffer from back pain and wish to enter parinirvāṇa. He then proceeded to the Śi...
He proceeded to the banks of the river, beneath the twin *śāla* trees. Lying on his right side with his feet叠疊 (placed one upon the other), he remained in profound, tranquil stillness.
He then rose from his coffin to preach the Dharma for his mother. He specifically displayed his two feet to convert Bakkula and spoke the verse on impermanence:

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss. At that time, the disciples immediately [prepared] incense...

They vied with one another to cremate [the body] with firewood. After the embers subsided, the golden coffin remained as it was. At that time, the great assembly immediately praised the Buddha before him in verse, saying:
"How could the fierce and blazing fires of ordinary mortals Ever succeed in burning [this body]? We pray that the Honored One’s fire of samādhi May cremate this golden-hued body.
At that moment, the golden coffin rose from its seat to a height of seven *tāla* trees and moved back and forth through the air.
Through the Fire Transformation Samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), ashes were produced in an instant, and eight *hu* and four *dou* of śarīra were obtained.

This was on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign, the *Ren-shen* year. One thousand one hundred and seventeen years had passed since the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One when the teaching reached the Central Lands;
this was the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han, the *Wu-chen* year. —The World-Honored One.
As soon as he was born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, walked seven steps in every direction, and looked around the four quarters, saying:
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am honored. One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat; when the great assembly had gathered and settled, [he spoke].
Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said, "Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from his seat.
On another day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat and sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, "I request the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said, "In this assembly there are two bhikṣus who have violated the Vinaya. For this reason, I do not preach the Dharma. Thus spoke Ānanda.
Using his supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, he observed these bhikṣus and subsequently expelled them. The World-Honored One remained silent once more. Ānanda spoke again:
"Just now, because two bhikṣus had violated the precepts, those two bhikṣus have already been expelled. Why does the World-Honored One not preach the Dharma?
The World-Honored One said, "I have vowed never to preach the Dharma for those of the Two Vehicles, such as the śrāvakas. Thereupon, he descended from his seat.
One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat. When the great assembly had gathered and settled, Kāśyapa struck the gavel and said, "The World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. The World-Honored One remained in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for ninety days, preaching the Dharma for his mother.
When he was about to descend from the celestial realm, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all went to the sky to welcome him.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Padmavarṇā who thought to herself: "I am a female monastic; I will surely see the Buddha after the great monks.

It would be better for me to use my supernatural powers to transform myself into a universal monarch (cakravartin) surrounded by a thousand sons, so that I may be the very first to see the Buddha. Thus, her wish was fulfilled.
The World-Honored One, upon merely seeing her, rebuked her, saying: "Lotus-Color Bhikṣuṇī, how is it that you bypass the great bhikṣus to see me?
Although you see my physical body (rūpakāya), you do not see my Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Subhūti, sitting in meditative seclusion within a mountain cave, beheld my Dharma-body. Furthermore, in the past, when Mañjuśrī arrived at the assembly of all Buddhas, the Buddhas—
Each returned to their original place, except for one woman who sat near that Buddha and had entered into samādhi.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying, "Why is it that this person is able to sit near the Buddha while I am not?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "Simply awaken this woman and cause her to rise from her samādhi; you may ask her yourself. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times and [shook her]...
He pointed with his finger. Then, exerting all his supernatural powers, he supported her up to the Brahma Heaven, yet he was unable to release her from her concentration.
The World-Honored One said, "Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs, they too would be unable to release this woman from her concentration.
Forty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* worlds below, there is a Bodhisattva named Vimalaprabhā who can release this woman from her concentration. In an instant, Vimalaprabhā arrived.
A man emerged from the earth, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One commanded Wuming to come forth.
Wuming went back to the woman and snapped his fingers once; the woman thereupon emerged from her meditative concentration. Subsequently, the World-Honored One was asked by King Prasenajit:
"Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), does conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) exist? If one says it does not, then wisdom would not be dual. If...
"If one says they exist, wisdom should not be singular. What is the meaning of 'one' and 'two'?
The Buddha said, 'Great King, in the past, under the Dharma of the Buddha Dragon-Light (Nāgaprabha), you once asked about this meaning. Now I have nothing to say, and you have nothing to hear.
This absence of speaking and absence of hearing—this is called the meaning of one and the meaning of two. One day, the World-Honored One saw Mañjuśrī at the gate.
Standing outside, [the Buddha] said, “Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī, why do you not enter through the gate? Mañjuśrī replied, “I do not see a single dharma outside the gate;
why do you instruct me to enter? One day, while the World-Honored One was sitting, he saw two men carrying a pig past him.
He asked, “What is this? They replied, “The Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom; even a piglet does not escape it.”
[The monk] said, “World-Honored One, you ought to have asked [the question] back. The World-Honored One replied: Once, a follower of another school asked me, “Are all phenomena eternal?
I did not answer. He asked again, “Are all phenomena impermanent? I likewise did not answer. The follower of another school said, “The World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom;
why do you not answer me? The World-Honored One said, “What you have asked consists entirely of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).”
One day, the World-Honored One showed a multicolored mani-jewel to the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions and asked them, "What color is this jewel?

At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions each described it as being a different color. The World-Honored One then concealed the jewel in his sleeve and raised his hand, asking again, "What color is this jewel?
The Heavenly Kings replied, "There is no jewel in the Buddha’s hand; where could there be any color?"
The Honored One sighed and said, "How can your delusion be so extreme? When I showed you the worldly pearls, each of you insisted that they were blue, yellow, red, or white.
Yet when I showed you the true pearls, you knew nothing at all. At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions...
All have awakened to the Way. Once, when the Gandharva King presented music to the World-Honored One, at that time the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all became the sound of lutes.
Kāśyapa rose and danced. The King asked, "Is Kāśyapa not indeed an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted?
How can he still have residual habits? The Buddha said, "In truth, there are no residual habits. Do not slander the Dharma. The King again...
The king played the zither three times, and Kāśyapa likewise danced three times. The king said, "Kāśyapa has danced; is this not so?
The Buddha said, "In truth, he never danced. The king said, "How can the World-Honored One speak falsely? The Buddha said, "It is no falsehood."
“When you play the lute, do not the mountains, rivers, the great earth, wood, and stone all produce the sound of the lute? “Is this not so? the King asked. “It is,” the King replied.
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa was also like this; therefore, he truly never performed the dance. The King then accepted and believed the World-Honored One’s words.

Once, when a non-Buddhist asked the Buddha, “What Dharma did you teach yesterday? the Buddha replied, “I taught the Dharma of concentration (samādhi). The non-Buddhist asked, “What will you teach today?”
"What dharma? he asked. "The indeterminate dharma," [the Buddha] replied. The non-Buddhist said, "Yesterday you spoke of the determinate dharma; why do you speak of the indeterminate dharma today?
The World-Honored One said, "Yesterday was determinate; today it is indeterminate. This was because the World-Honored One had been questioned by a seer possessing the five supernormal powers.
"The World-Honored One possesses six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); I possess five. What is that one power?
The Buddha summoned the rishi with five supernormal powers, who responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "Ask me about that one power.

Because of this, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (*Samantacakṣus*) desired to see Samantabhadra but could not find him. He entered into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) three times in succession, surveying the three thousand great [thousandfold world systems].

Throughout a thousand worlds, he sought Samantabhadra but could not find or see him. He then returned and informed the Buddha, who said, "If you simply give rise to a single thought within the samādhi of stillness, you will immediately see Samantabhadra.

Thereupon, as soon as Wenyuan gave rise to a single thought, he saw Samantabhadra riding upon a six-tusked white elephant in mid-air. On the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, Mañjuśrī... [the text continues].
While they were spending the summer retreat, Kāśyapa intended to strike the gavel to expel them. As soon as he raised the gavel, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs.
Although Kāśyapa exhausted all his supernatural powers, he could not lift the gavel. The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? Kāśyapa was speechless.
Later, the World-Honored One received a request from the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha to engage in a debate on the principles of doctrine. He prepared...
They made a pact, saying, "If my doctrine falls into error, I shall cut off my own head. The World-Honored One asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine?
Zhi replied, "My tenet is that I do not accept anything at all. The World-Honored One asked, "Do you accept this view [of non-acceptance]?

Zhi then shook out his sleeves and departed. When he reached the middle of the road, he suddenly realized the truth. He said to his disciples, "I must return and cut off my head to apologize to the World-Honored One."
The Venerable One said, "My disciple, before this assembly of devas and humans, you should surely have been victorious. Why then did you cut off my head?
Zhì replied, "I would rather have my head cut off before one who possesses wisdom than achieve victory before one who lacks it.

He then sighed and said, "In my doctrine, there are two ways of falling into defeat. If this view is accepted, the door of defeat is coarse; if this view is not accepted, the door of defeat is subtle."
All humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles do not know where my meaning falls; only the World-Honored One and the great bodhisattvas know where my meaning falls.
Returning before the World-Honored One, he said, "My meaning has fallen into two points of defeat; therefore, I shall cut off my head to apologize.
The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing as this. You should turn your mind toward the Path. At that—
These were the same five hundred followers who at once threw themselves before the Buddha to leave the household life and realize arhatship.

World-Honored One, in the past, when you wished to lead the assembly of sages to the sixth heaven to preach the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, you commanded all the fierce and malevolent ghosts and spirits from other lands, this land, the human realm, and the heavens to assemble together;
they received the Buddha’s entrustment to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Should there be any who do not attend, the Four Heavenly Kings shall fly fiery iron wheels to pursue them and compel their assembly.
Once assembled, there shall be none who do not comply with the Buddha’s command; each shall make a great vow to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Only one Māra King spoke thus to the World-Honored One: "Gautama, I shall wait until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood and the realm of sentient beings is emptied."
"There is no such thing as a 'sentient being' by name; it is for this reason that I have resolved to attain Bodhicitta.
Once, while the World-Honored One was walking with Ānanda, they came upon the stupa of an ancient Buddha. The World-Honored One paid his respects, whereupon Ānanda asked, "Whose stupa is this?"
The World-Honored One said, "These are the stupas of the Buddhas of the past. Ānanda asked, "Of whom were the Buddhas of the past disciples?
The World-Honored One said, "They were my disciples. Ānanda said, "It should be so.

Once, when a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One a question, he neither spoke of existence nor spoke of non-existence. After a long silence, the World-Honored One remained still, and the non-Buddhist offered words of praise.
He said, "World-Honored One, with your great kindness and great compassion, you have cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter [the Way]. He then prostrated himself and departed.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "What principle did this non-Buddhist realize that he praised you so and then departed?

The World-Honored One replied, "It is like a fine horse that, upon seeing the shadow of the whip, immediately gallops forward. One day, the World-Honored One instructed Ānanda, "The time for the meal is approaching; you should [prepare the offerings]."
"Enter the city with your alms-bowl. Ānanda assented. The World-Honored One said, "Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past.
Ānanda then asked, "What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past? The World-Honored One called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda assented.
The World-Honored One said, "Go, carrying the bowl. Because of this, a bhikṣu asked the World-Honored One: "I..."
"Within the Dharma of the Blessed One, the place of seeing exists, but the place of realization does not yet exist. What, then, will the Blessed One demonstrate?
The Blessed One said, "Bhikṣu so-and-so, what will you demonstrate? This is your question. [This occurred] after the Blessed One had attained enlightenment.
In the Jeta Grove, beneath a tree, he sat cross-legged. Two merchants, traveling with five hundred wagons, passed by the edge of the grove;
two of their oxen refused to move forward. The merchants were surprised to see this, and a mountain deity informed them:
"Within this grove there is a holy man who has attained the Way. Forty-nine days have passed since he last ate; you ought to..."
He made offerings. The merchant entered the forest and saw a man sitting upright and motionless.
He asked, "Are you the Brahma King? Or Śakra? A mountain deity? Or a river deity? The World-Honored One smiled and held up a corner of his *kāṣāya* robe to show him.
The merchant prostrated himself and then presented offerings to the World-Honored One. Because Jīvaka was skilled at distinguishing sounds, [the narrative] proceeds to—
Once, while at a cemetery, the World-Honored One saw five skulls. He struck one skull and asked Jīvaka, "Where was this person born? Jīvaka replied, "This person was born into the human realm.
The World-Honored One struck another and asked, "Where was this person born? Jīvaka replied, "This person was born into the heavenly realm.
The World-Honored One then struck yet another and asked, "Where was this person born? Jīvaka was ignorant of where this person had been born. Because of this, the World-Honored One...
The Brahmin Kāla, exercising his supernatural powers, held two *saṃpuṣpita* (合歡) *dhātrī* (梧桐) flowers in his left and right hands and came to make an offering to the Buddha.
The Buddha called out to the rishi, and the Brahmin responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "Put them down.
The Brahmin then set down the flower in his left hand. The Buddha called to the rishi again, "Put them down," and the Brahmin then set down the flower in his right hand.
In his hand he held a single flower. The Buddha again called to the immortal, saying, "Put it down. The Brahmin said, "World-Honored One, both my hands are now empty;
what more do you command me to put down? The Buddha said, "I did not instruct you to discard the flower."
"You should abandon the six external sense objects, the six internal sense faculties, and the six intermediate consciousnesses all at once.
When there is no place to abandon, that is the place where you escape birth and death. At these words, the Brahmin realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

The World-Honored One [taught this] because, during the assembly on Vulture Peak, five hundred bhikṣus had attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), yet they had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

By means of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*), each of them individually beheld their own past—having killed their fathers, harmed their mothers, and committed various grave offenses.
Within their own minds, each harbored doubts and was unable to enter into the realization of the profound Dharma.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, took a sharp sword in his hand and pressed it against the Tathāgata. The World-Honored One then said to Mañjuśrī: "Stop!"
"Abide! You must not commit an act of rebellion; do not seek to harm me. If I am inevitably to be harmed, let it be for the sake of doing good that I am harmed.
Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning you have had no self or person; it is only because of the internal mind that you perceive a self or person.
When the internal mind arises, 'I' am inevitably harmed—this itself is what is called 'harm. Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus realized their own fundamental minds."
"It is like a dream, like a magical illusion. Within dreams and illusions, there is no self, no person, nor even parents who give birth or are born from one another.
Thereupon, five hundred bhikṣus praised him in unison, saying: "Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Wisdom, has profoundly penetrated the very source and bottom of all phenomena."
Holding a sharp sword in his hand, he pressed it against the body of the Tathāgata. As the sword was, so too was the Buddha; they were of one single mark and not two.

Being without marks and without origination, how could there be killing therein? When the World-Honored One was on the path of practice, he spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara.
Seeing the place where the hair was spread, Dīpaṃkara then signaled for the assembly to withdraw. He then pointed to the ground and said: "This one..."

The ground was measured out, and it was deemed appropriate to establish a Buddhist monastery there. At that time, among the assembly was a wise elder who held up a measuring rod and, pointing to a spot, said, "Once the monastery is completed.
Then the devas scattered flowers and praised him, saying, "This son of a concubine possesses great wisdom!
Subsequently, when the World-Honored One was wandering through the Śītavana cemetery with the seven virtuous women, one of the women pointed to a corpse and said, "The corpse is right here."
"Where has this person gone? One woman said, "What? What? Sisters, observe closely! Each of them attained realization.
Moved by this, Empress [Wu Zetian] scattered flowers and said, "I only wish that you, Noble Sister, would let me know what you require; I shall provide for you for the rest of my life."
The woman said, "In my home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided; however, I require three things: first, a single rootless tree;
second, a patch of ground where neither sun nor shade exists; and third, a mountain valley that echoes not when called.
Śakra said, "Of everything you require, I have it all; as for those three things, I truly do not possess them."
[He] attained it. The girl said, "If you did not possess this, how could you have understood how to save others? Śakra was at a loss for an answer, so he went together with her to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika, even my great disciples, the Arhats, do not understand this meaning;
only the great Bodhisattvas understand this meaning. [Śakra asked,] "World-Honored One, because of Devadatta’s slandering of the Buddha, he entered hell while still in his physical body."
He then ordered Ānanda to ask, "Are you well in the hells? He replied, "Although I am in the hells, it is as pleasant as the Third Dhyāna Heaven.
The Buddha again ordered him to ask, "Do you still seek to leave? He replied, "I shall leave as soon as the World-Honored One arrives."
Ānanda said, "The Buddha is the Great Teacher of the three realms; how could he have any portion of entering hell?
[The Master] replied, "If the Buddha has no portion of entering hell, how could I have any portion of escaping from hell?

World-Honored One, because Mañjuśrī suddenly gave rise to views of the Buddha and views of the Dharma, he was subdued by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and led away toward the two Iron Ring Mountains. To the east of the city, there was an old woman.
He was born at the same time as the Buddha, yet he did not wish to see him. Every time he saw the Buddha approaching, he would immediately turn away to avoid him.
Nevertheless, wherever he looked toward the east or west, everywhere was the Buddha. He then covered his face with his hand, but even within the palms of his ten fingers, everywhere was the Buddha.
Aṅgulimāla, while carrying his alms bowl, arrived at the gate of a certain elder’s house; the woman of that household—
It was at a time when there were complications in childbirth and the mother and child had not yet been separated. The elder said, "Gautama’s disciple, you are a most holy one;
what dharma do you possess that can free one from the perils of childbirth? Aṅgulimāla said to the elder, "I have only recently entered the Path and am not yet aware of this dharma.
Wait while I return to ask the World-Honored One, and I shall come back to inform you. Upon his return, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"Kūṭadanta, go quickly and report this: 'Since I followed the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones, I have never killed a living being.
Kūṭadanta, having received the Buddha’s words, went swiftly to inform her. Upon hearing this, his wife gave birth at that very moment.
Once, while the World-Honored One was sitting beneath a nyagrodha tree, two merchants asked him, "World-Honored One, did you see any carts pass by? He replied, "No."

[The Buddha] looked. The merchant asked, "Did you hear it? He replied, "I did not hear it. The merchant asked, "Were you in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)? He replied, "I was not in meditative concentration.
[The merchant] asked, "Were you asleep? He replied, "I was not asleep. The merchant then sighed and said, "Excellent, excellent!
The World-Honored One is awakened yet does not see. Thereupon, he offered two pieces of white cotton cloth. While the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up [a flower].
Vimalakīrti showed this to the assembly. At that time, the multitude were all at a loss as to its meaning; only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said:
"I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate of the true mark which is signless.

It does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside of the teachings. I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. The World-Honored One then proceeded to the Śāla Grove of the Seven Mulberry Trees.
Previously, he summoned Mahākāśyapa, assigned him a seat, and wrapped him in his *saṃghāṭī* robe. He then declared:
"I entrust the treasury of the True Dharma Eye to you in secret; you must protect and uphold it, transmitting it to future generations.

When the World-Honored One was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, the Great Being Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma once more. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "Mañjuśrī!"
“I have dwelt in this world for forty-nine years, yet I have never uttered a single word. You ask me to turn the Wheel of Dharma once more;
have I ever turned the Wheel of Dharma? At the assembly of the Great Parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One rubbed his chest with his hand and addressed the multitude, saying:
“You should all carefully observe my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold. Behold it to your heart’s content, lest you later regret it.”
"If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, you are not my disciple; if you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa, you are likewise not my disciple.
At that time, an assembly of hundreds of billions all attained realization.

The First Patriarch of the Western Heaven, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. His clan was Brahmin; his father was named Yinze (Drinking Moisture), and his mother was Xiangzhi (Fragrant Will).

In former times, he served as a goldsmith and was skilled in understanding the nature of gold, enabling him to temper and subdue it. [From] the *Chuanfabaoji* (Record of the Transmission of the Dharma).
It is said that once, in the distant past during the kalpa of Vipaśyin Buddha, after the Buddha had entered nirvana, the fourfold assembly erected a stūpa.

Within the stūpa, the face of the Buddha image was damaged and its golden color was marred. At that time, there was a poor woman who took a gold bead to a goldsmith and requested that he adorn the Buddha’s face.
Subsequently, they both made a vow together, wishing: "May we two become an untainted husband and wife. From this...
Regarding the causal conditions: for ninety-one kalpas, his body was entirely golden in color. Subsequently, he was born in the Brahma Heaven.

When his celestial lifespan ended, he was born into a Brahmin family in Madhyama-Magadha, named Kāśyapa—translated here as "Drinking Light" or "Victorious Radiance"—a title derived from his golden hue.
Consequently, he resolved to seek renunciation, hoping to cross over the various realms of existence. The Buddha said to him, "Welcome."
Bhikṣu, with beard and hair naturally removed and the kāṣāya robe upon your body, you have always been praised as the foremost among the assembly.
One day, at the place where the World-Honored One held up a flower to show the multitude, you thoroughly perceived the source of the Dharma; thereupon, you broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One then conferred upon you the gold-threaded *kāṣāya* and further said: "I entrust to you the pure Dharma-eye. You—
"You should circulate this so that it does not become extinct. Once, when the Venerable One was questioned by a non-Buddhist, the latter asked, "What is this 'self' of mine?
The Master said, "That which seeks the self is your self. The non-Buddhist said, "This is my self; where is your self?
The Master replied, "You ask me, and I seek it. One day, while the Venerable One was treading mud, a novice saw him and asked:
"How can the Venerable One act on his own behalf? He replied, "If I do not act for myself, who will act for me? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvāṇa, Kāśyapa was not present among the assembly.
The Buddha addressed the great disciples, saying, "When Kāśyapa arrives, you may together proclaim the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. At that time, Kāśyapa was at Vulture Peak.
At the Pipphalavana Cave on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he beheld a magnificent radiance and immediately entered into samādhi.

With his purified divine eye, he saw that the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa by the side of the Hiraṇyavatī River. He then addressed his disciples, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa!
How swift was it! He then went to the space between the twin trees and wailed in grief and longing. The Buddha manifested himself from within the golden coffin.
[The two feet. At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus: "The Buddha has already been cremated; the diamond-like *śarīra* relics are not our concern.
We ought to convene a council (*saṃgīti*) of the Dharma-eye so that it may not be severed. He then spoke this verse: "Disciples of the Tathāgata, do not yet enter *nirvāṇa*.
Those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) should attend the council. Thereupon, those who had attained supernatural powers...
They all assembled at the Piṇḍola Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. At that time, Ānanda was unable to enter the assembly because his outflows were not yet exhausted;
later, having realized the fruit of Arhatship, he was thereby able to enter. Kāśyapa then addressed the assembly, saying:
"This bhikṣu Ānanda is one of great learning and retention, possessing vast wisdom.
He has constantly followed the Tathāgata, his brahmacarya is pure, and the Buddha-dharma he has heard has been transmitted like water from one vessel to another without any remainder.

Praised by the Buddha as foremost in intelligence and quick-wittedness, it is fitting that he be requested to compile the Sūtra Piṭaka. The great assembly remained silent. Kāśyapa then addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now proclaim the Eye of the Dharma. Hearing these words, Ānanda accepted them with faith. He surveyed the minds of the assembly and spoke in verse:
"O monks and all your followers, Separated from the Buddha, you lack adornment, Just as in the empty sky, The multitude of stars is without the moon."
Having spoken these verses, he prostrated at the feet of the Sangha, ascended the Dharma seat, and proclaimed these words: "Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was dwelling in such-and-such a place, preaching such-and-such a sutra and teaching, [extending] even unto the humans and devas, who paid homage and practiced accordingly.
Then Kāśyapa asked the bhikṣus: "Is what Ānanda has spoken free from error? They all replied: "It is no different from that which the World-Honored One [taught]."
Having spoken thus, Kāśyapa addressed Ānanda, saying: "The time for my life is not long; I now entrust the True Dharma to you.
Guard it well. Listen to these verses of mine: 'Phenomenon after phenomenon are fundamentally the Dharma; there is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon.'"
"How can there be both the Dharma and non-Dharma within a single dharma? Having spoken this verse, he took up his saṃghāṭī robe and entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await the descent of Maitreya;
this was the year of Bingchen, the fifth year of King Zhou Xiaowang.
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan was Kṣatriya;
his father was King Droṇodana, who was indeed the younger brother of the Buddha. In Sanskrit he is called Ānanda, which here means "Joyous" or "Rejoicing.

He was born on the night the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, and thus he was named accordingly. He was widely learned and profoundly erudite, possessing unimpeded wisdom. The World-Honored One regarded him as...

He was foremost in dhāraṇīs and had always been praised for them. Furthermore, due to his great merit from past lives, he received and upheld the Dharma-treasury like water being passed from one vessel to another. The Buddha then appointed him as his attendant.

One day, the Venerable said to the Buddha, "Today, upon entering the city, I witnessed a most extraordinary thing. The Buddha asked, "What extraordinary thing did you see? He replied, "As I entered the city, I saw..."
A troupe of musicians was performing a dance. Upon leaving the city, they all witnessed impermanence. The Buddha said, "Yesterday when I entered the city, I also saw a most extraordinary thing.
They asked, "We do not know what extraordinary thing you saw. The Buddha said, "When I entered the city..."
He saw a troupe of musicians performing a dance. When he left the city, he again saw the musicians performing a dance.
One day he asked Kāśyapa, "Elder brother, besides the golden-brocade *kaṣāya* transmitted by the World-Honored One, what else did he transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Knock down the banner-pole in front of the gate. Later, Ānanda...
King Ajātaśatru said, "Venerable one, the two masters, the Tathāgata and the honored Kāśyapa, have both already entered parinirvāṇa;

due to my many affairs, I was unable to behold them both. When you, Venerable One, enter parinirvāṇa, I pray that you will grant me leave. The Venerable One granted his permission. Later, he thought to himself:
"My body is fragile and brittle, like a mass of foam; how much more so now that I am aged and decrepit—how could it endure for long?"
"Long ago, King Ajātaśatru made a pact with me. I have therefore come to the royal palace to inform him, saying: 'I wish to enter nirvāṇa; I have come to bid you farewell.
The gatekeeper said, 'The King is asleep and cannot be awakened. I replied, 'Wait until the King awakens, and I shall speak for him.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru saw in a dream a precious parasol, adorned with the seven treasures, worth ten million..."

Surrounded by hundreds of millions of followers who gazed up at him in reverence, a sudden storm of wind and rain broke out. It blew and snapped the handle of his bowl, causing the precious jewels and necklaces to fall all over the ground.
He was deeply struck with wonder and alarm. Upon waking, the gatekeeper reported these events in detail. When the King heard this, he let out a cry of lamentation that moved both heaven and earth.
He immediately went to the city of Vaiśālī and saw the Venerable One standing in the middle of the Ganges River.
He sat cross-legged. The king then paid homage and spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms; having abandoned me, you have come here.
For the sake of the power of your compassionate vow, pray do not enter parinirvāṇa for a while. At that time, King Vaiśālī was also by the riverbank and spoke this verse:
"O Venerable One, why so soon? Why return to the field of quiescent extinction? I pray that you remain for but a moment..."
Having received the offerings, the Venerable One saw that the two kings had both come to entreat him. He then spoke this verse: "O two kings, dwell well-composed; do not grieve or lament.
Nirvāṇa is my purity, for it is free from all states of existence. The Venerable One further reflected:
"If I were to favor one kingdom over the other, the various kingdoms would fall into strife. Such a thing must not be; I should act with equanimity."
Having delivered all sentient beings, he then proceeded to enter parinirvāṇa in the middle of the Ganges River.
At that time, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways. Five hundred rishis from the Snowy Mountains, beholding this auspicious omen, flew through the air and arrived.
He prostrated at the feet of the Venerable One, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and said: "I shall realize the Buddha-dharma under the Elder;
I pray that you will grant us great compassion and deliver us. The Venerable One accepted the request in silence.

He immediately transformed the Ganges River so that it became entirely golden ground, and for the sake of that assembly of sages, he preached various great Dharmas. The Venerable One then thought: "The disciples I previously delivered should now come."
In a short while, five hundred arhats descended from the sky. They granted the śramaṇa ordination to the various sages.
Among the assembly of sages were two arhats: the first was named Śāṇakavāsin, and the second was named Madhyāntika.
Knowing them to be vessels of the Dharma, the Venerable One said to them: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa."
Kāśyapa entered meditative absorption and entrusted it to me. Now that I am about to pass away, I transmit it to you.
Receive my teaching; you must listen to these verses: "The Dharma originally entrusted exists; Having been entrusted, one says there is no Dharma. Each must awaken for themselves;

Once awakened, there is neither Dharma nor non-Dharma. The Venerable One, having completed the entrustment of the Treasury of the Eye of the Dharma, leaped into the void and manifested the eighteen transformations.
He entered the *Vāyu-vega-vikrīḍita-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Swift Play of Wind) and divided his body into four parts. One part he offered to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
one part he offered to the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King; one part he offered to King Viśālā; and one part he offered to King Ajātaśatru.
Each erected a jeweled stūpa to make offerings to them. This was in the twelfth year of King Zhou Li, the year of Guisi.
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, was a native of the kingdom of Mathurā. He was also named Śāṇavāsa;
his clan name was Viśākha, his father was Vanavāsin, and his mother was Kauśalyā. He was born after remaining in the womb for six years.
In the Sanskrit language, "Śāṇaka" means "naturally clothed," which refers to the name of a nine-branch exquisite grass from the Western Regions. When a sage descends [into the world],...
As for its birth: this grass grows in pure and clean places. When Andhaka was born, these auspicious plants appeared in response.
Long ago, when the Tathāgata was traveling to convert beings, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā and saw a grove of green trees with lush branches and leaves. He said to Ānanda:
This forest grove is named Uruvelā. One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall turn the sublime wheel of Dharma here.
A hundred years later, Śāṇakavāsin will be born; he will leave the household life, realize the Path, receive the Dharma-eye of the Venerable Ānanda, and guide sentient beings.
He will dwell in this grove and subdue two fire-dragons, causing them to take refuge in the Buddha.

The Dragon King offered him land so that he might establish a Brahma-palace. After the Venerable One had long been engaged in converting beings through his conditions, he reflected upon the entrustment of the True Dharma.
He subsequently found Upagupta in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā and took him as his attendant. Thereupon, he questioned Upagupta, saying:
"How old are you? he asked. He replied, "I am seventeen years old. The other said, "Is it your body that is seventeen, or your nature that is seventeen?
He replied, "My teacher’s hair has turned white; is it his hair that is white, or his mind that is white? The other said, "It is only my hair that is white; my mind is not white.
Guptaka said, "My body is seventeen, but my nature is not seventeen. Venerable sir, you understand this Dharma."
Three years later, he finally shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him. He then said: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the unsurpassed Dharma-eye to Kāśyapa;
it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; do not let it be severed.
Receive my teaching and listen to these verses of mine: 'Neither dharma nor mind, neither mind nor dharma. He spoke thus.

At that time, while this was a mental phenomenon (*cittadharma*), that phenomenon was not a mental phenomenon. Having spoken these verses, he immediately vanished into the Elephant White Mountain (*Hastivāhana*) to the south of Kaśmīra.
Later, while in samādhi, he saw his disciple Guptaka with a retinue of five hundred followers who were frequently indolent and arrogant.
The Venerable One then went to them and, manifesting the Dragon’s Impetuous Samādhi (*nāgavikrīḍita-samādhi*), subdued them and spoke:

The verse says: "Thoroughly penetrating that there is neither 'this' nor 'that,' the Noble Ones have neither long nor short. Cast away your thoughts of contempt, and you shall swiftly attain Arhatship.
Upon hearing this verse, the five hundred bhikṣus followed the teaching and practiced accordingly; they all attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
The Venerable One then manifested the eighteen transformations and entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi) to cremate his own body. Kujūta collected the relics and interred them.
At Mount Vaṅkara, five hundred bhikṣus, each holding a banner, escorted [the relics] there to erect a stūpa and make offerings;
this was in the twenty-third year of King Zhou Xuan’s reign, the year of Yiwu.
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. He was also named Upagupta and alternatively called Upagupta.
His clan name was Śūdra; his father was Subhadra. He left home at the age of seventeen and realized the fruit [of Arhatship] at twenty.

Traveling to various regions to propagate the teachings, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā, where those who received ordination were exceedingly numerous. Consequently, the palace of Māra trembled. Wave...
Pāpīyān was filled with grief and fear; he then exhausted all his demonic powers to harm the True Dharma. The Venerable One immediately entered *samādhi* to observe its cause.
Pāpīyān again sought an opportunity and secretly took a necklace, binding it around [the Venerable’s] neck. When the Venerable emerged from *samādhi*, [he saw it].
He then took the three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—and transformed them into flower garlands. He spoke with words of consolation to Pāpīyan, saying:
"The necklaces you gave me were truly exquisite and wonderful; I have these flower garlands to offer in exchange. Pāpīyan was greatly delighted and craned his neck to receive them.
Immediately, they transformed into three kinds of putrid corpses, infested with maggots and rotting away. Pāpīyan felt loathing and revulsion, and great [disgust arose within him].
Distressed, he exerted all his supernatural powers but was unable to move it. He then ascended to the six heavens of the desire realm and informed the various lords of those heavens;

he further went to the Brahma King to seek deliverance. They each replied, "The miraculous transformations performed by a disciple of the One of Ten Powers—how could we, who are ordinary and lowly, be able to remove them?
Pāpīyas asked, "If that is so, what then shall I do? The Brahma King said, "You should return."
The Venerable One was able to sever [the affliction] immediately. He then spoke a verse to cause him to dedicate his merit, saying:
"If one falls upon the ground, one rises from the ground; to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible.

Having received these instructions, Pāpīyas descended from the celestial palace, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable One, and offered a piteous confession. The Venerable One told him: "From this day forward, regarding the Tathāgata..."
"Will you no longer cause harm to the True Dharma? Pāpīyān replied, "I vow to turn toward the Buddha-way and forever sever all that is unwholesome.
The Venerable One said, "If this is so, you may yourself proclaim with your own mouth your taking of refuge in the Triple Gem.
The Māra joined his palms and recited it three times; his flower garlands were all cast off, whereupon he leaped for joy, prostrated before the Venerable One, and spoke this verse:
I prostrate to the Honored One of Samādhi and the noble disciples of the Ten Powers. I now make this dedication of merit:
may there be no venerable ones of inferior strength remaining in the world to guide and transform others. May those who have realized the fruits of the path be most numerous;

for every person they deliver, let them place a tally-stick within a stone chamber. Let that chamber be eighteen cubits in length and twelve cubits in width, until it is filled to capacity. At the very end, there shall be one...

The son of a householder named Gandharva came to pay homage to the Venerable One, seeking to leave the household life. The Venerable One asked him, "Do you leave the household life with your body, or do you leave it with your mind?

He replied, "I have come to leave the household life, not for the sake of body or mind. The Venerable One said, "If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who is it that leaves the household life?
He replied, "As for leaving the household life, because there is no self and no 'mine,' there is neither self nor 'mine'."
Therefore, the mind itself is neither born nor extinguished. That the mind is neither born nor extinguished is the eternal Way;

the Buddhas are likewise eternal. The mind has no form or appearance, and its essence is the same. The Venerable One said, "You shall attain great enlightenment and the mind will naturally be realized.

You should rely upon the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha to perpetuate the lineage of the Sages. He then performed his tonsure, conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*), and further addressed him, saying, "Your father..."
"I once dreamed that you were born from a golden sun; you may be named Tiṭṭhoga (Ditika). He further said:

'The Tathāgata transmitted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma in succession until it reached me. Now I entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: "The mind is the original mind; the original mind is not a dharma.
If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind; but being neither mind nor dharma, it is the fundamental reality. [This concludes] the Entrustment of the Dharma.
Having finished speaking, he leaped into the air and manifested the eighteen transformations. He then returned to his original seat and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Dhitika used the counting sticks from the room to cremate his master’s body, collected the relics, and constructed a stupa for offerings.
This was the gengzi year, the thirty-first year of King Ping of the Zhou dynasty.

The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Diṭṭhika, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. In the Sanskrit language he is called Diṭṭhika, which translates here as Tongzhenliang (Measure of Penetrating Reality).
When he was first born, his father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, illuminating heaven and earth;
before it stood a great mountain adorned with various jewels, from the summit of which a spring gushed forth, flowing in torrents in all four directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Guptaka.
The Master then explained it for him, saying: "The mountain of jewels is my own body; the gushing spring is the inexhaustibility of the Dharma;
the sun rising from the house is the sign of your current entry into the Way; and its illuminating of heaven and earth is the transcendence of your wisdom.
Having heard the Master's words, the Venerable One leaped for joy and sang this verse: "Lofty is the mountain of the seven treasures!"

He constantly brings forth the spring of wisdom, which transforms into the true flavor of the Dharma; he is able to deliver all who have a karmic connection. Venerable Guptaka also spoke a verse, saying:
"I transmit my Dharma to you; you shall manifest great wisdom. Like the golden sun rising from the house, it shall illuminate heaven and earth.
When Kṛṣṇa (Tiduojiaye) heard his teacher’s sublime verse, he prostrated and received it with reverence. Later, he traveled to Central India.
In that country there were eight thousand great seers, with Mīcaka at their head. Hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they led their assembly to pay him homage.
Addressing the Venerable One, they said: "In the past, we were born together in the Brahma Heaven. I encountered the seer Asita, who bestowed the methods of the seers upon me;
you, Master, met a disciple of the One of Ten Powers, under whom you practiced *dhyāna*. Since then, our karmic destinies have followed divergent paths for six [eons]."
The other said, "To have wandered through kalpas in such a fragmented state—truly this is no empty boast! Now you may abandon heterodoxy to return to the orthodox and enter the Buddha-vehicle.
Mīchaka replied, "Long ago, the seer Asita gave me this prophecy: 'Six kalpas hence, you shall become a Buddha.'"

"When we encountered our fellow student, he attained the fruit of the outflow-free state (*anāsrava-phala*). Our meeting today—could this not be due to past affinities? I pray that the Master, in his compassion, will grant me liberation.
Thereupon, [the Master] ordained him as a renunciant and commanded the noble ones to confer the precepts upon him. As for the rest of the assembly of sages, they initially gave rise to pride;
however, when the Venerable One displayed great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), they all simultaneously resolved their minds on Bodhicitta and were ordained at once.
On the day he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed Micchaka, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa;
it was passed down through successive generations until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and cherish it. He then spoke this verse:
"The mind that penetrates the fundamental Dharma Is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Realization is the same as non-realization; Even a mindless state is [the same]."
Unable to do so, he spoke these verses. Having finished speaking, he leaped into the void and performed the eighteen transformations.

Entering the fire-light samādhi (*tejo-dhātu-samādhi*), he spontaneously incinerated his own body. Mucalinda and eight thousand bhikṣus together collected the relics and erected a stūpa for worship on Mount Paṇḍava.
This was the year Jichou (己丑), the seventh year of King Zhou Zhuang’s reign.
The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Mīchaka, was a native of Central India. Having transmitted the Dharma, he traveled to North India to propagate the teachings.
There, seeing auspicious golden clouds above the city walls, he sighed and said, "This is the spiritual aura of a person of the Way."
"There must be a Great Being who shall be my successor. He then entered the city. In the midst of the marketplace, there was a man holding a wine vessel.
Approaching him, he asked, "From where have you come, Master? Where do you intend to go? The Patriarch replied, "I come from my own mind; I intend to go nowhere.
The man asked, "Do you recognize what is in my hand? The Patriarch said, "This is a vessel for contact, yet those who carry it are pure."
[The monk] asked, "Does my teacher recognize me? The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize you; if I were to recognize you, it would not be myself.
He further said to him, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall subsequently reveal your original cause. The monk replied with a verse:
"From immeasurable kalpas past, until my birth in this land, My original surname was Bharadvāja, and my name was Vāsukṣema. The Patriarch said, "My teacher..."
Tidūka said: "In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through Northern India, he spoke to Ānanda, saying:
'In this land, three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a holy man of the Bharadvāja clan named Vasumitra, who shall become the seventh in the lineage of the Dhyāna patriarchs.
The World-Honored One has prophesied this for you; you should leave the household life. Thereupon, [the disciple] set down his bowl and paid homage to the Master, standing to one side.
Standing, he said: "I recall a past kalpa when I once acted as a donor and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha gave me this prediction:
'In the Śākya Dharma of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall propagate the ultimate teaching. This now accords with what the Master has said; I pray that you grant me liberation.
The Patriarch immediately shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts, then told him: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now entrusted to you."
"Regarding you, do not allow [this lineage] to be severed. He then spoke a verse, saying: "No mind can be apprehended; What is spoken of cannot be called a dharma.

If one realizes that mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and mental dharmas. After the Patriarch had spoken the verse, he entered the Lion’s Vigorous Display Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*).
He leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, then returned to his original seat and transformed into fire to cremate himself. Vāsula...
He secretly collected the sacred relics and stored them in a casket made of the seven precious substances; he then erected a stupa and placed them on its upper level.
This was the year Jia-shen, the seventeenth year of King Xiang of the Zhou dynasty.
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of Northern India. His family name was Bharadvāja.
He habitually wore pure garments and carried vessels for wine as he wandered through the streets and neighborhoods, sometimes chanting and sometimes whistling; people regarded him as mad.

Upon meeting the Venerable Mīdhaka, who proclaimed the Tathāgata’s past prophecy, he reflected upon his own prior karmic conditions. He cast aside his vessels, left the household life to receive the Dharma, and traveled to propagate the teachings.

Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kāmarūpa, he extensively promoted Buddhist affairs. One day, before the Dharma seat, there was a man who suddenly appeared and declared himself to be named Buddhanandi, saying, "I shall now debate the meaning of the Dharma with you, Master.
The Patriarch said, "O worthy one, where there is debate, there is no true meaning; where there is true meaning, there is no debate.
If you intend to debate the meaning, it will ultimately not be a discussion of the true meaning. Nandi realized that the Master’s principle was superior, and his mind...

He immediately expressed his reverence and said, "I wish to seek the Way so that I may be moistened by the flavor of the nectar. The Patriarch then granted him the tonsure and bestowed upon him the full precepts.
He further told him: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you; you must protect and uphold it. Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When the realization of empty space is attained, There is neither 'is' nor 'is not'."
There is no un-Dharma. He immediately entered the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind. At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas all came together to pay homage and spoke these verses:
"O Patriarch of the sages of this Bhadrakalpa, you shall occupy the seventh position.
Venerable One, have compassion for us and please proclaim the Buddha-ground. The Venerable One arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma which I have attained..."

Because it does not exist as a substantial entity. When he had finished saying that consciousness in the Buddha-ground is free from both existence and non-existence, he returned to samādhi and manifested the signs of nirvana.
Nandi immediately erected a stupa of the seven precious gems upon his original seat to enshrine his entire body;
this was the year of Xīnwèi, the nineteenth year of King Zhōu Dìng’s reign.
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhānanda, was a native of the kingdom of Kāmala. His surname was Gautama.

He possessed a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his crown and was endowed with swift and unimpeded eloquence. Initially, he encountered Vasumitra, from whom he left the household life and received instruction.

Subsequently, leading his disciples, he traveled to propagate the Dharma until he arrived at the home of Viśāla in the kingdom of Ti-ga. There, he observed a white light ascending from atop the house and said to his disciples:
He said, "In this household there is a sage who speaks no words; he is a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He does not walk the four crossroads, for he knows that contact is defilement.
Having finished speaking, the elder came forth to pay his respects and asked what was required.
The Patriarch said, "I seek an attendant. The elder said, "I have a son named Buddhabhadra; he is already fifty years old and has never spoken with his mouth. His feet... [were paralyzed].
[The Master] had never stepped upon it. The Patriarch said, "As you have spoken, you are truly my disciple. When Votuo heard this, he rose immediately to prostrate and spoke a verse, saying:
"Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my Way; [who is the true Way?]"
"Who is the one most realized in the Way? The Patriarch replied with a verse: "What you say accords with the mind; even your parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice accords with the Way;
the minds of all Buddhas are precisely this. To seek externally for a Buddha with attributes is not to resemble your own nature."
"I wish to know your original mind; it is neither joined nor separated. Having heard this verse, Vovada (Bodhidharma) immediately took seven steps.

The Patriarch said, "This child has encountered Buddhas in the past; his compassionate vows are vast and great. Fearing that his parents' affection would make him difficult to part with, he remained silent and did not walk.
The elder then relinquished him to allow him to leave the household life. The Patriarch soon conferred upon him the full precepts and further told him:
"I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s treasury of the eye of the true Dharma; do not let it be severed. He then spoke a verse:
"Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so. If one thoroughly understands space, One penetrates the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Fotuo Cheng, receiving this entrustment, praised him in verse: "Among the patriarchs of Chan, my teacher Shall become the first..."

8. He transformed immeasurable multitudes through the Dharma, and they all attained arhatship. At that time, the Patriarch immediately manifested supernatural transformations and returned to his original seat, remaining solemnly in parinirvāṇa.
The assembly erected a precious stūpa and interred his entire body; this was the year of Bingyin, the twelfth year of King Jing of the Zhou dynasty.
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of the country of Ti-ga. His secular surname was Viśāla.
Having received the entrustment of the Eighth Patriarch, he later traveled to Central India to propagate the Dharma.

At that time, there was an elder named Gandhacchattra who brought his son to pay homage to the Patriarch and said, "This child remained in the womb for sixty years; therefore, he is named Duṣprasaha (Difficult to Be Born). He once encountered an immortal."
"This child is no ordinary person; he shall become a vessel for the Dharma. Now that he has met you, Venerable One, you may cause him to leave the household life.

The Patriarch then shaved his head and conferred the precepts upon him. At the moment of the *karmavācanā*, auspicious light illuminated the seat, and furthermore, thirty-seven śarīra relics manifested before them.
From then on, he practiced with such diligence that he forgot all fatigue. Subsequently, the Patriarch said to him: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye..."
"I now entrust this to you; you must protect and keep it in mind. He then spoke a verse, saying: "Ultimate Truth is originally nameless; through names, Ultimate Truth is revealed.
Having received the True Dharma, it is neither true nor false. Having thus transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch entered the Samādhi of Extinction and passed into Parinirvāṇa.
The assembly cremated his remains with fragrant oils and sandalwood, collected the relics, and erected a stupa.
Regarding Nālandā Monastery: it was the year Jia-yin, the thirty-third year of King Jing of the Zhou dynasty.
The tenth patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of Central India. His original name was Duṣprasaha.

When he was about to be born, his father dreamed of a white elephant with a jeweled throne upon its back; atop this throne sat a bright pearl, which entered through the gate, its radiance illuminating the fourfold assembly.
Upon awakening, he was subsequently reborn. Later, he encountered the Ninth Patriarch and attended upon him at his side, never once sleeping;

it is said that his ribs never touched his mat, and thus he was given the title "Venerable Flank" (Pakṣika). When he first arrived in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, he rested beneath a tree and pointed to the ground with his right hand, declaring to the assembly:
"When this ground turns golden in color, a holy man shall enter this assembly. Having finished speaking, immediately—
[The Master’s body] transformed into the color of gold. At that time, the elder’s son Pūrṇayaśas stood before him with palms joined.

The Patriarch asked, “From where have you come? He replied, “My mind does not go. The Patriarch said, “Where do you dwell? He replied, “My mind does not stop. The Patriarch said, “Are you not settled?
He replied, “All Buddhas are likewise so. The Patriarch said, “Are you not a Buddha? He replied, “All [Buddhas are likewise so].”
The Buddha was not [the one who did so]. The Patriarch then spoke a verse, saying: "This ground turns golden; it is known in advance that a Sage has arrived.

He shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree and, having perfected the awakening flower, [attain enlightenment]. Yaśas then spoke another verse: "The Master sits upon the golden ground and constantly proclaims the true meaning.
May he turn his light to illuminate me, causing me to enter samādhi. The Patriarch understood his intention and immediately ordained him.
He left the household life and further perfected the categories of the precepts. He then addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma is now entrusted to you;
you must protect and cherish it. He then spoke this verse: "The true essence is naturally true; Because of the truth, there is the principle of explanation.

Having realized the dharma of true truth, There is neither practice nor cessation. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he immediately manifested spiritual transformations and entered nirvana.
He manifested a fire that consumed himself. The fourfold assembly each took the relics in their robes and, at various locations, erected stupas to make offerings to them.
This was the year Jihai, the twenty-eighth year of King Zhengding of the Zhou dynasty.
The eleventh patriarch, Venerable Punayaśas, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. His clan name was Gautama; his father’s name was Ratnakāya.
Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Pārśva, he soon traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
There, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa came forward to greet him with prostrations and asked: "I wish to recognize the Buddha. Which one is he? The Patriarch replied: "You wish to recognize the Buddha?"

[Asanga] said, "This is consciousness. Vasubandhu replied, "Since the Buddha did not recognize it, how can you know it is this? Vasubandhu said, "Since he did not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is not?

[Asanga] said, "This is the meaning of the saw. Vasubandhu said, "That is the meaning of the wood. Vasubandhu asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? [Asanga] replied, "It is leveled out together with the Master.
Vasubandhu then asked, "What is the meaning of the wood? Vasubandhu said, "You have been cut by me," [and thus] Asanga was defeated.
Suddenly, he attained awakening. He prostrated himself in refuge and subsequently requested ordination. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This Great Being was formerly the King of Viśālā.
In that kingdom, there was a class of people who were as naked as horses; the King exercised his supernatural power to divide his body into silkworms so that they might obtain clothing.
Later, the King was reborn in Central India, and those 'horse-people' felt deep attachment and longing for him."

He cried out in lamentation, and thus he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Cry). The Tathāgata’s prophecy stated: "Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a worthy one named Aśvaghoṣa in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
He shall subdue the followers of heterodox paths and deliver immeasurable beings, continuing my transmission of the Dharma.
Now is precisely that time. He then addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now entrusted to you. Thus it was said.

He spoke in verse: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; light and darkness are never separate. Now I entrust this dharma of concealment and manifestation, which is neither one nor two.
Having thus entrusted the Dharma, the Venerable One manifested miraculous transformations and entered profound, perfect nirvana. The assembly then erected a precious stupa for him.
His entire body was enshrined in a sealed stupa; this was the year Wuxu, the nineteenth year of King An of the Zhou dynasty.
The Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

He was also named Kāśyapa (Gongsheng), a name derived from the fact that his various merits, both conditioned and unconditioned, were most preeminent. Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Yaśas, he...
Later, while he was turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, a certain old man suddenly prostrated himself on the ground before him.
The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This is no ordinary person; there shall be extraordinary signs. Having finished speaking, the man vanished.

A moment later, a golden-colored man emerged from the earth, who then transformed into a woman. Pointing her right hand toward the Patriarch, she spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Venerable Elder."
"You shall receive the Tathāgata’s prediction. Now, upon this ground, you have proclaimed and disseminated the ultimate truth.

Having spoken these verses, he vanished instantly. The Patriarch said, "A māra is about to come to contend with me for power. After a short while, wind and rain arrived violently, and heaven and earth became dark and obscured.
The Patriarch said, "It is certain that the māra has come; I shall eliminate him. He then pointed into the air, and there appeared—

The great golden dragon exerted its majestic spiritual power, causing the mountains and peaks to tremble. Yet the Patriarch remained solemn upon his seat, and the demonic disturbances were extinguished accordingly.
After seven days, a small insect as large as a mayfly appeared, hiding beneath the seat. The Patriarch took it up with his hand.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation wrought by a māra, who has come to eavesdrop upon my Dharma. He then released him to depart, but the māra was unable to move.
The Patriarch said to him, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers.
Thereupon, he returned to his original form, prostrated himself, and repented. The Patriarch asked, "What is your name? How many followers do you have? He replied, "My name is Ka..."
Vimalakīrti had three thousand followers. The Patriarch asked, "Exerting all your supernatural powers, what kind of transformations can you perform?
He replied, "I could transform a vast ocean; that would be a very minor matter. The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the ocean of nature? He asked, "What is meant by the 'ocean of nature'?"
"I have never known this. The Patriarch then explained the Ocean of Nature (xinghai) to him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it;
the three samādhis and six supernormal powers are manifested through it. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra conceived faith and, together with three thousand disciples, sought ordination.
