The Patriarch then summoned five hundred arhats to confer the full precepts (upasaṃpadā) upon them, and further addressed them:
He said, "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye shall now be entrusted to you. Listen to these verses: 'Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma;

light and darkness are originally not two. Now I entrust this Dharma of realization, which is neither grasped nor abandoned. Having finished the entrustment, he immediately entered the Dragon’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi.
He rose upright into the air, appearing like the orb of the sun, and then manifested his parinirvāṇa. The fourfold assembly..."
The True Body was enshrined in a dragon niche; this was the year Jiawu, the forty-second year of King Xian of the Zhou dynasty.
The thirteenth patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra.

Initially a non-Buddhist, he had three thousand disciples and was well-versed in various heterodox doctrines. Later, he received the Dharma from the venerable Aśvaghoṣa and led his followers to Western India.
He had a crown prince named Meghasvāmin (Yún Zìzài). Looking up to the Venerable One’s reputation, he invited him to the palace to provide offerings.
The Patriarch said, “The Tathāgata has taught that śramaṇas must not draw near to kings, ministers, or families of power.
The Prince said, “To the north of my kingdom and city there is a great mountain. On that mountain is a stone cave where you may practice meditative seclusion.”

“This is not so,” the Patriarch replied, “I accept. He then entered that mountain. After traveling several li, he encountered a large python. The Patriarch walked straight ahead without looking back; the serpent coiled itself around his body. The Patriarch then conferred the Three Refuges upon it, and having heard them, the serpent departed. As the Patriarch was about to reach a stone cave, an old man dressed in plain white robes came out, joined his palms in greeting, and asked, “What do you seek? The Patriarch said, “I am seeking the Dharma. The old man said, “The Dharma is not something that can be sought. The Patriarch said, “If it cannot be sought, how can it be attained? The old man said, “It is like a person who has lost their way and wanders through the mountains and marshes for ten thousand *li*, yet still thinks they have not reached their destination. If they suddenly turn back and rest at the very place where they started, they will realize that they have returned home. The Patriarch said, “If one has already returned home, why must one still look for the gate? The old man said, “If you have already returned home, you need not look for the gate. But if you have not yet returned home, how can you avoid looking for the gate? The Patriarch said, “I have already returned home; I do not need to look for the gate. The old man said, “If you have already returned home, you should know the name of your house. The Patriarch said, “I do not even know my own name; how could I know the name of my house? The old man said, “If you do not even know your own name, how can you say you have returned home? You should go back and search for it. The Patriarch said, “I have searched for it for many years and have never found it. The old man said, “If you have searched for it for many years and never found it, it means you have been searching in the wrong place. You should stop searching there and instead look within yourself. The Patriarch said, “If I look within myself, what shall I see? The old man said, “If you look within yourself, you will see nothing at all. That which sees is your original face. The Patriarch said, “If there is nothing to be seen, how can there be seeing? The old man said, “Seeing is precisely because there is nothing to be seen. If there were something to be seen, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is nothing to be seen, this is called the Unconditioned. The Patriarch said, “If there is nothing to be seen, how can there be knowing? The old man said, “Knowing is precisely because there is nothing to be known. If there were something to be known, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is nothing to be known, this is called the Unknowable. The Patriarch said, “If there is nothing to be known, how can there be practice? The old man said, “Practice is precisely because there is nothing to be practiced. If there were something to be practiced, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is nothing to be practiced, this is called Non-practice. The Patriarch said, “If there is no practice, how can there be realization? The old man said, “Realization is precisely because there is nothing to be realized. If there were something to be realized, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is nothing to be realized, this is called Non-realization. The Patriarch said, “If there is no realization, how can there be liberation? The old man said, “Liberation is precisely because there is nothing to be liberated from. If there were something to be liberated from, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is nothing to be liberated from, this is called Non-liberation. The Patriarch said, “If there is no liberation, how can there be Nirvana? The old man said, “Nirvana is precisely because there is nothing to be extinguished. If there were something to be extinguished, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is nothing to be extinguished, this is called Non-extinction. The Patriarch said, “If there is no extinction, how can there be a Buddha? The old man said, “A Buddha is precisely because there is no Buddha. If there were a Buddha, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no Buddha, this is called the Unborn. The Patriarch said, “If there is no birth, how can there be death? The old man said, “Death is precisely because there is no death. If there were death, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no death, this is called the Deathless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no death, how can there be suffering? The old man said, “Suffering is precisely because there is no suffering. If there were suffering, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no suffering, this is called the Unconditioned. The Patriarch said, “If there is no suffering, how can there be a teacher? The old man said, “A teacher is precisely because there is no teacher. If there were a teacher, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no teacher, this is called the Teacherless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no teacher, how can there be a disciple? The old man said, “A disciple is precisely because there is no disciple. If there were a disciple, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no disciple, this is called the Discipleless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no disciple, how can there be a Dharma? The old man said, “The Dharma is precisely because there is no Dharma. If there were a Dharma, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no Dharma, this is called the Dharmaless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no Dharma, how can there be a Sangha? The old man said, “The Sangha is precisely because there is no Sangha. If there were a Sangha, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no Sangha, this is called the Sanghahless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no Sangha, how can there be a path? The old man said, “The path is precisely because there is no path. If there were a path, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no path, this is called the Pathless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no path, how can there be a vehicle? The old man said, “The vehicle is precisely because there is no vehicle. If there were a vehicle, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no vehicle, this is called the Vehicleless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no vehicle, how can there be a destination? The old man said, “The destination is precisely because there is no destination. If there were a destination, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no destination, this is called the Destinationless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no destination, how can there be a beginning? The old man said, “The beginning is precisely because there is no beginning. If there were a beginning, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no beginning, this is called the Beginningless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no beginning, how can there be an end? The old man said, “The end is precisely because there is no end. If there were an end, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no end, this is called the Endless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no end, how can there be a middle? The old man said, “The middle is precisely because there is no middle. If there were a middle, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no middle, this is called the Middleless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no middle, how can there be a self? The old man said, “The self is precisely because there is no self. If there were a self, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no self, this is called the Selfless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no self, how can there be others? The old man said, “Others are precisely because there are no others. If there were others, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there are no others, this is called the Otherless. The Patriarch said, “If there are no others, how can there be a distinction between self and other? The old man said, “The distinction between self and other is precisely because there is no such distinction. If there were a distinction between self and other, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no distinction between self and other, this is called Non-duality. The Patriarch said, “If there is no duality, how can there be a third? The old man said, “A third is precisely because there is no third. If there were a third, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no third, this is called the Thirdless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no third, how can there be a fourth? The old man said, “A fourth is precisely because there is no fourth. If there were a fourth, it would be a conditioned phenomenon. Since there is no fourth, this is called the Fourthless. The Patriarch said, “If there is no fourth, how can there be a fifth? The
Zhi said, "I replied: 'In the past, I was once a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in stillness and solitude.

A novice bhikṣu would frequently come to request instruction, but I grew weary of responding to him and gave rise to thoughts of resentment. When my life ended, I fell into the body of a python and have dwelt in this cave for a thousand years.
Having just encountered the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the precepts, I have come to express my gratitude. The Patriarch asked:
He asked, "Who else dwells on this mountain? He replied, "Ten li to the north, there is a great tree that provides shade for five hundred great nāgas.
This king of trees is named Nāgavṛkṣa (Dragon Tree), and he constantly preaches the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas; I too have listened to it."
The Patriarch then went with his disciples to that place. Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is secluded and desolate, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons.
You, O Virtuous One of supreme honor, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet? The Patriarch replied, "I am not one of supreme honor; I have come to visit a worthy man.
Nāgārjuna thought to himself, "Has this master attained the nature of certainty? Does he possess the clear eye of the Way? Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle? The Patriarch—
[The Master] said: "Though you speak with your mind, I have already known it with my mind. Simply prepare for your renunciation; why worry that I am not a sage?
Upon hearing this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Patriarch immediately granted him ordination, as well as to five hundred dragon followers, and conferred the full precepts upon them all.
He further addressed them, saying: "I now entrust the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to you. Listen attentively to these verses. [He spoke: "Not..."
The hidden is not a manifest dharma; this is called the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). To awaken to this dharma of the hidden and the manifest is neither folly nor wisdom.
Having transmitted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations, using fire to cremate his body. Nāgārjuna collected his five-colored *śarīra* relics and erected a stūpa there.
This was the year Renchen, the forty-sixth year of King Zhou Nanwang’s reign.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was a native of Western India; he was also named Nāgasena.

He first received the Dharma from Venerable Māra and later traveled to South India. The people of that country were largely devoted to the cultivation of merit and karma. For their sake, the Patriarch...
While preaching the Dharma, they said to one another, "Among all people, there are none whose meritorious karma is greater than his; yet we speak in vain of 'Buddha-nature'—who can truly perceive it?
The Patriarch said, "If you wish to see Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your pride. The man asked, "Is Buddha-nature large or small?
The Patriarch replied, "It is neither large nor small; it is neither broad nor narrow. It has no merit and no retribution; it neither dies nor is born."
Hearing that the principle was superior, they all returned to their original resolve. The Patriarch then manifested a body of sovereign mastery upon his seat, like a full moon disc;
the entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma and could not perceive the Patriarch’s form.

Among the crowd was the son of an elder named Kanadeva, who asked the assembly, "Do you recognize this manifestation? The assembly replied, "We have never seen such a thing with our eyes; how can we identify it?"
Deva said: "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essence and characteristics of the Buddha-nature to demonstrate it to us.
How do we know this? It is because through the signless samādhi, his form is like the full moon; the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous. Having finished speaking, [he prostrated].
The wheel-mark immediately vanished, and he returned to his original seat, where he spoke these verses: "The body manifests the form of the full moon, To represent the essence of all Buddhas.

The preaching of Dharma has no fixed shape, Employed to discern that which is neither sound nor form. Upon hearing these verses, the assembly suddenly attained realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
They all vowed to leave the household life in order to seek liberation. The Patriarch immediately shaved their hair and commanded the various sages to confer the full precepts upon them.
Previously, there had been more than five thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths in that country who practiced great magical arts and were venerated by the masses;

the Patriarch transformed them all, causing them to take refuge in the Triple Gem. Furthermore, he composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, which he bequeathed [to the world].
Having transmitted [the Dharma] to the world, he later addressed his chief disciple, Kāṇadeva, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma shall now be entrusted to you.
Listen to my verse: 'To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, one speaks of the logic of liberation;

yet regarding the Dharma, the mind does not realize it—there is neither anger nor joy. Having completed the transmission of the Dharma, he entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi and extensively manifested miraculous transformations."
He returned once more to his original seat and remained in profound meditative stillness. Kanadeva, together with the fourfold assembly, constructed a precious stupa to enshrine him;
this was the year Jichou (49 B.C.), the thirty-fifth year of the First Emperor of Qin.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśāla.
Initially, he sought to cultivate meritorious deeds and also delighted in philosophical debate. Later, he went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.

As he was about to reach the gate, Nāgārjuna, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent his attendant to place a bowl filled with water before the seat. Upon seeing this, the Venerable [immediately...]

He cast a single needle into it and it advanced; [Nāgārjuna] joyfully attained realization. Nāgārjuna immediately preached the Dharma for him without rising from his seat, manifesting the form of a lunar disc;
they heard only his voice but did not see his physical form. The Patriarch said to the assembly: "This auspicious omen of today—"

The Master’s manifestation of Buddha-nature signifies that the preaching of the Dharma transcends both sound and form. After the Patriarch had attained the Dharma, he traveled to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
There lived an elder named Brahmā-Śuddhaguna. One day, mushrooms grew upon the trees in his garden; they were of exquisite flavor.
Only the elder and his second son, Rāhulabhadra, took them and ate them. Having taken them, they followed [the growth].

The elder grew old, and after his life ended, he was reborn again; none of his other relatives were able to see him. His grandfather, knowing the cause from their past lives, went to the elder’s house.
The elder then asked for the reason. The grandfather said, "In the past, your family once made offerings to a bhikṣu.
However, this bhikṣu’s insight into the Way was not yet clear; because he had falsely partaken of the faithful offerings, his retribution was to become a wooden fungus. Only you and [the others]..."
"Son, it is through sincere devotion in making offerings that one may partake [of the merit]; otherwise, it is not so. He asked again, "How old is the elder?
He replied, "Seventy-nine. The Patriarch then spoke this verse: "If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, One returns to the world to consume the faithful offerings.
At eighty-one years of age, This tree shall not grow. Having heard the verse, the elder was filled with even greater admiration and reverence.

Furthermore, he said, "I, your disciple, am aged and infirm and can no longer serve my master. I pray that you will allow me to relinquish my second son so that he may follow you and leave the household life.
The Patriarch replied, "In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this son would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period. That we have met now—"
This was indeed in accordance with his past causes and conditions. He immediately had [the master] shaved his hair and attended him.

Later, when they reached the city of Pāṭaliputra, he heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma. After deliberating on this for some time, the Patriarch took up a long banner and entered among their assembly.
They asked the Patriarch, "Why do you not go forward? The Patriarch replied, "Why do you not go backward? They said, "You seem like a lowly person. The Patriarch replied, "You..."
He resembled a man of noble character. The other asked, "What Dharma do you understand? The Patriarch replied, "You do not understand anything at all.

The other said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood. The Patriarch said, "I have certainly attained Buddhahood. The other said, "It is not fitting for you to attain it. The Patriarch said, "Originally, I say that I have attained it."
"You truly have not attained it," [the Master] said. He replied, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have? The Patriarch said, "Because you possess a self, you do not attain it.
Since I am without a self, I naturally attain it. When his words were thus defeated, he asked the Patriarch:
"What is your name? The Master replied, "My name is Kanadeva. Since he had previously heard of the Master's reputation, he repented his errors and offered his thanks.

At that time, those in the assembly continued to raise various challenges and objections, but the Master analyzed them with unimpeded eloquence; consequently, they all submitted and took refuge in him.
He then informed his senior disciple, Rāhulata, and transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse: "The original intent was to transmit the Dharma."
He expounded the principle of liberation for the sake of people; yet in reality, there is no realization within the dharmas, neither end nor beginning.
After the Patriarch had spoken this verse, he entered the Samādhi of Agility, emitted light from his body, and returned to nirvāṇa. The assembly of disciples erected a stūpa to make offerings to him;
this was precisely the third year of the Later Yuan era of Emperor Wen of the Former Han, the Gengchen year.
