Compiled by the monk (Chao Yong), Abbot of Shenggan Chan Temple in the Capital.
Verified and presented for the Patriarchs of the Western Heaven by the Abbot (Subject) Monk Chaokeui of Kyoto’s Ancient Kegon-ji Temple.
The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulabhadra, was a native of Kapilavastu.

While traveling to Śrāvastī to propagate the Dharma, he came upon a river named Suvarṇodaka (Golden Water), whose taste was exceptionally fine. In the middle of its current, the reflections of five Buddhas appeared.
The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away; there dwells a holy one named Saṃghanandi."
At that place, the Buddha prophesied that one thousand years hence, he would succeed to the holy position.

Having spoken, he led his assembly of disciples upstream until they reached that location, where they saw Saṃghanandin sitting peacefully in meditative absorption. The Patriarch and the assembly waited for him;
after twenty-one days had passed, he finally arose from concentration. The Patriarch asked, "Is it your body that is concentrated, or is it your mind? Saṃghanandin replied, "Both body and mind..."
[The Master] said, "Both body and mind are settled. How can there be entering and exiting? Daitetsu said, "Although there is entering and exiting, one does not lose the characteristic of samādhi.
It is like gold in a well: the essence of the gold is always tranquil. The Master said, "Whether the gold is in the well or whether the gold has been taken out of the well,"
"Gold has neither motion nor stillness; what is it that enters and exits? Daiten replied, "If you say gold has motion and stillness, what is it that enters and exits?

If you say gold enters and exits, then gold itself is neither motion nor stillness. The Patriarch said, "If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that comes out? If the gold comes out of the well..."
"What is it that remains? Dashi said, "If the gold has come out of the well, what remains is not the gold. If the gold is still in the well, what has come out is not the object.
The Patriarch said, "This interpretation is not correct. Dashi said, "That interpretation is not attached [to the truth]. The Patriarch said, "This interpretation shall fall [into error]."
Tishya said, "Your position is not established. The Patriarch said, "Your position is not established; my position is established.
Tishya said, "Although my position is established, the Dharma is not mine. The Patriarch said, "My position is already established, for I have no self.
Tishya said, "Since I have no self, what further meaning is established? The Patriarch said, "Because I have no self, your position is established. Tishya said, "O Virtuous One..."
"Who is your teacher? Who has attained this non-self? The Patriarch replied, "My teacher is Kanadeva;
he realized this non-self. Nandī praised him with a verse: "I bow my head to Teacher Deva, From whom you, O Benevolent One, have emerged.
Because you, O Benevolent One, are without self, I wish to take you as my teacher. The Patriarch answered with a verse: "Since I am already without self, You must see my self. You..."
"If you take me as your teacher, you shall know that 'I' is not 'I'. When Nandi heard this, his mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately sought ordination and liberation.
The Patriarch said, "Your mind is autonomous; it is not bound by me.

Having spoken, he took the golden bowl in his right hand and lifted it up to the Brahma Heaven to fetch fragrant food, intending to serve it to the assembly. However, the assembly suddenly felt a sense of revulsion. The Patriarch—
He said, "This is not my fault; it is the result of your own karma. He then commanded Nandi to share his seat and eat with him. The assembly again marveled at this.
The Patriarch said, "That you are unable to eat is entirely due to this reason. You should know that he who shared his seat with me was the Tathāgata Śālarāja of the past.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he manifested his traces here. You all, too, belong to the same Bhadrakalpa."
They had attained the third fruit [of the path] but had not yet realized the untainted (*anāsrava*) state. The assembly said, "The spiritual power of our teacher is indeed credible.
However, they harbored secret doubts regarding his claim that he was a Buddha of the past. Knowing the arrogance of these beings, Nandika said:

"When the World-Honored One was in the world, the earth was level and even, without hills or mounds. There were no great rivers, streams, ditches, or canals; all water was sweet and delicious. The grasses and trees..."

"The lands will flourish and be abundant; the eight sufferings will cease to exist, and beings will practice the ten wholesome deeds. Since my passing away between the twin trees, more than eight hundred years have elapsed.

The world has become a desolate ruin, and the trees are withered and parched. People lack profound faith; their right mindfulness is slight and they do not believe in *tathatā* (Suchness), but cherish only supernatural powers.
Having finished speaking, he gradually extended his right hand into the earth until it reached the limit of the *vajra-maṇḍala*, and took hold [of it].

Taking a vessel of lapis lazuli filled with ambrosial water, he brought it to the assembly hall. When the great multitude saw this, they immediately felt deep admiration, repented their transgressions, and prostrated themselves.
Thereupon, the Patriarch entrusted the Dharma-eye to Saṃghanandin, speaking this verse:

"In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; Neither grasped nor abandoned. The Dharma has no characteristics of existence or non-existence; How could it arise from within or without? The Patriarch thus transmitted the Dharma.

Having finished [his teaching], he sat peacefully and returned to stillness. The fourfold assembly erected a stupa for him; this was in the fourth year of the Yuanding era of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty, the Wuchen year (57 BCE).
The seventeenth patriarch, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyuha of the city of Śrāvastī.
From birth he was able to speak and constantly praised the deeds of the Buddha. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents in verse, saying:
"I bow my head to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I pay homage to my Mother of flesh and blood. I now wish to leave the home life; I pray you will have pity on me.

His parents tried to dissuade him firmly, whereupon he refused to eat for an entire day. They finally permitted him to leave the home life while remaining within the household, and he was given the name Seng.
Ganḍī further appointed the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin as his teacher. For nineteen years, he never once grew weary or indolent.
He often thought to himself, "I dwell within a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, a divine light shone down, illuminating a path that was level and smooth.
Without realizing it, he walked slowly along it for about ten *li* until he reached a great cliff, where there was a stone cave.
He then dwelt in tranquil seclusion within. When the father lost his son, he immediately banished Śāṇakavāsin from the country and went abroad in search of him, but did not know where he was.
Ten years passed; having received the Dharma and the prediction of his attainment, the Patriarch traveled to spread the teaching and arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā.
Suddenly, a cool breeze swept over the bodies and minds of the assembly, bringing them an extraordinary sense of joy and comfort, though they did not know its cause.
The Patriarch said, "This is the wind of the Way and its Virtue. A sage shall appear in this world to continue the ancestral lamp.

Having spoken, he used his supernatural powers to lead the great multitude through the mountains and valleys; in the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak. He said to the assembly, "This peak..."
At the summit, there were purple clouds like a canopy; a sage dwelt there. He and the great assembly lingered for a long time before seeing a mountain cottage.
A young boy holding a round mirror came straight before the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "How old are you? He replied, "A hundred years.
The Patriarch said, "You are still a child; why do you say you are a hundred years old? The boy said, "I do not understand principle; I am truly a hundred years old."
The Patriarch said, “Are you skilled in the pivot? The boy replied, “The Buddha said:

‘If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the pivot of the Buddhas, it would be better to live for a single day and attain decisive realization. The Patriarch asked, “What does that which is in your hand signify?
The boy replied, “It is the great perfect mirror of all Buddhas; without flaw or obscuration within or without, both persons see it together with their mind-eyes.”
They were all alike. When his parents heard their son’s words, they immediately allowed him to leave the household life.

His grandfather took him back to his original home and, having conferred upon him the full ordination (*upasampadā*), gave him the name Gayāsīta. Later, hearing the sound of wind blowing through the palace bells, his grandfather asked, "Are the bells ringing, or is it the wind?
Sīta replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells that are ringing; it is my own heart that is ringing. His grandfather said:
The Master asked, "And who is this mind? She-t'o replied, "Because both are utterly quiescent. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could succeed to my Way?
He then transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse: "The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth; The ground arises from conditions.
Condition and seed do not obstruct one another; Flower and fruit are likewise so. Having transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch grasped the tree with his right hand and—
The assembly deliberated, saying, "The Venerable One has entered parinirvāṇa beneath this tree; shall its shade continue to shelter his descendants?

We intend to enshrine his entire body on the high plateau and erect a stūpa there. However, the multitude's strength was insufficient to lift him. Thus, they erected the stūpa directly beneath the tree.
This occurred in the first year of the Yuanying era of Emperor Zhao of the Former Han, the Dingwei year.
The eighteenth patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the kingdom of Mathura. His clan name was Uttara, his father was Devavarma, and his mother was Bhadra.
She once dreamed of a great deity holding a mirror, and consequently became pregnant. He was born after exactly seven days;
his body was as translucent as lapis lazuli, and though he never bathed, he was naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood, he delighted in solitude and quietude, and his speech was extraordinary.
As a youth, he took a mirror and went out for a stroll, where he encountered Venerable Nandī and received ordination. Later, leading his disciples, he arrived at the kingdom of Mahācīna.
Seeing an unusual aura over a Brahmin’s house, the Patriarch was about to enter it when the householder Kumāralata asked, "Who are these followers?
The Patriarch replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, Kumāralata’s spirit was suddenly stirred.
He immediately closed the door. After a long while, Sengzhu knocked on the door. Luopo said, "There is no one in this house. Sengzhu asked, "Who is it that says there is no one?
Upon hearing these words, Luopo realized he was an extraordinary person; he hurriedly opened the door and invited him in. Sengzhu said, "In the past, the World-Honored One made a prophecy:
'One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Mozhī (Yuezhi) to propagate and uphold [the Dharma].'"

"Original Transformation. Now you have encountered me; you should respond to this auspicious destiny. Thereupon, Kumārajīva developed the wisdom of his past lives and devotedly entered the monastic order.
Once he had received full ordination, [the Patriarch] bestowed upon him the Dharma verse, saying: "When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, causes and conditions can cause sprouts to emerge.
If these conditions do not obstruct one another, then birth will arise from non-birth. Having transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch leaped into the void and manifested—

Having displayed eighteen kinds of supernatural transformations, he entered the Samādhi of the Emanation of Fire-Light and spontaneously cremated his own body. The multitude erected a stupa for his relics;
this was in the fourth year of the Yongshi era of Emperor Cheng of the Han dynasty, the Wushen year.
The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Gandhāra.

In a former life, he was a deva of sovereign power (the sixth heaven of the desire realm). Upon seeing the jeweled ornaments of a bodhisattva, he suddenly conceived a heart of attachment and fell to be born in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven (the second heaven of the desire realm).
There, he heard Kauśika preach the Prajñāpāramitā; because the Dharma was supreme, he ascended [to a higher realm].
His son was Brahmadeva (of the Form Realm). Because his faculties were sharp, he skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma; all the devas honored him as their teacher.

As the time had come to succeed to the ancestral lineage, he subsequently descended to the country of the Yuezhi. Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Central India, where there was a Mahāsattva named Jayanta.
The questioner asked: "In my family, our parents have long been faithful to the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by chronic illness, and whatever we undertake never turns out as we wish.
On the other hand, my neighbor has long followed the profession of a *caṇḍāla*, yet his body is always vigorous and healthy, and everything he does succeeds.
Why is he so fortunate, while I am so guilty? The Patriarch said: "Why is there any need for such doubt? Furthermore, regarding the retribution of good and evil—"

There are three points here. Ordinary people, seeing only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, and that those who act contrary to the Way meet with good fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune, conclude that cause and effect do not exist and that merit and retribution are empty.
They fail to realize, however, that shadow and echo follow one another without the slightest discrepancy;
even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they shall never perish. When Śāṇakavāsin heard these words, his doubts were instantly dispelled. The Patriarch said: "You..."

Although one has already gained faith in the three types of karma, one has not yet clarified that karma arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), that afflictions exist because of consciousness (*vijñāna*), that consciousness depends upon non-awakening (*avidyā*), and that non-awakening depends upon the mind (*citta*).
This mind is fundamentally pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, without retribution, and without victory or defeat.
"Tranquil and still; numinous and alert. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may become one with all Buddhas.

All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions. Śāṇakavāsin received these words and grasped their meaning; his latent wisdom was immediately awakened, and he earnestly sought ordination.
Once he had received full precepts, the Patriarch told him: "The time for my final nirvana has now arrived. You shall succeed me."

Having completed his travels to transform and guide others, he then transmitted the Dharma-eye. He spoke in verse: "In the fundamental nature, there is originally no birth; it is spoken for the sake of those who seek.

Since nothing can be attained within the Dharma, why harbor doubts about being resolved or not? He further said, "These are the words of the Tathāgata Sublime Sound regarding the purity of seeing one's nature.
You must propagate them for future students. Having finished speaking, he immediately scratched his face with his fingernails while sitting upon his seat.
Like a red lotus in bloom, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the fourfold assembly before entering parinirvāṇa.
Śāṇakavāsa erected a stūpa for him during the Renwu year of the reign of Emperor Ziying of the Han dynasty.
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Jayata, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and deep; he transformed and guided immeasurable beings.
Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and propagated the teachings of the sudden school (*tun-jiao*). There was a community of students there who valued only dialectical debate.

Their leader was named Vasu-bandhu (translated as "Pianxing" or "Universal Walker"), who constantly ate only one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha six times daily. He was pure...
Śuddhavīra was revered by the multitude. When the Patriarch was about to deliver him, he first asked the assembly, "This ascetic Pūrṇa is able to cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*);
can he attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied, "Our teacher is diligent; why should he not be capable?
The Patriarch said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice austerities for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would all be in vain."

This is the fundamental principle. The assembly asked, "What virtues and conduct does the Venerable One possess that he should disparage our Master? The Patriarch replied, "I do not seek the Way, yet I am not deluded.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I do not treat him with contempt. I do not sit perpetually, yet I am not indolent."
"I do not eat but once a day, nor do I consume mixed foods. I am neither discontented nor greedy;
my mind has no expectations—this is what is called the Way. When Pūrvavāsī heard this, he attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully praised him.
The Elder then said to the assembly, "Do you understand my words? It is because his resolve for the Way is so earnest. Now, as for the lute strings...
He immediately cut it off. Therefore, I do not praise such things; rather, I cause them to dwell in the ground of peace and bliss and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas.
He then addressed Samantagupta, saying: "I have just now, before this assembly, suppressed and rebuked you, my worthy friend. Are you not troubled in your heart? Samantagupta replied:
"I recall that seven kalpas ago, I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Bliss. My teacher there was the Wise One Candravimala, who prophesied that I would [attain enlightenment] before long."
When I was realizing the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, there appeared in the world a Bodhisattva named Mahāprabha. Because I was old, I leaned on a staff to pay my respects to him.
The Master rebuked me, saying, "To honor the son and slight the father—how vulgar this is! At that time, I considered myself blameless and requested the Master to point out my fault.
The Master said, "When you paid homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, you leaned your staff against the wall where a painted Buddha stood."
[The Master] said: "Because of this overweening pride (*adhimāna*), you have consequently lost two fruits [of the path]. I have reproached myself and repented my errors;

since then, when I have heard various harsh words, I have regarded them as being like the wind or an echo. How much more so now that I have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar (*amṛta*)—how could I instead give rise to feverish affliction?
I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said: "You have long planted many virtues and shall succeed to my lineage. Listen to me..."

The verse says: "In the moment the words fell, he merged with the non-arising; he became one with the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand in this way, one has fully mastered both phenomena and principle.
After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he did not rise from his seat and suddenly returned to quiescence. His body was cremated, the relics were collected, and a stupa was erected.
This occurred in the seventeenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, the year of Jiashu.
The twenty-first patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Viśākha;
his father was named Prabhācchada and his mother, Śrīmatī. Although his family was wealthy, they had no son. Consequently, his parents prayed at a Buddhist stūpa, seeking an heir.
One night, his mother dreamed that she swallowed two pearls, one bright and one dark. Upon waking, she became pregnant.

After seven days had passed, an arhat named Bhadrayaśas arrived at her home. She prepared a radiant canopy and offered him her respects; Bhadrayaśas sat upright and accepted them. Then Yan came forward and prostrated himself.
The virtuous assembly rose from their seats and said, "We return our salutations to the Great Being of the Dharma-body. Guanggai could not fathom the reason for this;
he then took a precious jewel and knelt to offer it, testing whether they were genuine or false. The virtuous assembly accepted it immediately, without any sign of modesty or thanks.
Unable to restrain himself, Guanggai asked, "I am a man, yet when I offered my respects, you paid me no heed. What virtue does my wife possess that you avoid her?"
The virtuous assembly said, "We accepted your prostration and the pearl only to bestow blessings upon you.
Your wife is pregnant with a holy son who, when born, shall become a lamp for the world and a sun of wisdom; therefore, we avoided him, not out of any regard for women.
The virtuous assembly further said, "Your wife shall give birth to two sons: the first shall be named Vasiṣṭha, whom I shall honor; the second shall be named Kātyāyana (which means..."
The Wild Magpie: Formerly, when the Tathāgata was practicing the Way on Mount Himavat, a female crane nested upon his head.
Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, the crane received her karmic retribution by becoming the Queen of King Nadi. The Buddha prophesied, saying:

"In the second five-hundred-year period [after my passing], you shall be born into the family of Viśākha in the city of Rājagṛha as a sibling to a noble one; now there is no discrepancy. One month later, she indeed gave birth.
The two sons—Venerable Vāṣpa (婆修盤頭)—reached the age of fifteen and, having paid homage to the arhat Prabhāsa, left the household life.
Moved by the bodhisattva Vibhāṣa, he was granted the precepts. While traveling to spread the teachings, he arrived at the kingdom of Nadī.
Its king was named Nityeśvara (常自在) and had two sons: the first was named Mahāla (摩訶羅), and the second was named Maṇḍala (摩拏羅). The king asked his grandfather: "Rājagṛha..."
[The King asked: "How does the climate and customs of that land differ from this? The Patriarch said: "In that land, three Buddhas have appeared in the world.
Now, in your kingdom, there are two masters who provide guidance. The King asked: "Who are these two masters? The Patriarch said:

"The Buddha prophesied that in the second five-hundred-year period, there would be two Great Beings of supernatural power who would leave the household life to succeed the Sages. One of them is your second son, Maṇiratha."

[The King replied: "Indeed, although my virtue is meager, I dare to accept one [of these offerings]. The King said, "Truly as the Venerable One has spoken, I shall renounce this son to become a śramaṇa.
The Patriarch said, "Excellent, Great King! You are able to follow the Buddha’s intent. He immediately conferred full ordination upon him and bestowed the verse of the transmission of the Dharma:
"Phenomena like bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded; why is it that one does not awaken to this? To penetrate the Dharma within them—this is neither of the present nor..."

This was not according to ancient custom. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he leaped into the air to a height of half a yojana and remained suspended there motionless. The fourfold assembly gazed up at him with reverence and earnestly requested him to sit down again;
he then passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His body was cremated, and śarīra relics were obtained for which a stūpa was erected.
This occurred in the fourth year of the Yuanchu era of Emperor An of the Han dynasty, the year of Ding-si.
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍara, was the son of King Nitya-vaśavartin of the country of Nādi.
At the age of thirty, he encountered the patriarch Vasu and left the household life. He transmitted the Dharma to Western India, where the king’s name was Pradyota;
he was of the Gautama clan and had turned toward the Buddha Vehicle, practicing with diligent perseverance. One day, at the place where he practiced the Way, [he...]
A small stūpa appeared, and when [the king] wished to take it to offer worship, the multitude was unable to lift it.

The king immediately convened a great assembly of the three groups—the Brahma-farers (*brahmacārin*), those in meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), and those of incantations (*mantra*). He intended to ask about his doubts. At that time, the Patriarch also attended this assembly;

none of these three groups were able to discern [its origin]. The Patriarch then explained to the king in detail the causes and conditions of the stūpa (as for the stūpas built by King Aśoka, they are not recorded here at length). Now, it emerged...
"This is manifested by the power of the King's merit. Upon hearing these words, the King said, "The ultimate truth is difficult to encounter, and worldly pleasures are not enduring.
He immediately abdicated the throne to his crown prince and went forth as a renunciant under the Patriarch. Within seven days, he realized the fruit of Arhatship.

The Patriarch comforted and instructed him deeply, saying, "While you remain in this kingdom, skillfully deliver others. Now, there is one of great Dharma-capacity in a foreign land; I shall [go there]."

When he was about to go and convert others, [the King] said, "The Master’s manifested traces pervade the ten directions; whenever you stir a thought, you shall arrive. Why trouble yourself with the journey? The Master replied, "Indeed.
Thereupon, he burned incense and spoke from afar to the Bhikṣu Helunana in the Kingdom of Mozhī: "You are in that kingdom..."
He instructed the flock of cranes, saying, "The Way and its fruits are about to be realized; you should know this for yourselves.
At that time, Hakena recited a sūtra verse for King Ratnamudrā. Suddenly, he beheld a wondrous fragrance forming into a cluster. The king asked, "What omen is this?
He replied, "This is the fragrant token sent in advance by the Patriarch Mañjuśrī, who transmits the Buddha’s Mind-Seal from the Western Land of India and is about to arrive."

[The King] said, "What is the spiritual power of this master like? [Huike] replied, "This master has received a distant prediction from the Buddha that he shall widely proclaim the profound transformation in this land.

At that time, the King and Helena both paid homage from afar. The Patriarch, knowing this, immediately took leave of the bhikṣu De-du (Deduo) and went to the kingdom of Moji (Yuezhi), where he accepted the offerings of the King and Helena. Later, Helena asked:
The Patriarch said, "I have resided among the forests for nine white years. I have a disciple named Longzi, who was intelligent and wise from his youth;

though I have investigated through the three periods of time, I could not discover his origin. The Patriarch continued, "In the fifth kalpa, this child was born into a Brahmin family in the Land of Wondrous Joy (Abhirati).
He once offered sandalwood to a Buddhist temple to serve as a mallet for striking the bell, and thereby received [the fruit of his merit]."
Baocongming was revered and admired by the multitude. Again, [Baofu] asked, "By what conditions did I attract this flock of cranes?
The Patriarch said, "In the fourth kalpa, you were once a bhikṣu. You were about to attend a gathering at the Dragon Palace, and your disciples all wished to follow you.
You observed that among the five hundred members of the assembly, not a single person was fit to receive such sublime offerings. At that time, your disciples said:"
"The Master constantly preached the Dharma, being equal toward food and equal toward the Dharma. Now that he is not so, how can he be considered a sage?
You must immediately go to the assembly. From the moment you leave this life and enter the next, you shall travel through various kingdoms to convert them. As for your five hundred disciples..."
Because my merit was slight and my virtue thin, I was born among the feathered tribes. Now, moved by your kindness, I have come to follow this flock of cranes.
Helan asked, "By what skillful means can you cause them to attain liberation? The Patriarch replied, "I possess the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma;

you should listen and receive it so that it may transform beings throughout the limits of the future. He then spoke a verse: "The mind turns following the myriad objects; in the place where it turns..."
"Truly able to penetrate the profound; following the stream, one recognizes the nature. Without joy and without sorrow. When the flock of cranes heard this verse, they flew away with cries.
The Patriarch sat in the *paryaṅka* posture and passed away in silence.
Harelana and King Baoyin erected a stupa for him in the eighth year of the Yanxi era of Emperor Huan of the Later Han dynasty, the year of Yisi.
The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Harelana, was a native of the country of Moji (Yuezhi).
His family name was Brahmin; his father was Qiansheng, and his mother was Jinguang. Because they had no son, she prayed before the golden pillar of the Seven Buddhas.
She then dreamed of a divine youth atop Mount Sumeru holding a golden ring and saying, "I have come. Upon waking, she became pregnant. At the age of seven, he wandered through the marketplace.

He fell [into a state of realization]. Seeing the vulgar sacrifices practiced among the common people, he entered the temple and rebuked them, saying: "You recklessly invoke calamity and fortune to delude and confuse the people.
Year after year you waste livestock and inflict great harm. Having finished speaking, the temple structure suddenly collapsed.

From this, the local community called him the "Holy Child" (Shengzi). At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life; at thirty, he met the Venerable Maṇḍarava, who transmitted [the Dharma] to him.
Fayan Zhang traveled to Central India to propagate the Dharma. The king there was named Abhayasāgara; he held deep faith in the Buddha’s Way.
The Patriarch preached the True Dharma for him. Later, the king suddenly saw two men dressed in vermilion and white robes bowing before the Patriarch.
The king asked, "Who are these people? The Patriarch replied, "These are the Sun and Moon Devas. Because I once preached the Dharma for them in the past, they have come to pay their respects."
He prostrated. After a long while, [the Master] was no longer seen; only a wondrous fragrance was perceived. The King asked, "How many suns, moons, and lands are there in total?
The Patriarch replied, "In the worlds transformed by the thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas, there are each ten billion Mount Merus, suns, and moons.

If I were to explain this extensively, I could not finish. Upon hearing this, the King was filled with joy. At that time, the Patriarch expounded the Unsurpassed Way and delivered those sentient beings with whom he had a karmic affinity.
The Dragon Prince Yishangzu died young. He had an elder brother named Shizi, who was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory; he served a Brahmin teacher.
When that teacher passed away and his younger brother also died, Shizi took refuge with the Venerable One and asked:

"I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind? The Patriarch said: "If you wish to seek the Way, there is no place for the mind to be applied. Shizi asked: "If there is no application of the mind, who is it that acts?"
[The Master said: "Buddha-work. The Patriarch said: "If you have something to employ, it is not merit; if you have no action, that is Buddha-work. As the Sūtra says:
"The merits I have performed are without the notion of 'mine'. Having heard these words, Śiṃha immediately entered the Buddha-wisdom.
At that time, the Patriarch suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked: "What kind of phenomenon is this? Śiṃha replied: "I see a vapor."
It was like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth, with five paths of black vapor stretching horizontally across its center.
The Patriarch asked, "What is the significance of this omen? He replied, "It cannot be known. The Patriarch said, "Fifty years after my passing, in the kingdom of Northern India..."
"When a time of difficulty arises, you shall bear the infant within your person; I am about to pass away. Now, I entrust the Dharma-eye to you.
Guard and uphold it well. He then spoke a verse, saying: "When the nature of mind is recognized, It can be spoken of, yet cannot be deliberated upon.

It is perfectly clear, yet nothing can be grasped; When it is attained, one does not say 'I know. Upon hearing this verse, the Bhikṣu Siṃha was filled with joy and satisfaction, yet he did not yet understand its meaning.
"What difficulty have you encountered? The Patriarch then secretly revealed it to him. Having finished speaking, he manifested eighteen transformations and returned to stillness.

After the cremation was completed and the śarīra relics were distributed, everyone wished to erect a stūpa for their share. The Patriarch again appeared in mid-air and spoke this verse: "One dharma encompasses all dharmas; All dharmas are subsumed within one dharma.
My body is neither existent nor non-existent; Why divide it into various stūpas? When the great assembly heard this verse, they [ceased their efforts].

Consequently, they were no longer divided; instead, a stūpa was erected at the site of the Dhadu field. This was the year Jichou (49th year of the sexagenary cycle), the fourteenth year of the Jian’an era of Emperor Xian of the Later Han dynasty.
The twenty-fourth patriarch, Venerable Siṃha, was a native of Central India. His family name was Brahmin. Having attained the Dharma, he traveled abroad.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was a man named Parika who had originally practiced dhyāna-vipaśyanā.

Consequently, he had five groups of followers—those who clung to signs, those who abandoned signs, and those who remained silent through meditative concentration and insight. The Patriarch interrogated them and transformed them; the four groups all remained silent, submitting their hearts in reverence.
Only Dharmatrāta, the master of dhyāna-concentration, heard that the fourfold assembly had been rebuked and came in a state of indignant agitation.

The Patriarch said, "Virtuous one, you practice concentration; why have you come here? Now that you have arrived here, how can you say you practice concentration? He replied, "Though I have come here, my mind is not distracted.
Concentration follows the person who practices it; how could it depend on a particular location? The Patriarch said, "Since you have come here, virtuous one..."

"Practice also reaches [the practitioner]. Since there is no fixed location, how could it depend on the person practicing? He said, 'It is certainly the person who practices; it is not that the person practices concentration (samādhi).
When I come here, that concentration will be constantly practiced. The Master said, 'It is not that the person practices concentration; rather, it is concentration that practices the person.

Therefore, when you come here of your own accord, who will be practicing that concentration? He said, 'It is like a pure, bright pearl with no obscurations inside or out. If concentration is thus pervasive..."
"Penetrated! It must certainly be so. The Patriarch said, "If it were truly penetrated, it would be like a bright pearl.

Now that I see you, sir, you are not of the class of pearls. The man replied, "That pearl is clear and transparent; inside and out it is entirely settled. My mind is undisturbed, just as this [pearl] is pure.
The Patriarch said, "That pearl has no interior or exterior; how can you, sir, be 'settled'? Impure things are subject to agitation; this is not true stillness."

"It is not pure. Dhamadatta received the patriarch’s instruction and attained enlightenment; his mind became luminous and clear. The patriarch immediately gathered him as one of the fivefold assembly, and his fame spread far and wide.
Just as he was seeking a dharma heir, he encountered an elder who led forth his son and addressed the patriarch, saying:

"This boy is named Sthavira. From the moment of his birth, his left hand has been clenched in a fist; now that he has grown up, he is still unable to open it. I pray that the Venerable One will instruct him."
The Patriarch perceived his past causes and immediately reached out his hand, saying, "Return my pearl to me. The boy suddenly opened his hand and presented the pearl.
The assembly was all struck with wonder. The Patriarch said, "In a previous life, I was a monk named Basha.
Once, when I went to a vegetarian feast by the Western Sea, I received this embroidered pearl and entrusted it to him. That he now returns my pearl is but natural. The elder [was thus moved].

He then abandoned his son to enter the monastic life. The Patriarch immediately bestowed the *saṃkakṣikā* robe upon him; because of these prior conditions, he was named Vasiṣṭha. The Patriarch then said to him:
"My teacher had a secret prophetic prediction that you would encounter hardship before long. Now, the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is transmitted to you.
You must protect it so that it may universally moisten all beings until the end of time. He spoke in verse: "When the true teaching of knowledge and vision is expounded,"
"Knowledge and vision are both the mind; when the mind is present, there is knowledge and vision; knowledge and vision exist right now.

Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch secretly entrusted his *saṃghāṭī* robe to Suta, instructing him to go to another country and transform beings according to their capacities. Suta received the teaching and traveled directly to Southern India.
The Patriarch said, "One cannot evade destiny through mere whim," and thus he remained alone in Kaśmīra. At that time, there was a foreigner in that country...
There were two men, one named Māmuta and the other named Durlabha. Having studied various magical arts, they plotted together to incite a rebellion;
they then stole the appearance of Śākya disciples and secretly entered the royal palace. They thought to themselves: "If we do not succeed, the guilt will fall upon the sons of the Buddha.

Since we have committed this sorcery ourselves, the calamity will surely follow us immediately. The King was indeed enraged and said: "I have long since placed my heart's devotion in the Triple Gem. Why..."
Thus, his malice reached such an extreme that he immediately ordered the destruction of the monasteries and the expulsion of the Śākya community.

Furthermore, he personally took up a sword and went to where the Venerable was, asking: "Has the Master realized the emptiness of the aggregates? The Patriarch replied: "I have already realized the emptiness of the aggregates. The King said:
"Are you free from birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I am already free from birth and death. The King said, "Since you are free from birth and death, you may give me your head.
The Patriarch said, "This body is not mine; why should I begrudge my head? The King then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable’s head.
White milk gushed forth several feet high, and the King’s right arm immediately fell to the ground. He died seven days later. His son was named Guangshou (Light-Head).
He sighed and said, "Why has my father brought this calamity upon himself? At that time, there was an ascetic named Śvetaśaila who deeply understood the law of cause and effect;
he then extensively explained the past causes for Kāśyapa’s sake, unraveling the net of his doubts (the details of which are found in the *Shengzhou ji* and the *Baolin zhuan*).
Thereupon, he constructed a stūpa as an act of requital for the Venerable Siṃha. This was in the second year of the Jingshao era of Emperor Huan of the Later Han, the year of Jihai.
The year was the Year of the Hare.
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Vasiṣṭha (Póshè斯多) Bhadanta, was a native of Kaśmīra. His clan was Brāhmaṇa;

his father was named Śāntacaryā (Jíxíng), and his mother was Nityasukha (Cháng'ānlè). Initially, the mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword, and consequently became pregnant. Upon his birth, his left hand remained in a fist.

Handu met the Venerable Siṃha, who revealed his past causes and secretly transmitted the seal of the mind (cittamudrā) to him. Later, he traveled to South India and reached Central India, where the king was named Kaniṣka;
the king paid him homage and provided offerings. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner known as Nirātman-bhadra.
Previously, the King had held him in high esteem. Envious of Bodhidharma’s arrival, he wished to debate with him, hoping to defeat him and thereby consolidate his own position.
Thus, before the King, he requested of Bodhidharma, saying, "I understand silent debate, which does not rely on spoken words. Bodhidharma asked, "Who shall determine victory and defeat?
He replied, "I do not contend for victory or defeat; I seek only the meaning. Bodhidharma asked, "By what do you define 'meaning'? He—

He said, "To be without mind is the meaning. The Patriarch said, "Since you are already without mind, how can you attain the meaning? He replied, "When I speak of being without mind, it is a name, not the meaning.
The Patriarch said, "When you speak of being without mind, it is a name, not the meaning; when I speak of non-mind, it is the meaning, not the name.
He asked, "If it is the meaning and not the name, who is able to discern the meaning? The Patriarch said, "Your 'name' is not the meaning; this..."

"What is the name of that which is called 'name'? He replied, "It is for the sake of distinguishing non-meaning; therefore, it is called 'the nameless name. The Patriarch said, "If the name is not a name, then the meaning is also not a meaning.
Who is it that distinguishes? And what is there to be distinguished? Thus they conversed back and forth forty-nine times. The outsider was silenced and filled with conviction.
At that moment, the Patriarch suddenly turned northward, joined his palms, and sighed deeply, saying, "My teacher, the Lion."

"Venerable One, today we have encountered a calamity; this is truly lamentable. Having thus taken leave of the king, he traveled southward and reached Southern India, where he lived in seclusion within the mountain valleys.
At that time, there was a king of that land named Devaśrī (Heavenly Virtue) who welcomed him and offered him sustenance. The king had two sons:

the first was named Guṇajaya (Victorious in Virtue), who was fierce and violent yet possessed of great physical vigor; the second was named Upamanyu (Not Inferior), who was gentle and mild, but had suffered from chronic illness since childhood.
He was suffering from illness. The Master then explained the law of cause and effect for him, and the king immediately had his doubts resolved.

Furthermore, there was a master of incantations who resented the Master’s Way; he secretly placed poison in food and drink. The Master knew of it and ate it, whereupon the other man instead met with disaster and subsequently sought refuge with the Master to leave the household life.
The Master then conferred the full precepts upon him. Sixty years later, Emperor De-sheng ascended the throne once again.
He believed in non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) and presented difficulties to the Patriarch. He was not as [fortunate] as Guṇamati, who was imprisoned for offering remonstrance.

The King suddenly asked the Patriarch, "In my kingdom, heterodox and deceptive teachings have long been absent. What school is that which you have transmitted? The Patriarch replied, "In Your Majesty’s kingdom, there has indeed been no false dharma since ancient times.
That which I have attained is precisely the Buddha-dharma. The King said, "It has been over twelve hundred years since the Buddha's parinirvāṇa."
[The King asked: "For a hundred years, from whom did you receive [this teaching], Master? The Master said: "The Mahāsattva Prabhāsa directly received the Buddha’s seal.
It was transmitted successively down to the twenty-fourth generation, the Venerable Siṃha; I received it from him. The King said: "I have heard that there was a Bhikṣu named Siṃha."
"You cannot escape execution; how then can you transmit the Dharma to future generations?

The Patriarch replied, "When my teacher’s time of peril had not yet arisen, he secretly bestowed upon me the robe of faith and the Dharma verses to manifest the lineage of succession. The King asked, "Where is that robe?

The Patriarch immediately took the robe out from his bag and showed it to the King. The King ordered it to be burned; its five colors remained vividly distinct, and even when the wood was consumed, it remained as it was before. The King then—
He repented and paid his respects. Once it was clear that Shizi Zhen had truly succeeded him, he then pardoned Mita. Mita then requested to leave the household life.
The Patriarch asked, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you do so? Mita replied, "If I leave the household life, I shall not engage in that business.
The Patriarch asked, "What business will you not engage in? Mita replied, "I shall not engage in worldly affairs. The Master said, "Then you shall engage in this."
"What task shall it be? Guṇamati replied, "It shall be a Buddha-act. The Patriarch said, "The Prince’s wisdom is innate; he must surely be an incarnation of a sage.
He then granted him permission to leave the household life. He served [the Patriarch] for six years, and later received full ordination within the royal palace. At the moment of the *karmavācanā*,...
Heaven and earth shook, and many miraculous signs appeared. The Patriarch then addressed him, saying: "I am already worn out by age; how can I remain much longer?
You must well protect the Eye of the True Dharma and universally deliver all sentient beings. Listen to my verse:

"The Sage speaks of knowledge and vision, Yet within the objective realm there is neither right nor wrong. I have now awakened to the true nature: There is neither Path nor Principle. It is better to remain silent."

Dawen bowed again and addressed the Patriarch, saying, "You should transmit this robe to me. The Patriarch said, "This robe was used as a provisional means of verification because of the difficulties involved.
You have no such difficulties; why should you need the robe? When your transformation reaches the ten directions and people naturally turn toward you with faith, [the purpose will be fulfilled]."

It is better to hear the teachings in secret. Having paid his respects, he withdrew. The Patriarch manifested supernatural transformations, transforming himself into a fire of samādhi to cremate himself.
The śarīra remained level with the ground, standing one chi high. King Deśeng (Dekseng) built a stūpa to enshrine them.
This was in the year of Yiyou, the third year of the Taining era of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulamitra, was the second son of King Devaśrī of South India.
Having received ordination and attained the Dharma, he traveled to East India. There, the king was named Sthira; he venerated the non-Buddhist teacher, the Brahmin Dīrghanakha.
As the Venerable One was about to arrive, the king and the Brahmin both beheld a white vapor piercing through the heavens from above to below. The king said:
"What auspicious omen is this? The Brahmin, having foreknowledge that the Elder was about to enter the kingdom, feared that the King would convert to the true path.

He then said, "This is merely a sign that Māra is coming; what auspicious omen could there be? He immediately gathered his disciples and deliberated, saying, "It will not do to let him enter the capital city.
Who among us can defeat him? A disciple replied, "Each of us possesses incantations capable of shaking the heavens."
"Entering earth, water, or fire—what trouble could there be? When the Patriarch arrived, he first saw black vapors over the palace walls and said, "There will be a minor difficulty.

He went straight to the King's location. The King asked, "For what purpose have you come, Master? The Patriarch replied, "I have come to deliver sentient beings. The King asked, "By what means do you deliver them?
The Patriarch replied, "I deliver each according to their own kind. At that time, a Brahmin heard these words and could not contain his anger.
He immediately used his illusory power to manifest a great mountain atop the Patriarch’s head. The Patriarch pointed at it, and suddenly it appeared above the heads of the entire assembly.

The brahmins and others, seized with fear, threw themselves at the Patriarch’s mercy. The Patriarch, pitying their ignorance and delusion, pointed his finger at them once more; the mountain was transformed and vanished accordingly.
He then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the King, leading him toward the True Vehicle. He said to the King: "In this country, there shall be a holy man who will succeed me.
At that time, there was the son of a Brahmin, about twenty years of age, who had lost both parents in childhood and knew nothing [of his origins].
As for his name, he sometimes called himself "Sragdharin" (The Garlanded One); thus people called him the "Girland-Wearing Boy.

He wandered through the streets and villages, begging for his daily sustenance, much like the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta. When people asked him, "Why do you walk so hurriedly? he would reply, "Why do you walk so slowly?
Or when asked what his surname was, he would say, "It is the same as yours. No one knew the reason for this. Later, the King and the Venerable... [text ends]
They departed together in the same carriage and encountered the youth Maṇicūḍa. [The Master] prostrated before him. The Patriarch said, "Do you remember past events?
The youth replied, "I recall that in a distant kalpa, I lived with my teacher. My teacher expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and I recited the profound *Sūtras*.
Today’s encounter is surely in accord with our former causes. The Patriarch further said to the King, "This youth..."
"You are none other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. After this holy one, two more individuals appeared:
one was destined to convert South India, while the other had a karmic connection with China (Zhendan). Within four or five years, he returned to this land;
thus, due to his past causes, he was named Prajñātāra and entrusted with the treasury of the Dharma-eye. The verse says: "The true nature is the treasury of the mind-ground."

Having neither head nor tail, he transforms beings in accordance with conditions; this skillful means is called "wisdom. Having transmitted the Dharma to his successor, the Patriarch took leave of the King, saying:
"My karmic conditions for transformation have ended; I shall now return to quiescent extinction. I pray that Your Majesty will not forget to provide external protection for the Supreme Vehicle.
He then returned to his original seat, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. A fire spontaneously emerged to cremate him. His relics were collected, enshrined in a stupa, and interred.
This occurred in the thirteenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin dynasty, the wuzi year.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of East India.

After he had received the Dharma, the King of East India invited the Patriarch for a vegetarian feast. During the meal, the King asked: "Everyone here recites the scriptures; why is it that you alone do not?"
"It does not turn. The Patriarch said, "In my breathing out, I do not follow external conditions; in my breathing in, I do not dwell within the aggregates or realms.
I constantly recite this sutra in hundreds of thousands of ten-thousands of millions of scrolls, not merely one or two scrolls. While traveling to propagate the teaching, I reached South India."
That king was named Xiangzhi (Gandhāra). He venerated the Buddha Vehicle with such profound respect and made offerings so surpassingly magnificent that they exceeded those of all others.
Furthermore, he bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. At that time, the king had three sons named Yuejingduoluo (Candravimala), Gongdeduoluo (Guṇavimala), and Putiduoluo (Bodhivimala);
the youngest was a bodhisattva. Desiring to test what each had attained, the grandfather took the jewel he had been given and questioned the three princes.

The Master said, "This pearl is perfectly round and luminous; is there anyone capable of receiving it? The first prince and the second prince both replied, "This pearl is the most honored among the seven treasures;
indeed, nothing surpasses it. Were it not for the power of the Honored One’s Way, who could receive it?
The third prince said, "This is but a worldly treasure; it is not sufficient to be considered supreme. Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme."
This is the light of the world; it is not yet supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is the clarity of the world; it is not yet supreme. Among all clarities, the clarity of the mind is supreme. The radiance of this jewel cannot illuminate itself.
One must rely upon the light of wisdom; it is through this light that [the jewel] is discerned here. Once it has been discerned, one knows it is a jewel;

once it is known to be a jewel, its preciousness is clarified. Now, the preciousness of the jewel does not exist inherently within the jewel; likewise, if one discerns the jewel, the jewel does not exist inherently as a jewel.
A worldly jewel is not a jewel in itself; it must rely upon the jewel of wisdom to be distinguished as such. A treasure is not a treasure in itself;

it must rely upon the treasure of wisdom to illuminate the Dharma-treasure. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, that treasure immediately manifests; so too, when sentient beings possess the Way...
The Jewel of the Mind is likewise so. The Patriarch praised his eloquence and wisdom, and then asked again: "Among all things, what thing is without characteristics? He replied:
"Among all things, that which does not arise is without characteristics. He asked again: "Among all things, what thing is the highest?"
[The King] said, "Among all things, the human self is the highest. He was asked again, "Among all things, what is the greatest?

[The King] replied, "Among all things, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the greatest. The Patriarch, knowing he was his Dharma heir, remained silent and mingled with the crowd as the time had not yet arrived.
When King Xiang passed away, the multitude all wailed and fainted; only the third son, Bodhidhara, did not.
Luó entered meditative absorption before the coffin and emerged after seven days, whereupon he requested ordination. Once he had received full precepts, his master told him:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; in this manner it was passed down successively until it reached me."
"I now entrust this to you. Listen to my verse: 'The mind-ground gives rise to all seeds; from cause, phenomena arise again.
When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; when the flower blooms, the world emerges.

Having thus transmitted the Dharma, the Venerable One rose from his seat, extended his left and right hands, and emitted twenty-seven rays of light from each, brilliant with five colors. He then leaped into the void."
It was seven *tāla* trees in height. He transformed himself into fire and consumed his own body. Śarīra relics fell like rain from the sky; they were collected and used to build a stūpa.
This was in the Dingyou year, the first year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty.
One day, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, a holy sage manifested in the Western Heaven, commanded Sudhana to gather medicinal herbs, saying: "Bring back those herbs.
Sudhana surveyed the great earth and found that there was nothing that was not medicine. He returned and reported: "There is nothing that is not medicine. Mañjuśrī said:
"Bring this medicine. Sudhana then picked up a blade of grass from the ground and handed it to Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī received it and held it up, showing it to the assembly, saying: "This medicine can kill a person, and it can also bring a person to life."
Mañjuśrī asked the woman Aṅgulimālā, "What is the meaning of 'birth'? The woman replied, "The meaning of birth is that which is born through non-birth.
Mañjuśrī asked, "How is it that the meaning of birth is that which is born through non-birth?
The woman replied, "If one can clearly know that the four conditions—earth, water, fire, and wind—have never attained self-existence and yet are able to harmonize according to their circumstances..."
This is what is appropriate; this is the meaning of birth. Zhu asked, "What is the meaning of death?
The woman said, "Death takes the non-death of death as its meaning. Zhu asked, "How is it that death takes the non-death of death as its meaning?
The woman said, "If one can clearly know that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never been self-acquired and are subject to dispersal, yet one can follow them..."

This is what is appropriate; this is the meaning of death. The woman Antichā asked Mañjuśrī, "If you clearly understand that the principle of birth is non-birth, why is it that you are nevertheless still transmigrating through birth and death? Mañjuśrī replied, "Because my power is not yet sufficient."
When Bodhisattva Vasubandhu descended from Maitreya’s inner palace, Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked him:

"Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for those devas. During a single period, Maitreya brings five billion devaputras to accomplishment and enables them to realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
I wonder what dharma he preaches? Vasubandhu replied: "He preaches only this very dharma."
It was simply that his Brahma-voice was pure and elegant, causing those who heard it to rejoice.
At the assembly of Vimalakīrti, thirty-two bodhisattvas each expounded the gate of non-duality. Mañjuśrī said: "Regarding all dharmas, I have no speech and no discourse;
there is no demonstration and no cognition. It is free from all questioning and answering; this is the bodhisattva’s entry [into the gate of non-duality]."
Regarding the Gate of Non-dual Dharma: thereupon Mañjuśrī again asked Vimalakīrti, "Virtuous One, you should speak:

what is the bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of non-dual dharma? Vimalakīrti remained silent. Mañjuśrī praised him, saying, "The absence of even speech and written words—this is the bodhisattva’s true entry into the gate of non-dual dharma."
After Sudhana had visited fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), he finally arrived before the pavilion of Maitreya.
He saw that the door of the pavilion was closed; gazing up at it with reverence and offering praise, he beheld Maitreya approaching from another direction.
Sudhana prostrated himself and said, "I pray that the door of this pavilion may open, so that I may enter. Immediately, Maitreya came before Sudhana and snapped his fingers once. The pavilion—
The gate to the pavilion opened; once Sudhana had entered, the gate closed immediately.
He saw hundreds of thousands of millions of pavilions, and within each pavilion stood a Maitreya leading his retinue, with a Sudhana standing before him.
Because the Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked him, "I wish to see Mañjuśrī; which one of these is he? Sudhana replied:
"You give rise to a single thought of pure mind; that itself is it. Wuzhuo said, "I give rise to a single thought of pure mind;
why do I not see it? Cui said, "This is truly seeing Mañjuśrī."
The Venerable Subhūti was sitting in meditative seclusion within a mountain cave. The devas rained down flowers and offered praise. A person asked, "Who is it raining flowers from the sky to praise?
And for what reason do they praise him? The deva replied, "I am Brahmā. I respect the Venerable One’s excellent exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Venerable One said, "Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, I have never spoken even a single word. How can you say this?"
[Subhūti] praised him. The deva said: "In this way, Venerable One, there is no speaking, and thus I have no hearing.
That which is without speaking and without hearing is the true teaching of Prajñāpāramitā. One day, while the Venerable One was preaching the Dharma, Śakra rained down flowers.
Subhūti then asked: "From where did these flowers come? Did they come from heaven, from the earth, or from humans? Śakra replied: "No. Subhūti asked: "From where then?"
"Have you attained it? Śāriputra then raised his hand, and the girl said, "So it is, so it is.
As the Venerable Śāriputra was entering the city, he saw the girl Candrottarā coming out from the city.
Śāriputra thought to himself: "This sister has seen the Buddha; I do not know whether she has attained the stage of patience (kṣānti) or not. I shall ask her. Just as he drew near...
He then asked, "Sister, where are you going? The woman replied, "I go as Śāriputra goes.
Śāriputra said, "I have just entered the city, while you have just left it; how can you say you go as I do? The woman asked, "In what should the disciples of the Buddhas abide?
Śāriputra replied, "The disciples of the Buddhas abide in the Great Nirvāṇa. The woman said, "The [disciples of the] Buddhas..."
The Buddha’s disciples, having already taken their abode in the Mahāparinirvāṇa, I too am like Śāriputra in departing.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Is that which is spoken of as the six pāramitās within a dream the same as or different from [that spoken of] when awake?"
Śāriputra said, "This meaning is profound and far-reaching; I am unable to explain it. Within this assembly is the Great Being Maitreya; go to him and ask.
Śāriputra then questioned Maitreya, and Maitreya asked, "Who is named Maitreya? Who is Maitreya?
Śāriputra then asked the goddess, "Why do you not transform your female body? The goddess replied, "It has been twelve years since I began."
When seeking the characteristics of a woman, they are utterly unfindable; what, then, is there to transform?
At that moment, the goddess used her supernormal powers to transform Śāriputra so that he appeared exactly like herself, while she transformed her own body to appear like Śāriputra.
She then asked, "Why do you not transform this female body? Śāriputra, appearing in the form of the goddess, replied, "I do not know how."
How did he transform and become a female body?
Before the Venerable Aṅgulimāla had left the household life, he was a follower of the non-Buddhists named Kosiya, who desired to ascend the throne as king.
He used the thumbs of a thousand people to fashion a flower crown; he had already obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine, lacking only one.
He pointed [at his mother’s finger] and intended to kill his mother to take the finger. At that time, the Buddha was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;

observing this with his divine eye, he manifested as a śramaṇa before Aṅgulimāla. Aṅgulimāla then released his mother, intending to kill the Buddha. The Buddha walked slowly, while Aṅgulimāla ran after him in haste but could not catch up.
He then called out, “Gautama, stop! Stop! The Buddha said, “I have long since stopped; it is you who have not.”
He did not abide [in worldly things]. When Aṅgulimāla heard this, his mind was suddenly awakened; he then cast away his blade, took refuge with the Buddha, and left the household life.
Venerable Piṇḍola, while King Aśoka’s inner palace was providing a meal for thirty thousand great Arhats, personally went to offer incense and saw that there was no one in the first seat.
When the King asked the reason for this, the Venerable Sāgaramati replied, "This is Piṇḍola..."
Pindola was present. Seeing that the Buddha was approaching, the king asked, "Where is he now?
Pindola replied, "Wait but a moment. Having spoken, Pindola descended from the sky. The king invited him to take a seat and paid his respects, but Pindola did not look at him.
The king then asked, "I have heard that you, Venerable One, personally saw the Buddha come; is this true? Pindola raised his eyebrows with his hand and said, "Understood."
The Master said, "I do not understand. The other replied, "The Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta once invited the Buddha for a meal;
at that time, I was also included among those present."
The Mara Śambara, leading his retinue, followed the Bodhisattva Vajrasama for a thousand years, seeking the place of his arising without success.
Suddenly, one day, he beheld him and asked: "Upon what do you rely to dwell? For a thousand years I have sought the place of your arising without finding it.
Vajrasama replied: "I do not dwell relying on existence; I do not dwell relying on non-existence."
He dwelt thus. He dwelt in this manner.

Prince Naci divided his flesh and returned it to his mother; he divided his bones and returned them to his father. Thereafter, manifesting his true body and exercising great supernatural power, he preached the Dharma for his parents.
The butcher Wide-Forehead, at the assembly of the Great Parinirvāṇa, cast down his butcher’s blade and immediately became a Buddha.
He declared himself to be one among the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
The First Patriarch of the Eastern Land, the Great Master Bodhidharma, was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
His clan was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitāra. Later, he encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra.

Upon arriving in his own country, he received the offerings of the king. Recognizing that his teacher was Guhyapada, the king tested him by having him distinguish between the precious jewels bestowed upon his two elder brothers;
through this, the essential points of the mind were revealed. Thereupon, the Venerable One said, "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery.
Now, 'Dharma' carries the meaning of 'thorough penetration. You should be named Dharma. Consequently, he changed his name to Bodhidharma. This was the Patriarch.
He then addressed the Venerable One, saying, "Now that I have attained the Dharma, to which country should I go to perform the Buddha-work? I pray you grant me your instruction.
The Venerable One replied, "Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not travel far yet. Stay for now in the south.

Wait until sixty-seven years after my passing, then you shall go to China (Zhendan) and administer the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of superior faculties. Be careful not to act too hastily, lest you suffer decline."
Under the sun, the Patriarch asked again, "Is there a Great Being there who is capable of being a vessel for the Dharma? Will there be obstacles for a thousand years to come?
The other replied, "In the regions you shall convert, those who attain Bodhi will be beyond counting.
More than sixty years after my parinirvāṇa, that country will face a crisis; at that time, Wenbu will naturally subdue it from within the waters. When your time comes," he said.
"Do not dwell in the south. There, people care only for conditioned achievements and do not perceive the principle of the Buddha.
Even if you were to reach that place, you must not remain for long. Listen to my verse: 'On the road one meets one crossing water, then again one meeting a sheep;

All alone and weary, one crosses the river in the dark. At sunset, how pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses; Two young cassia trees have long flourished in prosperity. He asked again: 'This...'"
"What further events will there be after this? He replied: "From now until one hundred and fifty years hence, there will be minor difficulties.

Listen to my prophecy: 'Though auspicious within the heart, it is ominous on the outside; a house added beneath the stream bears an ill-fated name. Because of encountering a venomous dragon, a martial son is born;
suddenly meeting a small mouse, there will be endless stillness. He asked again: 'What will happen after this? He replied:"
Two hundred and twenty years hence, you shall see a man beneath the forest trees who will attain the fruit of the Way. Listen to my prophecy: "Though China is vast, there is no other path;
it must be traversed by the feet of one's own descendants. A golden rooster knows how to hold a single grain of millet in its beak to offer as sustenance to the Arhat monks of the ten directions.
He further recited various verses, all of which were prophecies concerning the rise and decline of the Buddha-dharma. (The details of these matters are contained in...)

In the *Baolin Zhuan* and the *Shengzhou Ji*, it is recorded that Master Zu Gong received the teachings and served at his [the Master’s] side with devotion for nearly forty years, never failing in his duties.
Upon the passing of the Venerable One, he proceeded to propagate the Dharma in his native country. At that time, there were two masters; one was named Buddhaguhya.
The second was named Buddhabhadra (Fo-da-sheng-duo). Originally, he studied the Hinayana meditative contemplations of Buddhabhadra alongside his master;
Buddhabhadra was senior to him. Having encountered the Venerable Prajñātāra, he abandoned the Hinayana for the Mahayana and engaged in propagation together with his master.
At that time, they were known as the "Two Gateways to Ambrosia. Buddhabhadra further divided his followers into six schools, the first of which was the Satkāya-vāda (First-Existence School).

The School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa), the second, the School of Signlessness (Nirābhāsa), the third, the School of Samādhi and Prajñā, the fourth, the School of Preceptual Practice (Śīla-caryā), the fifth, the School of Non-attainment (Anupalambha), and the sixth, the School of Quiescence (Upaśama)—each clung to its own understanding and separately expanded their sources of conversion.

Their monastic settlements were vast and imposing, and their followers were exceedingly numerous. The Patriarch sighed deeply and said: "If even one teacher among them has already fallen into the tracks of an ox, how much more so those who are fragmented and divided?"
It was flourishing and divided into six schools. [The Master] thought, "If I do not eliminate these, they will remain forever entangled in false views.

He manifested a subtle supernatural power and went to the place of the school that maintains characteristics (*lakṣaṇavāda*). He asked, "Regarding all dharmas, what is called 'true reality' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?

Among that assembly, there was a venerable elder named Sarvāla who replied, "Among all characteristics, that which does not interact with other characteristics is called true reality. The Patriarch said:
[The questioner asked: "If all characteristics do not interact with one another, and if they are called 'true characteristics' (dharmatā), how can they be fixed?
He replied: "Among all characteristics, there is truly no fixedness. If characteristics were fixed, how could they be called 'true'? The Patriarch said: "All characteristics are not fixed."
"This is precisely what is called the true mark (dharmatā). You are currently not fixed; how can you attain it?

He replied, "When I say 'not fixed,' I am not speaking of various marks; rather, I am speaking of the various marks. The meaning is the same. The Patriarch said, "Your statement that it is 'not fixed' shall itself be the true mark."
"Because it is not fixed, it is not the true mark (dharmatā). He replied, "If that which is fixed is not fixed, then it is not the true mark;

I know this because it is not so. [The Master said,] "It is neither fixed nor changing. The Patriarch said, "If you are now unchanging, how can you be called the true mark? That which has already changed and passed away—[is that the true mark?]"
The meaning is likewise so. He said: "If it were unchanging, it would have to exist; because it both exists and does not exist, the reality-mark (dharmatā) changes.

Thus, one establishes its meaning through this. The Patriarch said: "If the reality-mark is unchanging, then change is not the reality-mark. Within the realm of existence and non-existence, how can it be called the reality-mark?"

Śubhakarasiṃha knew in his heart that the Holy Master had attained profound liberation and reached the depths of understanding. He immediately pointed his finger at empty space and said, "This is a conditioned phenomenon of the world, yet it can also be made empty.
Can my body become like this? The Patriarch replied, "If you understand the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), you will see that there is no mark.
If you realize that there is no mark, then its form is likewise so. You must not lose yourself within form."
The substance of form does not obstruct existence within the signless; if one can understand it thus, this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

When that assembly heard this, their minds became clear and bright; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it with faith. They proceeded to the school of the Signless (*animitta-vāda*), where they asked:
"You speak of the signless; how should it be realized? Among them was one named Pratītya, who replied: "I clarify the signless through the mind."

"Do not grasp or reject. At the time of clarity, there is likewise no one who 'should.'* The Patriarch said: 'Regarding all existence and non-existence, the mind neither grasps nor rejects, and furthermore, there is no one who "should.

The other said: 'Even when entering the Buddha-samādhi, nothing is attained; how much more so for that which is formless—how could one wish to know it? The Patriarch said: 'Since form itself cannot be apprehended, who speaks of existence or non-existence? He went to the abode of Dinghui Zong and asked: "In your study of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), are they one or two?
Among the assembly was one named Póluántuò, who replied: "This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two. The Patriarch said: "Since they are neither one nor two, why..."

The Patriarch said: "When it is one, it is not one; when it is two, it is not two. Since it is neither concentration nor wisdom, by what means can concentration and wisdom be defined? He replied: "One is not one and two is not two;

"Because they are not fixed. But how is this known? They are neither one nor two; who is concentration and who is wisdom? When Pārāśarya heard this, his doubts were completely dispelled.
He went to the master of the school of precepts and conduct and asked: "What is called 'precept' (śīla), and what is called 'conduct' (caryā)?"
Regarding this practice of precepts, is it one or two? Among that assembly, there was a worthy man who replied: "One is two, and two are one; both are born from that.
To rely on the teaching without defilement—this is called the practice of precepts. The Patriarch said: "Your statement that 'one relies on the teaching' implies there is still defilement.
Since both 'one' and 'two' are shattered, how can you say one relies on the teaching? These two are contradictory and do not reach the true practice within."
