Among them was a venerable one who replied, "This mind is unmoving; this is called 'quiescence' (śamatha). To be unstained by phenomena is called 'tranquility' (praśrabdhi).

The Patriarch said, "If the fundamental mind were not itself quiescent, it would require the support of quiescence and tranquility. Since it is quiescent from the very beginning, what use is there for further quiescence and tranquility?"
The other said, "All dharmas are fundamentally empty; because they are empty through emptiness, they are called 'quiescence' within that emptiness of emptiness.
The Patriarch said, "Emptiness itself is already empty, and all dharmas are likewise so. Being quiescent and signless, what is there to be quiescent, and what is there to be still?

Upon hearing the Master’s instruction, the Venerable One attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Thereafter, the six groups of disciples all vowed to take refuge [in him], and from this, his transformation spread abroad.
In Southern India, his fame spread throughout the Five Indias. Over the course of sixty years, he delivered immeasurable multitudes.

Later, he encountered King Vikramāditya, who held heterodox views and disparaged the Triple Gem. The king would often say: "The ancestors of my lineage all believed in the Buddhist Way, yet they fell into false views;

consequently, their lifespans were not long and their reigns were brief. Furthermore, I myself am a Buddha—why should I seek anything further outside? As for the retribution of good and evil," [he continued].
Because those possessed of much learning had fabricated false doctrines, even the country’s elders who had been honored by former kings were all dismissed and deposed.
Knowing this, [the Patriarch] sighed, lamenting their meager virtue, and wondered how he might save them.

He then thought of two leaders within the School of Formlessness (*animitta-yāna*): one was Pārali, who shared a karmic affinity with the king and was on the verge of realizing the fruit of his practice. His...

The two masters were both eminent and possessed great erudition and eloquence; yet, they had no prior karmic connection [with the Emperor]. At that time, the disciples of the six schools each thought to themselves:
"The Buddha-Dharma is under threat; why does our Master remain so composed? The Patriarch perceived the thoughts of the assembly from afar and immediately snapped his fingers in response.
Hearing this, the six groups exclaimed, "This is the reverberation of the faith of our Master Bodhidharma! We should proceed with haste to fulfill his compassionate command."
He immediately went to the Patriarch’s location, prostrated himself, and inquired after his well-being. The Patriarch said, "A single leaf obscures the sky; who is able to trim and sweep it away?

Zongsheng replied, "Though I am shallow and insignificant, how could I dare shrink from this task? The Patriarch said, "Though you possess eloquence and wisdom, your power of the Way is not yet complete.
Zongsheng thought to himself, "My Master fears that I might see the King, perform great Buddhist services, and achieve such fame and renown that I would eclipse his own dignity."
"O King, even if you were to employ all your merit and wisdom as a sovereign, I am but a śramaṇa who has received the Buddha’s instructions; how could I be difficult to oppose?

Having spoken thus, he vanished and went to the king's location. There, he extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma, as well as matters concerning the suffering and happiness of the world, and the good and evil of humans and devas.
The king engaged him in a series of dialogues and interrogations, yet there was nothing that did not accord with principle. The king said, "The Dharma that you now understand—"
"Where does it reside? Zongsheng replied, "As for a king's governance and transformation of the people, it should accord with the Way. The King asked, "The Way you possess—where does that Way reside?
The King continued, "The Way I possess is intended to eliminate heterodox teachings; as for the Dharma you possess, whom do you intend to subdue?

The Patriarch did not rise from his seat, already intuitively knowing that Zongsheng’s argument had fallen into error. He immediately told Pratītyasamutpāda, "Zongsheng has failed to receive [the true transmission]."
"My teaching has been secretly transforming the King; in a mere moment, his arguments will be exhausted. You must save him quickly.

Pāṭaliputra respectfully received the Patriarch’s instructions and said, "I pray you grant me your supernatural power. Having spoken, clouds rose from beneath his feet, and he went before the Great King, standing there in silence.
At that time, while the King was in the midst of questioning Zhongsheng, he suddenly saw Pāṭali arriving by riding upon the clouds.
Startled, he forgot his question and looked toward Pāṭali, saying, "One who comes through the air—is this right or wrong? Pāṭali replied, "I am neither wrong nor right;
I come because of right and wrong. If your mind, O King, were right, I would have no wrongness or rightness. Although the King was struck with wonder, he remained arrogant.
As the debate was reaching its peak, the King immediately expelled Zongsheng. Pratibha said, "Since Your Majesty possesses the Way, why do you expel a śramaṇa?
Although I have no understanding, I pray that Your Majesty will put me a question. The King asked angrily, "What is the Buddha? Pratibha replied, "Seeing one's nature is the Buddha.
The King asked, "Does the Master see your own nature? Pratibha replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside?"
Yunju Daoci said, "The nature is present within activity. The King asked, "What is this activity? I do not see it now. Daoci said, "It is manifesting as activity right now;
it is simply that you yourself do not see it. The King asked, "Is it present within me? Daoci said, "If you were to engage in activity, there would be nothing that is not it.
If you do not engage in activity, its essence is difficult to perceive. The King asked, "When it is being used, from how many places does it emerge?"
Pāṭaliputra said, “When it manifests, there shall be eight manifestations. The King said, “Tell me of these eight manifestations.
Pāṭaliputra then spoke in verse: “In the womb, it is the body; In the world, it is the person; In the eye, it is called seeing.”
In the ears it is called hearing; in the nose, the discernment of fragrance; in the mouth, discourse; in the hands, grasping; in the feet, running.

It manifests everywhere, encompassing all within the sands of the universe, yet when withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute speck of dust. Those who recognize it know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*prāṇa*).
Upon hearing these verses, the King immediately attained awakening; he repented his former errors and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.

Morning and evening he forgot weariness, continuing until the ninety-day period had concluded. At that time, Zongsheng, having been expelled, withdrew to hide in the deep mountains. He thought to himself, "I am now a hundred years old;
for eighty years I committed wrongs, and only in the past twenty years have I returned to the Buddha-way.

Though my nature is dull and ignorant, my conduct has been free from blemish. Unable to withstand this calamity, what is life compared to death? Having finished speaking, he immediately threw himself off a cliff. Suddenly—
A divine being appeared, received [the body] in his hands, and placed it upon a rock; it remained there peacefully without damage.

Zongsheng said, "I am a śramaṇa by title and ought to be the master of the True Dharma. Yet I have been unable to suppress the king's transgressions; for this reason, I cast away my body to reproach myself."

"What deity has bestowed such divine protection? How could it have reached this point? I pray you grant me a word so that I may preserve my remaining years. Thereupon, the divine being spoke this verse:
"The Master’s lifespan shall be one hundred years. At eighty, he committed a transgression.

Because he drew near to the Most Honored One, he cultivated his practice and entered the Way. Although he possessed some wisdom, he harbored much attachment to self and others. Regarding the various worthies he encountered..."
He had long cherished rare reverence. Yet, despite twenty years of meritorious practice, his mind remained unpeaceful because of his cleverness and arrogance;
thus he reached this state. One who gains a king’s lack of respect shall experience such a karmic fruit.

From now on, I shall not be negligent; before long, I shall achieve wondrous wisdom. All the sages will keep me in their thoughts, and the Tathāgata likewise. Upon hearing these verses, Zongsheng was filled with joy.
He was then sitting in meditation amidst the cliffs. The King again asked Prajñātāra, "Virtuous one, you possess such wisdom and eloquence; whom do you take as your teacher?
Prajñātāra replied, "As for my teacher of the precepts, he is the Tripitaka Master Upasena of Śālā Monastery, from whom I received my training.
As for my teacher of the Way, he is the Great King’s uncle, Bodhidharma. When the King heard the Patriarch’s name, [he was deeply moved].

After being struck with awe for a long time, he said, "I, a person of humble and shallow merit, have the misfortune of succeeding to the royal throne, yet I inclined toward the heterodox and turned my back on the orthodox, forgetting my venerable uncle.
I hastily commanded my close attendants to specially invite you here. Zu then followed the messenger and arrived, performing repentance for the King’s past transgressions.
Upon hearing this counsel, the king wept and apologized to his grandfather. He then issued an edict for Zongsheng to return to the kingdom.
A high minister reported, "Zongsheng was exiled and cast down a cliff; he has now perished. The king said to his grandfather, "The death of Zongsheng is entirely my own doing."
"How may Great Compassion cause him to be spared from this transgression? The Patriarch replied, "Zongsheng is currently resting in seclusion within the crags.

Simply dispatch a messenger to summon him, and he shall arrive immediately. The King immediately sent a messenger into the mountains, who indeed found Zongsheng sitting upright in meditative stillness.
Upon receiving the summons, Zongsheng said: "I am deeply ashamed of Your Majesty's intention. This poor monk has vowed to dwell among the crags and springs.

Furthermore, in Your Majesty’s kingdom, virtuous men are as numerous as a forest. Bodhidharma is Your Majesty’s own uncle and the teacher of the Six Groups; he is a dragon-elephant within the *Prātimokṣa* Dharma."

"I pray that Your Majesty will revere and honor these two sages, thereby securing the foundation of the imperial throne. Before the messenger had returned with his report, Nanyue Zuzhao said to the King, "Do you know whether you have obtained the victory?
The King replied, "I do not yet know. Zuzhao said, "One invitation has not yet arrived; upon the second summons, they will surely come."
After a long while, the messenger returned. Indeed, it was just as the Patriarch had said. The Patriarch then took his leave of the King, saying, "You should cultivate virtue well;
before long, illness will arise. I shall now depart. Seven days later, the King fell ill. The court physicians examined and treated him, yet his condition only worsened and did not improve.

The high-ranking relatives and close attendants recalled the Master’s previous prediction and urgently dispatched a messenger to inform the Patriarch, saying: "The King’s illness has reached a critical stage;

we pray that you, Uncle, will show compassion and come from afar to examine and save him. The Patriarch immediately arrived to offer his condolences. At that time, Zongsheng was summoned once again by the King.
He then withdrew to a separate cave. Bodhidharma also came to inquire after his illness and asked the Patriarch, "What should be done to enable the King to escape his suffering?

The Patriarch immediately instructed the Crown Prince to grant clemency to the King and bestow favor upon him, to venerate the Triple Gem, and further to perform repentance on his behalf, praying that his transgressions might be extinguished.
This was repeated three times, and the King’s illness subsequently abated. The Master then reflected that the conditions for China were ripe, and he set out.
When the time for his departure arrived, he first took leave of the ancestral stūpa, next bid farewell to his fellow students, and finally went to the king’s presence.
He comforted and exhorted him, saying: "You should diligently cultivate pure deeds and protect and uphold the Triple Gem. My departure is not late; I shall return after one year.

Upon hearing the Master’s words, the king’s tears flowed profusely, and he said: "What sin has this country committed? What auspiciousness does that land possess? Since you, my elder brother, have such a karmic connection there, it cannot be otherwise."
"I shall remain here; I only pray that you do not forget your native land and will return early once your mission is complete.
The King immediately prepared a great ship, filled it with various treasures, and personally led his ministers and officials to escort him to the seashore.

Setting out upon the vast ocean, he traveled for three full cycles of winter and summer before arriving at Nanhai County of Guangzhou Prefecture in the ninth month of the first year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the year of Gengzi.
On the twenty-first day, Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, prepared a full reception with the honors due to a host and sent a memorial to Emperor Wu.

Upon reading the petition, the Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree to invite him. (The dates in the old edition were erroneous; here they are corrected according to Liang Sengbaochang’s *Xu faji* and Song Shaogong’s *Zhengzong ji*.)
He still felt some doubt. (There is another account regarding this later. In the eleventh month, he arrived in Jinling.

The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built temples, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting. What merit do these deeds possess? The Master replied, "They possess no merit whatsoever. The Emperor said:
"Why does it lack merit? The Patriarch replied, "This is merely a minor fruit of humans and devas, a cause of outflows (*āsrava*).
It follows the body like a shadow; though it exists, it is not real. The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect;
its essence is inherently empty and tranquil. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked again, "What is the First Noble Truth?"
The Emperor asked, "What is the One Meaning? The Patriarch replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me?

The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain realization. Knowing that his timing was not in accord, on the nineteenth day of that month, he secretly returned north of the Yangtze River.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived at Luoyang, which was the first year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty. He took up residence there.
At Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, he sat facing a wall, remaining silent all day long; no one could fathom him, and thus he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin.
At that time, there was a monk named Shen Guang, a man of vast and open spirit who had long resided in the region of Yi and Luo.

He had read extensively across many books and was skilled at discussing the profound principles of the Ultimate. He often sighed, "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi, as well as their rites, arts, and moral precepts, and the writings of Mengzi, Zhuangzi, and others, do not exhaust the subtle truths.
Recently, he heard that the Great Being Bodhidharma was residing at Shaolin; thus, the Sage was no longer far away.

When Daoxuan first arrived at the Yuanjing Monastery, he went there every morning and evening to attend upon the Patriarch. However, the Patriarch would always sit facing a wall and no instructions were heard.

Daoxuan thought to himself: "In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow, pierce their flesh to provide nourishment for the hungry, spread their hair to cover the mud, and throw themselves off cliffs to feed tigers.
If the ancients were already like this, what kind of person am I? On the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year..."
At night, it rained and snowed heavily. Guo Guang stood firm and motionless. By dawn, the accumulated snow had risen above his knees.
The Master, moved by pity, asked him, "You have stood long in the midst of this snow; what do you seek? Guang wept with sorrow and said, "I only pray that the Master will show me compassion."

He opened the gate of the nectar of immortality to extensively deliver all classes of beings. The Patriarch said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort through vast eons;

one must perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is difficult to endure. How can you hope for the True Vehicle with meager virtue and meager wisdom, or with a frivolous and arrogant mind?
Your toil and hardship will be in vain. Upon hearing the Patriarch’s admonition, Huiguang secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it—
Before the Patriarch, the Patriarch, knowing that he was a vessel for the Dharma, said: "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma.
Now that you have severed your arm before me, your seeking is likewise acceptable. The Patriarch then changed his name to Huìkě.
Huìkě asked: "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? The Patriarch replied: "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another person. Huìkě...
[The monk] said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall grant you peace.
After [the monk] had searched for a long while, he said, "I have sought my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. The Patriarch said, "I have finished granting you peace.
Nine years later, wishing to return to India, he addressed his disciples, saying, "The time has come. You should each speak of what you have attained. At that time—
Daowu replied, "As I see it, the Way is not grasped through words and letters, yet it is not separate from words and letters;
this is its application. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my skin. Nizi Tongzhi said, "My current understanding is like that of Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha:
having seen it once, one does not need to see it again. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu said, "The four great elements..."
"Empty! The five aggregates do not exist, yet in my field of vision, not a single dharma can be apprehended. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my bones.
Finally, Huik’e prostrated himself and stood in his place. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my marrow. He then turned to Huik’e and told him:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to the Great Being Kāśyapa, and it was passed down through successive entrustments."
And so you have come to me. I now entrust this to you; you must protect and uphold it. Furthermore, I bestow upon you this *kāṣāya* robe as a token of the Dharma.

Each of these has its own symbolic significance, which you should understand. [The disciple] said, "I pray that the Master will explain them. The Patriarch said, "Internally, the Dharma-seal is transmitted to accord with and realize the mind;
externally, the *kāṣāya* robe is bestowed to establish the fundamental tenet. In future generations, people will become degenerate and frivolous, and doubts will compete for precedence."
Śāṇavāsa said, "I am a man from the Western Heaven; you are a native of this land. By what means did you obtain the Dharma, and by what do you realize it?
Now that you have received this robe and the Dharma, it will be difficult for you to survive in the future. Simply produce this robe along with my Dharma-verses to manifest your realization;
then your transformation will be unimpeded. Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the robe shall cease and no longer be transmitted, while the Dharma will circulate throughout the world."
Throughout the sands of worlds, those who understand the Way are many, but those who practice the Way are few; those who discourse on principle are many, but those who penetrate principle are few.

There are more than ten million who secretly accord with it and silently realize it; you should propagate this teaching and never underestimate those who have not yet awakened. A single thought that turns the faculty of mind is identical to original attainment.
Listen to my verse: I originally came to this land To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower opens into five petals...

Leaves. The fruit ripens spontaneously. (The old record states: The Patriarch said, "I have four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*; I also entrust them to you. This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter it.

According to the *Rendiyantumu*, Daguan Ying repeatedly debated this to correct its errors, making it most explicit. I now follow this teaching and delete the following: "Since I arrived here, I have been poisoned five times.
I once went out myself to test [the poison] by placing it on a stone; the stone split. This was because I had originally departed from the South..."

Master Yin: "I came to this Eastern Land and saw that the Great State of China possessed the atmosphere of the Mahāyāna. Consequently, I crossed the seas and traversed the deserts to seek the Dharma and its seekers.
As our fates had not yet converged, I remained as if dull-witted and reticent. Now that I have received your transmission, my purpose is fulfilled. (Separate Record:

When the Master first resided at Shaolin Temple for nine years, he preached the Dharma for the Second Patriarch, teaching only: "Cease all external conditions; let the internal mind be free from agitation. Let the mind be like a wall; then one may enter the Way. Yet Huike spoke variously about the nature of the mind.)

Hitherto, he had not yet realized the principle. National Teacher Zhi forbade his error and did not explain the essence of the mind of non-thought to him. One day, Ke said, "I have already stilled all conditions. The National Teacher asked, "Do you not fall into annihilationism? Ke replied, "I do not fall into annihilationism.

The National Teacher said, "This is the essence of the mind transmitted by all Buddhas; do not doubt it further. Thereupon, he went with his disciples to Qiansheng Temple at Yumen, where they stayed for three days.

There was Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Qicheng, who had long admired the Buddha-vehicle. He asked the Patriarch, "In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, the lineage of teachers is considered the Patriarchs;
what is their Way like? The Patriarch replied, "One who clarifies the essence of the Buddha-mind and whose practice accords with understanding is called a Patriarch.
He asked again, "What about beyond this? The Patriarch said, "One must clarify the minds of others, know the present and the past, and never weary of existence."
There is nothing. Regarding all phenomena, there is no grasping; one is neither virtuous nor foolish, neither deluded nor awakened. If one can understand it thus, one is called an Ancestor.
Yang said, "I have turned my heart toward the Triple Gem for many years, yet my wisdom has been clouded and dull, and I remain confused regarding the True Principle.
Having just heard the Master’s words, I do not know how to proceed. I pray that the Master will, out of compassion, reveal the essential teaching. The Ancestor knew [his intent].
He spoke earnestly, immediately reciting a verse: "One does not harbor aversion upon seeing evil, nor does one strive to practice virtue merely because it is seen as good.
One does not abandon wisdom to draw near to folly, nor does one cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment. To realize the Great Way is to transcend all measure."
Penetrating the Buddha-mind, he emerged to deliver beings; not sharing the same orbit as ordinary people or sages, he was transcendentally named a Patriarch.

Upon hearing the verse, Yang was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy, saying, "I pray that you, Master, will remain long in this world to transform and guide all sentient beings. The Patriarch said, "I shall depart immediately; I cannot stay long.
The capacities of beings differ by ten thousand degrees, and many encounter the difficulties of ignorance. Yang asked, "May I inquire who these people are?"
The disciple asked, "May I remove [the obstacles] for my master? The Patriarch said, "I have transmitted the Buddha’s secret mysteries to benefit those lost on the path.
To harm others for one's own peace is certainly not possible. Yang said, "If you, Master, refuse to speak, how can you manifest the power of your penetrating transformation and contemplative insight?
The Patriarch, having no other choice, then uttered a prophecy: "The raft upon the river divides the jade waves; the torches open the golden locks. Five..."
They conversed together; for ninety days there was no sense of "self" or "other. Yang heard these words but did not investigate their source;
he silently took them to heart, paid his respects, and departed. Although the Master’s prophecies could not be fathomed at the time, they were all later proven true.

At that time, the Wei dynasty honored the teachings of Śākyamuni, and eminent Chan masters were as numerous as a forest. When the Vinaya Master Daoguang and the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha witnessed the Master expounding the Way, they [were deeply impressed].
He rejected external forms and pointed directly to the mind. Whenever he debated doctrine with his teacher, points of contention arose like swarms of bees.

The Patriarch [Huike] loftily sustained the primordial wind and universally bestowed the rain of Dharma, yet the narrow-mindedness of [Sengcan] could not bear this; he gave rise to malice and repeatedly administered poison.
By the sixth time, as his mission for conversion was complete and he had found one to whom the Dharma could be transmitted, he finally ceased to save him. He sat upright and passed away.
This was the fifth day of the tenth month in the first year of the Yong’an era of Emperor Zhuang of the Wei dynasty, the year Wushen (498 CE).
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of that same year, he was buried at Xiong’er Mountain, and a stupa was erected at Dinglin Monastery. Three years later, Song Yun of the Wei dynasty...

He saw the Patriarch carrying a single sandal, walking gracefully and alone toward the west. Huìyún asked, "Where are you going, Master? The Patriarch replied, "I am going to the West. Upon his return, Huìyún related these events in detail. Later, when the disciples opened the tomb, they found it empty. Only the single sandal remained. When they tried to lift it, it was as heavy as a mountain; when they let go, it vanished like a feather. They then understood that the Patriarch had indeed departed for the West. Subsequently, the Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the title "National Teacher of the Great Tang" (Dàtáng Guóshī). His remains were enshrined in a stupa at the Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. Failing to recognize the original source, one’s efforts to contemplate stillness are in vain. Perfectly identical to the great void, it lacks nothing and has no excess. It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting that one does not [attain it].

Cease movement by returning to stillness, yet stillness itself further intensifies movement. To linger only in these two extremes, how could one know the "one kind"? If this one kind is not penetrated, both sides fail in their efficacy.
To dispel existence and non-existence is to turn one's back on emptiness from within emptiness. Much talk and much deliberation only lead further away from correspondence. Cut off words; cut off...

Contemplation has no place where it does not penetrate. To return to the root is to attain the essential meaning; to follow after illumination is to lose the source. A moment of returning-illumination surpasses the previous emptiness.

That the previous emptiness underwent transformation was entirely due to deluded vision. Do not seek the Truth; you need only cease your views. When these two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them.
As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes distracted and loses the mind. The two arise because of the one; yet even the one must not be grasped.
Maintain this: when the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. When there is no fault, there are no dharmas; when there is no arising, there is no mind.
The capacity [of the mind] is extinguished by objects, and objects sink as they pursue the capacity. Objects exist because of the capacity, and the capacity exists because of objects.

If you wish to know these two segments, they are originally one emptiness. One emptiness is identical to the two, equally encompassing the myriad phenomena. Seeing neither the refined nor the coarse, how could there be partiality? This is the essence of the Great Way.

Be expansive. There is neither ease nor difficulty. With narrow views, one harbors doubt; as one becomes more anxious, one becomes more sluggish. To cling to it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path.

To let it be natural, the essence has no coming or staying. To follow one's nature is to accord with the Way; to roam at ease is to be free from affliction. To bind one’s thoughts is to deviate from the truth;
to be muddled and heavy is not good. Do not labor your spirit; what use is there for intimacy or estrangement? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six [senses].
Dust. The six dusts are not evil; they are identical to perfect enlightenment. The wise act without effort; the ignorant bind themselves.

There is no dharma apart from the Dharma, yet they delusively cling to it with their own affection. To employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error? Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation; awakening is free from likes and dislikes.
All dualistic extremes arise from one's own deliberations. They are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky—why labor to grasp them? Gain and loss are...
No. Let them all be cast off at once. If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of themselves. If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are as one.
In the fundamental essence of this oneness, one is suddenly oblivious to conditions. When the myriad dharmas are viewed as equal, one returns to spontaneity.

When that which constitutes [this state] is extinguished, it cannot be compared to anything. Where movement ceases, there is no movement; where movement ceases, there is no cessation. Since both are unestablished, how can there be one?
Thus, reaching the ultimate limit, no rules or regulations remain. The mind accords with equality; all that is done ceases. Doubts are completely purified; right faith is harmonized and balanced.
Nothing remains to be retained; there is nothing to be remembered. Empty clarity illuminates itself spontaneously, without taxing the power of the mind.

This is not a place for discursive thought, difficult for the consciousness and emotions to fathom. Within the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self. One must urgently [realize] this mutual...
It should be understood that it is simply called "non-duality. Where there is non-duality, all things are identical; there is nothing that is not encompassed within it.

All wise ones of the ten directions enter this school. This school is neither constricted nor expansive: in a single thought-moment there are ten thousand years; it is neither here nor not here, yet it is before the eyes of all throughout the ten directions.

The extremely small is identical to the great, as all boundaries and limits are forgotten and severed. The extremely great is identical to the small, as no outer periphery is seen. Existence is itself non-existence; non-existence is itself existence.
There is. If it were not thus, there would be no need to maintain it at all. One is all; all is one. If you can simply be like this, why worry about not reaching completion?
Faith is non-dual; non-duality is faith. The path of words is cut off; it is neither past, future, nor present.
The Great Master Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of Huangmei in Huangzhou, was surnamed Sima. His family had resided for generations in Henei, later migrating to Guangji County in Qizhou.

From birth he was exceptionally gifted; from childhood he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and his mastery of the various gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) seemed as if it were the result of past habituation.
Having succeeded to the patriarchal tradition, he concentrated his mind without sleep; for sixty years, his side did not touch his mat. During the Sui dynasty...
In the Dingshou year of the Daye era, he led his disciples to Jizhou. There they encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city, which remained besieged for seventy days without resolution.
The multitude was filled with terror, and the Master took pity on them; he instructed them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, the rebel forces, looking toward the battlements...
There was a divine army that addressed one another, saying, "There must be an extraordinary person within this city; it is not possible to attack it.
They gradually withdrew. In the Jia-shen year of the Tang dynasty’s Wu-de era, the Master returned to Qichun and resided at Mount Poutou, where disciples gathered like clouds.
One day, while traveling to Huangmei County, he encountered a young boy on the road whose physical features were remarkably refined and extraordinary, unlike those of ordinary children.
The Patriarch asked the boy, "What is your surname? He replied, "I have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one.
The Patriarch asked, "What is it? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Patriarch asked, "Then you have no surname? He replied, "Because nature is empty, there is none.

The Patriarch silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and immediately dispatched an attendant to the boy's mother to request that she allow him to leave the household life. His mother, due to past karmic conditions...
Therefore, he showed no sign of reluctance and accepted him as a disciple. This continued until the transmission of the Dharma and the handing over of the robe.
He spoke in verse: "The nature of the seed of a flower exists; Depending on the ground, the flower grows. When the great conditions unite with this nature, That which is born is, in truth, unborn.
He then entrusted his students to him. One day he told the assembly: "During the Wude era, I traveled to Mount Lu and ascended its summit."
Looking toward Mount Pòtóu, he saw purple clouds like a canopy, beneath which white vapors divided into six horizontal paths. "Do you all understand? he asked.
The assembly remained silent. Huìrěn said, "Could this not be the Dharma-branch that will emerge crosswise after the Master's passing?

The Patriarch replied, "It is well. In the year Guǐmǎo of the Zhèngguān era, Emperor Tàizōng, drawn by the flavor of the Master’s Way and desiring to behold his dignified bearing, issued an imperial decree.
He proceeded to the capital. His master, the Patriarch, submitted a memorial declining the honor. After three successive refusals, he finally declined on the grounds of illness.

On his fourth visit, the Emperor commanded the envoy, saying, "If he truly does not rise, then bring his head here. When the envoy arrived at the mountain and delivered the imperial decree, the Patriarch extended his neck toward the blade.
His countenance was solemn and dignified, which caused others to marvel at him. Dao-hui reported these circumstances to the Emperor, who thereafter held him in even greater esteem and admiration.

He bestowed upon him precious silks so that he might fulfill his aspirations. On the fourth day of the intercalary ninth month in the *xinhai* year of the Yonghui era of Gaozong, he suddenly issued an admonition to his disciples, saying:
"All dharmas are entirely liberation. You each must protect and mind yourselves, and spread this transformation among those who have not yet heard it."
"Come," he said, and having finished speaking, he sat peacefully and passed away at the age of seventy-two. His stūpa was erected at his home mountain.

On the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, the door of the stūpa opened spontaneously for no apparent reason; his countenance remained as if alive. Thereafter, his disciples did not dare to close it again.
Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dayi.
This is the pagoda of Ciyun. The Great Master Wuzu Hongren of Huangmei in Huangzhou was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou.
Previously, while serving as a "pine-planting practitioner" at Mount Poutou, he once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "You..."

The woman said, "I have parents and brothers; you may go ask them. He replied, "Very well, I shall do so immediately. The woman nodded her head in agreement, and he turned his steps back.
There was a woman named Zhou, the daughter of Li. As soon as she married, she became pregnant; her parents detested her greatly and cast her out.

Having nowhere else to go, she spent her days spinning for hire in the village and stayed at night beneath a public inn. Afterward, she gave birth to a son. Thinking him an ill omen, she threw him into a muddy stream.
The next day, she saw him swimming upstream against the current, his physical form radiant and clear. She was greatly astonished.
He was subsequently taken in. When he reached the age of a young boy, he followed his mother to beg for food; the villagers called him "The Child Without a Surname.
He encountered a man of wisdom who sighed and said, "This child lacks seven marks of excellence and thus falls short of the Tathāgata.

Later, he met the Great Master Xinxing and attained the Dharma, succeeding him in spreading the teachings on Mount Pòtóu. During the Xiánhēng era of the Tang Emperor Gāozōng, there was a lay practitioner (jūshì) surnamed Lú, named Huì.

Lu said, "I only seek to become a Buddha. The Patriarch said, "The people of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can they become Buddhas?
Lu said, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could that be the case for Buddha-nature? The Patriarch knew he was an extraordinary man and rebuked him.

He said, "Go and work in the fodder shed. Lu prostrated at his feet and withdrew, then entered the rice-husking room. There he applied himself to labor at the pestle and mortar, working day and night without rest for eight months.
The Patriarch, knowing that the time had come to transmit the Dharma, addressed the assembly, saying:

Among them was the Elder Shenxiu, whose learning permeated both Buddhist and secular classics, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to.

They all recommended him, saying, "Were it not for the Venerable Shenxiu, who else would dare to receive this? Hearing these public praises, Shenxiu did not reflect further; he then inscribed a verse upon a wall in the corridor.

When Huineng saw the sketches and the inscribed verse on the wall, he stopped painting and instead had everyone recite it.
While Lu was at the mill, he suddenly heard the verse being recited and asked his fellow students, "What are these lines? His companions replied, "You do not know.
The Master is seeking a Dharma heir and has ordered each of us to compose a verse expressing our realization. This is the one composed by the Venerable Xiu, and the Master holds it in high regard."
[The Master] praised him, saying, "He will surely be entrusted with the Dharma and the robe. Lu asked, "What was the verse? His fellow student recited it for him.
After a long while, Lu said, "It is beautiful, yet it is not fully realized. The fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How can a common person like you know this?
Do not utter such mad words. Lu replied, "Do you not believe me? I wish to respond with a verse of my own. The fellow student did not answer, but merely looked at him.
He looked at him and smiled. That night, Lu secretly told a young boy to lead him to the corridor.
Lu himself held a candle and invited Zhang Riyong, the Regional Inspector, to write a verse beside Xiu’s verse, saying: "Bodhi originally has no tree; / A bright mirror is likewise not a stand.
/ From the beginning, there is not a single thing; / Where could dust and grime gather? Later, when the Patriarch saw this verse, he said:
"Who made this? You have not yet seen its nature. When the assembly heard the Master’s words, they paid them no further heed.

That night, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-hulling shed and asked, "Is the rice white yet? Lu said, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted. The Patriarch struck the pestle three times with his staff;
Lu immediately beat the drum three times and entered the room. The Patriarch told him, "The Buddhas appear in the world for one purpose..."

This is a matter of great importance. According to the capacity of beings—whether large or small—they were guided accordingly, resulting in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the doctrines of sudden and gradual enlightenment as pedagogical gateways.

Nevertheless, the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *Dharmaparyāya*—the Treasury of the True Eye of the Dharma (*dharmadharmacakṣuskośa*)—was entrusted to the foremost Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
It was transmitted in succession through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma.
It was transmitted through Mo, reaching this land where it was received by the Great Master Ke (Huineng) and passed down to the present day.
I now entrust to you these Dharma treasures and the robe he transmitted; protect them well so that they shall not be severed. Listen to my verse:
"When sentient beings come to plant seeds, the fruit arises from the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, they lack nature and thus do not arise.
The Practitioner Lu knelt to receive the dharma of the robe and asked, "Now that the dharma has been received, to whom shall the robe be entrusted?
The Patriarch said, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him; therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest his attainment of the Dharma. Now, faith has matured."
"The robe is a source of contention; let it remain with you and no longer be passed on. For now, you should go into seclusion in a remote place and wait for the time to manifest your transformation.
As it is said, the life of one who receives this robe is like a thread suspended from a string. Lu asked, "Where should I go into seclusion?
The Master said, "When you encounter Huai, stop there; when you meet Hui, hide away. After Lu had prostrated at his feet, he took the robe and departed. That night, he traveled southward. Great.
The assembly did not know [the reason]. From that time on, the Fifth Patriarch no longer ascended the hall. The great assembly, filled with suspicion and wonder, questioned him.
The Patriarch said, "My Way shall now proceed; why inquire further? They asked again, "Who has obtained the robe and the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "He who is capable has obtained it.

Thereupon, the assembly deliberated: the name of Layman Lu was Huineng. Since he had been lost during their search, they secretly knew that he must have obtained it, and so they all set out to pursue him together.

After the Fifth Patriarch had transmitted the robe and the Dharma, another four years passed until the year of Yihai in the Shangyuan era. He suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "My work is now complete;
it is time for me to depart. He then entered his room, sat upright, and passed away at the age of seventy-four.
A stupa was erected on the Eastern Mountain of Huangmei. Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Daman, and the stupa was named Fayu (Dharma Rain).
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was surnamed Lu. His ancestors were from Fanyang;

his father, Lu Xingtáo, was transferred as an official to Xinzhou in Nanhai during the Wude era and subsequently registered his residence there. He lost his father at the age of three, and his mother remained steadfast in her resolve to raise him.
When he grew up, the family was particularly impoverished, and the Master provided for them by gathering firewood. One day, while carrying a load of wood through the marketplace, he encountered...
Hearing a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he reached the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere," and was moved by a profound realization.
He asked the guest, "What teaching is this? From whom did you receive it? The guest replied, "This is called the *Diamond Sutra*.
It was received from the Great Master Ren at Huangmei. The Patriarch immediately informed his mother of his intention to seek a teacher for the sake of the Dharma, and set out directly for Shaozhou.
In the province, he met the man of lofty conduct Liu Zhilüe and formed a friendship with him.
There was a nun named Wujinzang, who was Zhilüe’s paternal aunt; she regularly recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. When the Master briefly listened to her, he immediately explained its meaning for her.

The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters. The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize the characters, but as for the meaning, please ask me. The nun said, "If you do not even recognize the characters..."
"How can one possibly comprehend the ultimate meaning? The Patriarch replied, "The wondrous principle of all Buddhas has no connection with written words.

The nun was struck with wonder and amazement, and she told the elders of her village, "Neng is a man of the Way; you should invite him to receive our offerings. Thereupon, the local inhabitants vied with one another to come and pay their respects.
Nearby was the site of an old temple formerly known as Baolin; the community deliberated and decided to restore it so that the Patriarch might dwell there. Thus did the fourfold assembly [gather].
Mist gathered, and in an instant it formed a jeweled monastery. One day, the Patriarch suddenly thought to himself, "I have sought the Great Dharma; how could I stop midway?
The next day he set out and reached a stone grotto in the Western Mountains of Changle County, where he met Zhiyuan. The Patriarch then requested instruction from him.
Zhiyuan said, "Observing your spiritual bearing, you are exceptionally outstanding; you are surely no ordinary man. I have heard that in the Western Regions there is a Bodhi..."
Dharmatrāta transmitted the mind-seal at Huangmei. "You should go there to seek resolution," the Patriarch said as he departed.
He proceeded directly to Mount Dongshan in Huangmei; this was the second year of the Xianheng era of the Tang dynasty. Upon seeing him, Master Ren recognized him silently.
Later, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma, instructing him to remain hidden between Huaiji and Sihuai. This was the Bingzi year of the Yifeng era.
On the eighth day of the month, he arrived at Nanhai. There he met the Dharma Master Yinzong, who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Fǎxìng Monastery.
The Patriarch took up residence in the corridors. One evening, as the wind blew the banner atop the stupa, he heard two monks debating one another; one said, "The banner moves."

The first [theory] was that it was the wind moving. They exchanged words back and forth, yet none had ever grasped the principle. The Patriarch said, "Can one allow worldly people to rashly participate in such lofty discourse?
It is simply that the wind and the banner do not move; movement arises from the mind itself. When Yinzong overheard these words in secret, he was struck with awe and marveled at them.
The next day, he invited the Patriarch into his chamber and inquired about the meaning of the wind and the banner. The Patriarch explained it to him in full according to the principle. Yinzong—
Master Zong, unaware [of his identity], rose and said, "This practitioner is certainly no ordinary person. Who is your teacher? The Patriarch had nothing further to conceal;
he directly recounted the circumstances of how he had attained the Dharma. Thereupon, Master Zong assumed the etiquette of a disciple and requested the transmission of the essentials of Chan.
He then addressed the fourfold assembly, saying, "I, Yinzong, am a complete ordinary man, yet now I have encountered an incarnate Bodhisattva," and he pointed [to the Patriarch].
The layman Lu, seated below, said, "This is it indeed. He then requested that the robe of transmission be brought forth so that everyone might gaze upon and pay homage to it.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, he assembled various eminent and virtuous monks to shave his head.

On the eighth day of the second month, he received the full ordination from Vinaya Master Zhiguang at Faxing Monastery. That ordination platform was the very one established during the Liu Song dynasty by Guṇavarman.

This was established by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra. The *Record of the Tripiṭaka* states: "In the future, there shall be an incarnation Bodhisattva who will receive the precepts upon this altar.
Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha personally planted two Bodhi trees beside the altar and said to the assembly:
"One hundred and twenty years hence, there will be a Great Mahāsattva who shall expound [the Dharma] beneath these trees."

The Unsurpassed Vehicle. Having delivered immeasurable multitudes and completed his observance of the precepts, the Patriarch, beneath this tree, opened the Dharma-gate of Dongshan as if in accordance with a prior covenant.
On the eighth day of the second month of the following year, he suddenly said to the assembly: "I do not wish to dwell here;
I desire to return to my former retreat. Thereupon, Yinzong and over a thousand monastics and laypeople escorted the Patriarch back to Baolin Temple in Shaoyou Prefecture.
The Provincial Governor Wei Ju invited him to the Dafan Temple to turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma and receive the precepts of the Non-characteristic Mind-Ground.

His disciples recorded these teachings, titling them the *Platform Sutra*, which became widely circulated throughout the world. Later, he returned to Caoqi and rained down the great rain of the Dharma.
The number of scholars did not fall short of a thousand. In the year of Yisi (705) during the Shenlong era of Emperor Zhongzong, an imperial edict was issued stating:

"I have invited the two masters An and Xiu to provide offerings within the palace. In my leisure from the myriad affairs of state, I have frequently investigated the One Vehicle. Both masters, however, declined, saying:"
In the south there is Master Neng, who received the robe and dharma of Great Master Ren in secret; you may consult him on this matter.

I have now dispatched the Inner Attendant Xue Jian to ride with an imperial edict to invite you. I hope that the Master will look upon me with compassion and proceed quickly to the capital. The Patriarch submitted a memorial declining the invitation on the grounds of illness.

Huineng wished to remain at the foot of the mountain forests. Jian said, "The virtuous monks of the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It has never happened that anyone attained liberation without relying on meditation and concentration. I do not know how the Dharma you teach differs from this.
The Patriarch replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; why should it depend on sitting? As the Sūtra says: 'If one sees the Tathāgata...'"
Whether sitting or reclining, these are the practices of a deviant path. Why? Because there is nowhere from which one comes, nor anywhere to which one goes.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna. All dharmas are empty and quiescent; this is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting.

Since ultimately there is nothing to be realized, how much less can there be "sitting"? Jian said: "When your disciple returns, the Sovereign will surely question me. I pray that the Venerable Master will show compassion."
The Master pointed to his mind-essence and said: "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of alternation.

Since light and darkness are inexhaustible, they are names established through mutual dependence and finitude. Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'Dharmas have no peer, for they do not depend on one another.'"

Jian said: "Clarity is a metaphor for wisdom; darkness is an analogy for afflictions (*kleśa*). For one who cultivates the Way, if they do not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, by what means could they escape from beginningless birth and death?
The Patriarch said: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi; they are non-dual and without distinction.
If one uses wisdom to illuminate afflictions, this is the limited view of the Two Vehicles—the level of the sheep, the deer, and so forth."
Ji was of great wisdom and superior capacity, yet none were like him. Jian asked, "What is the insight of the Mahāyāna?
The Patriarch said, "Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual in their nature. This non-dual nature is the true nature. As for the true nature:
it is not extinguished among the foolish and ordinary; it does not increase among the sages and saints; it remains undisturbed amidst afflictions; and it dwells in meditative concentration."
It is not quiescent; it is neither interrupted nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes; it does not abide in the middle, nor in the interior or exterior;
it is neither born nor extinguished. Its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*); it is eternally abiding and never shifting—this is called the Way.

Jian asked: "The Master speaks of 'neither born nor extinguished. How does this differ from the non-Buddhists? The Patriarch said: "What the non-Buddhists call 'neither born nor extinguished' is [a state] that will eventually be extinguished."
Cessation arises; by means of arising, cessation is revealed. Yet cessation is not yet ceased, and arising is said to be non-arising.

When I speak of that which is neither born nor extinguished, it is because it was originally unborn and is now likewise unextinguished. This is why it differs from the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever. You will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and serene.
"Constantly quiescent, yet its wondrous function is as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Having been briefly instructed by the Master, Jian attained sudden and great enlightenment.

Jian returned to the capital and memorialized the Emperor regarding the Patriarch’s words. An imperial edict was issued to thank the Master, and he was granted a *kāṣāya*, five hundred rolls of silk, and a precious alms bowl.
On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, an imperial decree changed the name of the ancient Baolin Monastery to Zhongxing Monastery. (The third year, November 18th.)
One day, an imperial edict was issued to the Prefect of Shaoshan to further embellish and adorn the site, granting it the name Fajian Monastery (Dharma Spring Monastery).
Zu’s former residence in Xinzhou was designated as Guoen Monastery (State Kindness Monastery). One day, Zu addressed the assembly, saying:

"O virtuous friends, each of you should purify your minds and listen to my preaching of the Dharma. You all should know that your own mind is the Buddha; do not harbor any further doubt. There is nothing external..."
That a single thing can establish [all things] means that all myriad phenomena are produced from the fundamental mind. Therefore, a sutra says: "When the mind arises, all phenomena arise;

when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease. If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one must attain the samādhi of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇasamādhi*) and the samādhi of the single practice (*ekakāryasamādhi*).
If, in all places, one does not dwell upon characteristics, then within those characteristics, aversion will not arise.
There is no attachment, nor is there any grasping or rejecting. One does not dwell upon matters such as benefit or ruin, success or failure.

Being at ease, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene—this is called the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic. If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely straightforward mind.
The immovable site of enlightenment is truly the Pure Land; it is named the Samādhi of Single Practice.

If a person possesses two or three samādhis, it is like the earth with seeds, which can contain and nurture them until their fruit is realized. The same applies to the single characteristic and the single practice.
I now preach the Dharma like a timely rain that universally moistens the great earth. Your Buddha-natures are like various seeds;
encountering this soaking moisture, they shall all sprout and grow. Those who receive my intent will certainly attain Bodhi; those who follow my practice...
Having definitively realized the wondrous fruit, Emperor Minghuang, in the *Renzi* year of the Xiantian era, addressed the fourfold assembly, saying:

"I have humbly received the robe and the Dharma from the Great Master. Now I shall preach the Dharma for you all, yet I do not transmit the robe to you. This is because your roots of faith are pure and mature;
you are resolute and free from doubt, and thus capable of undertaking the great task. Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds; it rains everywhere...'"
All were born [into awakening]. Having suddenly realized the essence of the flower, the fruit of Bodhi was spontaneously attained. After speaking these verses, he said again:
"The Dharma is non-dual; the mind is likewise so. The Way is pure and free from all marks. You must be careful not to perceive it as pure."
"Furthermore, empty your mind. This mind is fundamentally pure; there is nothing to be grasped or rejected. Each of you must exert yourselves. Go as you please according to conditions.
A monk recited the verse of Wōluán: "Wōluán has skillful means; he can sever a hundred thoughts.
When facing objects, his mind does not arise; thus Bodhi grows day by day. Upon hearing this, the Patriarch said, "This verse has not yet clarified the ground of the mind. If you rely upon it..."
To practice this is to add further fetters. To illustrate this, he spoke a verse: "Wisdom can eliminate artifice; It does not sever the hundred thoughts.
When encountering objects, mental states arise; How could Bodhi grow? The Patriarch preached the Dharma to benefit sentient beings for forty years.

On the sixth day of the seventh month of that year, he instructed his disciple residing at Guoen Temple in Xinzhou to construct a stupa for repaying his parents' kindness, ordering him to redouble his efforts.
Furthermore, a monk from Shu named Fangbian came to visit and said, "I am skilled at modeling and sculpting. The Patriarch looked at him with a stern expression and said:
"Try sculpting one and see. Fangbian did not grasp the intent, so he instead sculpted a true likeness of the Patriarch, seven feet in height, capturing every nuance of its excellence.

When the Patriarch saw it, he said, "You are skilled at shaping material form, but not at understanding Buddha-nature. He rewarded him with clothing and goods, and Fangbian bowed in thanks before departing.
On the first day of the seventh month in the Gui-chou year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Minghuang, he said to his disciples, "I wish to return."
"New State. You must quickly prepare the boats. At that time, the great assembly was filled with grief and longing, entreating the Master to remain.

The Patriarch said, "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they still manifest *nirvāṇa*. That there is coming, there must be going; this principle is constant. This physical form of mine must also have a place to which it returns.
The assembly asked, "If the Master departs from here, when will you return? The Patriarch replied, "Leaves fall and return to their root; when I come..."
Wumu remained silent. Again he asked, "Whom did your Dharma-eye transmit to? The Patriarch said, "Those who possess the Way shall attain it; those without a mind shall penetrate it.
He asked again, "Will there not be difficulties after my passing? The Patriarch said, "Five or six years after my death, there will be a man who comes to take my head.

Listen to my prediction: 'To support one's parents, one must nourish them upon one's head; for one's own sustenance, one must eat from one's mouth. When you encounter the one named Man (Manzhi), give him my head.'"

It was difficult [to understand]. He said, "The willows shall become officials. He further said, "Seventy years after I have departed, two Bodhisattvas shall come from the East—one a householder and one a renunciant—who shall simultaneously propagate the Dharma, establish my school, restore monasteries, and cause the lineage of the Dharma to flourish.
Having finished speaking, he went to Guoen Temple in Xinzhou, bathed, sat in the lotus position, and passed away, while a wondrous fragrance permeated the air.

A white rainbow stretched toward the earth on the third day of the eighth month of that same year. At that time, the two prefectures of Shaozhou and Xin'an were each constructing a stupa for the spirit;

neither the clergy nor the laity could decide where it should be located. The Prefectural Governors of both prefectures together burned incense and prayed, saying: "Wherever the smoke of our incense leads..."

As the Master was about to return [to his homeland], incense rising from the burner surged upward, piercing straight through to Caoxi. On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, he entered the stupa;
his age was seventy-six. At that time, Wei Ju, the Imperial Commissioner of Shaoyang Prefecture, composed the inscription for the stele.

In the Gengzi year of the Shangyuan era, Emperor Suzong dispatched an envoy to request the Master’s robes and alms bowl to be brought back to the palace for veneration. This continued until the first year of the Yongtai era.

On the fifth day of the fifth month, Emperor Daizong dreamed that the Sixth Patriarch Master requested his robe and alms bowl. On the seventh day, he issued an edict to the Regional Inspector Yang Jian, saying:
"In my dream, I was moved by the Chan Master’s request to return the Dharma-transmitting cassock to Caoxi.
I have now dispatched Liu Chongjing, General of the State Guard, to carry it upon his head and deliver it. I regard it as a national treasure; you may [receive it] at the local monastery."

He was enshrined according to the Dharma, and those among the monastic community who had personally inherited the essential tenets were strictly charged with guarding them so that they would not be lost or allowed to fall into decline.
Subsequently, whenever anyone attempted to steal them, they were recovered before they could travel far. This occurred several times.
Emperor Xianzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dajian, and his stupa was named Yuanhe Lingzhao.

Kuang marveled at where he had come from, and Man said, "Does the Dharma have a place from which it comes? Kuang sent someone to search for his point of entry, but there was only snow on all four sides.
The pile reached about five chi in height. Daokuang said, "It cannot be measured. He once told people: "The Buddhas taught that the mind is to be understood as having illusory characteristics;
now, by adding further mental characteristics, one deeply violates the Buddha’s intent. Furthermore, to increase the proliferation of discursive arguments is utterly contrary to the Great Principle.
Later, while engaged in metalworking, he passed away while sitting peacefully, without illness.

The layman [Hui] had previously lived in seclusion among the forests and wilds, eating from the trees and drinking from the mountain streams. At the beginning of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi dynasty, he heard of the flourishing transformation of the Second Patriarch and sent him a letter, saying:
"Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow sounds. To dally with shadows is to weary the form; yet one does not realize that form is the root of the shadow.
To raise a sound is to seek to stop the echo; yet one does not know that sound is the source of the echo. To eliminate afflictions and seek Nirvana..."
It is like seeking a shadow by removing the form; it is like seeking the fruit of Buddhahood apart from sentient beings; it is like seeking an echo while silencing the sound.
Thus we know that delusion and awakening are one path, and folly and wisdom are not distinct. Where there is no name, one creates names; because of these names, right and wrong arise.
Where there is no principle, one creates principles; because of these principles, disputes arise. These are illusory transformations and not real; who is right and who is wrong?
"No. It is false and illusory, without reality. What is empty? What exists? You should know that what is gained is nothing gained, and what is lost is nothing lost.

He had not yet paid his respects again when he briefly set forth this meaning, humbly hoping for a reply. The Second Patriarch returned with this instruction: "I have fully observed the intent of your letter; it is entirely as you say.
The principle of the truly profound is ultimately no different [from my own]. Originally, you mistook the *maṇi* jewel for a pebble, but now you have suddenly awakened on your own."
Awakening is the true pearl; ignorance and wisdom are equal and without distinction. One should know that all phenomena are thus.

Out of compassion for those who hold these two views, I have composed this book with pen and ink. When one contemplates that the body and the Buddha are no different, why seek that which is beyond remainder?
Layman, having received and read these ancestral verses, you then prostrated yourself in audience and secretly received the seal of transmission.
The second-generation successor of the Second Patriarch,
Chan Master Hui-man of Longhua Temple in Zhangde Prefecture,
was a native of the Zhang family of Yingyang. He first encountered [the Dharma] at this very temple.
The Second Patriarch’s instructions were to maintain a life of frugality and simplicity. He said of himself, "Throughout my life, my mind has been free from fear; I do not dream while sleeping.

He constantly practiced begging for alms and never stayed overnight in the same place twice. During the *Ren-yin* year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, he stayed in an ancient tomb beside Huishan Monastery in Luoyang.
When heavy snow fell, he entered the monastery at dawn and met the Dharma Master Tanguang. Tanguang was surprised by his origins.
[Someone] came. The Master said, "Does the Dharma come? Kuang was sent to search for its place of origin; he found it lodged five chi deep within a pile of snow.
Later, hearing that there were matters concerning the registration of monks, the other monks fled and hid themselves. The Master alone carried his alms bowl into the villages, meeting no obstruction;
whatever he received, he immediately distributed, remaining thus empty and at ease. Furthermore, he once told people: "The Buddhas speak of the mind to cause one to know it."

The characteristics of the mind are illusory; to now further add to these mental characteristics deeply contradicts the Buddha’s intention and increases the proliferation of discursive debate, which is utterly at variance with the Great Principle.
Therefore, he constantly carried the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as his essential core, practicing exactly as it was taught.
This was indeed to follow the legacy entrusted to him by generations past. Later, while engaged in metalworking, he passed away while sitting peacefully without illness at the age of seventy.
From the third generation after the Second Patriarch down to the eighth, the chapter headings are not listed.
Regarding the Fourth Patriarch, Chan Master Dayi: his collateral successor was the First Generation, Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou.
He was a native of Yanling in Runzhou, surnamed Wei. At the age of nineteen, he...
His learning encompassed the Classics and Histories. Upon searching through and reading the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtras, he attained a profound understanding of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One day, he sighed and said: "The secular texts of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma; the correct contemplation of Prajñā is the vessel for transcending the world.

He subsequently retired to Mount Mao, where he entered the monastic order under a master and shaved his head. Later, he entered a stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou. There, hundreds of birds brought [offerings].

Regarding the wonders of this flower: During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Fourth Patriarch observed the atmospheric signs from afar and knew there was a person of extraordinary character on that mountain.

He went in person to seek him out and asked the temple monks, "Is there any practitioner of the Way here? They replied, "Among those who have left the household life, which one is not a practitioner of the Way?
The Patriarch said, "Which one among them is the practitioner of the Way? The monks were speechless. Another monk said, "This..."
About ten *li* into the mountains, there was one named Lanrong. He would not rise when seeing people, nor would he join his palms.
"Could this be a man of the Way? the Patriarch thought, and so he entered the mountains. He saw the Master sitting upright and composed, with no regard for anything at all. The Patriarch asked:
"What are you doing here? the Master asked. The Teacher replied, "I am contemplating the mind. The Patriarch asked, "Who is it that contemplates? What is this 'mind'? The Teacher was speechless.
He then rose, prostrated himself, and asked, "Where does the Great Virtuous One dwell? The Patriarch replied, "This poor monk has no fixed abode;
sometimes I go east, sometimes west. The Teacher asked, "Do you know Meditation Master Daoxin? The Patriarch asked, "Why do you ask about him?"
The Master said, "I have long admired your virtue and have hoped to pay my respects. The Patriarch said, "I am that very Daoxin, the Chan Master.

The Master asked, "For what reason have you descended here? The Patriarch replied, "I have come specifically to visit you. The Master asked further, "Is there perhaps another place where you might rest?"

The Master pointed behind him and said, "There is another small hermitage. He then led the Patriarch to the site of the hermitage; when they circled it, they saw nothing but tigers, wolves, and other such beasts.
The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of fear. The Master said, "There is still this remaining. The Patriarch replied:
"What is this? The Master was speechless. After a short while, the Patriarch again inscribed the character for "Buddha" (佛) upon a stone where the Master was sitting in formal meditation.

Upon seeing it, the Master stood in awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this remaining. The Master did not yet understand, so he bowed his head and requested an explanation of the essential truth.
The Patriarch said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind; the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all..."
At the source of the mind, all gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are entirely and spontaneously complete;
they do not depart from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are fundamentally empty and still. All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions.
There are no three realms from which to escape, and there is no bodhi to be sought. Humans and non-humans are equal in their essential nature and characteristics. Great!
The Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation. Such a Dharma you have now attained; it lacks nothing and differs not from that of the Buddha.
There is no other separate Dharma. You need only allow the mind to be free and at ease. Do not engage in contemplative practices, nor do you need to clarify the mind.
Do not give rise to greed or anger, nor harbor anxiety or worry. Be broad and unimpeded, moving freely in all directions, and do not perform any [conditioned] deeds.

"Excellent! Not committing any evil, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whenever the eyes encounter objects or the mind meets with conditions—all is the wondrous function of the Buddha, joyful and free from sorrow;
therefore, he is called 'Buddha'. The Master asked: "Since the mind is already complete, what is the Buddha and what is the mind?

The Patriarch said: "If it is not the mind, one does not inquire about the Buddha; if one inquires about the Buddha, it is not apart from the mind. The Master said: "Since you do not permit the practice of contemplation..."
"When an object arises before you, how does the mind counteract it? The Patriarch said: "The objective conditions have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind.
If the mind does not apply forced designations, from where can deluded sentiments arise? Since deluded sentiments do not arise, the true mind is free to know all things.
You need only follow the mind with ease and freedom; there will be no further need for counteraction. This is what is called the eternally abiding Dharmakāya. There is nothing more to it.

[The Master] said, "My transmission of the Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching from Master Huicán is now entrusted to you. You must now receive my words with earnest attention and remain on this very mountain.
Hereafter, there shall be five men who attain realization and will carry forward your great transformation.

Having finished transmitting the Dharma, the Patriarch returned to Shuangfeng to spend the remainder of his life there. From that time on, the master’s Dharma seat flourished greatly. During the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, his disciples...
The community was short of provisions. The Master traveled to Danyang to seek alms;

though it was eighty li from the mountain, he personally carried one shi eight dou of rice, going in the morning and returning by evening, providing for three hundred monks without fail at both meal times. The district magistrate, Xiao Yuanshan, invited him to the Jianchu Monastery to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Listeners gathered like clouds. When they reached the "Chapter on Cessation and Tranquility," the earth shook.
Dong Bolingwang asked the Master, "When an object-condition arises from form, you do not say that it arises because of the object-condition. How, then, can one know the condition?
Is it intended to cease its arising? The Master replied, "At the very moment the objective form first arises, both the nature of form and the nature of the object are empty."

Fundamentally, there is no knower of conditions; the mind-measure (*cittamātra*) is identical with knowing. Illumination is the original source, yet its arising is non-arising. At that time, one gives rise to the cessation of self-clinging and the darkness [of ignorance].
When the perceiving mind arises in relation to conditions, those conditions do not follow after it; they are as they were before birth. Form and mind are not what is nurtured.

From emptiness, fundamentally there is no thought. Perception, sensation, and verbal recollection arise from thought. That which has never arisen is now being activated; how could one use the Buddha’s teachings to inquire about this?
With eyes closed, one does not see forms, yet mental objects and deliberations become manifold. Since forms do not concern the mind, from where do these objects arise? The Master said:
"With eyes closed, one does not see forms, yet the inner mind stirs with manifold deliberations. These are the provisional functions of illusory consciousness arising."

Names ultimately do not transcend [reality]. Know that form does not engage the mind, and the mind likewise does not engage persons. As one follows in practice, there is the turning of signs. When a bird flies away into the sky, its trace is true.
Question: The objective realm arises without a fixed location; through conditions, awakening realizes its birth.

When the object fades, awareness turns back; awareness then transforms into the object. If one uses the mind to drag the mind, it returns to being what is perceived by awareness. Following this, it follows along with each subsequent state.
"Go! Do not depart from the boundary of arising and ceasing. The Master said: "In the beginning, middle, and end of form and mind, there is truly no object of dependent origination.

When one moment of self-doubt is forgotten, who can calculate movement and stillness? This knowing is itself without knowing; knowing and the objects of knowing do not meet. You should examine your own fundamental form for yourself;
why must you seek it beyond this realm? The preceding object does not change or pass away; the subsequent thought does not come into the present. To seek the moon..."
Grasping at reflections and shadows, tracing footprints and pursuing flying birds—to seek to know the fundamental nature of the mind is like looking into a dream.
It is likened to ice in the sixth month: everywhere it is the same. One cannot escape by avoiding emptiness, nor can one achieve it by seeking emptiness.
I ask you, O mirror-image: from where does the mind arise? Question: When the mind is applied with such precision, how can it be made peaceful and secure?

The Master said: "Precisely when the mind is applied, precisely there is no mind to apply. To discuss names and forms in a circuitous way is wearying; to speak directly of non-existence is not cumbersome.
When there is no mind, it is precisely applied; what is constantly used is precisely non-existent. Now, where I speak of the state of no-mind, it is not different from that which has a mind.
Question: "When the Wise One cites wondrous words, they accord with what is being explained. Yet words and the path of the mind are distinct; how can they be unified?"
