He replied, "I am upright; how could I be arbitrary? The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean whether your actions accord with the Will of Heaven before and after. He replied, "I can. The Master said:
"Have you not been ruined by wine? He replied, "I have. The Master said, "The above constitutes the Buddha's precepts.

He further said, "Maintain them with a focused mind, yet remain free from the mind that clings; act for the sake of others with a conscious mind, yet remain free from the thought of a self-centered body.

If one can do so, then though born before heaven and earth, one does not become a mere vital essence; though dying after heaven and earth, one does not become old. Throughout the day, one undergoes transformation."

Transforming yet not being moved; reaching ultimate stillness yet not ceasing. Believing this, then though one marries, it is not for the sake of a wife; though one feasts, it is not for the sake of taking;
though one holds office, it is not for the sake of power; though one acts, it is not for the sake of habit; though one is intoxicated, it is not for the sake of delusion.

If one can be without mind regarding the myriad things, then even if ensnared by desires, it does not constitute lust. Even if blessings fall upon the licentious and calamities upon the virtuous, it does not constitute [the workings of] fortune or misfortune.
Stealing, negligence, error, doubt, and confusion do not constitute killing; violating the laws of Heaven in sequence does not constitute falsehood;

being dazed, deluded, or inverted does not constitute intoxication. This is called being "without mind. Without mind, there is no precept; without precepts, there is no mind. There is no Buddha and no sentient beings;
there is neither you nor me. Who, then, would have precepts? The Spirit said, "My spiritual powers are second only to the Buddha's. The Master said:

"Your supernatural powers consist of ten items: five abilities and five incapacities. Those of the Buddha, however, consist of ten items: seven abilities and three incapacities. Shen [the deity] was struck with awe, rose from his seat, knelt, and asked, "May I hear them? The Master said, "Can you cause the Supreme Deity to turn eastward and make the Seven Luminaries travel westward? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you seize the Earth Deity and melt the Five Peaks? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you draw the Four Seas into a single drop and place it upon your tongue? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take Mount Sumeru and place it within a mustard seed? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the entire world and place it within a single pore? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take all the Buddhas of the three times and place them within a single atom? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within your own mind? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single hair-pore? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single thought-moment? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single dust mote? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single speck of dust? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single grain of sand? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single drop of water? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single bubble? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single spark of fire? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single breath of wind? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single atom? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you take the minds of all sentient beings and place them within a single thought-instant? He replied, "I cannot. "Can one bind the four seas? He replied, "No. The Master said, "This is called the five 'cannots.

The Buddha can empty all phenomena and achieve the wisdom of the myriad dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma. The Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaustively understand the events of billions of kalpas, yet he cannot transform and guide those who lack the karmic affinity.
The Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot bring them all to an end."
The realm of sentient beings—these are the three impossibilities. Even determinate karma is not fixed or enduring; even the absence of conditions constitutes a single lifetime.
The realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease. Throughout all time, there is not a single person who can master this dharma. Where there is a dharma, there is no master.

"This is called the non-existence of dharmas. Where there are no dharmas, there is no master; this is called the absence of mind. As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*);
he is simply able to penetrate all dharmas through the state of no-mind. The deity said, "I am indeed shallow and ignorant, having not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
I shall faithfully observe the precepts you have bestowed upon me. Now I wish to repay your compassionate virtue by demonstrating what I am capable of. The Master [consented].
He said, "I observe that the body is nothingness; I observe that all phenomena are impermanent. Being as solid as a clod of earth, what further desire could I have?

The Spirit said, "The Master must surely command me to perform a worldly task to display my minor divine powers, so that those who have already resolved their minds, those who have first resolved their minds, and those who have not yet resolved their minds—or those who do not believe—will surely come to believe.
May these five classes of people behold the traces of my spirit and know that there is both Buddha and Spirit."
[The Master said: "There is capability and incapability; there is that which is spontaneous and that which is not spontaneous. The Teacher said: "Non-action is it. Non-action is it. The Spirit said:
"The Buddha also commands spirits to protect the Dharma. How could you, Master, ever rebel against the Buddha? I pray that you will instruct me as you please."
The Master, having no choice, spoke, saying: "The barrier of Dongnamsa Temple is desolate and treeless;
while there are trees on the northern peak, its back is not shielded by them. Can you move the trees from the north to the eastern ridge? The spirit replied: "I have already received your command."

However, as it was already deep night, there was inevitably a great clamor and commotion. "I pray that you, Master, will not be startled," he said, and immediately performed a prostration and took his leave.

The Master saw him off at the gate and watched him go; he beheld the ceremonial guards winding along like the retinue of a sovereign, amidst swirling mists and rosy clouds, while banners, streamers, and tinkling ornaments vanished into the air.
That very evening, indeed, a violent wind howled, thunder crashed, and clouds rushed forth.

A flash of lightning struck; the buildings shook and swayed, and the birds roosting there cried out in a tumultuous clamor. The Master said to the assembly, "Do not fear, do not fear! The deity has entered into harmony with me.
At dawn the next day, when the weather was clear and bright, the pine and cypress trees on the northern cliff had all been moved to the eastern ridge, standing there in dense, orderly rows.
The Master said to his disciples, "After my passing, do not let outsiders know of this. If it becomes a subject for idle talk, people will surely regard me as a sorcerer."
In the *Bingchen* year of the Kaiyuan era during the Tang dynasty, Emperor Minghuang instructed his disciples, saying: "I originally resided on the eastern ridge of this temple;
when I pass away, you must place my remains there. Having finished speaking, he was like one casting off a sloughed skin. He was seventy-two years of age.
His disciples honored him by constructing a stupa.
He was the third-generation descendant of the Fifth Patriarch (branch line).
He was a dharma heir of Chan Master Ji of Mount Song.
Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan Mountain was the son of Zhou [surname] of Pingyuan.

He received his formal training under Dharma Master Quancheng of Yanyang Temple in his native prefecture and attained the Dharma from Chan Master Pujì of Mount Song. He subsequently entered Mount Taiyi, where students filled his quarters.
Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty was fond of eating clams; the officials along the coastal regions were exhausted by the constant task of presenting them to him. One day—
Among the imperial offerings, there was one that had been split open but did not close back together. The Emperor, finding it extraordinary, immediately burned incense and prayed to it;

upon opening it, he beheld the form and countenance of a Bodhisattva, complete with the marks of a Brahma. The Emperor then enshrined it in a casket made of gold and grain, covered with fine brocade, and bestowed it upon Xingshan Monastery, ordering the monks to gaze upon and worship it.
He then asked his ministers, "What auspicious omen does this portend? Some replied: [The rest of the response would follow here.]

Chan Master Weizheng of Taishan was profoundly enlightened in the Buddha-dharma and possessed vast learning and a powerful memory. The Emperor requested that he be summoned for an audience. An imperial edict was immediately issued.
When the Master arrived, the Emperor questioned him regarding the matter. The Master said, "Your servant has heard that nothing occurs without a corresponding cause;
this is merely to inspire Your Majesty’s faith. Thus, a sutra says: 'To those who are to be saved by this body, [the Buddha] manifests in this form.'"
[The Master] manifested his body and preached the Dharma for him. The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has already appeared, yet I have not heard him preach the Dharma.
The Master asked, "Your Majesty, regarding this which you behold—is it permanent or impermanent? Is it real or unreal? The Emperor replied, "It is a most rare and marvelous thing."

"I believe this deeply," the Emperor said. The Master replied, "Your Majesty has already heard the Dharma teaching in its entirety. The Emperor’s heart was filled with joy, a state he had never before experienced.
He issued an edict for all monasteries throughout the realm to establish an image of Avalokiteśvara in order to repay this extraordinary grace.

He invited the Master to remain at the Inner Sanctuary (Neidaochang), but the Master repeatedly declined and requested to return to the mountains. The Emperor then decreed that he reside at Shengshou Monastery. When Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne, the Master suddenly entered Mount Zhong.
He lived in seclusion on the South Mountain. When people asked him the reason for this, the Master said, "I am avoiding my enemies. After his death, he was cremated;
forty-nine śarīras were collected, and a stūpa was erected over them.
A monk asked Master Puo-zao-duo, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Junji of Mount Song: "What is one who practices good? The Master said, "Shouldering the cangue and wearing the shackles.
The monk asked, "What is one who commits evil? The Master said, "Practicing dhyāna and entering samādhi. The monk said, "My faculties are shallow."
"Please, Master, point directly. The Master said, "If you ask me about evil, evil does not follow from good. If you ask me about good, good does not follow from evil.
After the monk had been silent for a long while, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "An evil person has no thoughts of goodness."
"A good person has no evil mind. Thus it is said that good and evil are like floating clouds; both have no place of arising or ceasing.
At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Later, when Puzhuo heard this statement being cited, he remarked, "This man has fully realized that all dharmas are non-arising."
The Fourth Generation under the Fifth Patriarch:
Chan Master Wuxiang of Yizhou and his Dharma heir, Chan Master Wuzhu of Baotang Temple in Yizhou.
Having initially received the Dharma from Great Master Wuxiang, he then resided in the South.

Yang Bai resided at Yaishan, devoting himself exclusively to the practice of tranquil meditation for many years. As students gradually arrived and their earnest requests never ceased, he began to offer instruction from that time forward.
Although he extensively expounded upon verbal teachings, he maintained that non-thought alone constitutes true concentration.

When Du Hongjian, the State Councilor of the Tang Dynasty, was dispatched to govern the region of Sichuan (Kunwei), he heard of the Master’s reputation and desired to pay his respects. He sent an envoy to the mountain to extend an invitation, arriving during the Master’s seasonal retreat.
The Regional Inspector Cui Ning also commanded the monastics of various temples to travel a long distance to welcome and escort him.
Upon arriving at Konghui Temple, Lord Du and the military commander summoned eminent masters of the Three Studies to assemble within the temple.

After the formal greetings were concluded, Lord Du asked, "I have heard, Master, that you now teach the Dharma-gate of the three phrases: 'no recollection,' 'no thought,' and 'do not be deluded. Is this so? The Master replied:

The Duke said, "Regarding these three phrases, are they one or are they three? The Master replied, "'No recollection' is called precept; 'no thought' is called concentration; 'do not delude' is called wisdom. When the single mind does not arise, one possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom; it is neither one nor three. The Duke asked, "In the last phrase, the character for 'delusion' (妄), is it the 'wàng' that is written with the 'heart' radical? The Master said, "It is the one written with the 'woman' radical. The Duke said, "I have a source for this. The Master said, "I too have a source. The Duke said, "What is your source? The Master replied, "The *Shuo Wen* says: 'Delusion (妄) means to deceive. The Duke said, "Excellent! Excellent! He then bowed and withdrew. The Master then composed the following verse:

"Recollection is the thief of the Way; Thought is the enemy of the mind. If you do not give rise to them, The myriad phenomena are naturally extinguished. Precept, concentration, and wisdom are complete within yourself; They are neither one nor three. The Duke then had this verse inscribed on a stele and erected it at the monastery. It was titled "The Stele Inscription on the Three Phrases of the Diamond Sutra. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he said to his disciples, "The Duke of Xiangyang has long been my friend. I hope you will take care of him. After the Master passed away, the Duke visited the temple and saw the inscription on the stele.

He sighed and said, "How could I have known that the Master’s words were so profound? I have heard that the Master said, 'When the single mind does not arise, one possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom. I have always wondered what the 'single mind' is. Now I know it is the mind that does not give rise to recollection or thought. This is truly the gate of liberation. The Duke then had the inscription copied and distributed throughout the world. It became widely circulated and is known as "The Inscription on the Three Phrases. The Duke also composed a preface to it, which begins: "The Buddha’s teaching is vast and boundless; Its essence is subtle and difficult to fathom. The ancients transmitted it through the written word; The sages expounded it through oral instruction. Now, the Master’s three phrases are like a key That opens the gate of the Tathāgata’s treasury. They are the ultimate meaning of the sutra; They are the essential principle of the Dharma. If one can practice according to them, One will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood. The Duke further stated: "The Master’s three phrases are the very marrow of the Buddhas and patriarchs. They are the true path for those who seek liberation. I hope that all practitioners will study and uphold them. Thus, the inscription was widely disseminated, and its influence spread throughout the land. It remains a testament to the profound realization of the Sixth Patriarch. The Duke’s inquiry and the Master’s response demonstrate the seamless integration of the Mahayana teachings with the practical application of mindfulness and the eradication of delusion. This dialogue serves as a timeless guide for those seeking to realize the non-dual nature of reality.
"No. The Master said, "The *Dharmapada* states: 'If one gives rise to a mind of diligent effort, this is delusion, not diligence.

If one can keep the mind free from delusion, diligence will be boundless. Upon hearing this, the official’s doubts were completely dispelled. The official asked again, 'Does the Master still instruct people using the three phrases?
The Master replied, 'For a beginner practitioner, one must first cause them to cease discursive thought and settle the waves of consciousness until the water becomes clear.'"
Manifesting as reflections, one awakens to the essence of non-thought; with quiescence manifest before one, even "non-thought" does not stand. At that time, a crow cawed in a tree in the courtyard.
The Master asked, "Did you hear it? The Master replied, "I heard it. After the crow had flown away, he asked again, "Did you hear it? The Master replied, "I heard it."
[The Master] said, "When the crow flew away, there was no sound. How can you say you heard it? The Master then addressed the assembly at large:
"A Buddha’s world is difficult to encounter; the Dharma of the world is difficult to hear. Each of you listen attentively. To 'hear' is to have no hearing;
it does not concern the nature of hearing. It is originally unborn; how could it ever cease? When there is sound, that sound-object arises of itself. When there is no sound, it is..."
The auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) perishes of its own accord, yet this nature of hearing does not arise following the sound, nor does it perish following the sound.
To realize this nature of hearing is to escape being turned by the auditory object. You should know that within the intervals there is neither arising nor ceasing; hearing has no coming or going.
[Then] Gong, together with his officials and the great assembly, bowed their heads and asked: "What is called the primary truth (paramārtha)? From what sequence does the primary truth proceed?"
[The monk] entered. The Master said, "The primary truth (paramārtha-satya) has no sequence; it neither enters nor exits. In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), everything exists;

in the primary truth, there is nothing. All phenomena lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva); this absence of nature is what is called the primary truth. The Buddha said, "That which has existence is named the conventional truth; that which lacks intrinsic nature is the primary truth.
The Master [Dongshan] said, "As the Master has revealed, it is truly inconceivable. Your disciple..."
"My nature of consciousness is shallow and superficial. Previously, during my leisure time, I composed two fascicles of commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*.

May these be called the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "In composing commentaries, one always employs the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*)—employing deliberation and discrimination, the conditioned and the contrived, and the stirring of thoughts and intentions;
it is only through these that they can be produced. According to the text of the treatise, it says: 'One should know that all dharmas, from the very beginning...'"
Since time immemorial, it has been free from the marks of verbal expression, free from the marks of names and designations, and free from the marks of mental objects;

it is ultimately equal, without change or variation, and consists solely of the one mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (Suchness). Now, you, Excellency, are attached to the marks of verbal expression, attached to the marks of names and designations, and attached to the marks of mental objects.
Since you are attached to such various marks, how can this be the Buddha-dharma? The Excellency rose, prostrated himself, and said:
"Disciple, I have also previously questioned various venerable monks who attend the court, and they all praised you as being inconceivable.

You should know that they were merely following worldly sentiment. Now, Master, please explain from the perspective of understanding; this must accord with the mind-ground. The Dharma is truly the ultimate truth and is indeed inconceivable.
The Duke asked again: "How is it that there is no arising? How is it that there is no ceasing? How does one attain liberation?"

“Deliverance. The Master said: “When the mind does not arise upon encountering objects, this is called ‘non-arising. Non-arising is itself non-extinction. Since there is neither arising nor extinction, one is not bound by external sensory realms;
one is liberated right where one is. Non-arising is called ‘no-thought’ (amanasikāra). No-thought is itself non-extinction. No-thought is itself non-bondage.
No-thought is itself non-deliverance. To state the essential point: when the consciousness-mind is realized, it is free from thought.”
To see one's nature is itself liberation. Apart from seeing one's nature through the mind that transcends consciousness, there is no other dharma-gate by which one may realize unsurpassed bodhi;
such a thing is impossible. The Official asked, "What is meant by 'seeing one's nature through the mind of consciousness'? The Master replied, "All those who study the Way..."
One wanders about in accordance with these thoughts because one does not recognize the true mind. As for the true mind: when thoughts arise, it does not follow their arising;
when thoughts cease, it does not rely on their stillness. It neither comes nor goes; it is neither fixed nor distracted; it neither grasps nor abandons; it neither sinks nor floats.
It is unconditioned and signless, lively and agile, ordinary and sovereign. This essence of mind is ultimately ungraspable.
There is nothing that can be known or perceived; everything encountered by the eye is thus, for there is nothing that is not the nature of seeing.
The official and the assembly prostrated themselves, praising him with great joy before departing. Later, the Master resided at Baotang Temple until his passing.
The First Generation of Dharma Heirs Branching from the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Mirror Chan Master:
Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions, a native of India, attained realization upon hearing the words of the Sixth Patriarch.

Later, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he saw a monk sitting in meditation within a thatched hut. The Master asked him, "What are you doing sitting here alone? The monk replied, "I am practicing the contemplation of stillness. The Master said:
The monk asked, "Who is the observer? What is that which is still? He prostrated and asked, "What is the principle of this?
The Master said, "Why do you not observe yourself and find stillness within yourself? The monk was bewildered. The Master said, "Whose lineage do you follow? He replied, "Master Xiu.
The Master said, "Even the lowest practitioners among the heterodox paths of the Western Regions do not fall into such views; they remain in a state of profound, empty stillness."
"Seated meditation—what benefit does it bring to the Way? The monk countered by asking, "Who is your teacher? The Master replied, "My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch.
Why do you not go quickly to Caoxi to resolve the essential truth? The monk immediately went to visit the Sixth Patriarch.
The instructions he received from the Sixth Patriarch accorded perfectly with those of the Master, and the monk attained realization. The Master's final whereabouts were unknown.

Chan Master Fahai of Shaoyou was a native of Qujiang. Initially, he went to see the Sixth Patriarch and asked, "Regarding the teaching that 'this very mind is Buddha,' I pray you will grant me an illustration.
The Patriarch said, "The non-arising of the preceding thought is the mind; the non-extinguishing of the succeeding thought is the Buddha.

The manifestation of all phenomena is the mind; the detachment from all phenomena is the Buddha. If I were to explain this in full detail, it would not be exhausted even throughout kalpas. Listen to me..."
The verse says: That which is mind is called wisdom; that which is Buddha is concentration. When concentration and wisdom are held in equal balance, the mind becomes pure.
To awaken to this Dharma-gate through your own habitual nature—that which is fundamentally unborn—is the correct dual cultivation. The Master accepted this with faith and praised him in verse:

"That which is mind is primordially Buddha; failing to awaken, one merely humbles oneself. I know the cause of concentration and wisdom: by cultivating them both, one leaves behind all [defilements]."
Wu. Chan Master Zhizheng of Jizhou was a native of Tahe in that same province. Initially, he studied under Chan Master Xiu.
Later, as the two schools flourished, the disciples of Xiu frequently disparaged the Southern School, saying: "Master Neng does not know a single character."
"What excellence does he possess? Xiu replied, "He has attained teacherless wisdom and profoundly realized the Supreme Vehicle; in these respects, I am not his equal.
Furthermore, my master, the Fifth Patriarch, personally entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma—how could this have been for naught?

What I regret is that I was unable to travel far to attend upon him in person, thus receiving the bounty of the state in vain. You all should not remain stagnant here; you may go to Caoxi to resolve your doubts."
"Another day, when you return, you must explain this for me. Upon hearing these words, the Master took his leave and went to Shaoyang.

He joined the assembly to seek instruction, yet he did not mention where he had come from. At that time, the Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "There is currently a thief of the Dharma hidden within this congregation.
The Master stepped forward, prostrated himself, and recounted the matter in detail. The Patriarch asked, "How does your teacher instruct the assembly? The Master replied, "He has often said..."

He instructed the great assembly, commanding them to dwell the mind in the observation of stillness and to sit for long periods without lying down. The Patriarch said: "To dwell the mind in the observation of stillness is a sickness, not Chan;
to sit for long periods while constraining the body—what benefit does this provide for the Principle? Listen to my verse: 'Since birth, I have sat and never lain down.'"
"Dead and lying down, not sitting; a single set of stinking bones. Why establish merit or fault? The Master asked, "I do not yet understand with what Dharma you instruct people, Reverend.
The Patriarch said, "If I were to say that I have a Dharma to give to others, I would be deceiving you.
I simply follow the occasion to untie the bonds; it is provisionally named 'Samādhi. Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind free from transgression is the precept of self-nature.'"
"The mind-ground free from doubt is the wisdom of self-nature; the mind-ground free from distraction is the concentration of self-nature.

Neither increasing nor decreasing, it is the original vajra; the body going and coming is the fundamental samādhi. Upon hearing this verse, the Master repented and apologized, immediately vowing to take refuge.
He then presented his own verse, saying: "The illusory body of the five aggregates—what is the ultimate end of illusion? Turning toward True Suchness, the dharmas are still not pure."
The biography of Chan Master Xiaoliao of Biandang Mountain is not recorded [in other sources].

Only the stele inscription for his pagoda, composed by Chan Master Hulei Cheng—a disciple of the Northern School—is widely circulated in the world. Its summary states: "The Master resided at Biandang Mountain and was styled Xiaoliao;
he was a successor of the Sixth Patriarch. The Master attained the mind that is without mind and realized the form that is without form. That which is without form is the myriad phenomena..."
The eyes are dazzled. For one who is mindless, conceptual discrimination burns fiercely. Cut off every word and every sound; a sound cannot be transmitted, yet it is transmitted as it proceeds.
A word cannot be exhausted, yet to seek its exhaustion is erroneous. The Master has attained the "non-existence" of non-existence, yet he does not remain non-existent within that non-existence.
I, for my part, now employ the "existence" of existence, yet I do not remain existent within that existence. This existence that is not existent—its coming and going is not [real].
Increase! This is the "non-existence" of that which is not non-existent; Nirvana is not annihilation. Alas! While the Master dwelt in the world, Caoxi was illuminated;
when the Master entered nirvana, the Dharma-boat capsized. The Master’s discourse on the ineffable filled the universe; the Master revealed the Vehicle of Definitive Meaning to deluded disciples.
The mountain colors of Biandang still hang over this place; in the empty valley, the name of "Xiaoliao" remains.
Chan Master Fada of Hongzhou was a native of Fengcheng in Hongzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.

After receiving full ordination, he went to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch, yet his head did not touch the ground. The Patriarch rebuked him, saying, "If your prostration does not reach the ground, how is it any different from not prostrating at all?
There must be something within your mind; what have you been habitually practicing? The Master replied, "I am reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*."

[The Master] said, "You have already mastered three thousand sections of the sutras. The Patriarch said, "If you were to recite ten thousand sections and attain the meaning of those sutras, yet did not consider yourself superior [to others], then you may walk with me.
You are now burdened by this task, yet you do not recognize your own transgression.

Listen to my verse: "Veneration is fundamentally for breaking the banner of pride; why does your head not touch the ground? When there is a self, faults immediately arise; when merit is lost, blessings cease."
The Patriarch asked again, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Fada. The Patriarch said, "Your name is Fada;
when have you ever truly mastered the Dharma? He then spoke a verse: "You are now named Fada, Diligently reciting without ceasing.

In vain you recite, merely following the sound; To clarify the mind is what is called a Bodhisattva. Because you now possess the karmic conditions, I shall now speak for your sake. Simply believe in the Buddha..."
He remained silent. A lotus flower emerged from his mouth. Upon hearing the verse, the Master repented his error and said, "From this day forward, I shall treat all with humility and respect.
I only pray that the Preceptor, out of great compassion, will briefly explain the meaning and principles within the sutras. The Patriarch replied, "Recite this sutra."
"What is its essential tenet? The Master said, "I am a dull-witted student; from the beginning, I have merely recited it according to the text, so how could I know its fundamental principle?
The Patriarch said, "Recite it for me once, and I shall explain it for you. The Master then recited the scripture aloud.
Upon reaching the "Chapter on Expedient Means," the Patriarch said, "Stop. This scripture fundamentally takes the appearance of the world through causes and conditions as its tenet."
Even if one were to provide many kinds of parables, they would not exceed this. What is the causal condition?
It is the single Great Matter, the One Great Matter, which is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). You must be careful not to misunderstand the intent of the sutra.

If you see that the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" belong solely to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and conclude that we have no share in it—if you interpret it thus, you are slandering the sutra and committing a transgression.
He is the Buddha. Since he is already a Buddha, having fully perfected knowledge and vision, what need is there for him to further open [this teaching]?
You should now believe that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is nothing other than your own mind; it has no separate essence. It is simply because all sentient beings obscure their own radiance.
Craving sensory objects, you are disturbed by external conditions and willingly subject yourself to their driving force;

thus, you trouble others by forcing them to arise from samādhi and speak various bitter words to urge you to rest and cease seeking outwardly, for you are no different from the Buddha. Therefore, it is said that "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened.
If you merely exhaust yourself in clinging to thoughts, claiming them to be your spiritual practice, how is this any different from a yak that loves its own tail?—Master [Shenxiu].

[The student] said, "If that is so, then one need only understand the meaning; is there no need for the labor of reciting the sutra? The Master said, "What fault is there in the sutra? How could it obstruct your mindfulness?
It is simply because delusion and awakening depend on the person, and benefit or harm arise from you.

Listen to my verse: When the mind is deluded, the Lotus Sutra revolves around it; When the mind is awakened, it revolves the Lotus Sutra. To recite for a long time without clarifying oneself Is to become an enemy to the meaning. Without thought, there is constant mindfulness."

This is precisely correct. There are those who fall into error moment by moment, and there are those who do not reckon with either existence or non-existence. [The Master] long drove the white ox-cart. Upon hearing this verse, the Teacher spoke again, saying:
"The Sūtra states that even all the Great Śrāvakas and even the Bodhisattvas, though they exhaust their thoughts and measure with their intellects, are still unable to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Now, you cause ordinary people to merely awaken to their own minds and immediately name this the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. From here...

"You do not possess superior faculties; you have not yet escaped doubt and slander. Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of three carts: the cart of the great ox and the cart of the white ox—how are these to be distinguished?
I pray that the Master will again deign to explain this. The Patriarch said: "The intent of the Sūtra is clear, yet you yourself are deluded and turn your back upon it.
That those of the Three Vehicles cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom lies in their reliance on intellectual measurement. Even if they exhaust all their thought..."
We pushed it together, yet it grew increasingly distant. The Buddha originally taught this for ordinary beings, not for Buddhas.

If you are unwilling to believe this principle, you may withdraw from the assembly at your pleasure; yet you do not realize that you have already boarded the white ox-cart, while instead seeking three carts outside the gate.
Furthermore, the sutra text clearly tells you: "There are neither two nor three. Why do you fail to understand? The three carts!
This is provisional, because it pertains to the past. The One Vehicle is real, because it pertains to the present. I am merely teaching you to abandon the provisional and return to the real.
Once you have returned to the real, even "reality" has no name. You should know that all precious wealth now belongs entirely to you;
you may enjoy it as you please, without further conceiving of yourself as a father, nor as a son, nor even as one who possesses it. This is called "upholding."
Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, from kalpa to kalpa he did not let go of the scroll from his hands; from day to night, there was no moment when he did not contemplate it.
Having received this inspiration, the Master leaped for joy and praised it with a verse: "Three thousand sections of the sūtras have been recited, yet a single phrase of Caoxi has been lost.

If the ultimate meaning of transcending the world is not understood, how can the madness of successive lives be stilled? The metaphors of the sheep, deer, and ox were provisionally established; at the beginning, middle, and end..."
Later, Shanyang remarked, "Who would have known that within this burning house dwells the original King of the Dharma?

The Patriarch said, "From now on, you may truly be considered a monk who recites the sutras. From that time forth, the Master understood the intent and never ceased his recitation and upholding of the teachings.

Chan Master Zhītōng of Shòuzhōu was a native of Ānfēng. Initially, he studied the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* approximately one thousand times, yet he could not comprehend the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
He went to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning. The Patriarch said: "As for the three bodies..."
The pure *dharmakāya* is your nature. The complete *saṃbhogakāya* is your wisdom. The thousands of billions of *nirmāṇakāyas* are your practice.
If one departs from the fundamental nature and speaks of the three bodies separately, it is called having bodies but lacking wisdom.
If one realizes that the three bodies have no self-nature, it is called the four wisdoms of *bodhi*. Listen to my verse: The fundamental nature is inherently endowed with...
The Three Bodies manifest and give rise to the Four Wisdoms; without departing from seeing and hearing conditions, one transcends and ascends to the Buddha-ground.
I shall now explain this for you: believe it with earnest faith and you will never again be deluded. Do not emulate those who rush about in pursuit, speaking of Bodhi all day long.

The Master asked: "May I hear the meaning of the Four Wisdoms? The Patriarch said: "Since you have already understood the Three Bodies, you have naturally clarified the Four Wisdoms. Why ask further?"
This is erroneous. If one were to speak of the four wisdoms separately from the three bodies, this would imply that there is wisdom without a body;
yet such wisdom would, in turn, become non-wisdom. Furthermore, a verse is spoken: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure; The Wisdom of Equality has no affliction in its mind;
The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. Five, eight, six, and seven...

The transformation of cause and fruit involves merely the use of names and conventions, devoid of any substantial nature. If one leaves no attachment to this process of transformation, then amidst all profuse activity, one dwells eternally in the *nāga-samādhi*.
(Regarding the transformation of consciousness into wisdom, the teachings state: the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done;

the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality; and the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Although the sixth and seventh are transformed during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth are transformed at the stage of fruition, it is only their names that are transformed, not their essence. The Master bowed in thanks.

He praised him with these verses: "The three bodies are originally my own essence; the four wisdoms are fundamentally the clarity of my mind. Body and wisdom merge without obstruction, responding to things by assuming forms as required.
To initiate cultivation is entirely deluded movement; to cling to a state is not true refinement. Through the teacher, I have understood the wondrous principle;
at last, the name of defilement has perished."
Chan Master Zhiche of Jiangxi was surnamed Zhang and named Xingchang. He had served as an official in Shanxi during his youth.

Since the division into the Northern and Southern Schools, although the two patriarchs themselves had transcended notions of self and other, their disciples vied with one another in displays of favoritism and animosity.

At that time, the followers of the Northern School established Chan Master Xiu as the Sixth Patriarch, yet they harbored resentment toward the transmission of the robe by Dajian (Huineng), which had become widely known throughout the world. However—
The Patriarch had foreknowledge of this matter and immediately placed eleven *liang* of gold in the abbot’s quarters.

At that time, Xingchang, acting on the instructions of a follower of the Northern School, entered the Patriarch’s room with a blade concealed, intending to do him harm. The Patriarch extended his neck toward him;

Xingchang struck three times with the blade, yet it caused no injury at all. The Patriarch said, "A true sword is not crooked; a crooked sword is not true. It is simply that you have failed to carry it."

"Jin, I shall not take your life. Startled, Xingchang fell prostrate; after a long time he regained consciousness, sought mercy, and repented his transgressions, immediately vowing to leave the household life.
The Master then gave him gold, saying, "Go for now; I fear that the assembly might instead harm you.
You may come at another time under a different guise, and I shall accept you. Having received these instructions, Xingchang fled by night, joined the monastic community, and received full ordination.

Diligent in his practice, one day he recalled the words of the Patriarch and traveled from afar to pay his respects and seek an audience. The Patriarch said, "I have long been mindful of you; why have you come so late?

He replied, "Yesterday I received the Master’s grace in having my offenses pardoned. Although I have now left the household life and engage in ascetic practices, they will ultimately be insufficient to repay your profound kindness.

Is it not only through the transmission of the Dharma and the salvation of sentient beings that one may do so? I have often perused the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet I have not yet understood the meaning of 'permanence' and 'impermanence.'"
[The monk] said, "Master, please be compassionate and briefly explain the meaning of 'permanence' (nitya). The Patriarch said, "'Impermanence' is the Buddha-nature.
'Permanence' is the discriminating mind regarding all phenomena, both good and evil. [The monk] said, "What you have said greatly contradicts the scriptural texts.
The Patriarch said, "I transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal; how would I dare to contradict the Buddha’s scriptures? [The monk] said, "The scriptures state that the Buddha..."
“Nature is permanent,” you said; yet the Master, on the contrary, says it is impermanent. All dharmas, whether good or evil, even up to the bodhicitta, are all impermanent;
yet the Master, on the contrary, says they are permanent. This is contradictory and causes students to become increasingly confused. The Patriarch said:
“In the past, when I heard the nun Wujinzang recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* once, I immediately expounded its meaning for her.”
There is not a single word or a single meaning that does not accord with the scriptural texts; even for you, I have never given two different teachings.
[The student] said, "My capacity for understanding is shallow and dull; I pray that the Master will explain this in detail. The Patriarch said, "Do you know? If Buddha-nature were permanent..."
What need is there to further speak of various dharmas, good and evil? Even until the exhaustion of kalpas, not a single person would have given rise to the bodhicitta.
Therefore, what I call impermanence is precisely the Buddha’s teaching of the Way of True Permanence.
Furthermore, if all dharmas were merely impermanent, then every single thing would possess its own self-nature that accommodates birth and death; yet, the nature of true permanence exists.
Because it does not pervade all places, what I call "permanent" is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the true meaning of impermanence.

Compared to ordinary people and non-Buddhists who cling to false permanence, and the followers of the two vehicles who reckon the permanent as impermanent, these together constitute the eight inversions.
Therefore, within the definitive teachings on Nirvāṇa, he refutes those biased views and explicitly proclaims true permanence and true [emptiness].
One delights in the true self and its utter purity. Yet you now rely on the words while turning your back on their meaning;

by taking annihilation as impermanence and determining death to be permanence, you have misinterpreted the Buddha’s final, subtle, and perfect words. Even if you were to read them a thousand times, what benefit would there be?
Xingchang suddenly felt as if he had awakened from a drunken stupor. He then spoke this verse: "Because one guards the mind of impermanence, The Buddha expounds the nature of permanence.
Those who do not understand skillful means Are like those picking pebbles from a spring pond. Now, without applying effort, The Buddha-nature appears before me."
"It was not transmitted to me by a teacher, nor did I myself attain anything. The Patriarch said, "You have now attained thorough penetration; you should be named Zhiche (Voluntarily Penetrating).
The Master bowed in thanks and departed.
Chan Master Zhichang of Xinzhou was originally from Guixi in his native province. He entered the monastic life at the age of seven, with a resolute aspiration to realize the nature.
One day he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch, who asked, "Where have you come from? What do you seek?

The Master replied, "I recently paid my respects to Dadao Wenheshang, who taught me the principle of realizing the nature to achieve Buddhahood; however, I have not yet resolved my doubts. He then proceeded to Jizhou.
He encountered a person who pointed out his confusion and directed him to seek out the Abbot. He prostrated himself, praying, "I beseech you to bestow your compassion and accept me.

The Patriarch asked, "What words did he say? Try reciting them for me; I shall provide testimony for you. The Master said, "When I first arrived there, three months had passed without receiving any instruction.
Because my longing for the Dharma was so intense, I entered the Abbot’s quarters alone during the middle of the night, prostrating and entreating him with grief. Then, Daotong—"
He said, "Do you see empty space? He replied, "I see it. He asked, "In seeing empty space, do you perceive any form or characteristics?
He replied, "Empty space has no shape; what form or characteristic could it have? He said, "Your original nature is like empty space.
When you turn back to observe your own nature, there is not a single thing that can be seen; this is called right view. That there is not a single thing that can be known is called..."
True knowledge is devoid of blue, yellow, long, or short; it is merely seeing the original source as pure, the essence of awakening as perfectly luminous.
This is what is called "seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood," and it is also called the "Land of Ultimate Bliss" and the "Tathāgata’s Knowledge and Vision.

Although the student has heard this teaching, he is still not yet fully resolved and requests the Master’s instruction so that there may be no further stagnation. The Patriarch said: "As for what that teacher [said]..."
I have spoken thus, yet you still harbor views and notions; this is why you have not yet attained realization. I shall now show you a verse:

"To see not a single dharma, yet persist in the view of non-existence, Is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun. To know not a single dharma, yet cling to the knowledge of emptiness, Is like lightning flashing within the vast void.
When such views and knowledge arise in an instant, You mistakenly recognize them; how could you ever understand the skillful means? You—

"When one realizes in a single thought that it was wrong, one's own spiritual radiance will be constantly manifest. Upon hearing this verse, the Master’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and he composed a verse in response:
"Groundlessly giving rise to intellectual understanding, Seeking Bodhi by clinging to forms. If the mind harbors even a single thought of awakening, How can it transcend its former delusion?
The source-body of self-nature is the ground of enlightenment; To follow after illumination is to wander in vain. One does not enter the lineage of the Patriarchs."
The room was vast and empty; he wandered aimlessly toward both ends.
Chan Master Zhidao of Guangzhou was a native of Nanhai. Having first visited the Sixth Patriarch, he asked:

"Since I left home to become a monk, I have studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for over ten years, yet I have not yet understood its great meaning. I pray that the Master will grant me instruction. The Patriarch said:
"What is it that you have not yet understood? He replied, "I am in doubt regarding this: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss. The Patriarch asked, 'In what way do you doubt this?
He replied, 'All sentient beings possess two bodies, namely the physical body and the Dharma-body. The physical body is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing. But as for the Dharma-body..."
It is eternal, yet it is without cognition or perception. As the Sūtra says: "When birth and cessation have ceased, nirvana is bliss. I do not yet understand: which body attains this nirvana?
Which body experiences this bliss? If it is the physical body (*rūpakāya*), then at the time of its death, the four great elements disperse.
It is entirely suffering; it cannot be called happiness. If the *dharmakāya* were quiescent extinction, it would be identical to grass, trees, tiles, and stones—who then would experience happiness?
Furthermore, the *dharmatā* is the essence of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are the function of arising and ceasing.

With one essence and five functions, arising and ceasing are constant. When there is arising, the function emerges from the essence; when there is cessation, the function is withdrawn back into the essence. If one listens...

"Rebirth" refers to the category of sentient beings; it is neither interrupted nor extinguished. If suffering does not permit further rebirth, then one returns forever to quiescent extinction, becoming identical to insentient things.
If this were so, then all dharmas would be suppressed and constrained by nirvana such that they could not even arise;
what joy would there be in that? The Patriarch said: "You are a son of the Śākya; why do you practice the severance of the heterodox?"

To constantly hold such false views and yet discuss the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle—according to your understanding, you claim that apart from the physical body there exists a separate Dharma-body, and that one seeks quiescence by departing from birth and death.
Furthermore, you extrapolate from the permanence and bliss of Nirvana to assert that there is a recipient of bodily sensation.

You should know that this is merely to cling tenaciously to birth and death and to be addicted to worldly pleasures. You must now understand that the Buddha [taught] for the sake of all deluded people who...
The conjunction of the five aggregates constitutes the characteristic of the self-substance; the discrimination of all phenomena constitutes the characteristic of external objects.

One takes birth as good and death as evil, migrating and flowing from moment to moment, unaware that these are like dreams and illusions, false and hollow, thereby undergoing the cycle of rebirth in vain instead of [seeking] the eternal bliss of nirvana.
This is instead characterized by suffering. Throughout the day, one rushes about in pursuit [of it]. Out of compassion for this, the Buddha revealed the true bliss of Nirvana:

in each *kṣaṇa* there is no characteristic of arising; in each *kṣaṇa* there is no characteristic of ceasing. Since there is no further arising or ceasing to be extinguished, this is quiescent extinction manifest before one.
At the very moment it is manifest before one, there is even no measure of that manifestation. This is called "eternal bliss. This bliss is without...
There is one who experiences [suffering], yet there is also no one who does not experience it. How could there be such a thing as a single entity with five functions?

How much more so when you speak further of Nirvana as that which restrains and subdues all dharmas, causing them never to arise again? This is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse: [Verse follows]
The unsurpassed Great Nirvana is perfectly luminous, eternally still, and illuminating. The ignorant and foolish call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation;
those seeking the two vehicles regard it as non-action. All these belong to the calculations of the deluded mind—the very root of the sixty-two views.
They falsely establish empty and artificial names; what, then, is the meaning of reality? Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate it without grasping or rejecting;
for they know the phenomena of the five aggregates as well as the "self" within the aggregates, and all external manifestations of forms and every single characteristic of sound.
Equal like a dream or an illusion, one does not give rise to views of ordinary or sage, nor does one form an understanding of nirvana. The two extremes and the three periods of time are severed.

One constantly employs the functions of the sense faculties, yet does not give rise to the thought of such employment. One discriminates all phenomena, yet does not give rise to the thought of discrimination.
When the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and winds drive mountains together in collision, the bliss of true permanence and quiescent extinction—such is the mark of nirvana.
I now speak these words by force to cause you to abandon false views; do not follow the literal meaning of my words, for I permit you to know only a small portion.
Upon hearing the verse, the Master rose with joy, prostrated himself, and withdrew.

The Chan Master Zhenjue of Yongjia, whose name was Xuangjue, was the son of the Dai family from his native district. He entered the monastic order in his childhood and extensively explored the Tripitaka.
He mastered the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of Tiantai’s *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), constantly engaging in silent meditative observation throughout the four modes of deportment.
Later, inspired by the Zen Master Zuo Xi Lang and together with the Zen Master Dong Yang Ce, he traveled to Caoxi.

Upon his initial arrival, he shook his staff, circumambulated the Patriarch three times, and stood there upright. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand subtle practices.
From what direction have you come, Venerable Sir, that you display such great arrogance? The Master replied, "I have come from the place where there is no birth."

"The matter of death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize that which is unborn, so that there would be no swiftness? The Master said, "Realizing it is itself unborn;
understanding its source, there is fundamentally no swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment.
The Master then assumed his full dignified demeanor to pay his respects, and after a short while, took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Your return is very swift."

The Master said, "Since it is fundamentally non-moving, how could there be speed? The Patriarch said, "Who knows that it is non-moving? The Master said, "It is you, O Benevolent One, who give rise to discrimination.
The Patriarch said, "You have deeply grasped the meaning of the non-arising. The Master said, "In the non-arising, how could there be any meaning?

The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who would engage in discrimination? The Master said, "Discrimination itself is not a matter of meaning. The Patriarch sighed in praise and said, "Excellent!"
"Excellent! Excellent! Stay for one night. Thus he was called "One-Night Awakening" (Yi-xiu-jue). The Master descended the mountain the following day and returned to Wenzhou.

Students gathered there like spokes converging at the hub. He composed the *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*) and the *Essential Meaning of Enlightenment and Cultivation in the Chan School* (*Chanzong wuxiu yuanzhi*), which proceed from the shallow to the profound.

Wei Jing, the Regional Inspector of Qingzhou, compiled them and wrote a preface, titling the work the *Yongjia Collection*, which has circulated in the world. *The Aspiration to Seek the Way* (Mudao zhi)
Section One: Rituals for Aspiring to the Way. Now, one who wishes to cultivate the Way must first establish their resolve and observe the proper protocols for serving a teacher;
since these manifest the standards of training, this section is designated as the first to clarify the rituals for aspiring to the Way. Section Two: Guarding Against Arrogance and Indulgence.

Although one may initially establish the resolve to cultivate the Way and properly understand the ritual protocols, if the three karmas are arrogant and indulgent and the deluded mind is disturbed, how can one attain concentration? Therefore, this follows next.
The second [section] clarifies the arrogance regarding precepts (*śīla-mada*). The third [section] concerns the pure cultivation of the three karmas.

Having briefly outlined the essential framework in the preceding section on arrogance regarding precepts, this section now conducts a detailed examination and reproof so that coarse transgressions do not arise; therefore, the third section follows by clarifying the pure cultivation of the three karmas.
Precepts pertain to body, speech, and mind. The fourth [section], the *Śamatha* verses, has already examined body and speech to eliminate coarse [faults].
Errors do not arise. Next, one must enter the gate. Regarding the gradual sequence of cultivating the path, there are no more than five ways of giving rise to the mind and six methods of discernment.
Therefore, the fourth section clearly elucidates the verses on *śamatha*, and the fifth section contains the verses on *vipaśyanā*.

Without morality there is no meditative concentration; without meditative concentration there is no wisdom. Having already cultivated concentration (*samādhi*) above, one’s wisdom becomes clear through long-standing concentration;

therefore, the fifth section clarifies the verses on *vipaśyanā*. The sixth section clarifies the verses on *yuganaddha* (the union of calm and insight). If one cultivates concentration alone, the mind sinks after a long time;
if one studies wisdom alone, the mind becomes restless when wisdom is excessive. Therefore, the sixth section clarifies the verses on *yuganaddha*, which brings them into balance.

Regarding concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*): they prevent one from sinking into dullness or being moved by agitation, ensuring that concentration and wisdom are balanced and that one abandons the two extremes.

This is the seventh stage of the gradual progression of the Three Vehicles. Once concentration and wisdom are equalized, there is stillness while constantly illuminating; with the three contemplations within a single mind, what doubt remains undispelled, and what illumination remains incomplete?

Although one’s own understanding is clear, one feels compassion for others who have not yet awakened. Since there are varying depths of awakening, the third [aspect] is clarified next in the seventh stage.
This refers to the gradual progression. The eighth [section], "The Non-duality of Phenomena and Principle," concerns the three vehicles’ realization of principle.

Since principle is inexhaustible, the thorough investigation of principle resides within phenomena; once phenomena are understood, they are themselves principle. Therefore, the eighth section clarifies the non-duality of phenomena and principle—realizing the truth within phenomena itself—in order to eliminate inverted views.
The ninth, "A Letter of Exhortation to a Friend," states that once phenomena and principle are harmonized, the inner mind naturally becomes luminous. Furthermore, there is compassion...
Distant learning wastes precious moments; therefore, the following nine sections clarify the "Letter of Exhortation to Friends. Section ten is the "Text on Making Vows.
Although the exhortation to friends involves compassion for others, its focus remains concentrated on a single object and the sentiment is not yet universal;

therefore, section ten clarifies the "Text on Making Vows," pledging to deliver all beings. The *Upacāra-gāthā* (Verses on Ritual Conduct) states briefly: "Furthermore, contemplate the mind in ten ways."
Section One: The Gate. First, it speaks of the natural law (*dharmatā*). Second, it sets forth the essence of the contemplation.

Third, it discusses its correspondence. Fourth, it warns against arrogance. Fifth, it admonishes against negligence. Sixth, it reiterates the essence of the contemplation. Seventh, it clarifies right and wrong.
Eighth, it distinguishes the purport of the teachings. Ninth, it demonstrates how to form contemplation wherever one encounters the path. Tenth, it achieves wondrous accord with the profound mystery.

Source. First, regarding the term "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena): Now, the nature of the mind is empty and pervasive; the source of movement and stillness is non-dual. True Suchness transcends thought;
the notions of conditional calculation are not distinct from it. When deluded views proliferate and race about, if one exhaustively investigates them, there is only a single tranquility.

The numinous source has no fixed form; when reflected upon, it appears as a thousand differences. Because these thousand differences are not the same, the name "Dharma-eye" is established. [Yet] that single tranquility...

They are not different; thus the designation of the "Wisdom Eye" (prajñā-cakṣus) endures. When both principle and quantity are simultaneously extinguished, the efficacy of the "Buddha Eye" (buddha-cakṣus) is fully realized.

Therefore, within the single realm of the three truths, the principle of the Dharma-body is eternally pure; within the single mind of the three wisdoms, the illumination of Prajñā is eternally radiant.

Object and wisdom merge in profound stillness; the response of liberation accords with the capacities of beings. It is neither vertical nor horizontal; it is the mysterious convergence of the Way of the Perfect *i*.
Thus we know that the wondrous nature of the three virtues is perfectly in accord with the one mind. Profound and vast, inconceivable—what essential means could possibly not be the path?
Therefore, those who take this very mind as the Way may be said to have traced the current back to its source. Part Two.
As for the essence of this contemplation: one simply knows that a single thought-moment is both empty and not empty, neither empty nor not empty.
Regarding the third point, its correspondence: when the mind corresponds with emptiness, then whether there is slander or praise, what cause is there for sorrow or joy?

When the body corresponds with emptiness, then whether it is cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, what cause is there for suffering or pleasure? When the external environment corresponds with emptiness, then as for giving...
Regarding giving and taking away, what is gained and what is lost? When the mind corresponds with both emptiness and non-emptiness, attachment and views are entirely forgotten;
compassion universally rescues others. When the body corresponds with both emptiness and non-emptiness, internally it is like a withered tree, yet externally it manifests dignified deportment.

When the environment and its resources correspond with both emptiness and non-emptiness, craving and seeking are forever severed, while wealth and goods are used to provide for and relieve others. When the mind corresponds with emptiness—
When emptiness corresponds with that which is neither empty nor non-empty, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is first revealed, and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened.
When the body corresponds with that which is empty, non-empty, neither empty nor non-empty, then a single mote of dust enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), and all motes arise in samādhi.

When the dependent retribution corresponds with emptiness, non-emptiness, neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, then the fragrant terraces and jeweled pavilions adorn the land for those born through transformation.
Fourth, this warns against those who harbor arrogance; if it were otherwise, then one would not be in correspondence.
Fifth, this admonishes those who are negligent; yet, to cross the sea, one must board a ship—without a ship, how could one cross? Thus it is with the cultivation of the mind.
One must enter into contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Without contemplation, there is no means to clarify the mind. As long as the mind is not yet clarified, when will you attain realization?

Reflect on this and do not rely on your own self-assurance. The sixth point clarifies the essence of emerging from contemplation: one merely knows that a single thought is both empty and non-empty, neither existent nor non-existent;
yet one does not know that the very thought is itself empty and non-empty, neither non-existent nor non-non-existent. The seventh point clarifies...
Regarding this right and wrong: the mind is not "is," nor is it "is not"; the mind is not "not-is," nor is it "not-is-not. To say "it is" or "it is not" is to fall into "is";
to say "it is not-is" or "it is not-not-is" is to fall into "not-is. Such [positions] are merely the negation of right and wrong;

they have not yet reached the non-negation of right and wrong, nor the affirmation of that which is neither right nor wrong. Now, by means of the double negation, one refutes both "is" and "is not," and by refuting "is," one refutes "not-is."
This is still "is" and "is not. Furthermore, by means of a double negation, one refutes both negations; the negation refutes the negation, and that negation is itself "is.
Such "is" is merely the "is" of the non-is and non-non-is; it is not yet the non-non-is of non-is, nor the non-not-is of non-is.
The delusion of right and wrong is subtle and difficult to perceive; only when the spirit is clear and the mind is tranquil can one examine it minutely.

Regarding the eighth section, which clarifies its essential meaning: yet the ultimate principle is wordless, so we rely on words and phrases to elucidate its intent. This fundamental intent is not something to be grasped through mere observation.

One relies on the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to realize its fundamental principle (*tattva*). If the purport is not yet clear, then the words are not yet precise; if the fundamental principle is not yet realized, then the contemplation is not yet profound.

Only through profound contemplation does one realize the fundamental principle, and only through precise words is the purport necessarily clarified. Once both the purport and the fundamental principle are clearly realized, how could words and contemplation still persist?

Ninth, regarding "realizing contemplation wherever one encounters [an object]": Now, [...]* *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "Now," indicating the fragmentary nature of the excerpt.*
The words are restated and the essence of contemplation is reiterated; this is because one wishes to clarify that the fundamental principle is no different.

To say that contemplation shifts according to the method is to mean that while the words shift, the underlying principle does not differ. To change the term "contemplation" is to mean that the essential meaning of contemplation remains unchanged. This unchanging essence is precisely the principle.
The principle of non-differentiation is the fundamental tenet (*zong*). While the tenet is one, it has two names; "contemplation" (*guan*) is merely mentioned to serve as an introductory lead-in.

Regarding the tenth point, "Mysteriously Accord with the Profound Source": Now, a practitioner who has awakened to the mind would never cling to contemplation while remaining confused about the essential meaning.

How could a person who thoroughly understands the teachings remain stuck in words and be deluded regarding the principle? Once the principle is clarified, the path of language is severed; how then can words be used to discuss it? This is the essential meaning.

When they meet, the sphere of mental activity ceases; how could any contemplation be able to conceive of it? That which cannot be conceived by mind or speech may be called a wondrous accord with the center of the ring.
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month of the Gui-chou year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang Emperor Minghuang, he sat peacefully and passed away.
His stupa was erected on the southern slope of the Western Mountain, posthumously titled Great Master Wu-xiang (Formless), and his stupa was named Jing-guang (Pure Light).

Chan Master Benjing of Sīkōng Mountain was a native of the Zhang clan from Jāngzhou. Having donned the black robes at a young age, he received a prediction of enlightenment in the presence of [the Sixth Patriarch] at Cáoxī.

He was affiliated with Wúxiàng Monastery on Sīkōng Mountain. In the third year of the Tiānbão era of the Táng dynasty, Emperor Xuānzōng dispatched the palace messenger Yáng Guāngtíng to enter the mountains to gather *chángchūn* (evergreen) vines;
consequently, he constructed a hall for the Master. Paying his respects, the messenger asked: "I, your disciple, admire the Way."

"It has been a long time. I pray that the Venerable Master will compassionately grant me a brief instruction. The Master said, "The eminent scholars of the Chan school throughout the empire have all assembled in the capital.
Since you are returning to court as an imperial envoy, you should consult them for a definitive resolution. I, a poor monk, dwell by mountains and beside waters, having no concerns to occupy my mind.
Guangting prostrated himself in tears. The Master said, "Cease your salutations to this poor monk. Does the imperial envoy seek the Buddha, or do you seek the Way?"
The disciple said, "My wisdom and understanding are clouded and dull. I do not yet comprehend the meaning of 'Buddha' and 'the Way' (dharma). What are their respective significances?

The Master said, "If you wish to seek the Buddha, then the very mind is the Buddha. If you wish to realize the Way, then no-mind is the Way. The disciple asked, "In what way is the very mind the Buddha?
The Master replied, "The Buddha is realized through the mind; the mind is manifested by the Buddha. If one realizes no-mind, even the Buddha does not exist."
[The Emperor] asked, "What is meant by 'mindlessness is the Way'? The Master replied, "The Way is fundamentally mindless; mindlessness is called the Way.

If one realizes mindlessness, then mindlessness is itself the Way. Guangting prostrated himself and accepted this with faith. Upon returning to the imperial court, he reported in detail all that he had encountered in the mountains.
The Emperor immediately issued an edict to Guangting to summon the Master to the capital and commanded him to reside at Bailian Pavilion. The following year, in the first month...

On the fifteenth day of the month, he summoned eminent monks and great scholars from the two monastic streets to attend the Inner Sanctuary, where they were to expound the principles of the Buddha together with the Master.
At that time, there was a Zen Master named Yuan, who raised his voice and said to the Master: "Now, in the presence of His Majesty, we shall deliberate upon the fundamental tenets;
one must question directly and answer directly, without resorting to redundant words. According to what the Zen Master perceives, what do you take as [the ultimate]?"
The Master said, "No-mind is the Way. Yuan said, "Since the Way arises because of the mind, how can you say that no-mind is the Way?
The Master said, "The Way is originally nameless; it is because of the mind that it is named 'the Way. If the name 'mind' were real, then the Way would not be empty.

Since the mind, when investigated to its limit, is non-existent, upon what could the Way rely to stand? Both are equally illusory; they are all merely provisional names. Yuan said, "Chan Master, you see existence..."
"Are body and mind the Way? The Master said, "The mountain monk’s body and mind have been the Way from the very beginning. Yuan said, "Just now you said that 'no-mind' is the Way;
now you say that body and mind are originally the Way. Are these not contradictory? The Master said, "'No-mind' is the Way because when the mind is extinguished, the Way is non-existent.
Mind and the Way are one and the same; therefore, I say 'no-mind' is the Way. Body and mind are originally..."
"Coming is the Way; the Way is fundamentally the body and mind. Since the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty, the Way is likewise exhausted at its source and non-existent.
Yuan said, "Master Guan’s physical form is quite small, yet he understands this principle.
The Master said, "Virtuous One, you see only my form, but you do not see my formlessness. To see form is what you, Virtuous One, perceive. As the Sutra says: 'Ordinary..."
"All marks are entirely false and illusory. If one perceives that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Way.
If one takes marks to be real, one will not be able to see the Way even after the exhaustion of kalpas. Yuan said, "I now request the Master to explain non-mark within the context of marks.
The Master replied, "The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: 'The four great elements have no master; the body likewise has no self. It is free from the view of 'mine.'"

"This accords with the Way. Venerable Sir, if you regard the four great elements as having a master, that is 'self. If you possess such a view of self, you shall not realize the Way even at the end of an eon.
Upon hearing these words from afar, [the monk] turned pale; he hesitated and withdrew from his seat. The Master spoke a verse:

"The four great elements have no master and are like water; Meeting bends and encountering straightness, there is neither 'this' nor 'that. In both purity and filth, no mind arises; Whether obstructed or flowing..."
"How has there ever been a dual intention? When contacting objects, one is simply like water—without mind. Moving freely through the world, what matter is there?

He spoke again: 'The one great element is thus; the four great elements are likewise. If you clearly understand that the four great elements have no master, you will immediately awaken to the absence of mind.
If you comprehend the absence of mind, you will naturally accord with the Way. Zhiming asked: 'If you say that being without mind is the Way, then tiles and pebbles are without mind.'"

"The mind should also be the Way. He further said, "Body and mind are fundamentally the Way. Since all beings of the four modes of birth and the ten classes possess body and mind, they too should be the Way.
The Master said, "Virtuous One, if you understand this through the conceptualization of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, you are worlds apart from the Way.
You are one who seeks seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; you are not one who seeks the Way. As the Sutra says: "No eye..."
The six sense organs—ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are themselves non-existent; upon what, then, can seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing be established?

When traced to their source, they do not exist; where, then, could the mind abide? How could one not be the same as grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles? Ming closed his mouth and withdrew. The Master then spoke a verse:
"Seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are without obstruction; Sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena are always in samādhi. Like a bird in the sky..."
Just so it flies. Without grasping or rejecting, without hatred or love. If you understand that in the place of response there is fundamentally no mind, only then can you be called Avalokiteśvara.
Zhencan asked: "If the Way is indeed without mind, does the Buddha have a mind? Are the Buddha and the Way one or two?
The Master said: "Neither one nor two. [Zhencan] said: "The Buddha delivers sentient beings because he possesses a mind; the Way..."
"I do not save beings, because I am without mind. To say that one saves some and does not save others—how can there be duality?
The Master said, "If you say that the Buddha saves sentient beings while the Way has no saving, this is for you, Great Virtue, to have falsely given rise to dualistic views.
As for me, it is not so. 'Buddha' is a hollow name; 'the Way' is also falsely established. Both are unreal; they are all merely provisional names. One is a provisional [name]."
"Within this, how can one distinguish between two? It is said: 'Buddha' and 'the Way' are both merely provisional names. When these names are established, who is it that establishes them?
If there were someone who established them, how could one say they do not exist? The Master said: "Buddha and the Way are established based on the mind.
If one investigates the mind that establishes them, the mind itself is also non-existent. Since the mind is non-existent, one realizes that both are unreal. Thus he knew.
Like a dream or an illusion, one realizes that all is fundamentally empty. To forcefully establish the two names "Buddha" and "Path" is the view and understanding of those of the Two Vehicles.
The Master then spoke this verse on non-cultivation and non-action: "One cultivates the Path after seeing it; if one does not see it, what is there to cultivate?
The nature of the Path is like space; what can space possibly cultivate? To look everywhere for one who cultivates the Path is like stirring ashes to seek a bubble. But...

Watching the puppet show: when the strings break, everything stops at once. Fakong asked, "If both 'Buddha' and 'the Way' are merely provisional names, then the twelve divisions of the teachings must also be unreal.
Why have the venerable masters of the past all spoken of cultivating the Way? The Master said, "Virtuous One, you have misunderstood the meaning of the scriptures.
The Way is fundamentally without cultivation; you, Virtuous One, are practicing it by force. The Way is fundamentally without action."
