Deqiang’s composition: "The Way is fundamentally without affairs; by striving, one creates many affairs. The Way is fundamentally without knowledge;
within it, one strives to know. Such a view is contrary to the Way. The venerable masters of the past would not have acted thus.

This is simply because you, Great Virtue, do not understand. Please reflect upon this. The Master spoke a verse, saying: "The essence of the Way is fundamentally without cultivation; without cultivating, one naturally accords with the Way. If one gives rise to..."
One who cultivates the mind of the Way does not understand the Way; they abandon the one true nature and instead enter into a state of chaotic turmoil.

If you should suddenly encounter a practitioner of the Way, do not first ask about the Way—ask about peace through meditation (*anśen*). Since the Way is a provisional name, the Buddha said it is established falsely.

The twelve divisions of the teachings are likewise for the purpose of engaging with sentient beings and delivering them across [samsara]; all of these are illusory. What, then, is real? The Master said:

"Because there is illusion, one uses the real to contrast it with the illusory. When one investigates the nature of illusion to its root and finds it to be fundamentally empty, one realizes that the real has never existed either.

Thus, know that both 'real' and 'illusory' are merely provisional names; these two matters are mutual remedies and possess no substantial reality whatsoever. If one investigates their ultimate source, they are one."
"Everything is empty. [The student] asked, "Since you say that everything is illusory, and illusion is identical to the Real, with no distinction between the Real and the illusory, what then is it?
The Master said, "If one speaks of 'what thing,' even 'what thing' is illusory. The Sūtra says there is no mark; it is beyond all comparison."

The path of language is cut off; like a bird flying through the sky, he was filled with shame and submission, not knowing what to do. The Master had a verse that said: "Pushing back to the Truth, the Truth has no marks;
Exhausting the delusion, the delusion has no form. Turning back to examine the mind that pushes back and exhausts, One knows that this mind is also a provisional name.
Realizing the Way is also like this; In the end, it is simply peace. Daxing asked: "The Chan Master’s ultimate subtlety and true reality—" the Master replied, "True."
Delusion and its opposite both vanish; Buddha and the Way are both lost. Cultivating practice is empty in nature; names and forms are not real. The world is like an illusion;
all things are provisional designations. When one understands in this way, one must not sever the two roots of sentient beings—good and evil.

The Master said: "The two roots of good and evil both arise because of the mind. If, upon investigating the mind, it were found to exist, then the roots would likewise not be empty. But since the mind, when scrutinized, is ultimately non-existent, the roots..."
On what basis is this established? A sutra states: "Wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are transformed and born from the mind;

the conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma are fundamentally without reality. The Master has a verse that says: "Since the wholesome arises from the mind, how could the unwholesome be apart from the mind? Wholesomeness and unwholesomeness are but external conditions."
"In reality, it does not exist within the mind. When evil is abandoned, where does it go? When good is grasped, who is there to guard it? Alas for those caught between dualistic views;
they run back and forth, clinging to both ends. If one awakens to the fact that the mind is fundamentally non-existent, only then will one repent of former faults.
Furthermore, an attendant asked: "From where does this body come? After a hundred years, where does it return? The Master replied: "It is like a person..."
"When one is dreaming, from where does it come? When one has awakened, to where does it go? [The Master] replied:

"When dreaming, one cannot say it is non-existent; once awakened, one cannot say it exists. Although there is existence and non-existence, its coming and going have no fixed location. The Master said: "This body of mine—"
It is also just like a dream. The Master had a verse that says: "Viewing life as being like a dream—within the dream, there is indeed clamor.
Suddenly awakening, all affairs cease; it is just like the realization one has while still sleeping. The wise understand the dream upon awakening; the deluded believe the dream to be real clamor.

Understanding the dream and the awakened state are as if two different things, yet once awakened, there is no separate awakening. Between wealth and honor and poverty and lowliness, there is no path of distinction. —Tang Suo.
Master Zong passed away in the year of Xinyou during the Upper Yuan era; he was posthumously titled Chan Master Daxiao.
Chan Master Xuance was a native of Jinhua in Wuzhou. While traveling, he arrived at Hesuo, where there was a man named Zhihuang.

He once visited Huangmei and claimed to have attained true meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Master [Huineng] knew that Huáng’s realization was not yet authentic, so he went to him and asked, "What are you doing sitting here?
Huáng replied, "I am entering meditative absorption. The Master said, "When you say you have entered the chamber, is there a mind or is there no mind?"
"If there were a mind, all classes of wriggling and moving creatures would surely attain concentration.

If there were no mind, even all things such as grasses and trees should likewise attain concentration. [The Master] said: "When I am truly entering concentration, I do not perceive the existence of a mind characterized by 'being' or 'non-being.
The Teacher said: "Since you do not perceive the existence of a mind characterized by 'being' or 'non-being,' this is constant concentration; how could there be entering and exiting?"
"If there is any coming or going, it is not Great Samādhi. Huíng remained silent for a long while, then asked, "Whom does your teacher follow?
The Master replied, "My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi. Huíng asked, "What does the Sixth Patriarch take to be meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi)? The Master said, "My teacher says:

'The wondrous, profound, and perfectly quiescent essence and its function are as they are (tathatā). The five aggregates are fundamentally empty; the six sense objects do not exist. There is no emerging and no entering.'"

"Concentration is non-distraction; the nature of dhyāna has no abiding, so it is detached from the stillness of abiding in dhyāna. The nature of dhyāna is non-arising, so it is detached from the conceptualization of arising in dhyāna.
The mind is like empty space, yet even the measure of empty space does not exist. Upon hearing this teaching, Xuánhuáng went to Caoḳī to request a resolution of his doubts and obscurations;
there, the Patriarch’s intent and the Master’s realization were in profound accord, and Huáng finally attained awakening. The Master later returned to Jīnhuá. Great...
The Dharma assembly was opened.
Chan Master Zhihuang of Hebei first visited the Fifth Patriarch; although he had once sought his instruction and resolution, he followed a gradualist approach.
He then went to Hebei, where he built a hermitage and sat in long-term meditation for over twenty years without showing even a trace of indolence. Later, he encountered Xuancè.
Inspired, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. Moved by his journey from afar, the Patriarch granted him instruction and resolution.
At these words, the Master attained a sudden and profound realization; the mind he had cultivated for the preceding twenty years vanished entirely, leaving no trace.
That night, lay devotees and commoners in Hebei suddenly heard a voice in the air saying, "Chan Master Huang has attained the Way today. Later, he returned...
The North China Plain was being transformed by the Dharma.

National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang, a son of the Ran family from Zhuji in Yue Province, received the seal of mind-transmission and resided at Dangzi Valley on Mount Baitia in Nanyang for over forty years without descending the mountain. His practice of the Way became renowned throughout the imperial capital during the Tang dynasty.

In the second year of the Shangyuan era of Emperor Suzong, an imperial messenger, Sun Chaolin, was dispatched with an edict to summon him to the capital, where he was accorded the honors due to a teacher.

Initially, he resided at the Xichanyuan (Western Meditation Cloister) of Qianfu Monastery; later, during the reign of Emperor Daizong, he was again invited to stay at Guanzhao Jinglan Monastery for sixteen years.
At that time, the Tripitaka Master Mahākarṇa from India arrived in the capital, claiming to have attained the power of knowing others' minds.

[The Master] possessed the supernormal power of penetrating others' minds. Emperor Suzong ordered the National Teacher to test him. As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw the Teacher, he prostrated and stood to his right.
The Teacher asked, "Have you attained the power of penetrating others' minds? He replied, "I dare not say so. The Teacher said, "Tell me, where am I right now?
He replied, "You, Preceptor, are the national teacher; how could you have gone to Sichuan to see [the Emperor]?"
[The Master] was watching a boat race. After a long while, he asked again, "Tell me, where am I right now?
Zang replied, "You are the National Teacher; how could you be on Tianjin Bridge watching monkeys perform?
After another long silence, the Master asked again, "Tell me, where am I right now? Zang was at a loss. The Master rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox!"

**Essence.** Where does the supernormal power of knowing others' minds reside? [In the *Zang* (Treasury), it is said: A monk asked Yangshan, "When the Tripitaka Master 'Large Ears' came for the third time, why did he not see the National Teacher?

Yangshan replied, "The first two times were when his mind was still engaged with external objects; on the last occasion, he entered the Samādhi of Self-Enjoyment, which is why he did not see him. Furthermore, a monk asked Xuansha, [to which] Xuansha said, "Do you say that during the first two times he saw him?

Xuanjue said: "He saw him during the first two times. Why then did he not see him later? Tell me, where does the point of significance lie? A monk asked Zhaozhou: "Regarding the Tripitaka Master 'Large Ears,' he did not see the National Teacher on the third occasion. I wonder, as for the National Teacher—"

"Where is the Master? The Master said, "He is on top of the Tripitaka Master's nostrils. Later, a monk asked Xuansha, "Since he is on the nostrils, why can't one see him? Xuansha said, "It is precisely because he is too close.
One day, the Master called to his attendant. The attendant responded. Thus he called three times and the attendant responded three times. The Master said, "I thought I had let you down."

"Rather, it is you who have failed me. (A monk asked Xuansha: "What was the meaning of the National Teacher calling for his attendant? Xuansha said: "Rather, it was the attendant who understood. Yunju Xi said: "Now tell me, did the attendant understand or not?
If you say he understood, the National Teacher also said, 'It is you who have failed me. If you say he did not understand, Xuansha also said, 'Rather, it was the attendant who understood.

How do you deliberate upon this? Xuanjue questioned the monk: "In what way did the attendant understand? The monk said: "If he had not understood, how could he have responded in such a manner? Xuanjue said: "You have little understanding. He also said: "If you can deliberate upon this point, then you will know Xuansha. A monk asked Fayan: "The National Teacher called [for his attendant]...")

The attendant asked, "What was the Master’s intention? Fayan said, "Go now; come back at another time. Yunju Xi remarked, "When Fayan spoke thus, did he clarify the National Teacher’s intention, or not?

A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What was the National Teacher’s intention when he called for his attendant? Zhaozhou replied, "It is like a person writing characters in the dark; though the characters themselves do not take shape, the traces of the brushstrokes are already manifest.

Nanquan arrived for an audience. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Jiangxi. The Master said, "Have you brought the portrait of Mazu with you? He replied, "This very one is it."

The Master said, "What about that which is behind you? Nanquan then ceased speaking. (Changqing Ling said, "It is very much like not knowing. Baofu Zhan said, "He nearly failed to reach the Patriarch here.

Yunju Xi of this place said, "These two venerable elders both supported [the truth] from behind; as for Nanquan’s ceasing, did he support it from the front or from behind? Magu arrived to pay his respects.
He circled the meditation seat three times, shook his staff, and stood there. The Master said, "Since you are thus, I am also thus. Magu then...
[The Master] shook his mendicant’s staff. The Teacher rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit, get out! Ascending the hall, he said: "Students of the Zen school should follow the Buddha’s words.
That which is the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle accords with the source of one's own mind. As for that which is not definitive, they do not permit one another;
they are like worms within the body of a lion. Now, if one who acts as a teacher for others involves himself in fame and profit, or opens up heterodox paths, then what of himself and others?"
[This is] beneficial. It is like a master craftsman of the world whose hands are not injured by his adze and axe; it is like the load carried by a fragrant elephant, which a donkey cannot endure.

A monk asked, "How can one attain Buddhahood? The Master said, "Relinquish both Buddha and sentient beings all at once; liberation occurs right where you are. The monk asked, "How does one achieve resonance with this?
The Master said, "Do not think of good or evil, and you will spontaneously see your own Buddha-nature."
[The student] asked, "How does one realize the Dharma-body? The Master said, "Transcend the realm of Vairocana.

[The student] asked, "How does one attain the pure Dharma-body? The Master said, "Do not seek it from the Buddha. [The student] asked, "Which one is the Buddha? The Master said, "This very mind is the Buddha.
[The student] asked, "Does the mind have afflictions? The Master said, "The nature of afflictions is itself detached. [The student] asked, "Is this not severing [afflictions]?"
[The questioner] asked: "Is it so? The Master said: "One who cuts off afflictions (*kleśa*) is called a follower of the Two Vehicles. That afflictions do not arise is called Great Nirvāṇa. [Question:

"Regarding sitting in meditation and observing stillness, how should this be practiced? The Master said: "It is neither defiled nor pure; why should you give rise to a thought to observe the appearance of purity? [Question:
"When a Chan master perceives the empty space of the ten directions, is that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)? The Master said: "It is by means of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*)."
The mind grasps it; this is a perverted view. Question: "If the mind itself is the Buddha, may one still cultivate the myriad practices?

The Master said: "All the Sages were endowed with the two kinds of adornment (dvi-saṃbhāra). How could they deny cause and effect? He further said: "If I were to answer you now, I could not finish even at the end of an eon;
excessive words distance one from the Way. Therefore it is said: 'To have something gained in preaching the Dharma is to be a rustic.'"

The dry bones cry out. To preach the Dharma without anything to be attained—this is called the lion’s roar. Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "The green creeper winds its way straight up to the summit of the cold pine;
the white clouds drift and flow, appearing and disappearing within the great void. All phenomena are fundamentally tranquil, yet it is people who create their own clamor.
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "From the South. The Master said, "As for the spiritual teachers in the South—"

"By what dharma do you instruct people? He replied, "The spiritual friend Jidao of the south says that once the wind and fire [of death] have dispersed, it is like a snake shedding its skin or a dragon changing its bones;
one's original true nature remains perfectly intact and undestroyed. The Master said, "Alas! Alas!"
The Master from the South speaks of a Dharma that is half-born and half-extinguished, saying, "The Master from the South teaches just this.
He asked, "I do not yet know, Master, what Dharma you teach here. The Master said, "In my place here, body and mind are one; outside the body there is nothing else."
[The student] said, "How can you, Master, equate this body of foam and illusion with the Dharma-body?
The Master said, "Why have you entered onto a deviant path? [The student] asked, "In what way have I entered a deviant path? The Master said, "Have you not seen it stated in the teachings:
'If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata'?"
Upon seeing the Tathāgata, Zhang Fen, a practitioner from Nanyang, asked:
"I have heard the Master speak of 'insentient things preaching the Dharma,' yet I have not yet realized the meaning of this matter. I beg the Master to grant me instruction. The Master said:

"If you ask about insentient things preaching the Dharma, you must first understand those insentient things before you can hear my preaching of the Dharma. You should simply go and listen to the insentient things preaching the Dharma. Fen said:
"Simply taking the present expedient means of sentient beings as our standard, what is the condition of the insentient? The Master said:
"Within all current activities and functions, whether among the two streams of ordinary people and sages, there is not the slightest arising or ceasing;

this is precisely 'transcending consciousness. It does not belong to existence or non-existence. There is a vibrant seeing and perceiving, yet one hears only that there is no attachment to emotional consciousness. Therefore..."

The Master said, "What is it? The monk had no reply. He asked, "What is liberation? The Master said, "All dharmas do not encounter one another; they are liberated in their own place.
[The monk] said, "If that is so, then they must be severed. The Master said, "I told you that all dharmas do not encounter one another.
What is there to sever? When the Master saw a monk approaching, he made a circular gesture with his hand and wrote the character for "sun" within it.
[The Master] wrote [the character]. The monk had no reply. The Master asked Benjing, "In the future, when you encounter extraordinary words, how will you respond?
Jing said, "I shall have not a single thought of attachment. The Master said, "This is a matter for your own house.
Emperor Suzong asked, "What Dharma did you obtain at Caoxi? The Master said, "Does Your Majesty see that single cloud in the sky? The Emperor said, "I see it."
The Master said, "It is nailed down and hung up. The Emperor asked again, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies?
The Master rose and stood, saying, "Do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Hand the pure pitcher to this old monk.
The Emperor asked again, "What is the Samādhi of Non-contention? The Master said, "Donor, you are walking upon the crown of Vairocana’s head."
The Emperor said, "What do you mean by this? The Master replied, "Do not mistake it for your own pure *dharmakāya*.
Whenever the Master was in the presence of the Emperor, he never looked at him. The Emperor said, "I am the Son of Heaven of the Great Tang; why do you pay me no heed at all?
The Master replied, "Do you see empty space? The Emperor said, "I see it. The Master said, "Does it ever blink its eyes and look at Your Majesty?"
"No. Yu Junrong asked, "When you, Master, dwell on Mount Baitia, how do you cultivate the Way throughout the twelve periods of the day?

The Master called a youth forward, rubbed his head, and said, "When it is alert, speak directly that it is alert; when it is clear, speak directly that it is clear. In the future, do not allow yourself to be deceived by others.

Chan Master Shenhui of Heze in the Western Capital was the son of Gao of Xiangyang. At the age of fourteen, he became a śrāmaṇera and went to visit the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch said, "My friend has come from afar with great hardship. Do you bring your original nature?

If you have this original nature, you ought to recognize its master; try to explain it to me. The Master replied, "Taking non-abiding as the foundation, seeing is itself the master. The Patriarch said, "This śrāmaṇera..."
"Mi," [the Master] said. "How can you speak so casually? He struck him. Under the staff, the Master reflected: "A great spiritual friend is difficult to encounter throughout kalpas.
Now that I have met one, how could I spare my own life? From then on, he served him. Later, the Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have an object that has no head and no tail, no name and no character, no back and no face. All of you..."
"Do you still recognize it? The Master then stepped forward and said, "This is the original source of all dharmas; this is the Buddha-nature of Shenhui.
The Patriarch said, "I told you that it has no name and no character, yet you immediately call it the 'original source' and 'Buddha-nature.
The Master bowed and withdrew. The Patriarch said, "In the future, even if this boy covers his head with a mere tuft of straw, he will achieve nothing more than intellectual understanding."
The patriarch’s disciple subsequently went to the Western Capital to receive the precepts. During the Jinglong era of the Tang dynasty, he returned to Caoxi to read the Tripitaka.
Having encountered doubts regarding six passages within it, he questioned the Sixth Patriarch. First, he asked about precept, concentration, and wisdom, saying:
"What is the substance of the precepts one employs? From where does concentration (samādhi) arise? From what cause does wisdom (prajñā) emerge? What is it that the vision does not penetrate?
The Patriarch said: "Concentration is the settling of the mind; the precepts are the restraining of conduct. When the nature is constantly illumined by wisdom, one sees for oneself and knows deeply.
The second question: "What is the thing that was originally non-existent but now exists? What is the thing that was originally existent but now no longer exists? [Recite.]
The sutras do not perceive the meaning of existence or non-existence; it is like one already riding a donkey who goes about searching for another donkey.

The Patriarch said: "The evil karma of the preceding thought was originally non-existent; the good arising in the succeeding thought is now existent. If you constantly practice wholesome deeds in every thought-moment, you will soon attain the state of humans and devas.
You are now listening correctly to my words; I am precisely that which was originally non-existent and is now existent. Third question: "If one uses arising to extinguish extinction, then using..."
To extinguish extinction is to extinguish birth; failing to understand the meaning of birth and extinction, what one perceives is like being deaf and blind.
The Patriarch said: "Using birth to extinguish extinction prevents people from clinging to their nature; using extinction to extinguish birth causes the mind to depart from its objects.

Yet, this does not immediately leave behind the two extremes; it merely removes the sickness of birth and extinction. The fourth question: Is it sudden first and gradual later, or gradual first and sudden later? No.
Those who understand the sudden and the gradual are constantly bewildered and distressed in their hearts. The Patriarch said: "In the teaching of the Sudden, there is the Gradual;

in the realization of the Dharma, there is the Sudden within the Gradual; in cultivation, there is the Gradual within the Sudden; and in the attainment of fruition, there is the Sudden within the Gradual. Sudden and gradual are constant causes;

thus, one is not bewildered or distressed within awakening. The fifth question: "Is it wisdom first and concentration later, or concentration first and wisdom later? Which arises first, concentration or wisdom? Which is correct?"
The Patriarch said: "Always give rise to a pure mind; within meditative concentration there is wisdom. Be without conceptual mind regarding objects; within wisdom there is concentration.
When concentration and wisdom are equal with no priority, cultivate both together so that one's own mind is correct. The sixth question: "Is it the Buddha first, or the Dharma?"
"First the Dharma, then the Buddha. "The fundamental source of the Buddha-Dharma—from where does it arise? The Patriarch said: "In explanation, one speaks of first the Buddha and then the Dharma;
in listening, one hears of first the Dharma and then the Buddha. But if we discuss the fundamental source of the Buddha-Dharma, it arises from within the minds of all sentient beings.
After the Patriarch’s passing, for twenty years, the sudden teaching of Caoxi remained submerged and neglected.
The [teachings of] Jingzhou and Wuchang, as well as the gradual approach of Mount Song, flourished in the regions of Qin and Luo.

When the Master entered the capital in the fourth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he finally established the two schools—the Southern School of Sudden Enlightenment (Nánéng) and the Northern School of Gradual Teaching (Běixiù)—and composed the *Xiǎnzōng Jì* (Record of Manifesting the School), which became widely circulated throughout the world.

He rebuked the assembly for practicing *prajñā*. As soon as the congregation had gathered, the Master struck the gavel and said, "I trouble you all.
In the Gengzi year of the Shao Yuan era under Emperor Suzong, the Master passed away suddenly; his stupa was erected at Longmen.

Chan Master Guangbao of Mount Meng in Yishui was a successor of Chan Master Heze. He was the son of the Zhou family from Bingzhou. When he first visited Heze, Heze said to him:
[Zhaozhou] said: "Your name is Guangbao (Light-Treasure). A 'name' is the substance determined by its designation; 'treasure' is that which you already possess. 'Light' does not come from without.

Even if you employ it according to your will, there is no lack whatsoever. Throughout the long night, you have been illuminated without interruption. Do you still believe this? The Master said: "I do indeed believe it.
But I wonder, is the light the same as the treasure, or are they different? Zhe said: "The light is the treasure; the treasure is..."

“Master Guang, how can there be such names as ‘sameness’ and ‘difference’? The Master said, “When the eyes and ears perceive forms and sounds, do they proceed independently, or do they interact with one another?
Dazhe said, “Setting aside for a moment the question of independence and interaction, what dharma do you point to as the substance of form and sound?”
The Master said, "According to what you have said, there is no sound or form to be apprehended.

Zhe said, "If you understand that the essence of sound and form is empty, you will also believe that the various faculties—the eyes and ears—as well as the ordinary and the sagely, are all equal and like an illusion.

Their oppositions and mutual interplay are clearly manifest in principle. Thereupon, the Master attained realization, paid his respects, took his leave, and departed. He had previously been in seclusion at Mount Meng by the Yi River.
He entered parinirvāṇa in the second year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty.
