Chan Master Zongmi of Mount Gui at Zhongnan Mountain was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuan of Suizhou. He was the son of the He family from Xichong in Guozhou. His family was originally of great wealth and status.

Having mastered Confucian classics by the age of seven, he explored the Buddhist scriptures upon reaching adulthood. In the Dinghai year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang Dynasty, as he was about to go to the imperial examinations, by chance—
He went to the Yuan Dharma-seat in Suizhou, where he felt a joyful resonance with the teachings. He subsequently requested ordination and received full precepts in that same year.
One day, while following the assembly of monks for a meal at the home of Ren Guan, a local official, he sat in a low position and received the scriptures in order.

Upon obtaining the twelve chapters of the *Nirvāṇa-samavasaraṇa-parivarta* (The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra), he had not yet finished reading the scroll when he was moved to tears by a profound realization. Returning home, he reported the essence of his awakening to Yuan.
Enchin patted him on the head and said, "You shall greatly propagate the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden (en-don). These are the instructions of all the Buddhas bestowed upon you.
Go now; do not remain stagnant in a single corner. The Master wept as he received this command, prostrated himself in farewell, and departed.
He then went to visit Nanyin Chū, who remarked, "This is a man who transmits the teachings. He ought to propagate them in the imperial capital. Subsequently, he met Hōkoku Shō in Rakuō.
Zhao said, "He is a bodhisattva; who could possibly recognize him? He traveled north to Mount Qingliang, and upon his return, resided at Caotang Monastery in Hu County.
Not long after, he entered the Lanruo Hermitage on Mount Zhongnan at Guifeng. During the Dazhong era, he was summoned to the imperial court and granted purple robes.

The Emperor repeatedly questioned him on the essentials of the Dharma, and court officials looked up to him with devotion. Among them, the Chancellor Pei Xu was particularly one who had penetrated the innermost sanctum of his teachings.
The Master, observing that scholars of Chan and the teachings were mutually disparaging one another, subsequently composed the *Chan Yuan Zhu Quan* (Explanations of the Various Sources of Chan).
He transcribed the accounts of various schools to elucidate the fundamental source of the Chan gate, compiling them into a single work to bequeath to future generations. Its preface states briefly:

"Chan is a term from India; in its full form it is called *dhyāna*. In Chinese, this is translated as 'cultivation through contemplation' (*sīwéi xiū*), and is also called 'tranquil reflection' (*jìnglù*)."
These are all general designations for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). "Source" refers to the fundamentally awakened true nature of all sentient beings;

it is also called Buddha-nature and also called the mind-ground. Awakening to it is termed wisdom; cultivating it is termed concentration. Concentration and wisdom together are collectively termed *dhyāna*.
This nature is the fundamental source of dhyāna; therefore, it is called the "Source of Dhyāna" (Chanyuan). It is also termed "dhyāna" (channa). Regarding "principle and practice":
this fundamental source is the principle of dhyāna, while forgetting the emotions to accord with it constitutes the practice of dhyāna; hence, it is called "principle and practice.

However, among the various works compiled here by different masters, most discuss the principles of dhyāna while little is said regarding its practice. Therefore, I have provisionally titled this work "The Source of Dhyāna. Now...

At that time, there were some who identified the true nature (*tathatā*) alone as *dhyāna*. This was a failure to comprehend the essential meaning of principle and practice, and it also failed to distinguish between the linguistic conventions of China and India.

However, it is not that there is a separate essence of *dhyāna* apart from the true nature. It is simply that when sentient beings are deluded regarding the true nature and unite with sensory dust (*rajas*), they are termed "distraction" (*vikṣepa*).

When they turn their backs on the dust and unite with the true nature, they are then termed "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*). If one discusses the fundamental nature directly, it is not [the case that the two are different].
It is true and not false; it is neither opposed nor conjoined; it is neither fixed nor chaotic. Who would call this "dhyāna"?

Moreover, this true nature is not only the source of the Dhyāna gate, but also the source of all dharmas; therefore, it is called *dharmatā*. It is also the source of the delusion and enlightenment of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. The *ālayavijñāna* (as set forth in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*) is also the [source] of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas.
It is the source; therefore it is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature), as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other scriptures. It is also the source of the myriad practices of a bodhisattva;
therefore it is called the "ground of the mind" (*cittabhūmi*). As the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the root of practicing the bodhisattva path.

Since the myriad practices do not exceed the six *pāramitās*, and meditation (*dhyāna*) is merely one among these six—specifically the fifth—how could the true nature itself be designated solely as the practice of "one meditation"? Nevertheless...
The single practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the most sublime and wondrous; it can give rise to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) inherent in one's nature.
All subtle functions, the myriad practices and myriad virtues, even down to supernatural powers and radiant light—all these emerge from concentration.

Therefore, those of the Three Vehicles who seek the Noble Path must necessarily cultivate meditation; apart from this there is no door, and apart from this there is no path. As for seeking [enlightenment] through the recitation of the Buddha’s name...

One is born in the Pure Land by practicing the sixteen contemplations of meditation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), as well as the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (recollection of the Buddha samādhi), the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (standing samādhi), and others.

Furthermore, the true nature (*tathatā*) is neither defiled nor pure; there is no distinction between ordinary beings and sages. However, within the gate of meditation, there are levels of shallowness and depth, with distinct stages and grades.

It is said that those who practice while harboring heterodox views, rejoicing in higher realms and loathing lower ones, are practitioners of non-Buddhist meditation (*tīrthika-dhyāna*). [In contrast,] correct faith...

To practice by means of both delighting in and loathing [the results] regarding cause and effect is the dhyāna of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). To practice having realized the principle of the partial truth of the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) is the dhyāna of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
To practice having realized the ultimate truth revealed by the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is the dhyāna of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
If one suddenly awakens to the fact that one's own mind is originally pure and primordially free from afflictions, it is the nature of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
It is inherently complete from the beginning; this mind is itself the Buddha, ultimately without distinction.

For those who practice based upon this, it is the Meditation of the Supreme Vehicle, also called the Tathāgata’s Pure Meditation, also called the Samādhi of One Practice, and also called the Samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the root of all samādhis. If one can cultivate and practice this in every thought-moment, one will naturally and gradually attain a hundred [samādhis].
The "thousand samādhis" transmitted successively from master to disciple within the lineage of Bodhidharma refer to this very Chan.

Prior to the arrival of Bodhidharma, the interpretations of various schools were all based on the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis; eminent monks who practiced these all attained functional efficacy.

Later, Nanyue and Tiantai directed practitioners to cultivate the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation according to the principle of the three truths. Although the doctrinal meanings...
It is most perfectly sublime. Nevertheless, the sequence of its entry points and gateways is nothing other than the various characteristics of the preceding meditative practices (*dhyāna*).

Only that which was transmitted by Bodhidharma is suddenly identical to the Buddha-body and stands in stark contrast to all other approaches; therefore, those who practice this school find it difficult to grasp its essential meaning.
To grasp it is to become a sage and swiftly realize *bodhi*; to miss it is to fall into error and quickly enter the mire and ashes of suffering. Thus spoke our former patriarchs.

To prevent the loss of what is obscured by ignorance, one person was first entrusted with the transmission to another; thus, later generations had something upon which to rely, and so a thousand lamps were permitted to illuminate one another.

However, as the Dharma became long-established and fell into decline, errors and misconceptions became numerous. Consequently, among those who study the sūtras and śāstras, instances of doubt and slander are also many. To examine the origin of this:
the Buddha taught both the sudden (sudden) and gradual teachings, and Chan opened both the sudden and gradual gates. These two teachings and two gates each...

They are in accord with one another. Yet nowadays, those who lecture on the sutras emphasize exclusively the meaning of the gradual path, while those who practice Chan propagate exclusively the Sudden school.

When a Chan practitioner and a lecturer meet, they are as far apart as Hu and Yue. As for Zongmi, I do not know what he did in his past lives to have been perfumed with such a mind; yet, he himself has not attained liberation.
Desiring to untie the bonds of others, he risked his own life for the sake of the Dharma; his compassion for humanity was more urgent than his own spirit.

He often lamented that people and the Dharma had diverged, and that the Dharma was becoming a sickness for people. Therefore, he separately compiled commentaries on the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, widely opening the gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom.

He manifested sudden enlightenment while supporting gradual cultivation, verifying that his teachings accorded with the Buddha’s intent. Having thus exhaustively revealed the meaning from beginning to end, [he passed away].

The texts are vast and profound, difficult to fathom; though those who study extensively are many, those who maintain their resolve are few. Moreover, when one's traces involve names and forms (*nāma-rūpa*), who can distinguish gold from brass?

One merely exhausts oneself without yet perceiving the stirrings of spiritual resonance. Although the Buddha taught that increasing compassion is the true practice, I feared that attachment and false views would be difficult to guard against.

Consequently, I abandoned the multitude to enter the mountains, practicing concentration (*samādhi*) and cultivating wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, my periods of stilling the mind followed one after another.
Following ten years, the subtle habitual tendencies of arising and ceasing became manifest within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);

the various meanings of the Dharma were arrayed, appearing within the empty mind like fine dust fluttering in sunlight through a crevice, or like reflections shimmering clearly at the bottom of a limpid pool.

How could this compare to the foolish meditation of those who merely maintain silence, or the frantic wisdom of those who seek only the literal text? Yet, it was fundamentally caused by [the realization of]...

One discerns the various teachings through one's own mind; therefore, one is earnest regarding the Mind-essence (cittagotra). Furthermore, because one understands the cultivation of the mind by means of discerning the various teachings, one is reverent toward the meaning of the teachings.
As for "Teachings" (jiao), these are the sūtras and śāstras left behind by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

As for "Chan," these are the verses and gāthās composed by the various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). However, the Buddhist sūtras are expansive, encompassing the eight directions of the great trichiliocosm.

This compendium of Chan verses is an abridgment intended for those of a certain disposition in this region. If one were to include every detail, the collection would be so vast and sprawling as to be difficult to rely upon;

by focusing instead on the specific needs of the practitioner, it provides clear guidance that is easy to apply. This present compilation is intended precisely for this purpose. Pei Xiu wrote its preface, stating:

"Under each of the various schools there are men of realization; yet each remains content with what they have practiced, such that those who achieve thorough mastery are few while those who remain narrow and limited are many."
Thus, for several decades, the methods of the masters have fallen further into decay. Taking the lineage of transmission as their own private doors, each has opened them wide;
taking the sūtras and śāstras as their weapons, they attack one another. Their sentiments shift back and forth like arrows and halberds; the Dharma rises and falls according to their personal egos.
Right and wrong are entangled in confusion, unable to be distinguished. This being so, how could the World-Honored One, the Bodhisattvas, and the various... [of former times]...?
The Master’s teaching was merely sufficient to incite disputes among later generations and increase the maladies of affliction; what benefit was there in it?
My late master, Guifeng, sighed for a long time and said, "I have arrived at this time and cannot remain silent.

Thereupon, he used the three types of doctrinal teachings of the Tathāgata to seal the three types of dharma-gates of the Chan school, melting the vase, the basin, the hairpin, and the bracelet into a single gold.

Churning the cream, curd, and clarified butter into a single flavor, he shakes the mainstay so that all who grasp it follow, and those who come according to the essential principles find themselves on the same path.
Yet, fearing that students might still find this difficult to clarify, he further directly demonstrates the beginning and end of the source of the school,

the harmony between the real and the false, the concealment and manifestation of emptiness-nature, the distinctions among dharmas and meanings, and the differences between the sudden and gradual approaches.
It is the same regarding the interplay between concealment and revelation, the depth and shallowness of the provisional and the real, and the right and wrong of the universal and the particular.
If one acts as a teacher, holding aloft the sun of the Buddha to shed its light in every direction, all doubts and obscurations will be entirely removed;

following the Buddha’s mind to extend great compassion across all realms, others will receive benefit throughout kalpas. Thus, while the World-Honored One is the master who expounds the teachings, the teacher is the person who synthesizes them; the beginning and the end thus correspond.
The talisman illuminates both near and far; it may truly be said to have fulfilled the essential tasks of the temporal teachings of an entire era.

On the sixth day of the first month of the Xinchou year of the Huichang period, the Master, at Xingfu Monastery, instructed his disciples: "Have my body carried out to be given to birds and beasts; cremate the bones and scatter them.
Do not indulge in grief or longing, lest they disturb your meditative contemplation. Every Qingming festival, he would ascend the mountain to preach the Way.
Seven days [passed]. As for the remaining rules for his residence and conduct, they should accord with the monastic codes (*vinaya*). "Those who violate this are not my disciples.

Having spoken thus, he sat and passed away. Monastics and laypeople alike enshrined his whole body at Mount Guifeng and performed cremation, from which they obtained *śarīra* relics that were brilliant, pure, and large.
Later, his disciples wept as they searched for his remains; they recovered them all from the ashes and embers and enshrined them in a stone chamber.
When Emperor Xuanzong reopened the True Teaching, he posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dinghui (Stabilized Wisdom), and his stupa was named Qinglian (Blue Lotus).
His secular age was sixty-two, and his monastic seniority was thirty-four.
Chan Master Huairang of Mount Heng in Hengzhou was a dharma successor of the Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Dajian. He was a native of the Du family from Jinzhou.

He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the Dingchou year of the Yifeng era of the Tang Gaozong Emperor. A white vapor appeared as an auspicious sign in the celestial phenomena. He was born in the region of Ankang. The Great...

The Grand Astrologer (Shi) observed this and reported it to the Emperor. The Emperor then asked what auspicious omen this was. The Grand Astrologer replied, "This is a vessel of the state's Dharma, untainted by worldly glory.
The Emperor issued an imperial decree to Han Jie, the Governor of Jinzhou, ordering him to go in person to offer condolences to the family.
The family had three sons, of whom the Master was the youngest; he was exceptionally brilliant and his nature was solely inclined toward yielding. His father therefore named him Huai.
When Reng was ten years old, he took pleasure only in Buddhist scriptures.

At that time, the Tripitaka Master Xuanjing visited his home and told his parents, "If this child leaves the household life, he will surely attain the Supreme Vehicle and extensively deliver sentient beings. This occurred during the Bingxu year of the Chuigong era.
At the age of fifteen, he took leave of his parents and went to Yùquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu, where he entered the monastic order under the Vinaya Master Hóngjǐng.

In the year Bǐshēn of the Tiāntōng cycle, he received full ordination. Thereafter, he studied the Piṇī-piṭaka (the Vinaya). One day, he sighed to himself, saying: "Now, one who has left the household life does so for the sake of the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Among all things in heaven and on earth, there is nothing superior to this. At that time, his fellow student Tǎnrán recognized the master’s resolute spirit.
Gaomei exhorted his teacher to visit An of Mount Song. An inspired him, whereupon he traveled directly to Caoxi to attend upon the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch said, "What thing comes in such a manner? The Master was speechless.
He remained thus for eight years until, suddenly, he attained realization. He then said to the Patriarch, "I have reached a point of understanding."
The Patriarch asked, "How is it? The Master said, "To describe it as a single thing is not correct. The Patriarch asked, "Is there still cultivation and realization?
The Master said, "There is no lack of cultivation and realization, yet one must not allow defilement. The Patriarch said, "It is precisely this non-defilement."
"You are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas; as you are thus, so am I. In the prophecy of Prajñātāra from the Western Heaven, it was foretold:
"From beneath your feet shall emerge a colt that will trample the people of the world to death. The Master attended upon him at his side for fifteen years.
In the *Gui-chou* year of the Kaiyuan era, he went to Mount Heng and resided at Panyue Temple. During the Kaiyuan era, there was a śramaṇa...

Daoyi (who was Mazu) was at Mount Heng, where he constantly practiced seated meditation. The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, went to him and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you hope to achieve by sitting in meditation?
Daoyi replied, "I hope to become a Buddha. The Master then took a brick and began rubbing it on a stone in front of the hermitage.
Daoyi asked, "What are you rubbing that brick for? The Master said, "I am rubbing it to make a mirror. Daoyi said, "How can you make a mirror by rubbing a brick?"
"Can a tile become a mirror? The Master said, "If grinding a tile cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation make one a Buddha?

The monk asked, "How then is it so? The Master said, "It is like an ox pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, would you strike the ox or strike the cart? The monk was speechless. The Master spoke again:
"In your practice of sitting meditation, do you study sitting as a Buddha? If you study sitting meditation, then [meditation...]"
"It is not sitting or reclining. If you study 'sitting as the Buddha,' the Buddha has no fixed characteristics; within the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject.

If you sit as the Buddha, that is precisely killing the Buddha. If you cling to the form of sitting, you do not penetrate its principle. Upon hearing this instruction once, [the student] was like drinking clarified butter (*amṛta*).
He prostrated and asked, "How should I apply the mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi? The Master said, "You..."

"Study the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. It is like a seed sown below; my teaching of the essential Dharma is like the rain from heaven. Because your conditions have converged, you shall perceive the Way.
He asked again, "The Way has no form or characteristics; how can it be seen? The Master said, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way.
It is the same with the signless samādhi. Another asked, "Is there arising and ceasing? The Master said: [The text here indicates the Master’s response follows].
He said: "If one perceives the Way through formation and destruction, gathering and dispersal, that is not seeing the Way. Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds;
When meeting moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is without form; What is there to destroy, and what is there to form? Once he received this awakening, his mind became transcendent.
He served [the Master] for ten years, and day by day he grew more profound and subtle. [He was thus named] an Inner Disciple.
There were six disciples, each of whom the Master certified, saying: "You six have collectively realized my person; each has attained one aspect of it.
One man attained my eyebrows—he excelled in dignified deportment (Chang Hao). One man attained my eyes—he excelled in his gaze (Zhida).

One man attained my ears—he excelled in listening to and discerning principles (Tanran). One man attained my nose—he excelled in perceiving the vital breath (Shenzhao). One man attained my... [text fragment]
Tongue. One who is skilled in discourse. (Yanjun) One person attained my mind. Skilled in both ancient and modern [teachings]. (Daoyi) He further said: "All phenomena arise from the mind;
the mind has no place of origin, and phenomena have no place of abiding. If one penetrates the ground of the mind, all actions will be unimpeded.

Unless one encounters a person of superior capacity, one should be careful and sparing in this matter. Question: It is like casting an image in a mirror; once the image is formed, I do not know where the light goes.
"Where have you been? The Master said, "When you were a young boy, Great Virtue, where was your appearance?
[The monk] said, "But after the image was completed, why does it not reflect? The Master said, "Although it does not reflect, it cannot deceive him by even a single point.
Later, when Mazu was spreading the Dharma in Jiangxi, the Master asked the assembly, "Daoyi has been preaching to the community."
“Did he preach the Dharma? the assembly asked. The Master said, “He has already preached the Dharma for the assembly.

The Master continued, “But no one at all has brought back any news. Thereupon, he sent a monk away, instructing him: “When he ascends the hall, simply ask him, ‘What is it? and memorize whatever words he says.
The monk went and acted exactly according to the Master’s instructions. Upon his return, he said to the Master, “Master Ma said, ‘Since—’”

For thirty years after his passing, there was never a shortage of salt and sauce. The Master approved of this. Emperor Minghuang passed away on the *xinchou* day of the eighth month in the *jiashen* year of the Tianbao era.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Mount Heng. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dahui. His stupa was named Zuishenglun (Supreme Wheel).
His secular age was sixty-eight, and his monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*-years) was fifty-four.
The Dharma Successor of Chan Master Nanyue Huairang (First Generation):
Chan Master Mazu Daoyi of Kaiyuan Temple in Nanchang. He was the son of the Ma family from Shifang in Hanzhou. He left home to become a monk at Luohan Monastery in his native district.
His appearance was extraordinary: he walked like an ox and gazed like a tiger; he could extend his tongue past his nose, and there were two marks beneath each of his feet.

Lunwen. He received the tonsure under Master Tang of Zizhou and received full ordination from Vinaya Master Yuan of Yuzhou. During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he practiced *dhyāna* concentration on Mount Heng.

There he met the Patriarch Xiangru (Shenxiu’s disciple), from whom he secretly received the Mind-Seal. (Ru was the first successor of Shenguang [Shenxiu], just as Zhixian was the successor of Sengcan;

though they stem from the same source, they form different lineages. Thus, the flourishing of the Chan Dharma began with these two masters. Liu Ke said: "Jiangxi is presided over by Dayi, and Hunan is presided over by Shitou. Those who come and go in great numbers do not realize that these two Great Beings are the ones responsible.")

The Indian Prajñātāra prophesied of Bodhidharma, saying: "Though China is vast, there is no other path; it must be traversed by the feet of one’s descendants. A golden rooster shall know how to hold a single grain of millet, providing sustenance for the arhats of the ten directions.

Furthermore, the Sixth Patriarch said to Master Ruang: "In the future, the Buddha-dharma shall proceed from your side; a colt shall trample the people of the world underfoot. Subsequently, the Dharma lineage flourished in Jiangxi and spread throughout the land, where he was popularly known as Mazu.
He first moved from Mount Foji in Jianyang to Linchuan, and next to Gonggong Mountain in Nankang. During the Dali era, his name was registered [in the official records].
At Kaiyuan Temple in Zhongling, the Regional Commander Lu Sīgōng heard of the Master’s reputation and, filled with admiration, personally received the core teachings from him.
Consequently, scholars from all quarters gathered at his seat like clouds. A questioner asked: "What is the cultivation of the Way? The Master said: "The Way does not belong to cultivation.
If one says it can be attained through cultivation, then once cultivated, it will eventually perish; this is the same as the Śrāvakas. If one says it is not to be cultivated..."

[The Master] said, "He is the same as an ordinary person. [The questioner] asked, "What kind of understanding must one have to immediately attain the Way? The Patriarch said, "The self-nature is inherently complete.

One is called a practitioner of the Way simply by not being obstructed by matters of good and evil. To grasp at goodness and reject evil, or to contemplate emptiness and enter meditative concentration, belongs to the realm of conditioned fabrication.
If you further seek it outwardly, you will become increasingly estranged and remote. Simply exhaust the mind of the triple world."
[Measurement]: A single thought of delusion is the very root of birth and death within the triple world.
If one simply lacks a single thought, the root of birth and death is eliminated, and one attains the unsurpassed, precious treasure of the Dharma King.

For immeasurable kalpas, the delusions of ordinary beings—flattery, crookedness, depravity, falsehood, self-conceit, and arrogance—have combined into a single entity; thus the Sūtra says: "It is merely composed of a multitude of dharmas."
This body, when arising, is only dharmas arising; when ceasing, is only dharmas ceasing. When these dharmas arise, they do not say "I arise";

when they cease, they do not say "I cease. The preceding thought, the subsequent thought, and the middle thought—thought after thought do not depend upon one another; each thought is quiescent and extinguished.
This is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), which encompasses all dharmas, just as hundreds of thousands of diverse streams all return to the great ocean.
All are called "sea water. Abiding in a single flavor, it encompasses all flavors; abiding in the great ocean, it blends all currents.
It is like a person bathing in the great ocean who uses every drop of water.

Thus, while Śrāvakas awaken from delusion and ordinary beings are deluded regarding awakening, the Śrāvakas do not know that the Sage’s mind fundamentally has no stages, causes, fruits, or hierarchical levels—these are merely the conceptual constructions of the mind's measure.

Cultivating the causes and realizing the fruit, they abide in the samādhi of emptiness for eighty thousand kalpas or twenty thousand kalpas; though they have already attained awakening, they subsequently fall into delusion.
To the various Bodhisattvas, this state appears as painful as the sufferings of hell; they sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence, failing to perceive the Buddha-nature.

If, however, these beings of superior capacity suddenly encounter a spiritual friend who points it out to them, they will comprehend it in a single word and no longer pass through the successive stages and grounds.
In this stage, one suddenly awakens to the fundamental nature. Thus, a sutra says: "Ordinary beings possess a regressive mind, whereas śrāvakas do not.
This is said in contrast to delusion; since there is fundamentally no delusion, awakening cannot be established either. All sentient beings, from immeasurable kalpas past...
He does not emerge from the samādhi of the dharma-nature; he remains perpetually within the samādhi of the dharma-nature.

Whether putting on clothes or eating food, whether engaging in conversation or responding to others, whether the six sense organs are active or performing any action whatsoever—all is entirely the dharma-nature. Failing to understand how to return to the source, you follow names and pursue appearances;
deluded sentiments arise falsely, and you create all manner of karma. If you can, for even a single thought-moment, reflect back upon yourself, your entire being will be the sacred mind. You—
All you people, each must realize your own mind; do not merely memorize my words. Even if you were able to explain as many principles as there are sands in the Ganges, your mind would not increase.
Even if you could not explain anything at all, your mind would not decrease. Whether you can explain it or cannot explain it, it is your own mind.
Even if you were to manifest by dividing your body, radiate light, and display the eighteen transformations, it would not equal returning to me.
"Dead ashes come. Ashes that have been doused with water are powerless; this is a metaphor for Śrāvakas who falsely cultivate causes and realize fruits.
Ashes that have not been doused with water are powerful; this is a metaphor for Bodhisattvas whose path and practice are fully matured and who cannot be defiled by any evils.

If one were to speak of the Tathāgata’s provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka, they could not be exhausted even if explained for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges; they are like a chain, never severed. If one awakens to this..."
The Holy Mind has no other concerns whatsoever. I have stood for a long time; take care. Pang Jushi asked:
"Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as companions? The Master said: "I shall tell you once you have swallowed up the waters of the West River in a single gulp.
He asked again: "Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations—please, Master, point directly to the meaning of the West. The Master said: "I am now..."
Dajian had no intention to speak. He said, "Go to Xitang and ask Zhizang. The monk went to Xitang and asked him.
Xitang pointed to his head and said, "I have a headache today; I cannot explain it for you. Go and ask my elder brother Hai."
The monk went to ask his elder brother Hai. Hai said, "When I arrived here, I did not understand. The monk returned and related this to the Master.
The Master said, "Zangtou’s head is white; Hai’s head is black. The Master then ordered a monk to deliver a letter to Qian of Mount Jing. In the letter, he drew a circle.
As soon as Qian opened it and saw it, he took up his brush and made a single dot in the center. Later, a monk brought this up for discussion.
Zhong Guoshi. Guoshi said, "Master Qin is still being deluded by Master Ma. [The monk] asked, "Why did the Master say 'this very mind is Buddha'?
The Master said, "To stop a small child from crying. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when the crying has stopped? The Master said: [He said,] "I tell you, it is not Buddha."
"It is neither mind nor Buddha. [The student] asked, "Setting aside these two types of people, how would you instruct them?
The Master said, "Tell them it is not a thing. [The student] asked, "What if someone who has already realized this comes along?
The Master said, "Simply let him realize the Great Way. [Another] asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "Right now, what is the meaning? The Master [continued].
He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Hunan. The Master said, "Is the water in Dong Lake full yet? The monk said, "Not yet.
The Master said, "After all this time of rain, it is still not full. [Another] asked, "Water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-bushel boat.
How is this principle to be understood? The Master said, "In this place there is neither water nor boat; what talk can there be of sinews and bones?"
The Inspector of Lianzhou asked, "Is it right to eat meat and drink wine, or is it not? The Master said, "If you eat, it is the official’s salary;
if you do not eat, it is the official’s merit. In the first month of the year Wuchen (788) during the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong, the Master ascended Mount Shimen in Jianchang.
While walking for exercise among the trees, he saw that a cave and ravine were level and open, and he addressed his attendant...
The man said, "I, of my withered form, shall return to this land next month. Having finished speaking, he turned back. Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness.
The head of the monastery asked, "How is the Master’s health these days? The Master replied, "The Buddha of the Sun’s Face; the Buddha of the Moon’s Face."

On the first day of the second month, he bathed and entered nirvāṇa while sitting in the full lotus posture. During the Yuanhe era, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Daji, and his stupa was named "Great Adornment.
His secular age was eighty, and his monastic seniority was sixty years.
The second generation descendant of Nanyue,
Chan Master Huaihaim of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou,
a successor of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi, was a native of the Wang family in Changle, Fuzhou. In his childhood, he accompanied his mother.

He entered a temple to pay homage to the Buddha and pointed to a statue, asking his mother, "What is this? His mother replied, "This is the Buddha. The Master said, "Its form and appearance are no different from a human being;
I shall become one like it later. At the age of seven, he left the secular world. He thoroughly mastered the three studies of the Buddhist curriculum.
When Mazu Daoci was propagating the Dharma in Jiangxi, the Master devoted himself wholeheartedly to him as a disciple, along with Xitang Zhizang and Nanquan Puyuan.
They entered the same room together; at that time, the three great adepts stood as peerless pillars.
While the Master was attending Mazu, they were walking along when a flock of wild ducks flew past. Mazu asked, "What is that? The Master replied, "Wild ducks.
Mazu asked, "Where have they gone? The Master said, "They have flown away. Mazu then seized the Master by the nose and twisted it. In agony, the Master let out a cry. Mazu said, "And..."
Dao Fei passed away. Upon hearing these words, the Master attained a realization; he returned to the attendants' quarters and wept bitterly.
A fellow practitioner asked him, "Are you thinking of your parents? The Master replied, "No. [The practitioner] asked, "Were you insulted by someone? The Master replied, "No."
[The colleague] asked, "Why are you weeping? The Master said, "My nostrils were pinched by the Great Master; it hurts unbearably.
The colleague said, "What circumstance is there that does not accord with you? The Master said, "You should ask the Abbot about it.
The colleague asked the Great Master, "Attendant Hai, what circumstance is there that does not accord with you, such that you are weeping in your quarters? Please inform the Abbot on my behalf."
He said this. The Master replied, "It is you who understand; you should ask him yourself.

Later, when they returned to the quarters together, the companion said, "The Master said you understood, so he told me to ask you myself. The Master then laughed heartily. The companion asked, "Just now you were crying;
why are you laughing now? The Master said, "Just now I was crying; now I am laughing. The companion was left bewildered.
The next day, Mazu ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master stepped forward and rolled up his seat. Mazu immediately descended from the seat.
The Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters, where Mazu said, "I have not yet spoken a word;
why did you roll up your seat so abruptly? The Master replied, "Yesterday, I was pinched by the Master until my nose hurt. Mazu asked, "Where did you leave yourself yesterday?"
The Master said, "Does the tip of your nose not ache today? The Patriarch replied, "You have thoroughly understood what happened yesterday.
The Master bowed and withdrew. On another occasion, while standing in attendance during a further visit, the Patriarch looked at the whisk in the corner of his meditation seat.
The Master said, "Is it used right here? Is it apart from being used here? The Patriarch asked, "When you open your two flaps of skin [your mouth] in the future, with what will you teach people?"
The Master took up his whisk and held it upright. The Patriarch said, "Use this very thing, yet remain detached from its use. The Master hung the whisk back in its original place.
The Patriarch let out a thunderous shout, which left the Master's ears deaf for three days. From that time on, the sound of his thundering voice was about to resound.
A donor invited him to the borders of Xinwu in Hongzhou to reside at Mount Daxiong; because the surrounding cliffs and peaks were extremely steep, it was named Baizhang.
Once he had settled there, before even a month had passed, guests seeking instruction arrived from all quarters like a swarm of deer. He asked:
He embraced his uncut jade and went to a master, requesting that the master provide a definitive judgment. The master said, "Last night, a tiger on South Mountain bit a large beast.
The student said, "This does not contradict the true teaching (*zhenquan*). "Why," he asked, "do you not employ skillful means? The master said, "A man who covers his ears while stealing a bell.

The student said, "Without the appraisal of the Marquis of Zhonglang, it remains the same as firewood in a wild shed. The master then struck him and said, "Heaven! Heaven! The master continued, "It can be given..."
The monk said, "Rarely do we encounter one who truly understands. He shook his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "Today Baizhang has lost half the battle.
That evening, an attendant asked, "Why did you stop as soon as that monk refused you?
The Master struck him and said, "Heaven! Heaven! The attendant said, "Rarely do we encounter one who truly understands. The Master said, "I accept this as a formal admission."

Once, a monk entered the Dharma Hall weeping. The Master asked, "What are you doing? The monk replied, "Both my parents have passed away; I ask the Master to select an auspicious day for their burial.
The Master said, "Tomorrow at the hour of the tiger (one o'clock), bury them all at once. A monk asked, "What is the extraordinary matter? The Master said, "Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak.
The monk bowed, and the Master struck him. A monk asked, "How will you act in the future? The Master said, [The text here is incomplete in the source].
He revealed this to the people. The Master [Nanquan] rolled up both sides of his sleeve with his hand and said, "What else is there to do?
The Master [Baizhang] nodded his head three times with his hand. Mazu sent a messenger with a letter and three jars of sauce for the Master.

The Master ordered them to be set out before the Dharma Hall. He then ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master pointed his staff at the jars of sauce and said, "If you can speak, then..."
He did not break it. When [the assembly] said they could not explain it, he broke it. The assembly was speechless, so the Master broke it himself.

He returned to the abbot’s quarters and ascended the hall; as soon as the assembly gathered, the Master drove them away with his staff. He then called out to the assembly, and when they turned their heads, the Master asked, "What is this?
Once, while returning from a communal labor of clearing the fields, the Master asked Layman Yun, "It was no small task to clear these fields."
Huangbo said, "The assembly of monks is performing manual labor. The Master said, "I fear it will trouble your practice. Huangbo said, "How would I dare decline such toil?
The Master asked, "How many fields have you plowed? Huangbo made the gesture of plowing a field. The Master then shouted. Huangbo covered his ears and departed.
Whenever the Master ascended the hall, an old man would follow the assembly to listen to the Dharma. One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, only the old man remained.
The Master asked, "Who are you? The old man replied, "In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain.
When a student asked me, 'Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect? I answered, 'He does not fall within cause and effect.
Consequently, I have been reborn as a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes. Now I beg the Master to provide a turning phrase in my stead, so that I may be liberated."
He was released from this body. The Master said, "Try asking me a question. The old man said, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect?

The Master replied, "One does not obscure cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment. He prostrated himself and said, "I have already cast off my wild fox body. I formerly lived behind the mountain;
I venture to request that you conduct my funeral according to the rites for a deceased monk. The Master ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) to announce it.
Dazhu addressed the assembly: "After the meal, we shall escort the deceased monk. After the meal, the Master led the assembly to the base of a cliff behind the mountain.
Indeed, they found a dead fox there; he then performed the cremation according to the Dharma. That evening, the Master ascended the hall and recounted the preceding circumstances. Huangbo then asked:
"The ancients said that by answering a single phrase incorrectly, one falls into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes. But as for this turning [of the wheel] after turning—"
“Not bad. What do you collaborate upon? The Master said, “Come closer; I will tell you. Baizhang stepped forward and struck the Master with his palm.
The Master clapped his hands and laughed, saying, “I thought the red-bearded barbarian was the only one; it turns out there is another red-bearded barbarian!
Dhyāna Master Sima raised the story of the Wild Fox and asked Attendant Wuyou, “What about this? Wuyou shook the door panels three times. Sima...
Maba said, "How very crude! Zuozhe said, "The Buddha-dharma is not this kind of principle. Guanglu said, "Since beginningless time, one has not been a Buddha;
do not form a conceptual understanding of 'Buddha. Buddha is a medicine for sentient beings; if you have no illness, there is no need to take it.
When both the medicine and the illness are eliminated, it is like clear water. Buddha is like licorice mixed with water, or like honey mixed with water—it is most so."
It is sweet. If one counts [the teachings] alongside clear water, they do not adhere. It is further said:

From the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, all the way to the tenth ground (*daśabhūmi*), whatever consists of words and phrases belongs entirely to the defilement of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*). Whatever consists of words and phrases is entirely subsumed under the side of affliction (*kleśa*).
Whatever consists of words and phrases is entirely of the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is that which upholds; it is not provisional.

The teachings on meaning (artha) concern transgressions; in the Buddha-ground, there is neither maintaining nor violating precepts. Both definitive (nītārtha) and non-definitive (neyārtha) teachings are entirely disallowed. It is further said:
"To be stained by craving for all existent and non-existent objects and phenomena, and to be deluded by all existent and non-existent objects—this is itself the Māra-king.
Illumination and function belong to the subjects of Māra. Only that which is presently reflected upon and awakened to does not rely upon or dwell in any existence."
There are no dharmas—neither mundane nor supramundane dharmas. One neither constructs a dwelling based on intellectual understanding, nor does one dwell in reliance upon non-understanding.

One’s own mind is the Buddha; its illumination and function belong to the Bodhisattva. Mind after mind is the sovereign master; illumination and function belong to adventitious dust. It is further said:

To say that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is likewise to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; to say that sentient beings lack Buddha-nature is likewise to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Furthermore, one slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. If one says that there is buddha-nature, it is called the slander of attachment. If one says that there is no buddha-nature, it is called the slander of falsehood.
As it is said: to say that buddha-nature exists is the slander of exaggeration; to say that buddha-nature does not exist is the slander of depreciation;
to say that buddha-nature both exists and does not exist is the slander of contradiction; and to say that the Buddha neither exists nor does not exist is...

It would be a frivolous fabrication and a slander if I were not to speak; yet, if I were to speak, sentient beings would develop understandings according to their own inclinations, resulting in more harm than benefit. Therefore, it is said: "I would rather not teach the Dharma and quickly enter parinirvāṇa.
However, looking back toward the past, all the Buddhas have taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. Thus, what follows is spoken provisionally and established as a provisional designation.
Names were not originally Buddhas, yet I have told them they are Buddhas. Bodhi was not originally present, yet I have told them it is Bodhi.
Regarding nirvana, liberation, and so forth—I knew they could not carry a load of a hundred piculs, so I gave them a load of only one sheng or one he.

Knowing they would find it difficult to believe the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), I have for now taught them the teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Thus, they have at least attained [something].
When wholesome dharmas prevail, they likewise surpass unwholesome dharmas. When the limit of wholesome fruits is fulfilled, the fruits of evil arrive.
If Buddhahood is attained, sentient beings arrive; if Nirvāṇa is attained, birth and death arrive. If light is attained, darkness arrives.
These are merely the inverted cycles of out-flowing causes and effects; there is nothing that does not reciprocate and present itself. If one wishes to avoid seeing these inversions...
Matters: merely severing both ends of the statement. It is further said: "To not take medicine when ill is the fool; to take medicine when not ill is the śrāvaka.
To dogmatically cling to a single dharma is called a śrāvaka of fixed nature. To be exclusively devoted to much hearing is called a śrāvaka of overweening pride.
To know others is called a śrāvaka in training (śaikṣa). To sink into emptiness, linger in quiescence, and [merely] know for oneself is called..."

For a śrāvaka who has nothing further to learn (*aśaikṣa*), greed, anger, and delusion are the poisons, while the twelvefold teaching of the Buddha is the medicine. If the poison has not yet been digested, the medicine cannot eliminate it;
to take medicine when one is not ill causes the medicine to turn into illness. It is also said: "A śramaṇa observes the fast and maintains the precepts."
Patience, gentleness, compassion, joy, and equanimity are the constant rules for the monastic community.
To understand them in this way is to remain perfectly in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings; it simply means that one must not allow for greedy attachment or clinging.

If one hopes to attain Buddhahood or the dharmas such as Bodhi, it is like a hand touching fire. Mañjuśrī said: "If you give rise to views of a Buddha or views of dharmas, you will surely harm yourself."
It is further said: "From the human stage up to Buddhahood is gain; from the human stage down to hell is loss.
The same applies to right and wrong. The Third Patriarch said: "Gain and loss, right and wrong—let them all go at once. It is also said:

"To cling to the view that one is oneself Buddha, or that one is oneself the Dharma, the Path, or a realized master, is called 'internal view. To cling to the view that one achieves realization through causes, conditions, cultivation, and verification is called 'external view.'"
Master Zhigong said: "To see internally and to see externally are both errors. He further said:

"Those who know the Buddha, see the Buddha, hear the Buddha, and speak of the Buddha are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; yet it is the Buddha who knows, the Buddha who sees, the Buddha who hears, and the Buddha who speaks."
"One in ten thousand. It is also said: "The Buddha enters among all classes of beings and acts as a boat or raft for sentient beings;
he undergoes suffering alongside them, experiencing boundless toil and exhaustion. When the Buddha enters places of suffering, he likewise undergoes suffering together with sentient beings.

The Buddha is simply one who possesses freedom of movement and dwelling, unlike sentient beings. The Buddha is not empty space; how could he not suffer when undergoing suffering? If one were to say he does not..."
"Suffering. These words are contradictory and self-defeating. Furthermore, it is said:

"Right now, simply be without the ten phrases of turbid mind—greedy mind, loving mind, defiled mind, angry mind, grasping mind, dwelling mind, dependent mind, attached mind, seizing mind, and longing mind.
There is only one phrase, yet each contains three phrases; let every one of them pass beyond these three phrases. This is simply all-encompassing illumination and function; let it be as it is."
"Transverse and vertical" refers to all movements and activities—whether speaking or remaining silent, crying or laughing—all are entirely the Buddha-wisdom.
Once, after the Master had finished preaching the Dharma and the assembly was descending from the hall, he called them. The assembly turned their heads; the Master said, "What is this?

When the monk Da finished reading the letter, he asked Zhunyu, "What is meant by 'its vastness is not external'? Zhunyu said, "It does no harm to ask one and receive a hundred answers."
The monk asked, "What is it that is 'solitude is not within'? Nan-yü said, "To perceive sounds and forms is not the work of a master.
The monk then asked Chang-sha; Sha stared at him with wide-open eyes. When the monk repeated his question, Sha closed his eyes to show him.
The monk then asked Chao-chou; Chou made the gesture of eating a meal. When the monk again repeated his question, Chou wiped his mouth with his hand.
Later, a monk brought this up to the Master. The Master said, "These three men will not fail to be my disciples.
Below the mountain of Nanquan, there was a hut-master. Someone said to him, "Recently, the Monk of Nanquan has appeared in the world;
why do you not go to pay him a visit? The master replied, "It is not merely that Nanquan has appeared in the world; even if the thousand Buddhas were to arise, I would still not go."
When the Master heard of this, he sent Zhaozhou to investigate. Upon arriving, Zhaozhou prostrated himself; the host ignored him.

Zhaozhou walked from west to east, and then from east to west, yet the host still paid him no heed. Zhaozhou said, "The grass-robber has been utterly defeated," whereupon he pulled down the curtain and returned.
He reported this to the Master, who said, "I have always suspected this fellow. The following day, the Master was with the monks...

Zhaozhou bowed and departed. Later, the Master went to a village estate. The headman had prepared a reception in advance.
The Master said, "I usually move about without letting anyone know; why have you made such preparations? The headman replied, "Last night..."

The Master then desisted. One day the Master asked Huangbo, "If the world were made of gold and the walls and gates of silver, whose dwelling would this be?

"Where does one person dwell? Huangbo then stood with his hands joined in *añjali*. The Master said, "If you cannot say, why not ask Old Teacher Wang?
Huangbo then asked in return, "Where does another person dwell? The Master said, "What a pity!
The Master asked Huangbo, "Regarding the equal cultivation of concentration and wisdom to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature—what is the principle of this? Huangbo replied, "The twelve hours."

Later, as the Master entered a vegetable garden, he saw a monk and struck him with a piece of tile. The monk looked back, and the Master then lifted his foot.
The monk remained silent. The Master then returned to his quarters. The monk followed him in and, after offering his greetings, said, "Just now, Master, you threw a tile and struck me;
was that not to alert me? The Master replied, "What about when you stood on one foot?"
The monk had no reply. Ascending the hall, the Master said: "Wang Laoshi is selling himself. Is there anyone who will buy him? A monk came forward and said, "I will buy him.
The Master said, "Neither as something precious nor as something cheap—how will you buy him? The monk had no reply.
The Master then went with Guizong and Magu to pay his respects to National Teacher Nanyang. On the road, the Master...
[The Master] drew a circle and said, "If you can express the Way, then you may go. Zong then sat within the circle. Gu bowed like a woman.
The Master said, "In that case, you shall not go. Zong asked, "What kind of mental activity is this? The Master then called out to him, and they returned together;
he did not go further to pay his respects to the National Teacher. While the Master was performing manual labor on the mountain, a monk asked, "Which is the road to Nanquan?"
“Where are you going? The Master picked up a sickle and said, “This sickle of mine was bought for thirty coins.
[The monk] said, “I am not asking about the sickle; where does the road to Nanquan lead? The Master said, “It is very convenient for me to use it.
There was a presiding master (zhu-zu) who took his leave of the Master. The Master asked, “Where are you going? He replied, “Down to the mountains. The Master said—
The Master said, "First, one must not slander the King and the Teacher. The monk asked, "How would we dare slander the Abbot?

The Master then sneezed and said, "How much? The monk immediately went out. One day, the Master closed the door of the abbot’s quarters and surrounded the exterior with ashes, saying, "If anyone can speak a word of response, I shall open it.
Many who attempted to respond failed to satisfy the Master's intent. Zhaozhou said:
"Blue Heaven! The Master then opened the door. While the Master was gazing at the moon, a monk asked, "When will I become like this?
The Master said, "Twenty years ago, I, Old Man Wang, was also like this—what else could there have been? The monk asked, "How about now?"
The Master then returned to his quarters. Grand Councilor Lu Xun asked, "Disciple, I have come from the six realms;
do they still possess bodies there? The Master said, "Keep this clearly in mind and present it to a master.
Lu said, "The Master is inconceivable; wherever you go, the world is perfected. The Master said, "Just now, all of that was a matter concerning you, Grand Councilor. Lu was struck with wonder.
Liu Zhilin said to Master [Linji], "I also have a slight understanding of the Buddha-dharma. The Master then asked, "In the twelve periods of the day, what do you do?
He replied, "Not a thread of silk hangs upon me. The Master said, "You are still a man standing on the steps. The Master spoke again, saying, "Have you not heard it said:
'A sovereign who possesses the Way does not accept ministers who possess mere cleverness'? Later, while ascending the hall, Liu Zhilin said, "I request..."
The Master was preaching the Dharma for the assembly when the Abbot said, "How would you have me preach? The Abbot asked, "Does the Master have no skillful means?
The Master replied, "Tell me, what is it that they lack? The Abbot asked, "Why then are there the six realms and four modes of birth?
The Master said, "I do not teach them. Later, while the Master and Layman Lu were watching people play double-sixes, the Master pointed at the dice and said:
"In such a way, not in such a way, or precisely in such a way—if one proceeds with full conviction, how is it?
The Master picked up a pair of dice and said, "A stinking bone, eighteen. He asked again, "In my home, there is a stone slab upon which I sometimes sit and sometimes lie.
Now, I intend to cast it as a Buddha; would this be permissible? The Master said, "It is permissible. Lu said, "Might it not be permissible?"
The Master said, "It cannot be attained. Zhaozhou asked, "The Way is not outside of things; that which is outside of things is not the Way. What is the Way outside of things? The Master struck him.
Zhaozhou seized the staff and said, "In the future, do not strike people in error.

The Master said, "Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish, but it is difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk. The Master called for the attendant in charge of the monastery. The attendant responded, "Yes? The Master said, "The Buddha [attained] ninety..."

When the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for his mother, King Udayana missed the Buddha and requested Maudgalyāyana to employ his supernormal powers three times to bring a craftsman there to carve a Buddha image. Yet, the craftsman could only carve thirty-one of the marks;
why was it that the mark of the Brahma-voice could not be carved? The King asked, "What is the mark of the Brahma-voice? The Master said, "It would have killed you."
The Master asked the *karmadāna*: "What are you doing today during the communal labor? He replied, "We are hauling the millstone.
The Master said, "You may haul the millstone as you please, but you must not touch the central tree of the mill. [The *karmadāna*] was speechless. One day, a *bhadanta* asked the Master:
"It is not permissible to say 'this very mind is Buddha,' yet it is also not permissible to say 'neither mind nor Buddha. What is your intention, Master?"
"What is it? the Master asked. The monk said, "Virtuous One, simply believe that mind itself is Buddha; once you have realized this, what more is there to say about 'attaining' or 'not attaining'?

It is just like when you, Virtuous One, have finished eating and walk from the eastern corridor to the western corridor—you certainly do not ask everyone along the way whether you have attained it or not.
When the Master was staying at his hermitage, a monk arrived. The Master said to him: "I..."
The Master went up the mountain to perform his labors. Waiting for the time of the midday meal, he prepared rice; having eaten some himself, he sent a portion up to the monk.
After a short while, the monk ate the rice he had prepared himself and then smashed all the household utensils at once, lying down upon the bed.
The Master, not seeing him come down, returned to the hermitage. Seeing the monk lying there, the Master also lay down beside him. The monk then got up and left; the Master remained.
Later, [the Master] said, "When I previously lived in a hermitage, there was a certain keen and talented practitioner whom I have not seen even until now.
The Master picked up a ball and asked a monk, "Which of those is like this one? The monk replied, "It is not like it. The Master said:
"Where did you see that person? [The Master] said, "I say it is not like that. [The Master] asked, "If you ask me for my own view, lay down the object in your hand.
The Master said, "I grant you one eye. Grand Master Lu said to the Master, "Dharma Master Zhao is truly extraordinary;
his interpretation that 'Heaven and earth share the same root as I, and all things are of one body with me' is most remarkable."
The Master pointed to the peony flowers in the courtyard and said, "Great Officer, when people of this age see this single stalk of flowers, it is like being in a dream.

Lu was at a loss for what to say. The Master asked again, "In what stage of realization does a Heavenly King (Devarāja) reside? The Master replied, "If one is a Heavenly King, that is not a 'stage' (bhūmi).
Lu said, "I have heard it said that a Heavenly King resides in the First Stage. The Master said, "One should [be seen] by means of the body of a Heavenly King."

To one who had attained liberation, he immediately manifested in the form of a celestial king and preached the Dharma for him. Lu then took his leave and returned to the administrative seat of Xuancheng.
The Master asked, "When you go there, Great Officer, how will you govern the people? He replied, "I shall govern the people with wisdom.
The Master said, "If that is so, then all the living beings there will surely suffer the calamities of fire and water. When the Master entered Xuanzhou, Great Officer Lu came out to welcome him.
At the city gate of Jiezhong, [Lu] said, "Everyone calls this the 'Yong Gate. I wonder, Master, what do you call it?
The Master said, "If I were to say, I fear it would disgrace Your Excellency’s virtuous governance. [Lu] asked, "What if bandits suddenly arrive?
The Master said, "This is the fault of Old Teacher Wuzhuo. Lu asked again, "The Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā uses so many..."
"What is the use of hands and eyes? The Master said, "As for the state, what further use is there for a high official?
While the Master was washing his clothes, a monk asked, "Does the Master still have this [attachment]? The Master picked up the garment and said, "What can be done about this?
The Master asked the monk Liangqin, "Is there a Buddha within the void kalpa? He replied, "There is. The Master said:
"Who is this? He replied, "Liang Qin. The Master asked, "In what land do you dwell? Qin was speechless. The Master asked, "The patriarchs have transmitted it from one to another;
what is it that they transmit? The Master said, "One, two, three, four, five. He asked, "What is the state of the ancients? The Master said, "One, two, three, four, five."
The Master said, "Wait until there is something, then speak. [The monk] asked, "Why does the Master tell lies? The Master said, "I do not tell lies;
it is you, Layman Lu, who tells lies. A question was asked: "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, what serves as the objective realm (*viṣaya*)?
The Master said, "Why do you not ask Old Teacher Wang? [The monk] said, "I have already asked. The Master said, "Has it ever served as an objective realm for you? A question was asked: "Green..."
The Master asked, "When the lotus is not dispersed by wind or fire, what is it? The monk said, "When there is no wind and no fire, what is it?
The monk was speechless. The Master asked, "When you do not think of good and do not think of evil, and when all thoughts have ceased to arise, show me your original face.
The monk said, "There is nothing that can be revealed. The Master asked a lecturer, "Explain the sutra for me."
"Is that so? [the monk] said, "I will lecture on the sutras for you, Master, but you must teach me Chan in return.
The Master said, "One must not trade golden pellets for silver pellets. [The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said:
“You say there is a single cloud in the sky: is it held fast by nails, or is it moored by ropes? [The monk] asked:
“If there is a pearl in the sky, how can it be obtained? The Master said: “Cut bamboo and lay out a ladder to take it from the sky. [The monk] asked: “How can one lay out a ladder in the sky?
The Master said: “What do you intend to do to obtain it? The monk took his leave, saying: “When a student arrives at various [monasteries]...”
One day, someone asked the Master, "What have you been doing lately? He did not know how to respond.
The Master said, "Just tell him that lately I have been learning to wrestle. The man asked, "How so? The Master said, "With a single clap, both vanish.
Another asked, "Before one's parents were born, where was the nose? The Master said, "Now that your parents are already born, where is the nose?"
Where will you go? As the Master was about to pass away, the First Seat asked, "After the Master’s hundred-year life has ended, where will you go?
The Master said, "I shall go to become a water buffalo on the mountain below. The Seat said, "If I follow the Master there, will I be able to do so as well?
The Master said, "If you would follow me, you must first bring back a blade of grass in your mouth. The Master [passed away].
In the twelfth month of the Jia-yin year of Emperor Wenzong’s Taihe era, he manifested illness and addressed his disciples, saying:

"The star-dust, the lamp-illusion, and so forth have long been so; do not say that I have coming or going. Having finished speaking, he passed away at the age of eighty-seven, with fifty-eight years since his ordination.
National Teacher Qian’an of Haichang Monastery in Yanguan, Hangzhou, was the son of the Li family of Haimen. At the time of his birth, a divine light illuminated the room.
Later, a strange monk said to him, "Is it not you who shall raise the banner of invincibility and cause the sun of the Buddha to shine its light back upon the world?
He subsequently relied upon Master Yuncong of Moku County, where he shaved his head and received full ordination. Later, he heard that Daji was traveling to transform beings.
Gonggong Mountain. [Dongshan] then shook his mendicant’s staff and went there. The Master possessed extraordinary features;
when Daji saw him, he regarded him with deep esteem and ordered him to enter the inner quarters, privately transmitting the True Dharma to him. A monk asked, "What is the original body, Vairocana?
The Master said, "Bring me the pure water pitcher. When the monk brought the pitcher to him, the Master said, "Return it to its original place."
The monks escorted him back to his original location, where he returned once more to interrogate him. The Master said, "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away. A lecturer-monk came to visit.
The Master asked, "Master of the Dharma, what is your field of study? He replied, "I lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The Master asked, "How many kinds of dharmadhātu are there?
He replied, "In an extensive explanation, they are infinitely layered; in a brief explanation, there are four kinds. The Master then held up [his finger].
The Bifuzi said, "Which kind of dharma-realm is this? The Master remained silent. The Bifuzi said, "To know through thinking and to understand through deliberation is the livelihood of ghosts.
A solitary lamp under the sun—surely it fails to illuminate. He asked Damei, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
Damei said, "There is no meaning in the Westward Journey. Upon hearing this, the Master said, "One coffin, two..."
"A dead man. One day the Master called to his attendant, saying, "Bring me the rhinoceros fan.
The attendant replied, "It is broken. The Master said, "The fan is already broken; give me back the rhinoceros. The attendant was speechless.
One day the Master said to the assembly, "With space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet, who can beat it? The assembly was speechless.
Yifa asked about various meanings from the *Pṛcchā-sūtra*; once the Master had answered each point, he said, "Since the Chan Master arrived, I have not yet been able to act as host.
Yifa said, "I request that the Venerable One now act as host."
The Master said, "It is night today; go back to your original place for now and return tomorrow. Fakan went down.
When morning came, the Master ordered a novice to invite Chan Master Fakan. When Fakan arrived, the Master looked at the novice and said:
"Ha! This śrāmaṇera does not understand matters. He has invited Chan Master Fākong; instead, he has brought a hall-attendant. Fākong was speechless.
The abbot Faxin came to pay his respects. The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "Faxin.
The Master said, "I do not know you. Faxin was speechless. Later, the Master passed away while sitting in meditation without any illness. His posthumous title was [bestowed].
Chan Master Wukong.

those noble gentlemen were unlike the common run. People of the present day cannot achieve self-reliance and thus waste their time in vain."
Guang: "Sons, do not err in your application of mind. No one can take your place, nor is there any place for you to apply your mind.
Do not seek it from others; from the beginning, you have merely relied on external interpretations. Consequently, every word you utter is obstructed, and your light does not penetrate through.

This is simply because there is something before your eyes. A questioner asked: "What is the original intent? The Master said: "No one is able to comprehend it. The questioner asked: "How was it before?"
The Master said, "To have a direction is already to deviate. [The monk] asked, "What of one who does not direct? The Master said, "Who seeks the original meaning?
Again [the monk] asked, "There is nowhere for you to apply your mind; is there no gate of expedient means by which a student may gain entry?

The Master said, "The wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can save the world from suffering. [The monk] asked, "In what way is this the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom? The Master struck [a bell].
[The Master] struck the lid of the tripod three times and said, "Did you hear that, Subhūti? [Subhūti] replied, "I heard it. The Master said, "Why did I not hear it? The monk was speechless.
The Master drove him away with his staff. The Master once traveled together with Nanquan.

Later, one day as they were about to part ways, while they were boiling tea, Nanquan asked, "From the beginning, we have discussed phrases and sayings with my elder brother; both of us already know them."
Later, someone asked about the matter of ultimate reality (*atyanta*). "How is it? the Master said. "This patch of ground is very good for establishing a hermitage.
Yuanquan said, "Setting aside the establishment of the hermitage for a moment, how is the matter of ultimate reality? The Master then overturned the tea kettle and rose immediately.
Yuanquan said, "Brother, you have finished your tea; I, Puyuan, have not yet drunk mine. The Master said, "To speak such words as these!"
"A single drop of water is difficult to dissolve. A question was asked: "This matter has existed for a long time; how should one apply the mind to it?
The Master said: "An ox-hide drum covers the pillar; the pillar shrieks and squeals. Ordinary ears do not hear it, but all the sages laugh aloud.
Because an official came to visit, the Master picked up the two straps of his hat and said, "Do you understand? The official replied, "I do not understand. The Master said: [He then donned the hat.]

"Do not wonder at this old monk’s head; the wind does not take off his hat. While the Master was entering the garden to gather vegetables, he drew a circle and enclosed a single stalk of vegetable within it.
He said to the assembly, "Do not dare to move this. The assembly did not dare to move it.
After a short while, the Master returned; seeing that the vegetable was still there, he struck the monks with his staff and drove them away, saying, "This lot of fellows—no sense at all!"
A master of great wisdom asked a newly arrived monk, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From Fengxiang. The master said, "Have you brought that thing with you? The monk replied, "I have brought it. The master said, "Where is it?
The monk raised his hand from the top of his head, holding up his staff to present it. The master immediately made a gesture of receiving it and tossed it behind him. The monk was at a loss.
The Master said, "This wild fox! While the Master was weeding grass, a monk who was a lecturer came to visit him.
Suddenly, a snake passed by, and the Master cut it with his hoe. The monk said, "I have long heard of Guizong; I never expected you would be such a coarse monk.
The Master said, "You are coarse, and I am coarse. The monk asked, "What is coarseness? The Master held up his hoe and said, "What is this?"
"This is subtle. The Master made a gesture of slaying a snake and said, "If it is so, then you shall act accordingly.

The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment acting accordingly, where did you see me slay the snake? The monk had no reply. Yunyan came to pay his respects. The Master made a gesture of drawing a bow.
After a long while, Yunyan made a gesture of drawing a sword. The Master said, "You have come too late. He ascended the hall and said, "I..."
"Now I wish to speak of Chan. All you sons, come forward together! The great assembly, come forward!

The Master said, "Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara, which responds appropriately to all places. A monk asked, "What is the practice of Avalokiteśvara? The Master snapped his fingers and said, "Do you hear that, everyone?
They replied, "We hear it. The Master said, "You lot of fellows! What are you looking for here? With his staff, he drove them out. Great!
Laughing, the Master returned to his quarters as the monk took his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to various places to study the 'five flavors' of Chan.
The Master said, "In other places there are five flavors of Chan; here, I have only one flavor of Chan. The monk asked, "What is this one flavor of Chan?
The Master struck him. The monk said, "I understand! I understand! The Master said, "Speak! Speak! The monk prepared to open his mouth—[and was struck again].
[The monk] spoke. The Master struck him again. Later, the monk went to Huangbo and recounted the previous conversation.
Huangbo ascended the hall and said: "Master Mazu produced eighty-four *kalyāṇamitras*; when questioned, each one was dripping wet. Only Guizong was slightly better.
