He did not doubt this, saying, "Is it not a false discourse to say that a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru? The Master asked, "It is said that you, Excellency, have read ten thousand scrolls of books;
is this true? He replied, "Yes. The Master said, "From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet, you are no larger than a coconut.
Where, then, would you place those ten thousand scrolls? Li bowed his head and remained silent. On another day, Li asked again, "What about the entire Tripitaka?"
The student asked, "In teaching, what kind of matter do you clarify? The Master raised his fist and showed it to him, saying, "Do you understand? The student said, "I do not understand.

The Master said, "This scholar does not even recognize the knuckle of my fist. The student said, "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "If you meet someone, bestow it upon them on the road;
if you do not meet anyone, let it flow as worldly truth. Because the Master had double pupils in his eyes, he subsequently... [text ends]
He massaged his eyes with medicine until both became bloodshot; thus he was popularly known as "Red-Eyed Guizong.
Later, when he manifested his passing, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhizhen.
Chan Master Fachang of Mount Damei in Mingzhou was the son of the Zheng family of Xiangyang. In his youth, he followed a teacher at Yuyuan Temple in Jingzhou.
He first visited Daji (Huairang), who asked him, "What is the Buddha? Daji replied, "Mind itself is the Buddha. Upon hearing this, the Master attained great enlightenment.
He subsequently went to the former retreat of Mei Zizhen on Mount Damei in Siming, where he thatched a cottage with reeds and dwelt there. This was during the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty.
Under the guidance of Master Yanguan, there was a monk who, while gathering firewood, lost his way and arrived at a hermitage. He asked the Master, "How long have you been here?
The Master replied, "I have only seen the four mountains turn green and then yellow. The monk asked again, "When one leaves the mountain path, where does one go?
The Master said, "Go with the flow. When the monk returned, he related this to Yanguan. Yanguan said, "When I was in Jiangxi..."
"I once saw a monk; since then I have had no news of him. Could it be this very monk? He then sent a monk to summon him.
The Master replied with a verse: "An withered tree, shattered and leaning against a cold forest, Through many springs, its heart remains unchanged."
Even when woodcutters encountered him, they paid him no heed; how could the people of Ying have troubled themselves to seek him out? With a pond of lotus leaves, his clothing was inexhaustible;
with several trees of pine blossoms, his food was more than sufficient. As soon as the world learned of his dwelling place, he moved his thatched hut deeper into the mountains.
When Daji heard that the Master was living in the mountains, he sent a monk to ask: "When you, Master, saw Mazu Daoshi, what did you obtain?"
"What? [the monk asked]. The Master said, "The Great Master told me, 'This very mind is Buddha,' so I have been dwelling right here.
The monk said, "Lately, the Great Master’s teaching on the Buddha-dharma has become different. The Master asked, "How so? He replied, "He also says, 'Neither mind nor Buddha.
The Master said, "This old fellow will continue to delude people without end; let him say 'neither' as he pleases."
"The mind is not the Buddha. I simply maintain that 'this very mind is the Buddha. When the monk returned and related this to Mazu, Mazu said, "The plum has ripened.
Hearing of this, Layman Pang wished to verify the Master’s realization and went specifically to visit him; as soon as they met face-to-face—
The scholar then asked, "I have long heard of Great Plum; I wonder if the plums have ripened yet? The Master said, "They have ripened.
Where will you apply your teeth? The scholar said, "In pieces. The Master reached out his hand and said, "Give me back the pit! The scholar was speechless.
From then on, students gradually flocked to him, and the Master's Way became even more renowned. He ascended the hall and addressed them: "All of you, each..."
Turn your mind back to reach the source; do not pursue its branches. If you merely attain the source, the branches will arrive of their own accord.
If you wish to know wood, you need only understand your own mind, for this mind is fundamentally the root of all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. Yet the mind does not cling to any good or evil as it gives rise to the myriad dharmas;
its original nature is simply suchness (*tathatā*). Question: "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said: "Reed flowers and willow catkins;
bamboo needles and hemp thread. Jiashan and Dingshan were traveling together. While they were conversing, Dingshan...

[The Master] said, "If there is no Buddha within birth and death, then there is no birth and death. Jia Shan said, "If there is a Buddha within birth and death, then one does not become deluded by birth and death.
They refused each other's views and went together up the mountain to see the Master.

Jia Shan then raised the matter and asked, "I wonder, between the two of you, whose realization is more intimate? The Master said, "One is intimate; the other is distant. Jia Shan asked again, "Which one is intimate?"
The Master said, "Go for now; come back tomorrow. The next day, Jia Shan went up again to question him. The Master said, "Those who are close do not ask;
those who ask are not close. A monk from Silla came to visit. The Master asked, "Where did you set out from? He replied, "I wish to communicate my place of origin."
Fearing he would be met with strange reproach, the monk said, "It must have a place of origin. The Master said, "Silla. The monk said, "How can you blame me?
The monk bowed, and the Master said, "Whether right or wrong, whether known or unknown, you are simply a person from the land of Silla.
One day, the Master suddenly said to his disciples: "Coming cannot be suppressed; going cannot be pursued. In this state of ease," he paused.
Upon hearing the cry of a flying squirrel, he said, "This very thing is not another thing. You all, protect and uphold this well; I am now departing.
Having finished speaking, he manifested his passing. Chan Master Yongming Shou praised him, saying: "When the Master first attained the Way, he realized that 'the mind is Buddha.
In his final instruction to his disciples, he showed that 'things are not other things. He exhausted the source of the myriad dharmas and penetrated the very bones of the thousand sages. Truly..."
Transformation does not involve shifting. How could it hinder appearing and disappearing?
During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Shunzong asked Chan Master Fuguang Ruyuan (who had previously resided at Jinguesi on Mount Wutai): "From what direction does the Buddha come?
To what direction does he go when he passes away? Since you say he dwells eternally in the world, where is the Buddha now? The Master replied: "The Buddha..."
Coming from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they go toward the unconditioned to cease. The Dharma-body is equal to space, eternally abiding in the state of no-mind.
Where there is thought, it returns to no-thought; where there is dwelling, it returns to non-dwelling. They come for the sake of sentient beings; they go for the sake of sentient beings.
In the ocean of pure *tathatā*, the essence is serene and eternally abiding. O wise ones, contemplate this well and do not give rise to further doubt.

The Emperor asked again: "The Buddha was born in the royal palace and passed away beneath the twin śāla trees. He dwelt in this world for forty-nine years, yet he also said there is no dharma to be taught.
Mountains, rivers, and the great ocean; heaven, earth, and the sun and moon—all must reach their end when the time comes.

Who can say they are subject neither to birth nor extinction? My doubts remain as they were; may the wise one skillfully discern them. The Master replied: "The essence of the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent."
This is due to the deluded mind’s false discrimination. The Dharmakāya is equal to empty space; it has never known arising or ceasing.

When conditions are present, a Buddha appears in the world; when conditions are absent, a Buddha enters nirvana. He transforms sentient beings everywhere, like the moon reflected in water—neither permanent nor annihilated, neither born nor extinguished.
Birth has never truly been born, and extinction has never truly been extinguished. To see this clearly is to realize the mindless state.
[This is] the place. It is naturally beyond words. When the Emperor heard this, he was greatly pleased and respected him all the more.
Chan Master Lingmo of Wuxie Mountain in Wuzhou was the son of the Xuan family of Piling. He first visited Mazu, whereupon he received the tonsure and the full precepts.
Later, he traveled far to visit Shitou and immediately asked: "If my words accord with yours, I shall stay; if they do not, I shall depart."
"Go! Shitou remained seated as the Master departed. Shitou called out after him, "Ācārya! The Master turned his head.
Shitou said, "From birth until death, it is simply this. Why do you turn your head and twist your brain? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment;
he then snapped his staff in two and settled there. In the early Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he resided at the White Sand Monastery (Bai Sha Daochang) and later lived elsewhere.
Wuye. A monk asked, "What thing is greater than heaven and earth? The Master said, "No one can recognize it. The monk asked, "Can it be carved or fashioned?
The Master said, "Try taking a hand to it and see. A monk asked, "In this gate, what is the matter from beginning to end?
The Master said, "Tell me, how much time has it been since that which is right before your eyes was formed? The monk said, "I, your disciple, do not..."
[The monk] arrived. The Master said, "In this place of mine, there is nothing for you to ask about. [The monk] asked, "Does the Master not have a way to receive people?
The Master said, "I will receive you once you seek to be received. [The monk] said, "Please, Master, receive me right now. The Master said, "What is it that you lack?
[The monk] asked, "How can one attain a state of no-mind? The Master said, "When mountains are overturned and the ocean is spilled, all is calm and still; the earth shakes."
"Peaceful Sleep; why heed this? On the *bingwu* day of the third month in the *wuxu* year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong, he bathed, burned incense, and sat upright.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma-body is perfect stillness; it manifests coming and going. The thousand sages share one source; the myriad spirits return to the One.
Now that I am like a bubble dispersing, why should you feign grief? Do not weary yourselves; you must maintain right mindfulness. If you follow this..."
"Obey my command; this is the true way to repay my kindness. If you stubbornly disobey my words, you are not my son. At that time, a monk asked, "Where will the Master go?
The Master replied, "I am going nowhere. The monk said, "Why do I not see you? The Master replied, "It is not something seen by the eyes.
Having finished speaking, he suddenly passed away in accordance with the natural course. His secular age was seventy-two, and his monastic seniority was forty-one. A stupa was built for him.
At Mount Ben, while Zen Master Baiyan Mingzhe was reading a scripture at Yaoshan, the Master said, "Stop, Preceptor; it is better for you to act like a monkey.
Yaoshan set aside the scripture and said, "Is it early or late in the day? The Master replied, "It is exactly noon. Yaoshan said, "There is still a trace of literary artistry there."
The Master said, "I have nothing, nor do I lack anything. Mount said, "You are far too clever. The Master said, "I am just like this;
what about you, Teacher? Mount said, "Limping and dragging along, a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses—just pass the time in this way."

Chan Master Baizhi of Panshan in Youzhou, a successor of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi, saw a guest purchasing pork.

At this, the Master attained realization. On another day, as he was leaving the gate, he saw people carrying a funeral bier with mournful songs;
he immediately shook his bells and said: "The crimson wheel is certain to sink in the west; I know not to which quarter the soul has departed. [The screen fell.]
The junior filial son wept, crying out, "Alas! Alas! The Master’s body and mind suddenly leaped with joy. Upon returning, he related this to Mazu, who certified his realization.

How could dust be established? The Way is fundamentally without substance; it is because of substance that a name is established. The Way has no original name; it is because of the name that it receives its designation.
If one says "this very mind is Buddha," at present one has not yet entered the profound mystery. If one says "neither mind nor Buddha," this is still merely pointing to the ultimate trace.
The path beyond this has not been transmitted by the thousand sages; students exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at shadows.
Ying ascends the hall: "The Great Way has no center; who, then, can speak of before or after? The vast sky reaches its limits; what use is there for measurement?
Since emptiness is thus, what more can be said of the Way? He ascends the hall again: "The moon of the mind is solitary and perfect, its light encompassing the myriad phenomena.
The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist [independently]. When both light and objects have vanished, what is this thing? Zen masters, consider this as an analogy."
It is like throwing a sword into the air; one cannot even discuss whether it reaches its mark or not. Thus, the wheel of emptiness leaves no trace, and the blade of the sword remains unimpaired.

If you can be thus, then mind after mind is without knowing. The whole mind is Buddha; the whole Buddha is the person. When the person and the Buddha are without distinction, only then have you begun the Way.
Ascending the hall, he said: "O virtuous Chan practitioners, in the midst of this, studying the Way is like the earth supporting a mountain—it is not conscious of doing so."
The mountain stands solitary and lofty; it is like a stone containing jade, yet one does not know that the jade is without flaw.
If it were otherwise, it would be called "leaving home. Thus the Great Teacher said: "Phenomena are fundamentally not mutually obstructive; the three periods of time are likewise so.

Ultimate emptiness leaves no trace; true suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words. Buddhas and *nirvāṇa* are merely figurative designations. All you practitioners of meditation, you must look directly within yourselves;
there is no one who can take your place. Ascending the hall, he said: "In the three realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind?
The four elements are fundamentally empty—upon what does the Buddha rely to abide? The celestial sphere is unmoving, silent and wordless, face-to-face."

[The Master] presented [the portrait]. There was nothing further to say. "Take care," he said. As the Master was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Is there anyone who can capture my true likeness?
The assembly presented the portraits they had painted, but none accorded with the Master’s intention. Puhua came forward and said, "I have captured it.
The Master said, "Why do you not present it to this old monk? Puhua then performed a somersault and left. The Master said, "This..."
Han: Later, he departed like one driven mad by the wind. The Master then passed away; his posthumous title was Great Master Ningji, and his stupa was named Zhenji.
While Chan Master Baoche of Mazu Shan in Puzhou was attending Mazu while traveling, he asked, "What is the Great Nirvana?"
The Master said, "Look at the water. While the Master was fanning himself, a monk asked, "The nature of wind is eternally abiding and reaches everywhere;

why does the Master still wave his fan? The Master replied, "You know only that the nature of wind is eternally abiding, but you do not yet know that it reaches everywhere. The monk asked, "What is it that reaches everywhere?"
The principle was not fully understood. The Master, however, shook his fan. The monk bowed. The Master said, "What benefit is there in having a thousand such monks?
A monk asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "I do not know. The Master asked again, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "Take care.
As the Master stepped down from his seat, he seized him and said, "When this monk is questioned, he immediately acts like a Buddha."
Fahui replied, "It seems as though you have no eyes. The Master let go of him and said, "I release your life; I allow you to breathe. The monk bowed.

The Master intended to seize him by the collar, but the monk shook out his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "Do not take a three-year-old bamboo and attempt to compare it with a ten-thousand-year-old pine.
Later, while the Master was traveling with Nanquan and two or three others to visit Jingshan, they encountered an old woman on the road. He asked her:
"Where does the Jingshan Road lead? The old woman said, "It goes straight ahead. The Master asked, "The water ahead is deep; can one cross it?
The old woman said, "Without getting one's feet wet. The Master asked again, "The rice on the upper bank is so lush, while the rice on the lower bank is so frail.
The old woman said, "It has all been eaten by the crabs. The Master said, "The grain is fragrant. The old woman said, [without speaking further].
When he had ceased breathing, the Master asked again, "Where does the old woman reside? She replied, "She resides right here.
The three men arrived at the inn, where the old woman brought a pot of tea and three cups. She said, "Monks, those who possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) may drink the tea.
The three looked at one another; the old woman said, "Behold, I shall now display my own supernatural powers myself. At that—
He picked up the cup, poured out the tea, and departed. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master remained silent.
The monk then asked Shishuang about this matter. Shishuang said, "The master raises his fists and brings trouble upon himself;
you, O *dārala*, drag through mud and wade through water."
Chan Master Ruhui of Dongsi Temple in Hunan was a native of Qujiang in Shixing. Initially, he visited Mount Jing; later, he studied under Daji (Nanyue Huairang).

As his disciples grew numerous, the beds and couches in the Sangha Hall were worn down and broken by their weight. Consequently, he was known at the time as "Zhechuang Hui" (The Master of the Broken Bed).
After Daji passed away, the Master often lamented that his followers incessantly recited and memorized the discourse on "the mind itself is Buddha."

Furthermore, he asked, "In what does the Buddha abide? and [the Master] replied, "It is precisely the mind. When [the questioner] said, "The mind is like a painter," [the Master] replied, "And it is precisely the Buddha.
He then addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. The sword has long since departed, yet you are still marking the boat.
At that time, he was known as Dongsi (East Temple) and served as a den of Chan. Prime Minister Cui Qun was appointed as the Inspector of Hunan; upon seeing him...
The Master asked, "By what means did you attain it? The Master [Nanquan] replied, "I attained it by seeing my nature. At that time, the Master was suffering from an eye ailment.

The official ridiculed him, saying, "If you say you have seen your nature, what can you do about your eyes? The Master said, "Seeing one's nature is not the eyes; what harm does an eye ailment do? The official bowed his head and apologized.
Later, the official saw a bird dropping excrement on the Buddha’s head and asked, "Does a bird also possess Buddha-nature?"
[This is] his nature. Wushan said, "There is a public saying: 'Why do you apply dung to the Buddha's head? The Master said, "It is he;
why does he not apply it to the hawk's head? Yangshan came to visit. The Master asked, "Where are you from?
Yangshan replied, "I am a man from Guangnan. The Master said, "I have heard that Guangnan possesses the 'Taming the Sea Bright Pearl. Is this true?"
Yang said, "This master says, 'How is this pearl? Yang replied, 'In the dark moon it is hidden;
in the bright moon it appears. The Master said, 'Have you brought it back? Yang replied, 'I have brought it back. The Master said, 'Why do you not present it to this old monk?"
Yang stepped forward with his hands joined in reverence and said, "Yesterday I arrived at Mount Gui, where I was also asked about this pearl.
I was left with no words to respond and no principle to defend. The Master said, "A true lion cub; you are well able to roar. Yang bowed in prostration, then withdrew to the guest quarters.
After arranging his formal demeanor, he went up again to pay his respects. As soon as the Master saw him, he said, "We have already met."
Yang said, "Meeting you in this manner—would that not be appropriate? The Master returned to his quarters and closed the door. Yang went back and reported this to Muzhou Daowu.
Muzhou said, "What kind of mental state is this, Jizang? Yang replied, "If he had not acted in this way, how could one have recognized him?
A layman asked the Master, "I wish to invite the Abbot to open the hall for teaching; would that be possible? The Master said, "Wait..."
He wrapped objects around stones; when they were warm, he would obtain [the desired result]. The earth remained silent. He entered nirvana in the gui-mao year of the Tang Changqing era.
His posthumous title was Grand Master Fuming, and his stupa was named Yongji.
Chan Master Zhizang of Xitang in Qianzhou was the son of the Liao family of Qianhua. At the age of eight, he followed a teacher; at twenty-five, he received full ordination.
A physiognomist, observing his extraordinary features, said to him, "Your bone and spirit are not ordinary; you shall become an assistant to the Dharma King.
The Master subsequently visited and paid respects to Mazu Daichi and entered the inner chamber together with Baizhang Huihai; both received [his transmission].
Seal of Transmission: One day, Daji sent the Master to Chang’an to present a letter to National Teacher Zhong.
The National Teacher asked, “What dharma does your master teach? The Master walked from east to west and stood there.
The National Teacher said, “Is that all? Is there something else? The Master then walked from west to east and stood there. The National Teacher said, “This is Master Ma.”

“Bottom. “Virtuous one, what do you say? The Master said, “I have already presented it to the Abbot long ago. Shortly thereafter, he sent a letter to Mount Jing (the words of which are in the *Guo Yi Zhang*).

While the Regional Commander Lu Sisi was inviting Daji to reside at his headquarters, where he flourished with a grand transformation in response to the times, the Master returned to the prefecture and received from Daji the transmission of the patched robe.
After Mazu passed away, the assembly requested [him to succeed him].
The opening of the hall. Once, Minister Li asked a monk, "What teachings did the Great Master Mazu have?
The monk replied, "The Great Master sometimes said 'This very mind is Buddha,' and sometimes he said 'Neither mind nor Buddha. Li said, "Both of those are on this side.
Li then asked the Master, "What teachings did the Great Master Mazu have? The Master called out, "Li Ao! Li responded, "Yes? The Master said:
The drums and horns were sounded. During a general work assignment (*pǔqǐng*), the Master said, "Cause and effect are manifest;

what can be done? What can be done? At that time, a monk stepped forward and pressed his hands against the ground. The Master asked, "What are you doing? The monk replied, "Save me! Save me! The Master said, [“... (implying he did not save him).
"This monk of the assembly is still somewhat lacking," [the Master said]. The monk brushed his sleeves and walked away.
The Master said, "A worm within the body of a lion eats the lion’s own flesh. A monk asked, "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined.
But when there is neither question nor answer, what then? The Master said, "I am afraid it will rot away! A layman asked, "Are there heavens and hells?"
"No. The Master asked, "Is there such a thing as the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha? He replied, "There is. The Master asked further questions, and he answered "Yes" to them all.
The Master said, "When you say 'Yes' to everything this way, are you not mistaken? He replied, "Have you ever met a venerable elder before?"
The man said, "I once visited Master Jingshan. The Master asked, "What did Jingshan say to you?
He replied, "He said that everything is entirely non-existent. The Master asked, "Do you have a wife? He replied, "Yes. The Master asked, "Does Master Jingshan have a wife? He replied, "No.
The Master said, "As for Master Jingshan, it is acceptable for him to say 'non-existent. [But you cannot say so of yourself]. The layman bowed in thanks and departed.
The Master entered nirvana on the eighth day of the fourth month in the Jiawu year of the Yuanhe era. He was eighty years of age and fifty years since his ordination.

Emperor Xianzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Great Propagation of Teaching (Daxuanjiao Chanshi). Emperor Muzong further conferred the title Chan Master Great Enlightenment (Dajue Chanshi). His stupa was named Yuanhe.
Chan Master Huahui of Zhangjing Temple in Jingzhao Prefecture was the son of the Xie family of Quanzhou. He first resided at Boya Mountain in Dingzhou, and subsequently at Mount Zhongtiao.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Xianzong issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Shangxuan Temple. Entering the hall, he said:

"The ultimate principle transcends words, yet people of this age do not understand it. They strenuously practice other matters, taking them to be spiritual efficacy, unaware that their own original nature is [the source]."

It is not an object of the sensory realms; it is this subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation. All its discerning awareness is unstained and unimpeded. Such radiance has never ceased or been abandoned.
From past kalpas until now, it remains eternally unchanged. It is like the solar disc, which shines equally upon both the distant and the near;
though it reaches all forms, it does not merge with anything. This spiritual lamp and wondrous clarity are not something produced by artificial refinement.

Refining. Because one does not understand, one grasps at objective forms; this is merely like pressing on the eyes and falsely perceiving flowers in the sky—exhausting oneself in vain and needlessly passing through kalpas.
If one can turn the light back upon oneself, there is no second person; every movement and action will not fall short of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Question:
When both mind and phenomena are simultaneously extinguished, where does the finger point? The Master said: "The man of Ying has no grime; his labor is in vain."
Jin said, "I request the Master’s words on not returning. The Master said, "There is no phrase for returning. Baizhang ordered a monk to come and wait upon him.
When the Master ascended the hall, the monk unfolded his sitting cloth, prostrated, and then stood up.

He took one of the Master’s sandals, brushed off the dust with the sleeve of his robe, and turned it upside down toward the ground. The Master said, "This old monk has committed an offense. Someone asked about the Patriarch.
The Master transmitted the Mind-Ground Dharma Gate, stating that the true mind is the *tathatā* (suchness) mind; the deluded mind is neither true nor deluded.
This is the mind established separately outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles. The Master asked, "Do you see the empty space before you?

He replied, "I know with certainty that it is always before one's eyes, yet people themselves do not see it. The Master said, "Do not mistake this for a reflected image. He asked, "How should I act, O Master?"
Sheng asked, "What is it? The Master struck the air with his hand three times and said, "How is this? You shall understand it later. A monk came to attend upon the Master;
he circumambulated him three times, shook his staff, and stood there. The Master said, "It is so, it is so. That same monk then went to Nanquan;
he likewise circumambulated Nanquan three times, shook his staff, and stood there. Nanquan said, "It is not so, it is not so. This...
"This is turned by the power of the wind; it will ultimately end in decay and ruin. The monk said, "Zhangjing says this is so. Why does the Master say it is not?
Quanshou said, "Zhangjing is indeed right; you are not. A junior monk returned from his travels.
The Master asked him, "How many years has it been since you left here? He replied, "It has been nearly eight years since I left the Master's presence."
The Master said, "What have you prepared? The junior monk drew a circle on the ground. The Master said, "Is there anything else besides this?
The junior monk then broke the circle and prostrated. The Master said, "Not it, not it.
A monk asked, "Within this body of the four elements and five aggregates, which one is the original Buddha-nature? The Master then called out to the monk.

[The Master] called his name. The monk responded, "Yes. After a long silence, the Master said, "You have no Buddha-nature. He entered nirvana in the twelfth month of the Wuxu year of the Tang Yuanhe era.
His stupa was erected by the Ba River, and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dajue; his stupa was named Dabaoxiang-ta.
Chan Master Dazhu Huihai of Yuezhou was the son of the Zhu family of Jianzhou. He studied under Dazhuan Zhi of Dayun Temple in Yuezhou.
When he first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dayun Temple in Yuezhou. Mazu said:
"What do you require by coming here? he asked. [The monk] replied, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. The Master said, "In this place of mine, there is not a single thing.
What Buddha-dharma do you seek? You fail to regard your own precious treasury; why do you abandon your home and wander about? [The monk] asked, "Which one is the precious treasury of Huihai?
The Patriarch said, "That which is currently questioning me is your own precious treasury; it possesses everything."

"It is sufficient; there is nothing further lacking. Its function is sovereign; why rely on seeking it externally? At these words, the Master recognized his own original mind for himself, not through intellectual cognition.
He leaped for joy and prostrated in gratitude. He served the Master for six years, after which, because his preceptor had grown old, he returned home abruptly to provide for him.

Thereupon, he concealed his traces and hid his capabilities, outwardly appearing dull and mute. He himself composed the *Tunwu rudao yaomen* (The Essential Gate to Sudden Enlightenment and Entry into the Way).
The treatise in one fascicle was privately produced by Fazhi Xuan’an and presented to Mazu. After Mazu had finished reading it, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"In Yuezhou there is a Great Pearl, perfectly round and bright, its light penetrating and free, with no place of obstruction. Among the assembly were those who recognized the Master;
they recommended him to go to Yuezhou to seek him out and rely upon him (at that time he was called Master Dazhu). The Master said to them: "O guests of Chan, I do not understand Chan," and so forth.
"There is not a single dharma that can be shown to others. Do not trouble yourself by standing here for long; please take your rest.
At that time, his disciples gradually increased in number, and they questioned and challenged him day and night. Having no choice, he answered each question as it arose; his eloquence was unimpeded.
Later, several *zhu-zu* (seminary masters) came to visit and said, "We intend to pose a question. Will you respond to us, Master? The Master replied, "The moon’s reflection in a deep pool."
While he was still pondering this, a monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Facing me in clear conversation—who else could it be? The assembly was all at a loss.
After a long while, the monk asked again, "What Dharma does the Master preach to save people? The Master replied, "I have never had a single Dharma to save people.
The monk said, "The houses of Chan masters are all like this. The Master then asked the monk, "What Dharma do you preach?"

Duren said, "I have been lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master asked, "How many times have you lectured on it? He replied, "More than twenty times. The Master asked, "Who preached this sūtra?
The monk raised his voice and said, "Master, you are mocking me! Do you not know that it was preached by the Buddha?
The Master said, "If one were to say that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma, they would be slandering the Buddha. Such a person does not understand my meaning."

Regarding the meaning of what has been taught: if one says that this sūtra was not spoken by the Buddha, that constitutes slandering the sūtra. "Venerable Sirs, please speak on this. The monks had no reply.
After a short while, the Master asked again: "The sūtra says: 'If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound...'"
"Such a person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. "Virtuous One," the monk asked, "tell me, which one is the Tathāgata?
The Master said, "When I arrived here, I was already lost; how can you say you have become lost now? The monk said, "I beg the Zen Master to explain this for me.
The Master said, "Virtuous One, you have lectured on the sutras more than twenty times, yet you do not recognize the Tathāgata. The monk [remained silent].
He paid his respects and said, "I pray that you will grant me an instruction. The Master said, "A Tathāgata is one whose meaning is the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.

How could you have forgotten this? He replied, "That is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. The Master said, "Virtuous One, even this is not yet it. He said, "The scriptural text is perfectly clear."

"That is not yet it. The Master asked, "Is 'suchness' (tathatā) like this, Venerable One? He replied, "It is like that. The Master asked, "Are wood and stone like that? He replied, "They are like that.
The Master said, "Venerable One, are 'suchness' and 'wood and stone' not the same? He replied, "There is no difference. The Master said, "What distinguishes you, Venerable One, from wood and stone?
The monk had no reply. After a long silence, he asked again, "How does one attain Great Nirvāṇa? The Master said, "By not creating birth."
[The questioner asked about] the karma of birth and death. [He] asked, "What is the karma of birth and death? The Master said, "Seeking great nirvāṇa is the karma of birth and death.
Abandoning defilement to grasp purity is the karma of birth and death. Having attainment and realization is the karma of birth and death. Not being liberated from the gate of antidotes."

"This is the karma of birth and death. [The student] asked, "How then can one immediately attain liberation? The Master said, "Originally there has been no bondage; there is no need to seek liberation.
Simply act directly and proceed straightforwardly—this is the peerless equality. [The student] said, "A Chan master such as you, Reverend, is truly rare indeed."
He bowed in thanks and departed. A practitioner asked, "Regarding 'this very mind is Buddha,' which one is the Buddha? The Master said, "Which one do you suspect is not the Buddha?
Point it out. The practitioner had no reply. The Master said, "To understand is to be pervasive; the object is non-awakening. [Those who hold such views] are forever estranged.
The Vinaya Master Faming said to the Master, "The followers of the Chan school mostly fall into emptiness. The Master said:
However, the Master of the Seat (the *zhuzu*) had fallen into emptiness. Ming was greatly startled and said, "How can you have fallen into emptiness?

The Master replied, "The sutras and treatises are but paper and ink characters. Since paper, ink, and characters are all empty, even if one establishes dharmas such as names and phrases based upon sounds, they are none other than empty.
You, Master of the Seat, cling to the substance of the teachings; how could you not fall into emptiness? Ming said, "Chan Master..."
"Does it fall into emptiness? The Master said, "It does not fall into emptiness. Ming said, "How can it be that it does not fall into emptiness?
The Master said, "Texts and words all arise from wisdom. When the Great Function manifests before one, how could it fall into emptiness?

Ming said, "Thus I know that if one does not penetrate even a single dharma, one cannot be called Siddhārtha. The Master said, "The Vinaya Master has not only fallen into emptiness; he has also misunderstood the name."
Mingzuo said, "Where is the error? The Master replied, "If you have not yet distinguished between the sounds of China and India, how can you lecture?
Mingzuo said, "I request the Chan Master to point out the specific error. The Master said, "Do you not know that *Siddhārtha* is a Sanskrit term?

Although Mingzuo recognized his mistake, his mind remained resentful. (In full, the Sanskrit is *Vaiśrāvaṇa-siddha*; in the Middle Kingdom [China], it is translated as "One by Whom All Meanings Are Accomplished.")
The old term "Siddhārtha" is likewise a corruption and abbreviation of the Sanskrit. He asked again: "The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are the words of the Buddha;
one recites them and practices according to their teachings. Why then do you not see your nature? The Master said: "It is like a mad dog chasing a clod of earth while a lion bites a man.
The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are the functioning of nature; those who recite them are the phenomena of nature. Ming said: "Does Amitābha Buddha have parents and a clan?"
"No. The Master said, "Amitābha’s surname is Kauśika; his father’s name is Candrāvatī and his mother’s name is Viśeṣacārumukhī.
Faming asked, "In which scriptural text does this appear? The Master replied, "It appears in the Drum-Sound King Sūtra (Dundubhisvara-rāja-sūtra). Faming bowed in thanks and withdrew with praise.
The Tripiṭaka Dharma Master asked, "Does True Suchness (Tathatā) undergo change? The Master replied, "It does undergo change. The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"The Chan Master is mistaken," [the Master] replied. The Master then asked, "Does the Tripitaka contain True Suchness? He said, "It does.

The Master said, "If it were without change, you would certainly be an ordinary monk. Have you not heard that a good spiritual friend can transform the three poisons into the three groups of pure precepts, transform the six consciousnesses into the six supernatural powers, transform afflictions into bodhi, and transform ignorance into..."
"Great wisdom! If True Suchness (*tathatā*) were without change, then the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) would truly be the same as non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).
Zang said, "If that is so, then True Suchness must possess change. The Master said, "If you cling to the notion that True Suchness possesses change, you are likewise a non-Buddhist.
[The monk] asked, "Just now, Meditation Master, you said that True Suchness possesses change; now you say it does not change. Which is it?"
"How is it that this is precisely the point? The Master said, "If one has clearly realized their nature, it is like a mani jewel manifesting colors:
one may say it changes, and one may also say it does not change. But for one who has not seen their nature, when they hear it said that True Suchness undergoes transformation," [they are confused].
He then interprets transformation as non-transformation, and interprets non-transformation as transformation. Baizhang said, "Thus one knows that the Southern School is truly unfathomable.
A practitioner asked, "Is there any dharma in the world that surpasses spontaneity (*ziran*)?
The Master said, "There is. The practitioner asked, "What dharma can surpass it? The Master said, "One who is able to know spontaneity. The practitioner said, "Is it not the primal qi (*yuanqi*)?"
"Is the Way not so? The Master said, "Original qi is original qi; the Way is the Way. [The monk] said, "If it is thus, then there ought to be two.
The Master said, "Know that there are not two people. He asked again, "What is called heterodoxy? What is called orthodoxy? The Master said:
When the mind pursues external objects, it is deviant; when objects follow the mind, it is correct. Master Yuanshou asked, "When you, Reverend, cultivate the Way, do you still apply effort?
The Master replied, "I apply effort. The Master asked, "How do you apply effort? The Master said, "When hungry, I eat; when tired, I sleep. The Master asked, "All people do this as well;
is your application of effort the same as theirs, Reverend? The Master said, "It is not the same. The Master asked, "In what way?"
Therefore, they are not the same. The Master said: "When others eat, he refuses to eat; he demands a hundred things. When others sleep, he refuses to sleep;
he devises a thousand schemes. This is why they are not the same. The Vinaya Master closed his mouth. Yunguang asked: "Does the Chan Master know where you were born?
The Master said: "I have never died; what use is there in discussing birth? To 'know birth' is itself non-existence."
"Arising. There is no dharma apart from arising; there is no dharma that has arising. The Patriarch said, "When there is arising, it is precisely non-arising.

[A monk] asked, "Can those who have not seen their nature also attain this? The Master said, "It is because they themselves have not seen their nature; it is not that they lack nature. Why is this so?"
Seeing is itself the nature; without nature, there can be no seeing. Consciousness is itself the nature; therefore, it is called the "nature of consciousness.
Awareness is itself the nature; thus, it is called the "nature of awareness. That which is able to give rise to the myriad dharmas is called the "dharma-nature," and is also named the "Dharmakāya.
The Patriarch Aśvaghoṣa said: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings. Because the mind arises, all dharmas arise. If the mind..."
Non-arising: phenomena have no source from which they arise, nor do they possess names. Deluded people do not know that the Dharma-body is formless, yet manifests forms in response to things;
they consequently claim that every verdant bamboo shoot is the Dharma-body, and that every lush yellow flower is nothing other than Prajñā.
If yellow flowers were prajñā, then prajñā would be the same as insentient matter; if green bamboos were the dharmakāya, then the dharmakāya would be the same as grass and trees.
If this were so, when a person eats bamboo shoots, they would be eating the dharmakāya in its entirety. How can such talk be worthy of being recorded?

Facing it face-to-face, they are deluded regarding the Buddha; for long kalpas they have sought it in vain. While the whole body is within the Dharma, they remain deluded and seek it externally. Therefore:

For one who understands the Way, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are none other than the Way. For one who awakens to the Dharma, moving forward or backward with ease is none other than the Dharma.
Guang asked again: "Can the great void give birth to spiritual wisdom? Does the true mind condition itself upon good and evil? Is a person possessed of greed and desire on the Way?
Will a person who clings to 'right' and 'wrong' attain penetration of the mind in the future? As for a person who gives rise to thoughts upon encountering objects..."

Is there concentration? There is none in one who dwells in silent seclusion. Is there wisdom? There is none in one who harbors arrogance toward all things. Is there selflessness? There is none in one who clings to emptiness or clings to a self. Is there true knowledge?
There is none in one who seeks proof by following texts, nor in one who seeks the Buddha through asceticism, nor in one who seeks the Buddha apart from the mind.

"You who grasp the mind as being the Buddha—does this wisdom accord with the Way? I pray that the Meditation Master will explain each point for me. The Master said: "The vast void does not give birth to numinous wisdom;
the true mind does not engage with good or evil. Those whose cravings are deep have shallow faculties; those who contend over right and wrong have not yet attained penetration.
Those who give rise to thoughts upon encountering objects lack stability; those who dwell in silence and forget their faculties have sunken wisdom. To be arrogant toward things..."

Those with haughty minds think, "I am strong. Those who cling to emptiness or cling to existence are all deluded. Those who seek proof by searching through texts become increasingly mired in stagnation.
Those who seek the Buddha through ascetic practices are equally lost. To seek the Buddha apart from the mind is the way of external paths; to cling to the mind as being the Buddha is to serve Māra.
[The monk] said, "If it is thus, then ultimately there is nothing at all. The Master said, "Ultimately, it is not that you, Great Virtue, do not exist;

it is that ultimately there is nothing at all. Guang leaped for joy, bowed in gratitude, and departed. [Another] asked, "Regarding the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism, how are they the same and how are they different?
The Master said, "For those of great capacity, when they employ them, they are the same; for those of lesser faculties, when they cling to them, they are different. All [arise] from..."

The single nature gives rise to function; through the differences in the capacities of those who perceive it, three [aspects] are formed. Delusion and enlightenment depend on the person; they do not reside in whether the teaching is identical or different.
There was an elder at Master Weizheng of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou who, seeing sunlight streaming through a window, asked the Master: "Is this..."
The sun moved toward the window, and the Master said, "Elder, there is a guest in your room; it would be well for you to leave.
The Master asked Nanquan, "Among the spiritual friends of all quarters, is there any who possesses a Dharma that cannot be described to others? Nanquan replied, "There is."
The Master said, "How is it? He replied, "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing. The Master said, "If that is so, then you have already explained it to people.
He replied, "I am just like this; what about you, Reverend? The Master said, "I am no spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra);
how could I know whether there is a teaching that is spoken or one that is not? He said, "I do not understand. I beg the Reverend to explain."
The Master said, "I have already told you quite enough. A monk asked, "What is the state where the Buddha and the Way are equal? The Master said, "It is settled.
Once, while on his way to the capital, the Master encountered an official who was eating.

Suddenly, he heard a donkey braying. The official called out, "Head-tato! (addressing the Master). The Master raised his head; the official pointed at the donkey. The Master, in turn, pointed at the official.
Chan Master Letan Fahui of Hongzhou asked Mazu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Mazu said, "Lower your voice and come closer; I will tell you. The Master stepped forward, and Mazu gave him a slap, saying, "Three ears make no secret;
go now and come back tomorrow. On the following day, the Master entered the Dharma Hall alone and said, "I request the Venerable One [to speak]."
The Master said, "Go for now. Wait until I have ascended the hall; I shall come forth and provide you with verification.
The Master suddenly attained realization and said, "I thank the great assembly for their verification. He then circumambulated the Dharma Hall once and departed.
When Chan Master Zhijian of Shanshan in Chizhou was first traveling on pilgrimage with Guizong and Nanquan, they encountered a tiger on the road.
Each passed by the tiger’s side. Nanquan asked Guizong, "What did that tiger just now look like to you?
Guizong replied, "It looked like a cat. Guizong then asked the Master, who replied, "It looked like a dog. He then asked Nanquan. Nanquan—
The Master said, "I see him as being like a great tiger. While the Master was eating his meal, Nanquan gathered up the raw rice and asked, "Is it raw?
The Master replied, "It is not raw. Nanquan said, "Even 'not raw' is still secondary. After Nanquan had walked several paces, the Master called out, "Elder!
Nanquan turned his head and asked, "What is it? The Master said, "Do not say that it is secondary. Later, while they were working together to select ferns, Nanquan—
Quán picked up a stalk [of a plant] and said, "This is a truly excellent offering. The Master said, "It is not only this;
he pays no heed even to a hundred flavors of delicacies. Quán said, "Even so, everyone must taste it before they can understand.
A monk asked, "What is the original body? The Master said, "In all the world, there is nothing like it."
One day, Chan Master Ledu Weijian of Hongzhou was sitting in meditation behind the Dharma Hall.
When Mazu saw him, he blew twice into the master’s ears. The master rose and, seeing it was Mazu, returned once more to his meditative absorption.
Mazu went back to his quarters and ordered an attendant to bring a bowl of tea to the master; the master paid no heed and simply returned to his hall.
Changsha Jingcen (Mingxi Daoheng) Chan Master once said: "I have a great illness that cannot be cured by the physicians of this world.
A monk asked, "How should one practice? The Master said, "What a fine master you are! Do not act like a hired laborer. The monk asked, "Ultimately, how is it?
The Master said, "It is unfit for being set down. The monk asked, "What is the path of true cultivation? The Master said, "It exists after nirvana."

[The student] asked, "What is it like to exist after nirvana? The Master said, "Not washing one's face. [The student] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "If there is no face, what is there to wash?"
Chan Master Huizang of Shigong in Fuzhou originally made his living as a hunter and harbored a deep aversion toward śramaṇas.
Once, while pursuing a deer, he passed before Mazu’s hermitage. Mazu went out to meet him, whereupon the Master asked, "Did you see a deer pass by?
Mazu replied, "Who are you? He said, "A hunter. Mazu said, "Are you skilled at archery? He replied, "I am skilled at archery. Mazu said, "You..."
"How many can one arrow shoot? he asked. The Master replied, "One arrow shoots one. The monk said, "You do not understand shooting.
The Master asked, "Do you understand shooting? The monk replied, "I do. The Master asked, "How many can one arrow shoot? The Master replied, "One arrow shoots a whole flock."
The monk said, "This is life and that is life. Why use this to shoot at that flock? The Patriarch said, "Since you know it is thus, why do you not shoot yourself?
The monk said, "If you were to have me shoot myself, I would truly have no place to begin.

The Patriarch said, "This fellow, the ignorance and afflictions of kalpas past are today suddenly stilled. The Master cast down his bow and arrows and entered the Patriarch’s community to leave the household life. One day—
While he was working in the kitchen, the Patriarch asked, "What are you doing? He replied, "I am herding an ox. The Patriarch asked, "How do you herd it?
He said, "Whenever it goes into the grass, I pull it back by the nose. The Patriarch said, "You truly herd an ox. The Master then ceased [speaking].
After the Master took up residence, he constantly used the bow and arrow to test people's mettle (as recorded in the *Sanping Zhang*). The Master asked Xitang, "Do you understand how to catch it?"
"Can one catch empty space? Xutang said, "I can catch it. The Master asked, "How do you catch it? Xutang reached out his hand and grasped at the air.
The Master said, "You do not know how to catch it. Xutang then asked the Master, "How do you, Elder Brother, catch it? The Master grabbed Xutang’s nostrils and pulled.
Xutang made a cry of pain and said, "You are pulling my nostrils too hard; I feel as though they will come right off! The Master said, "Exactly."
"You must grasp empty space in this way before you will succeed. During the assembly's period of inquiry, the Master said, "Where has that which was just now gone?
A monk said, "It is here. The Master said, "Where is it? The monk snapped his fingers once. A monk asked, "How can one escape birth and death?
The Master said, "What need is there to escape? The monk asked, "How then can one escape? The Master said, "This..."
"Fundamentally, there is no birth-and-death.
Master Lan Rang of Jiangxi asked Elder Liang of Hutang, "I have heard that you, elder brother, have painted a portrait of our late master;
I request to pay my respects to it for a moment. The Master opened his chest with both hands and showed it to him. As soon as Liang prostrated himself, the Master said: [The text ends here.]
[The Master] said, "Do not prostrate; do not prostrate. Huilang said, "Brother, you are mistaken. I am not prostrating to you, Brother.
The Master said, "You are prostrating to my late teacher, Zhenan. Huilang said, "Why then did you tell me not to prostrate? The Master said, "How could I have been mistaken?"
Chan Master Daoming of Nanyuan in Yuanzhou ascended the hall and said: "A swift horse requires but one whip; a swift man requires but one word.
If there is something, why not come forward? If there is nothing, each of you should take care of yourselves. A monk asked, "What about that one word?
The Master stuck out his tongue and said, "Wait until I possess the mark of a broad and long tongue, and then I shall tell you. Dongshan went to visit him. Just as he was about to ascend...
In the Dharma Hall, the Master said, "We have already met. Deshan then went down.
The next day he ascended again and asked, "Yesterday I was already graced by the Master’s compassion; I do not know where that place of mutual meeting with me is."
The Master said, "Mind after mind, without interruption, flows into the ocean of nature. Dongsan said, "How many times have you let this pass? Dongsan took his leave.
The Master said, "Study the Buddha-dharma extensively and bring great benefit to others. Dongsan said, "I do not ask about studying the Buddha-dharma extensively."
"What is it to extensively perform benefit? The Master said, "Do not oppose a single thing. Question: "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "One cannot say that you are him."
Chan Master Liman of Lichun in Xinzhou ascended the hall and said: "The past and present are not different; the Dharma is naturally so. What more is there to say?
Even so, there are many who are at a loss regarding this matter. A monk asked, "Since it does not fall within the past or present, I ask the Master to speak directly.
The Master said, "I knew well that you would be at a loss. As the monk was about to offer further words, the Master said, "I had thought..."
The old monk has fallen into the trap of "ancient and modern" (precedent). The monk asked, “What is it, then? The Master said, “A fish leaping into the azure heavens;
its scales make flight difficult. The monk asked, “How can one avoid this fault? The Master said, “If one has the form of a dragon, who would discuss high or low?
The monk bowed. The Master said, “How bitter! How unjust! Who is like me? He ascended the hall for a discourse: “Setting aside the brightness of day and the darkness of night.”
"What more could be said? Take care. Question: "What is the phrase that is free from contention? The Master said:
"It resounds through the heavens and shakes the earth.
Whenever Zen Master Hong'en of Zhongyi in Langzhou saw a monk approach, he would snap his fingers and make a "he-he" sound. Yangshan [observed this].
Xie Jie (Yangshan) clapped his mouth and made a "he-he" sound, then looked up and passed from west to east.

The Master also clapped his mouth and made a "he-he" sound, then looked up and passed from east to west. The Master again clapped his mouth and made a "he-he" sound, then looked up and stood in the center.
Thereupon, Xie Jie received the precepts. The Master asked, "Where did you obtain this samādhi? Xie Jie replied, "From the seal at Caoxi."
When Shishang came to visit, the Master asked, "Tell me, for what kind of person did Caoxi employ this samādhi?
Yang said, "To receive Yixiu Jue. Suiming asked, "Where did you, Master, obtain this samādhi? The Master replied, "I obtained this samādhi from Great Master Mazu.
Yang then asked, "How does one realize the meaning of seeing the Buddha-nature? The Master said, "I shall explain it to you."
He spoke a parable: "Suppose there is a room with six windows, and inside there is a monkey. Outside there is another monkey who calls from the east, 'Singing-sing!
and the monkey inside immediately responds. In this way, if called from all six windows, it responds to each.
Yangshan bowed in thanks and rose, saying, "I have now understood everything through the Master’s parable. However, there is one further matter: as for the one inside..."
The macaque was asleep. A macaque from outside wished to meet him; what then?
The Master descended from his rope-bed, took Yangshan’s hand, and danced, saying: "The *xingxing* has met you.
It is like a tiny gnat making a nest upon the eye-brows of a mosquito, crying out at the crossroads: 'The land is vast and people are few; those who meet here are rare!'"
[This is] brief. A monk asked Chan Master Létán Chángxīng of Hongzhou: "What is it like to be a guest under the gate of Caoxi?

The Master said: "A swallow coming from the south. The monk said: "I do not understand. The Master said: "It nurtures its feathers, awaiting the autumn wind. [The monk] asked: "What is it like to be..."

Regarding the ultimate matter of the Dharma-vehicle, the Master said: "The autumn rain causes the grass to wither and fall. When Nanquan arrived and saw the Master sitting with his back to the wall, he patted the Master on the back.
The Master asked, "Who are you? Nanquan replied, "Puyuan. The Master asked, "How is it? Nanquan said, "It is just as usual.
The Master remarked, "Why do you trouble yourself so much?"
Chan Master Wuye of Fenzhou was the son of the Du family of Shangluo in Shangzhou; his mother was Lady Li. Having heard a voice from the air asking, "May I take up residence here?
she then became aware that she was pregnant. On the night of his birth, a divine light filled the room. By the time he reached the age of childhood, he had already attained maturity.

When walking, he always kept his gaze straight; when sitting, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). At nine years of age, he relied upon Zhiben of Kaiyuan Temple to receive the Mahāyāna sūtras;

he could read five lines at once, reciting them without omission. At twelve, he shaved his head. At twenty, he received the full precepts from Master You of Xiangzhou and studied the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifenlü shu*);
he was able to expound it as soon as he had finished reading it. He frequently lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the assembly of monks.

He practiced the *Vasudhārā-dhāraṇī* extensively, never ceasing during either winter or summer. Later, hearing that the Chan school under Mazu was flourishing, he went specifically to pay his respects.
Upon seeing his extraordinary appearance and hearing his voice, which resonated like a bell, Mazu said, "Aloft is the Buddha hall, yet within it there is no Buddha."

The Master prostrated, knelt, and asked: "I have roughly exhausted the essential meanings of the literature of the Three Vehicles, yet I have often heard it said in the Chan gate that 'the mind itself is Buddha,' which I truly have not yet understood.
The Patriarch said: "It is precisely this very mind that you have not yet understood; there is nothing else besides it. The Master asked:
"What is the Mind-Seal that the Patriarch transmitted secretly when he came from the West? The Patriarch said: "Virtuous One, you are quite busy right now. And so he left.
He departed and returned at another time. As soon as the Master came out, the Patriarch called out, "Virtuous One! The Master turned his head; the Patriarch asked, "What is this?

At that moment, the Master attained realization and prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "You dull-witted fellow! Why do you prostrate yourself? From that point on, he understood the essential meaning.
He traveled to Caoxi to pay homage at the Patriarch’s stupa, and subsequently visited Mount Lu and Tiantai to seek out all the sacred sites.

Later, he resided at the Kaiyuan Vihāra; when students came to question him, he most often replied: "Do not engage in false conceptualization. Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty repeatedly summoned the Master, but each time he declined on the grounds of illness and did not go.
When Emperor Muzong ascended the throne, he longed to pay his respects in person and thus dispatched Ling... [the Director of Monks] from the two monastic districts.
Fu and the others brought the imperial decree to invite him. Upon arriving there, they prostrated themselves and said, "The Emperor’s gracious command this time is unlike those of ordinary times.

We pray that the Venerable Master will comply with the Heavenly Will and not speak of illness. The Master smiled and said, "What virtue do I, a poor monk, possess to trouble the sovereign so repeatedly?
Please proceed by the main path; I shall depart by another way. Thereupon, he bathed his body and shaved his hair.
At midnight, he addressed his disciples, Huìyìn and others, saying: "The nature of your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is coeval with the great void;
it is neither born nor extinguished. All realms of experience are fundamentally empty and still from the beginning; not a single dharma can be apprehended."
The deluded do not understand this and are thus deluded by objects. Once deluded by objects, they transmigrate without end.
You should know that the nature of the mind is inherently present from the beginning; it is not produced through artificial effort. It is like a vajra, indestructible.
All phenomena are like shadows and echoes; none possess substantial reality. As the Sūtra says: "Only this one thing is real; the other two are..."
"It is not truly eternal. To realize that all is empty, such that not a single thing remains within the reach of the mind—this is the place where the Buddhas apply their minds.

You all should practice this with diligence. Having spoken these words, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. On the day of his cremation, auspicious clouds of five colors appeared and a wondrous fragrance permeated the four directions.
The śarīra relics obtained were as brilliant as pearls and jade. His disciples stored them in a golden jar and interred them in a stone stupa.

On the twenty-first day of the twelfth month of the Gui-mao year during the Changqing era, at the age of sixty-two and forty-two years since his ordination, he was posthumously granted the imperial title of National Teacher Dada; his stupa was named Lingyuan.
A monk asked Chan Master Guangcheng of Dading in Lizhou, "How can one cause the six sense-faculties to cease?

The Master said, "A wheeling sword cast into the air does not harm anything. The monk asked, "What is the person of original nature? The Master said, "Sitting together, we do not recognize each other.
The monk said, "If that is so, then I, this student, shall depart with gratitude. The Master said, "In the dark, you write of a grieving heart to send to another."
Who was he? Chan Master Dayi of Gehu in Xinzhou, a native of the Xu family of Xujiang in Quzhou.

During the reign of Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty, he was once summoned to the palace to debate the principles of the Dharma at Lide Hall. A presiding master asked, "What are the Four Noble Truths? The Master replied, "The Sage..."
"Where are the former emperors and the three emperors? He asked again, "The realm of desire has no dhyāna, and dhyāna abides in the realm of form.
Upon what does this land rely for its establishment? The Master said, "Dharma Master, you only know that the realm of desire has no dhyāna; you do not know that the realm of dhyāna has no desire."
[The Emperor] asked, "What is Chan? The Master pointed at the empty space with his hand. The Dharma Master [Falin] had no reply.
The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master has lectured on infinite sutras and treatises, yet he is still at a loss for this single point. The Master then asked the eminent virtuous ones present:
"In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, what ultimately constitutes the Way? One replied, "Knowing is the Way. The Master said, "It cannot be so."
"Wisdom knows; it cannot be known by consciousness. How can one know that which knows? It is that which has an object but is without discrimination. The Master said:
"One who is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena yet remains unmoved within the ultimate truth—how could such a person be without discrimination?

It is that which has an object and corresponds to the four dhyānas and eight samādhis. The Master said: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it does not fall into any numerical categories."
When asked, "Where does one abide in the four dhyānas and eight samādhis? the assembly remained silent. The Master then cited Emperor Shunzong’s question to Chan Master Śīla:
"How can the sentient beings of this great earth see their nature and attain Buddhahood? Śīla replied, "Buddha-nature is like the moon in the water; it can be seen but cannot be grasped.
He then said to the Emperor, "Buddha-nature is not something to be seen by sight; it must be realized. It is like the moon in the water..."
"What do you seize? The Emperor then asked, "What is Buddha-nature? The Master replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has just asked.
The Emperor understood this in silence, and the True Lord (Emperor Zhenzong) honored him all the more. There was a monk who requested to be interred in a stupa.
When Minister Li Ao asked him, "The teachings do not permit carrying a corpse past the base of a stupa; how then shall it be? The monk had no reply. The monk, however, [departed].
He questioned his master, who replied: "He has attained great icchantika-hood. On the seventh day of the first month in the *wuxu* year of the Yuanhe era, he passed away at the age of seventy-four.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Huijue (Wisdom Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Jianxing (Manifesting Nature).
Chan Master Zizai of Mount Funiu at Yi Que was the son of Li of Wuxing. Initially, he received full ordination under Guoyi;
later, he studied with Mazu and realized the mind-ground. Mazu ordered him to deliver a letter to National Teacher Huizhong.
When the National Teacher asked, "With what Dharma does Master Ma instruct his disciples? he replied, "It is 'this very mind is Buddha. The National Teacher said, "What kind of talk is that?"
After a long silence, he asked again, "Beyond this, what further teachings do you have? The Master said, "Neither mind, nor Buddha.
Another said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. The National Teacher said, "That is still somewhat better.
The Master asked, "Master Mazu speaks thus; I wonder, how about here with you, Reverend? The National Teacher said, "The three dots are like flowing water."
His voice was like a sickle cutting grain. Later, the Master resided at Mount Funiu. He ascended the hall and said:

"‘This very mind is Buddha’ is a phrase for seeking medicine when one is not ill. ‘Neither mind nor Buddha’ is a phrase for counteracting the disease with the medicine. A monk asked, "What is the phrase of liberation?
The Master replied, "It has been passed down from ancient times beneath Mount Funiu. He entered parinirvāṇa at Kaiyuan Temple in Suizhou.
Chan Master Weikuan of Xingshan Monastery in Jingzhao was the son of the Zhu family of Xin’an, Quzhou.

At the age of thirteen, upon seeing those who were slaughtering living beings, he was struck with such compassion that he could not bear to eat meat; he therefore sought to leave the household life. Initially, he studied the *vinaya* and practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Later, he visited Daji (Huairang), through whom he attained the essential point of the mind. In the gengwu year of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he began his ministry for the transformation of beings among the regions of Wu and Yue. Eight...
When he reached Mount Poyang, a spirit requested that he receive the eight precepts. In the year Dingchou, he stayed at Shaolin on Mount Song.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "A truly fine mountain. The monk said, "I am asking about the Way; why do you speak of a fine mountain?
The Master said, "You only recognize a fine mountain; when have you ever realized the Way? [Another] asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master—
The monk said, "Does the Master have it? The Master said, "I do not. The monk said, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
why alone do you, Master, lack it? The Master said, "I am not among all sentient beings. The monk said, "If you are not a sentient being..."
"Are you not the Buddha? The Master said, "I am not the Buddha. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what thing are you?

The Master said, "Nor am I a thing. [The monk] asked, "Can you be seen or thought of? The Master said, "It is beyond the reach of thought and cannot be grasped by deliberation; therefore, it is called 'inconceivable' (*acintya*).
In the *Jihchou* year of the Yuanhe era, Emperor Xianzong issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital. The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Bai Juyi, once...
Question: Since you are called a Chan Master, why do you preach the Dharma? The Master said: "Unsurpassed Bodhi—when it is applied to the body, it is the Vinaya;
when it is spoken from the mouth, it is the Dharma; when it is practiced by the mind, it is Chan. These three applications are three in name, but their ultimate aim is one."
It is like the Yangtze, the Huai, the Jiang, and the Han rivers: each is given a name according to its location, yet though the names differ, the nature of water is one and the same.
The Vinaya is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is not separate from dhyāna. Why, then, give rise to false discrimination within it? [The student] asked:

"If there is no discrimination, why cultivate the mind? The Master said: "The mind is fundamentally without injury or damage; why must it be 'cultivated' or 'repaired'? Whether defiled or pure, it makes no difference."

[The student] asked, "If one must not give rise to any thoughts, then defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is indeed not to be thought of; but can purity (*viśuddhi*) be free from thought? The Master said, "It is like a speck upon the human eye: nothing may remain there.

Though gold dust is precious, when it is in the eye, it becomes a disease. [The student] asked, "If there is neither cultivation nor thought, how does this differ from an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?

The Master said, "Ordinary persons are characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*), while those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are characterized by attachment (*abhiniveśa*). [One who is free from these]..."
These two illnesses—this is called true cultivation. True cultivation means neither striving nor forgetting. Striving leads to attachment; forgetting falls into ignorance.
This is the essential point of the mind. Thus it was said. Question: Where does the Way reside? The Master said:
"It is right before your eyes. The monk asked, "Why do I not see it? The Master said, "Because you have the notion of 'I,' you do not see it.

The monk asked, "If I have the notion of 'I' and thus do not see it, does the Master see it? The Master said, "As long as there is 'you' and there is 'me,' we shall continue to fail to see each other.
The monk asked, "If there is neither 'I' nor 'you,' can you then see it? The Master said, "If there is neither 'I' nor 'you,' who is there to seek to see?"
On the final day of the second month in the year of Dingyou during the Yuanhe era, he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma; having finished, he passed away.

He was sixty-three years of age and thirty-nine years since his ordination. His stupa was erected on the western plain of Balingshan, and by imperial decree he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dache (Great Penetration), with his stupa named Zhengzhen (Correct Truth).
Chan Master Wudeng of Ezhou was a native of Wei County. His secular surname was Li. He left the household life on Mount Gonggong and secretly received the essential points of the mind.
Later, he went forth to reside at Tumen in Suizhou. One day, he went to visit the provincial governor, Attendant-in-Ordinary Wang. As he was taking his leave and about to step out the door, he said:

He summoned him, saying, "Upādhyāya. The Master looked back; the Cowherd struck the pillar three times. The Master made a circular gesture with his hand and then pushed it away three times before departing.
Later, while residing at Daji Temple in Wuchang, during the evening assembly, as everyone came forward, the Master stepped out from the front and said, "How do you do?
He then addressed the assembly, saying, "Where did the sound of the crowd just now go?"
There was a monk who raised one finger. The Master said, "Take care.
When that monk came for an audience the following morning, the Master turned his body away and lay down facing the wall, feigning groans and saying, "I have not been very well these past few days.
Great Virtue, do you have any medicine with you? Give me a little. The monk reached out his hand...
He struck the water jar and said, "From where did you get this water jar? The Master replied, "This one belongs to me, the old monk.
[The monk] asked, "Where is yours, Virtuous One? [The Master] said, "It belongs to you, the Monk, and it also belongs to me. The Master then struck him.
He passed away in the gengxu year of the Tahe era of Emperor Wen of the Tang dynasty at the age of eighty-two.

A monk asked Chan Master Zongyin of Sanjiaoshan in Tanzhou, "What are the Three Jewels? The Master said, "Rice, wheat, and beans. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The assembly joyfully accepts and upholds them. He ascended the hall and said, "If one discusses this matter, by the time you raise your eyebrows, you have already missed it. Magu then asked, "As for raising the eyebrows—" The Master said, "That is not it. Magu then bowed. The Master said, "You have missed it. Magu then struck the meditation seat once and departed. The Master called out to him; Magu did not turn his head. The Master said, "You have missed it. Magu then struck the meditation seat once more and left. The Master said, "This fellow has some spirit. Later, when Magu was about to pass away, he asked his disciples, "When I was at Sanjiaoshan, I received a single word from the Master. Now that I am about to die, what should I do? His disciples replied, "The Master’s Dharma body is already perfect; why do you still seek something else? Magu then struck the meditation seat once and passed away. His disciples reported this to the Master. The Master said, "This fellow has some spirit. He then composed a verse: "Magu was like a dragon without scales, Like a tiger without paws. He could not be captured by the hook, Nor could he be bound by the net. The Master then had Magu’s remains enshrined in a stupa. When the stupa was finished, the Master entered it himself and sat upright. He then had the doors sealed with a stone and departed. The next day, the monks opened the doors and found the Master gone. They searched everywhere but could not find him. They returned and reported this to the local governor, who said, "The Master has surely ascended to heaven. He then had a stele erected to commemorate him. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he told his disciples, "I am going to leave this world. He then composed a verse: "I have wandered through the five directions, And now I return to my original home. The great earth is vast and empty; Who can grasp its tracks? Having spoken this verse, he passed away. His disciples cremated his body and collected the relics. The local governor heard of this and sent an official to request the remains.
