every seven paces he would strike the staff once and chant the name of Avalokiteśvara once. Jiashan asked him, "I have heard from afar that you, Master, recite the name of Avalokiteśvara—is this true?"
The Master said, "So be it. Shanshan asked, "What if one were to ride upon the head? The Master said, "If you put your head out, I will let you ride;
if you do not put your head out, what is there to ride? Shanshan had no reply. A monk came for an audience. Just as he was unfolding his sitting mat, the Master said, "Slowly, slowly.
The monk asked, "What did you see, Master? The Master said, "What a pity—that you should have smashed the bell tower! From this, the monk attained realization.
The Inspector Pei Xiu visited him and asked, "Do you have any attendants?
The Master replied, "I have one or two, but they are not permitted to see guests. Pei asked, "Where are they? The Master then called out, "Dàkōng! Xiǎokōng!"
At that time, two tigers emerged from behind the hermitage. When Pei saw them, he was struck with terror. The Master said to the two tigers, "There is a guest here;
depart for now. The two tigers roared and left. Pei asked, "What kind of practice has the Master performed to move them to such an extent?"

The Master then remained silent for a long while and asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "This mountain monk constantly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara. Tingzhou Shuidang Wenheshang asked Guizong, "What kind of person are you? Guizong replied, "A person from Chenzhou. The Master asked, "How old are you? Guizong replied, "Twenty-two. The Master said, "Before you were born, where did this old monk go and come from? Guizong replied, [silently]. The Master said, "If you can speak like this, you may enter my gate. Guizong then bowed. The Master said, "You have entered my gate. Later, Guizong went to see the Master again. The Master asked, "Where have you been? Guizong replied, "I have been to the place of the Old Man of Mount Lu. The Master asked, "Did he teach you anything? Guizong replied, "He taught me nothing. The Master said, "Why did you say he taught you nothing? Guizong replied, "When I asked him about the meaning of the Patriarchs' coming from the West, he struck me with his staff and said, 'You have already gone too far. The Master said, "That fellow has a staff that knows no rest; it strikes people's heads and never misses. Guizong then bowed. The Master said, "You have entered my gate. Later, Guizong went to see the Master once more. The Master asked, "Where have you been? Guizong replied, "I have been to the place of the Old Man of Mount Lu. "Master, when were you born? The Master held up his whisk. Zong said, "Does this have birth?
The Master said, "If you understand it, there is no birth. Zong said, "I do not yet understand. The Master remained silent.
A monk asked Master Mengxi, "What is it like when not a single thought arises? The Master remained silent for a long while. The monk then bowed.
The Master said, "How do you understand this? The monk replied, "I truly dare not be shameless.
The Master said, "You have indeed gained conviction. Another asked, "How does one realize the fundamental matter? The Master said, "Why do you not ask? The monk said, "Please [instruct me]."
The Master answered the monk’s remark, saying, “You have asked well. The monk laughed loudly and departed. The Master said, “Only this monk possesses keen intelligence.
Another monk came from outside; the Master immediately shouted. The monk said, “What a fine occasion! The Master said, [“... (implying a similar response).
"Still, the staff remains with the monk. Having said "Take care," he departed. The Master remarked, "He has attained mastery.
Whenever Master Fota of Wenzhou saw someone coming, he would strike the ground with his staff and say, "The Buddhas of the past were like this;
the Buddhas of the future will be like this. A monk asked, "At that very moment, what is it? The Master drew a circle.
A monk performed a woman’s bow. The Master struck him. A monk asked, “What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, “Thief! Thief! A monk asked, “What is a being of a different species? The Master struck the bowl and said, “Huanu, Huanu, come eat your rice.”
The monk Wujou and the two senior monks Xuanshao visited the Master. The Master asked, "Where did you two Zen guests set out from?
Xuanshao replied, "Jiangxi. The Master struck him. Xuanshao said, "I have long known that the Master possesses such a vital pivot. The Master said:
"You do not understand; look at that monk behind you. As Shao was about to step forward, the Master struck him and said, "I knew it—there is no difference between soil from the same pit.
Go to the hall to attend to your duties. A monk asked, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "Dingzhou."
The Master said, "How does the Dharma-way of Dingzhou compare to here? The monk replied, "It is no different. The Master said, "If it is no different, then go back there!
He then struck him. The monk said, "There is an eye at the tip of the staff; one must not strike people so recklessly.
The Master said, "Today I have hit one who truly deserves it," and struck him three more times. The monk then departed. The Master said, "The staff was indeed a grievance [to have been used so]."
A man said, "Someone has already eaten it. The Master said, "What can you do? The handle of the ladle is in my hands.
The monk said, "If you want me to give it back to you, I will. The monk stepped forward, snatched the staff, and struck the Master three times.

The Master said, "An unjust blow! An unjust blow! The monk said, "Someone has already eaten it. The Master said, "I have carelessly struck a man. The monk bowed. The Master said, "And yet, it turns out like this."
"Go! The monk laughed loudly and departed. The Master said, "He can take it; he can take it.
In an ancient temple, the monk Danxia came to visit and stayed overnight.

The next morning, when the congee was ready, the attendant served only one bowl to the Master and filled another for himself to eat, paying no heed whatsoever to Danxia. Danxia also filled his own bowl and ate. The attendant—
He said, "At the fifth watch, people rise before dawn; yet there are still those traveling by night. Xiang asked the Master, "Why do you not instruct your practitioners?
How can they be so discourteous? The Master replied, "One must not defile the pure ground with the men and women of others. Xiang said, "..."
"I almost asked that old fellow about his faults.
When Master Shijiu first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Wujiao.
Mazu asked, "What has been said recently at Wujiao? The Master replied, "How many people here are utterly bewildered! Mazu said, "Bewildered..."
"Setting that aside for a moment, what about this single phrase of silence? How do you handle it? The Master then stepped forward three paces.
The Patriarch said, "I have seven blows to give; I am entrusting them to Wugou. Are you willing to accept them? The Master replied, "The Master shall eat them first; I will accept them later."
Master Benchxi was asked by Layman Pang, "When Danxia struck his attendant, what was his intention?
The Master said, "You old fellow, you still have the habit of judging others' faults. The Layman said, "Since we are fellow students of the same teacher, I venture to ask you this."
The Master said, "If you bring it up from the beginning like this, I will deliberate with you. The Layman said, "Great Elder, you must not speak of right and wrong with me.
The Master said, "I am mindful that you are old. The Layman said, "My fault, my fault."
When Master Shilin saw Layman Pang approaching, he held up his whisk and said, "This does not fall into the trap of Danxia’s device;
try and say a single phrase. The Layman snatched away the whisk and instead raised his own fist. The Master said, "That is precisely Danxia’s device.
The Layman said, "Let us see who does not fall into it. The Master said, "Danxia suffers from muteness; Master Pang suffers from deafness. The Layman said, "... (The text ends here).
[The Master] said, "Exactly so. The Master remained silent. The Layman said, "I told you it was merely a coincidence. On another day, he asked the Layman, "I have a question to ask;
do not be stingy with your words, Layman. The Layman said, "Please go ahead and ask. The Master said, "So you *are* stingy with your words?

The Layman said, "Regarding this very inquiry, I did not realize I had fallen into his trap. The Master then covered his ears. The Layman said, [“... (implying the Master’s action was a sign of his own defeat). The Layman said, [“...”]. (This concludes the exchange.)
"Teacher, teacher.
The presiding monk (zuozhu) Liang of Xishan in Nanchang was a native of Shu. He had lectured extensively on the sutras and śāstras.

Having gone to visit Mazu, Mazu asked, "I have heard it said that you, Master, lecture extensively on the sutras and śāstras—is this true? The Master replied, "I dare not say so. Mazu asked, "With what [do you lecture]?"
The lecturer said, "I shall lecture with my mind. The Patriarch said, "The mind is like a performing actor, and the intellect is like the conductor. How can you possibly understand how to lecture?
The lecturer raised his voice and said, "If the mind cannot be lectured upon, can empty space be lectured upon? The Patriarch said, "Indeed, it is empty space that can be lectured upon.
The lecturer did not accept this and was about to leave the hall when he descended the steps. The Patriarch called out, "Lecturer! The lecturer turned back.
[The Master] bowed his head. The Patriarch said, "How very, very [profound]. The Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment and immediately prostrated himself.
The Patriarch said, "Why does this dull-witted monk prostrate? The Master replied, "I thought that no one could equal me in the sutras and treatises I have studied.

Today, having been questioned by the Great Master, all the achievements of my life were instantly dissolved like melting ice. He withdrew after offering his thanks and subsequently went into seclusion.
There was no further news of him at Xishan in Hongzhou.
A monk asked Master Heyan, "What is the teacher who does not appear in the world? The Master said, "Śāriputra’s staff.
[Another] asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "A charcoal seller for ten years does not know the weight on the scale."
At Xingmi Ridge, a monk asked Master Heshang, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? The Master said, "Ugliness is left to your own disdain;
it does not wear the colors of clouds and mists. When the Master was about to pass away, he left behind this verse: "The patriarchs, one after another, are inconceivable; they do not permit..."
"Abiding eternally in the world. Great assembly, contemplate this carefully; in the end, it is only this. Having finished speaking, he became silent.
When Master Qifeng was visited by Layman Pang, the Master said, "A layperson entering the monastic quarters so frequently—what are you looking for?
The Layman looked to his left and right and said, "Who says such a thing? The Master then gave him a shout. The Layman said, "Right here!"
The Master said, "Is this not the Way of the Open Court? The scholar said, "What about that which is behind you? The Master turned his head and said, "Look! Look!
The scholar said, "The grass-thief has been utterly defeated. The scholar then asked, "How many li is it from here to the mountain peak? The Master said, "Where have you come from?
The scholar said, "It may be called steep and hard, yet one cannot question it. The Master said, "How much is it? The scholar said, [silently].
"One, two, three. The Master said, "Four, five, six. The scholar said, "Why do you not speak of seven? The Master said, "As soon as you speak of seven, there is already eight.
The scholar said, "I can stay here. The Master said, "Add as much as you wish. The scholar gave a shout and departed; the Master also shouted after him.

When Master Dayang met Yizhan, he asked him, "Yizhan, these days there is a certain class of teachers who instruct people regarding what is before their eyes, taking this very thing before them as the goal for helping others. Do you understand the state when the literary patterns have not yet emerged?
Yizhan said, "I intend to pose a question here; I do not know if it would be appropriate. The Master said, "It is already so."
The Master replied, "Do not speak of 'yes' or 'no' at all. He asked, "Do you recognize what is right before your eyes? The Master said, "If it is right before your eyes, how would you recognize it?
He replied, "In any case, it is subject to scrutiny. The Master said, "Who says so? He replied, "I do. The Master then gave a shout.
He stepped back and stood there. The Master said, "You only know how to look ahead; you do not know how to look behind. He replied, "Like adding snow to snow."
He added, "It is even more frosty. The Master said, "In either case, there is no benefit.
A monk from Hongluo Mountain in Youzhou presented a verse to his disciples, which says: "The son of Hongluo Mountain dwells near the borderlands."
Among those who have attained liberation, half are Xis. When spoken to and questioned, they do not understand a word; pitiable indeed, they only know "Nasiqi.
One day, when Master Bailin encountered Layman Pang on the road, he asked him, "Have you gained strength at Mount Nanyue?"
[The Master] said, "Have you ever brought this up to anyone? The Layman said, "I have. The Master asked, "To whom did you bring it up?
The Layman pointed at himself with his hand and said, "Pang Gong. The Master said, "This is truly Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) and Emptiness-Born (Śāriputra);
even praise cannot reach it. The Layman then asked, "Master, who knows the phrase by which you gained power? The Master put on his bamboo hat and walked away. The Layman— [followed him].
He said, "Excellent wayfarer! The Master will not look back again.
The Oxhead Ancestor of Zhenzhou used to prepare his own meals and offer them to the assembly of monks.
When it was time for the midday meal, he would carry the rice bucket to the front of the hall, perform a dance, and laugh heartily, saying, "Sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat!"
A monk asked the Venerable Heishui of Luojing, "What is the secret chamber? The Master said, "Cutting off one's ears and lying in the street.
The monk asked, "Who is the person within the secret chamber? The Master then crossed his hands and beat his breast.
A monk asked Master Lishan, “When all forms return to emptiness, where does emptiness return?

The Master said, “The tongue does not leave the mouth. The monk asked, “Why does it not leave the mouth? The Master said, “Because inner and outer are one and the same. Another asked, “Without passing through eons, one attains the Dharmakāya;
I pray that the Master will point this directly to me. The Master said, “The son inherits the father’s trade. The monk asked, “How should I understand this? The Master— [replied].
[The monk] said, "Is it that [the teaching of] disparagement and stripping away is not applied? [The Master] said, "If that is so, then the assembly will have something to rely upon.
The Master said, "Setting the assembly aside for a moment, what is the Dharma-body? The monk had no reply. The Master said, "Ask me and I will tell you. The monk asked.
"What is the Dharma-body? The Master said, "Blooming flowers in the sky; a mirage. The questioner asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
The Master said, "Do you not see how it is? He asked, "Why is it so? The Master said, "Precisely because it is so."
The Monk of Ruyuan in Shaoshan ascended the hall for formal instruction. "The direct meaning from the West—how difficult it is to express!
Is there anyone among you who can state it? Come forward and try to say it. At that time, a monk came forward and prostrated.
The Master struck him and said, "What kind of occasion is this to come forward? He then returned to his quarters. When Yangshan was a novice śrāmaṇera, he was reciting the sutras.
The sound was loud. The Master rebuked him, saying, "This śrāmaṇera, you recite the sutras as if you were weeping. Huaiji said, "I am simply like this;
I wonder, how about you, Master? The Master looked up at him and said, "If it is like this, how is it any different from weeping? Thereupon, the Master ceased speaking.
Master Songshan was drinking tea with Layman Pang. The Layman held up his tea bag and asked, "Everyone has their share;
why is it that they cannot speak of it? The Master said, "Precisely because everyone has it, they cannot speak of it.
The Layman said, "Why is it, elder brother, that you can speak of it? The Master said, "One must not remain without words. The Layman said, "Truly so."
"Clearly! The Master then drank his tea. The gentleman said, "Brother, you are drinking tea; why do you not bow to your guest? The Master asked, "Who?
The gentleman replied, "I am Pang. The Master said, "Why bother to bow further?

Later, when Danxia heard of this, he remarked, "Had it not been for Songshan, I might have been thrown into confusion by that old fellow. When the gentleman heard this, he sent someone to deliver a message to Danxia.
He said: "Why did you not grasp it when the bag had not yet been lifted?
Now, Master Chuanshan was a native of Shu. While he and Layman Pang were looking at one another, the Master asked, "Do you still remember the principle from when you saw Stonehead?
The Layman replied, "I am still able to have you, Master, raise it up once more. The Master said, "I knew for certain that you had long since practiced."
The official was arrogant. The layman said, "Master, you are old and decrepit; you are no match for Master Pang. The master said, "The two of them were contemporaries;
how much difference is there between them? The official said, "Master Pang was vigorous and healthy, surpassing you every day.

The master said, "It is not that he surpassed me; he simply lacked your head wrap (*fukutō*). The official took off his head wrap and said, "Now he resembles you, Master. The master merely laughed heartily.
While the Master was picking tea, the scholar said, “The Dharma-realm admits no person; does the Master still see me? The Master replied, “It is not that I, the teacher, am answering your question.
The scholar said, “To have a question and an answer is merely the ordinary. The Master continued picking tea and paid him no heed.
The scholar said, “Do not take offense at my having just asked so easily. The Master still did not look back. The scholar shouted:
"This man who lacks decorum—let me present him one by one to those with clear eyes.
The Master then cast aside his tea basket and returned directly to the abbot’s quarters.
The Monk Dazi of Xinzhou had received the imperial edict in Jiangxi and always kept his name concealed; whenever students came to question him...
He merely struck the ground with his staff to indicate [the meaning]. At that time, he was called "Master Striking the Ground" (Dadidi Heshang).
One day, a monk hid the staff away and then posed a question to him; the Master simply opened his mouth.
The monk asked a disciple, "When someone asks the Master every day and he strikes the ground, what is the underlying intent? The disciple immediately took a piece of firewood from inside the stove.
[The Master] threw a piece [of wood] into the cauldron.
Zen Master Xiuxi of Tanzhou asked Gushan, "When sound and form are pure and true, what is the Way? The Master said, "Why do you disturb the Way?
Gushan then moved from east to west and stood there. The Master said, "If it were not like this, it would be a disaster."
Mount Guishan again walked from west to east and stood still. The Master then descended from his meditation seat;
just as he had taken two steps, Guishan seized him and asked, "What is the matter with this pure reality of sound and form? The Master gave him a slap.
Guishan said, "Thirty years from now, there will not even be anyone left to serve tea. The Master replied, "What would you do with this fellow Guishan? Guishan—
He laughed heartily.
While Master Bibu of Jiangxi was lying down, Daowu approached and pulled the blanket over him. The Master asked, "What are you doing?"
I said, "It is the covering. The Master said, "Is it that which lies at the bottom? Is it that which sits upon it? I said, "It is not in either of these two places.
The Master said, "What then of the covering? I said, "Do not speak in confusion. While the Master was by the fire, I asked, "What is this?"
The Master said, "Harmony. Wuye said, "If that is so, you have already escaped at the very head.
The Master said, "How long has it been since we last met? Wuye then shook his sleeves and departed. One day, as Wuye returned from outside, the Master asked, "Where have you been?
Wuye said, "I have been attending closely. The Master said, "Why do you go to such lengths with these two pieces of skin? Wuye said, [silently].
"Borrowing. The Master said, "Does he have something to borrow from you? How about that? I replied, "It is precisely because he has it that he borrows it.
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A cat climbing a pillar. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Go ask the pillar."
When the Monk of Caotang in Jingzhao first ceased his studies under Daji and arrived at the place of Haichang, Haichang asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master said, "From Daochang. Haichang asked, "What is this place here? The Master said, "Thieves do not break into the homes of the poor.
He asked, "Before there was a single dharma, where was this body? The Master drew a perfect circle.
In the center of this, he inscribed the character for "body" (shen).
When a monk took his leave of Master Dong’an, the Master asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "Fundamentally, there is nowhere to go. The Master said:
The teacher said, "Be a good preceptor. [The disciple] replied, "I dare not. The teacher said, "When you travel to various places, explain this clearly.
While a monk was standing in attendance, the teacher asked, "What is today’s date? [The monk] replied, "I do not know. The teacher said, "I, however, remember it.
[The monk] asked, "What is today’s date? The teacher said, "Today is cloudy and dark."
When Master Xingping of Jingzhao came to pay his respects at Dongshan, the Master said, "Do not bow to an old decrepit man.
Dongshan said, "The one being bowed to is not the old decrepit man. The Master said, "That which is not the old decrepit man does not receive bows. Dongshan said, "He also does not cease [to exist].
Dongshan then asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? The Master said, "It is precisely your own mind. Dongshan said, "Even so..."
"This is still a point of doubt for me," said Xiangyan. The Master said, "If that is so, then go ask the wooden man.
Xiangyan said, "I have a phrase that does not borrow from the mouths of the sages. The Master said, "Try to say it. Xiangyan said, "It is not I.
As Xiangyan was taking his leave, the Master asked, "Where will you go? Xiangyan said, "Following the current, there is no fixed destination. The Master said, "The Dharma..."
"Body follows the stream; retribution-body follows the stream. Master Shan said, "I do not understand it in this way at all. The Master then clapped his hands.
Xiaoyao Wenheshi asked Lukxi, "Every thought clings to conditions; every mind is eternally still. The Master said, "Last night, someone also spoke like that.
Xiaoyao asked, "What did they say? The Master said, "I do not know. Xiaoyao said, "Please ask the Master [to explain]."

[The Master] spoke. The Master struck him over the mouth with his whisk. Xixi shook out his sleeves and departed. The Master called to the assembly, saying, "Keep your eyes open at the crown of your heads.
A monk asked Master Fuxi, "What is it like when the ancient mirror is without blemish? The Master remained silent for a long time. The monk said, "What is the Master’s meaning?"
"How is it? the monk asked. The Master said, "This mountain monk is deaf. The monk asked again. The Master said, "It is still somewhat better than that.
A monk asked, "What is one's own self? The Master said, "What are you asking? The monk replied, "Is there no expedient means?
The Master said, "What were you just now asking? The monk said, "How can you be so topsy-turvy? The Master said, "Today you deserve a blow from this mountain monk’s staff."

Question: "When conditioned phenomena disperse and return to emptiness, where does emptiness return? The Master then called to the assembly of monks; the monks responded with "Yes. The Master said, "Where is emptiness?
They replied, "We request the Master to tell us. The Master said, "The Persian eats black pepper."
When National Teacher Shuilao of Hongzhou first visited Mazu, he asked, "What is the very meaning of the coming from the West?
Mazu said, "Prostrate yourself. As soon as the Master prostrated, Mazu stepped on him right at the chest. The Master attained great enlightenment;
rising up, he clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Hundreds of thousands of samādhis, immeasurable wondrous..."
"Meaning! You must recognize the source upon a single hair-tip. Having said this, he bowed in thanks and withdrew. Later, whenever he addressed the assembly, he would say:
"Ever since I took that one bite from Mazu’s kick, I have been laughing without end until now.
A monk drew a circle, pinched it with his hand, and moved it toward the Master’s body. The Master pushed it away three times, then also drew a circle and returned it.
He pointed at a monk. The monk immediately bowed. The Master struck him and said, "This fellow of empty pretenses! A monk asked, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa?
The Master said, "Movement brings forth shadows; awareness gives rise to ice. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master clapped his hands and laughed loudly.
Master Fubei was visited by Ling Xingpo, who came to pay her respects. The Master offered her a seat and tea.
The woman then asked, "To whom do you entrust that phrase which cannot be spoken even with one's full strength? The Master replied, "Fubei has no superfluous words.

The woman said, "Before reaching Fubei, I could not help but harbor doubts. The Master said, "If you have another point of excellence, feel free to bring it forth. The woman folded her hands and wept.
He said, "The blue sky has yet another layer of grievous suffering added to it. The Master remained silent. The old woman said, "In speech you do not know the biased and the correct;
in principle you do not recognize the inverted and the crooked. To act as a teacher for others is to invite calamity. Later, a monk reported this to Nanquan. Nanquan said, "What a pity, Fubei!
You have been broken once by this old woman. When the old woman later heard of this, she laughed and said, "Master Wang still lacks some skillful means."
There was a Zen practitioner named Chengyi who encountered a laywoman (xingpo) and asked, "What is it that Nanquan still lacks in his skillful means?
The woman then wept, saying, "How tragic! How painful! Chengyi was at a loss for words. The woman asked, "Do you understand? Chengyi joined his palms and stood there.
The woman said, "Dead Zen monks are as numerous as hemp and millet. Chengyi reported this to Zhaozhou, who said, "I..."
When he saw this foul old woman, he questioned her until she was left speechless. One asked, "I do not understand, Master; how did you question her? Zhaozhou struck him.
The other said, "Why did you strike me instead? Zhaozhou replied, "If I do not strike a fellow like this dead man, when shall I ever do so?
He struck him several more times. Upon hearing this, the old woman said, "Zhaozhou deserves to eat from my hand."
[The Master] struck him with his staff. Later, a monk recounted this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou wept and said, "How tragic! How painful!

When the old woman heard these words, she joined her palms and sighed in admiration, saying, "Zhaozhou’s eye pierces through the four worlds. Zhaozhou then instructed the monk to ask her, "What is Zhaozhou’s eye? The old woman then raised her fist.
The monk returned and recounted this to Zhaozhou, who then composed a verse, which begins: "When the occasion arises, face it directly..."
"Face-to-face! Face-to-face, the response is swift and direct. I tell you, Laywoman Ling: why this weeping? Why this gain and loss? The laywoman replied with a verse:

"The Master has already understood the sound of my weeping; now that it is understood, who is there to know it? At that time in the kingdom of Magadha, how many would have lost the immediate opportunity before their eyes?"
The Monk of Longshan in Tanzhou asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From where the old master stays. The Master said, "What words or phrases did the old master speak?
The monk said, "If he speaks, there are a thousand phrases and ten thousand phrases; if he does not speak, there is not a single character.
The Master said, "In that case, it is like a fly laying its eggs. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him. Dongshan and Mimi... [text ends]
Fubo was traveling along when he saw vegetable leaves floating in a mountain stream. He said, "This deep mountain is uninhabited; why are there vegetables flowing here?

Is there perhaps a practitioner of the Way living here? They then consulted together and pushed through the grass to follow the stream for five or seven li, where they suddenly beheld the Master, whose emaciated form and extraordinary appearance struck them with awe.
Setting down their luggage, they paid their respects. The Master asked, "There are no paths on this mountain; from where have you come, O *jialuo*?"
Dong said, "Setting aside for a moment that there is no path, from where did you enter, Master? The Master replied, "I did not come from traveling among the clouds and waters.
Dong asked, "How long has the Master resided on this mountain? The Master replied, "I have not been involved with spring or autumn.
Dong asked, "Did the Master reside here first, or did the mountain reside here first? The Master replied, "I do not know. Dong asked, "Why do you not know?"
The Master said, "I have not come from the realm of humans or devas. Dongshan asked, "What principle did you realize, Master, that you dwell on this mountain?
The Master said, "I saw two earthen oxen fighting and entering the sea; until now, there has been no further news.
Only then did Dongshan assume his full ceremonial demeanor and prostrate himself, asking, "What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "Green mountains shroud the white clouds."
Yun asked, "What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "Never leaving the door for many years. Yun asked, "How far apart are the guest and the host?
The Master said, "Waves upon the waters of the Long River. Yun asked, "When the guest and host meet, what words are spoken? The Master said:
A pure breeze brushed against the bright moon. Dongshan took his leave, and the Master then composed a verse, saying:

"I have always dwelt in a thatched hut of three bays; A single ray of divine light leaves all phenomena at ease. Do not bring right and wrong to judge me; The worldly life of fabrication has no concern with this.
Because of this, he burned his hermitage and entered the deep mountains, where he was no longer seen. Later generations called him Master Yinshan (The Hidden Mountain).
The layman Pang Yun of Xiangzhou was a native of Hengyang County in Hengzhou. His courtesy name was Daoxuan. By family tradition, his ancestors had pursued the Confucian arts;

however, in his youth, he awakened to the weariness of worldly toil and resolved to seek the ultimate truth. At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he visited Shitou and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Shitou covered his mouth with his hand, whereupon Pang attained sudden enlightenment. Later, together with Dan...
With the clouds as his companions, one day Shitou asked him, "Since you first met this old monk, how have you conducted yourself in your daily activities?
The scholar replied, "If you ask about my daily activities, there is no opening for words. He then presented a verse: "In daily activities there is nothing different;
Only I myself am in harmony. At every point there is neither grasping nor rejecting; In every place there is no discord. Who distinguishes between crimson and purple?"
This was his title. "The peaks and mountains are free from a speck of dust; supernatural powers and wondrous functions consist in carrying water and hauling firewood.
Touzi asked, "Are you a monk (in black) or a layman (in white)? The man replied, "I wish to follow what I admire," and so he did not shave his head or dye his robes.
Later, he went to visit Mazu and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as its companion? Mazu said, "Wait until you..."
He said, "I shall drink up the waters of the West River with a single breath; I will tell you right now. At these words, the scholar suddenly grasped the fundamental principle.

He remained there for two years to attend upon him, composing a verse that says: "Having sons, they do not marry; having daughters, they do not wed. The whole family sits together in a circle, discussing the discourse on non-arising.
From then on, his wit and eloquence became swift and sharp, and he was sought after by all quarters. Thereupon, he took his leave of Yaoshan.

Zhaozhou Mountain summoned ten Chan practitioners and escorted them to the gate. Pointing to the snow falling from the sky, Zhaozhou said, "This fine snow, flake by flake, does not fall anywhere else.
A practitioner named Quan said, "Where does it land? Zhaozhou then gave him a slap.
Xuanquan said, "One must not be careless. The layman said, "If you call yourself a Chan guest like this, the Old Man Yama will not let you go.
Xuanquan asked, "How about you, Layman? The layman struck him again and said, "Seeing with eyes as if blind; speaking with a mouth as if mute.
[He] once frequented lecture halls and, while taking joy in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, when he reached the passage on "no self and no person," he posed a question, saying:
The Abbot said, "Since there is neither self nor person, who is it that lectures and who is it that listens? The Master had no reply.
The Layman said, "Although I am but a layperson, I have a rough understanding of faith and aspiration. The Abbot asked, "What, then, is your intention, Layman? The Layman answered with a verse:
"No self and no person, How can there be distance or intimacy? I urge you to stop circling the seats; It is not like being straightforward."
Seeking the Truth: The nature of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is utterly devoid of even a speck of dust from without.

What I have heard and accepted is entirely expressed through provisional names. Upon hearing this verse, the Master joyfully sighed in admiration. Wherever the Layman went, many senior monks would visit him to exchange questions and answers;
he responded to each according to their capacity, never constrained by fixed rules or standards. (The Yuanhe era).
He traveled north to Xianghan, dwelling wherever he found himself. He had a daughter named Lingzhao, who constantly sold bamboo water-strainers to provide for their daily needs.
A scholar composed a verse that said: "The mind is as it is, and the environment is likewise; Neither real nor unreal, Neither concerned with existence nor constrained by non-existence.
Not a sage or a holy one, but an ordinary person who has understood the matter. Easy indeed, easy! It is right here within these five aggregates."
There is true wisdom; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the One Vehicle is the same. How could there be two in the formless Dharmakāya?
If one abandons afflictions to enter Bodhi, one does not know in which direction the Buddha-ground lies. To protect life, one must kill; only when killing is exhausted does one dwell in peace.
If you understand the meaning within this, an iron boat will float upon the water. While sitting, [Dongshan] asked Lingzhao: "The ancients said..."
"Humanity! Clearly evident at the tips of the hundred grasses; clearly evident is the meaning of the Patriarch. How do you understand this?
Lingzhao said, "Old and decrepit as you are, why do you speak such words? The Master asked, "How about you? Lingzhao replied, "Clearly evident at the tips of the hundred grasses;

clearly evident is the meaning of the Patriarch. The Master then laughed. Later, while selling bamboo fishing screens, the Master tripped and fell off a bridge. Lingzhao... [ran to help him]. (The text ends here.)
She saw him and went to her father’s side to help him up. Layman Shou said, "What are you doing? Lingzhao replied, "I saw my father fall to the ground and am helping him up.
As the Layman was about to pass away, he said to Lingzhao, "Check the time of day and report back when it is noon.
Lingzhao quickly reported, "The sun has already reached its zenith, yet there is an eclipse. While the Layman went out the door to observe, Lingzhao immediately climbed onto her father's body.
He sat down, joined his palms, and passed away while seated. The scholar smiled and said, "My daughter’s wit is sharp. Thereupon, the period was extended for another seven days.
When the Prefect, Lord Yu Di, came to inquire after his illness, the scholar said to him, "I only wish that you would empty all that exists;

be careful not to fill what does not exist. The worlds of this life and the next are all like shadows and echoes. Having finished speaking, he rested his head upon Lord Yu’s knee and passed away. His final testament...
He ordered that [the master’s remains] be burned and cast into the rivers and lakes. More than three hundred poems and gāthās were transmitted to the world.
(From *Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume 6;
*Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume 7)
Compiled by the Abbot of Seikan Zen-ji Temple in Kyoto, the Monk (臣) Sō Chōei;
reviewed by the Abbot of Kokaigan-ji Temple in Kyoto, the Monk (臣) Sō Chōkei; presented for imperial inspection.
The Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo in Hongzhou,
a successor in the third generation under Nanyue and a dharma heir of Chan Master Baizhang Hai,
was a native of Min. In his youth, he left the household life at Mount Huangbo in his home prefecture.
The protuberance on his forehead was raised like a pearl; his voice and speech were clear and resonant, and his disposition was profound and serene.

Later, while traveling to Mount Tiantai, he encountered a monk who greeted him with laughter as if they were old acquaintances. Upon looking closely at him, [Huike] saw that the monk’s gaze pierced people; thus, he traveled together with him.

When they reached a mountain stream where the water had suddenly risen in a flood, the monk cast aside his hat, set down his staff, and stopped. The monk urged the Master to cross with him, but the Master said, “Brother, you must...”
The ferryman was crossing himself. He immediately lifted his robes and stepped upon the waves as if treading on level ground.
Looking back, he called out, "Come across! Come across! The Master said, "Tsk! You self-realized fellow. Had I known this earlier, I would have cut off your shins.
The monk sighed and said, "Truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma; I am not his equal. Having spoken, he vanished. Later, the Master traveled to the capital, where he was introduced by others.
Fafa then went to visit Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "Majestic and dignified, from where have you come? The Master replied, "Majestic and dignified, I have come from Lingnan.
Baizhang said, "Being so majestic and dignified, for what purpose do you come? The Master replied, "Being so majestic and dignified, I am not here for any other matter.
He was then made to prostrate and asked, "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of the Buddhas, how would you point it out to me? Baizhang—

After a long silence, the Master said, "I cannot allow the lineage to be severed for future generations. The Staff-bearer said, "I took you for someone of substance. He then rose and entered the Abbot’s quarters.
The Master followed him in and said, "I have come specifically for this purpose. The Staff-bearer asked, "If that is so, then hereafter you must not let me down.
One day, the Staff-bearer asked the Master, "Where have you been? The Master replied, "To the Great [Mountains]."
While at Mount Daxiong, Baizhang went out to gather mushrooms. Mazu asked, "Did you see the tiger? The Master immediately made a tiger’s roar.
Baizhang raised his axe and made a gesture as if to strike; the Master then struck Baizhang with a slap. Baizhang laughed heartily and returned.
Upon entering the hall, he said, "At the foot of Mount Daxiong there is a great tiger; all of you must watch out for it. Old Baizhang.
Han. Today I personally encountered this one mouthful. When Master [Zhaozhou] was at Nanquan, during a communal work period for selecting vegetables, Nanquan asked, "Where are you going?
The Master replied, "I am going to select vegetables. Nanquan asked, "With what do you select them? The Master held up his knife. Nanquan said, "You only know how to act as a guest;
you do not know how to act as the host. The Master pointed with the knife three times. Nanquan said, "Everyone, let us go select vegetables."
One day Nanquan said, "I, an old monk, have a 'Song of Herding an Ox. I ask you, Elder, to compose a response.
The Master replied, "I already have a teacher of my own. When the Master took his leave of Nanquan, Nanquan saw him off at the gate;

picking up the Master’s bamboo hat, he said, "Elder, your physical stature is of vast capacity, yet how small this hat is! The Master said, "Even so, the great trichiliocosm is entirely contained within it."

Xu Quan said, "What about Master Wang? The Master put on his bamboo hat and walked away. While the Master was prostrating before the Buddha in the hall of Yanguan Temple, the future Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty was there as a novice monk (śrāmaṇera).

He asked, "If one does not seek the Buddha, does not seek the Dharma, and does not seek the Saṅgha, for what purpose do you, Elder, perform this prostration? The Master replied, "I do not seek the Buddha; I do not seek the Dharma..."
[The Master] sought [the Dharma], yet did not seek it among the Sangha. He constantly paid homage in this manner. Mi said, "What is the use of paying homage?

The Master then struck him with his palm. Mi said, "That was quite crude. The Master replied, "What kind of place is this, where you speak of 'crude' and 'refined'? Following this, he struck him again.
When Minister Pei was stationed at Wanling, he established a Chan monastery and invited the Master to preach the Dharma. Because the Master deeply cherished his old [monastery], [Pei]...
The mountain was subsequently named after Huangbo. One day, the Duke placed a statue of the Buddha before the Master and knelt, saying, "I request that you bestow a name upon it.
The Master called out, "Pei Xiu! The Duke responded, "Yes. The Master said, "I have finished bestowing the name upon you.
The Duke prostrated himself. Later, six newly arrived monks came; five of them performed the ritual salutation, while one among them raised his sitting mat.
[The Master] drew a circle and said, "I have heard there is a very fierce hunting dog.
The monk said, "It comes seeking the sound of the antelope. The Master said, "The antelope makes no sound for you to seek. [The monk] said, "It comes seeking the tracks of the antelope.

The Master said, "The antelope leaves no tracks for you to seek. [The monk] said, "It comes seeking the footprints of the antelope. The Master said, "The antelope leaves no footprints for you to seek."
Xun said, "In that case, he is a dead antelope. The Master then ceased speaking. The next day, he ascended the hall and said, "The monk Xun who was the 'antelope' yesterday, come forward!
The monk immediately stepped out. The Master said, "Yesterday’s case was not yet finished; I, the old monk, simply stopped.
What do you have to say about it? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "I took you for one of true substance, but it turns out you are merely—"
This was a scholar-monk; the Master then struck him and drove him out. One day, the Master clenched his fist and said, "The old monks of the world are all here.
If I were to let loose a single thread, you could run wild in every direction;
but if I do not let it pass, one punch is enough. A monk asked, "What is it like when you let loose a single thread? The Master replied, "Running wild in every direction."
A monk asked, "If one does not let it pass and does not allow even a single pinch of time to elapse, what then? The Master said, "Puhui.

One day, Minister Pei invited the Master to his prefecture and presented him with a volume containing his own interpretations. The Master received it and placed it upon the seat, without glancing at it even briefly.
After a long silence, he asked, "Do you understand? Pei replied, "I have not yet fathomed it. The Master said, "If you could understand it in such a way, you would still be somewhat close;
but if it were expressed in ink on paper, what would remain of our school? Pei then presented him with a poem:
"Since the Great Being transmitted the Mind-Seal, A seven-foot body with a pearl upon his brow. Hanging his staff for ten years, he dwelt by the waters of Shu; Floating [upon the waves],..."
"Today I cross the banks of the Zhang River. A thousand dragon-elephants follow my lofty steps. Ten thousand miles away, fragrant flowers form a cause for excellence.
I wish to serve you as a disciple, Master, but I do not know to whom you will entrust the Dharma. The Master showed no sign of pleasure.
From that time on, the tradition of Huangbo flourished throughout the region south of the Yangtze. One day, he ascended the hall while the great assembly gathered like clouds. He then said:
He said, "What do you all seek? and drove them away with his staff; yet the assembly would not disperse.
The Master sat back down and said, "You all are nothing but fellows who eat dregs of wine. To travel on pilgrimage like this is to become a laughingstock to others.
You go wherever there are eight hundred or a thousand people; you cannot help but seek out such bustling crowds. The Old Man—
When traveling on pilgrimage, you might encounter a man beneath a patch of grass; you should then strike him with a goad right between his eyebrows.
If he recognizes the pain and itching, you may fill a cloth bag with rice and offer it to him as sustenance.
If everyone were as casual as you are, how could there ever be such a thing as "today's affairs"? Since you all claim to be traveling on pilgrimage, you must also apply some degree of earnestness.
"Divine, divine! Do you not know that within the Great Tang there is no Zen master?
At that time, a monk asked, "The venerable elders of all quarters gather assemblies to teach and transform; why do you say there is no Zen master? The Master said, "I do not say there is no Zen."
It is simply that there was no teacher, and you, O Kalyāṇamitra, did not see it. Under Master Māda (Mazu), there were eighty-four people who sat at the site of enlightenment;
those who attained Master Māda’s True Dharma Eye numbered only two or three. The Venerable Guizong of Mount Lu was one of them.
Now, those who have left the household life must first know the matters that have been handed down from of old before they can attain realization.

For instance, although the Oxhead under the Fourth Patriarch spoke both horizontally and vertically, he still did not yet know the pivot of the higher realm. Only when one possesses such an eye can one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

Furthermore, regarding the immediate needs of one's own practice, if one cannot realize them through personal experience but merely knows how to study words and recite [mantras], [one will remain deluded].
"You stuffed it into your bag and everywhere you go you claim, 'I am skilled in Chan. But can that possibly save you from birth and death?
To treat an elder with such contempt—you will enter hell as fast as an arrow. As soon as I saw you enter the gate, I already knew exactly who you were."

Do you understand yet? You must exert yourself with urgency; do not treat this lightly. To spend an entire life in vain, wearing but a single robe and subsisting on alms-food—clear-eyed people will laugh at you.
In the long run, you will be reckoned as nothing more than a common worldly man. You should examine for yourself how far you have come and how much further remains.
"Whose business is this? If you understand it, then understand it; if you do not understand it, then disperse.
Take care! He then said to Pei Gongmei: "The Buddhas and all sentient beings are nothing but this one mind; there is no other dharma."
This mind, from time without beginning, has never been born and never perishes. It is neither blue nor yellow; it is formless and signless.
It does not belong to existence or non-existence; it is reckoned neither new nor old. It is neither long nor short, neither large nor small.
It transcends all measures, names, and phrases, as well as all traces and dualistic oppositions. It is the very essence itself; to stir a thought is to deviate from it. It is like empty space.
It is without limit and cannot be measured; this single mind alone is the Buddha. There is no difference whatsoever between the Buddha and sentient beings.

It is only because sentient beings cling to appearances and seek outwardly that they lose [the truth] further as they seek it. Thus they cause the Buddha to search for the Buddha and use the mind to grasp the mind;

though they do so throughout kalpas and until the end of their lives, they will ultimately never attain it. They do not know how to let thoughts cease and forget deliberation, whereupon the Buddha manifests of itself.
This very mind is the Buddha; there is no other Buddha, nor is there any other mind. This mind is luminous and pure, like empty space, without a single mark or characteristic.
To raise the mind or stir a thought is immediately to deviate from the essence of the Dharma; it constitutes attachment to marks (*nimitta*).

Since beginningless time, there has been no Buddha who attached to marks while practicing the six perfections and the myriad deeds in a desire to seek Buddhahood—this would merely be a gradual process.
Since beginningless time, there has been no sequential succession of Buddhas; rather, it is simply the awakening to the One Mind, wherein not even the slightest dharma can be obtained.
This is the true Buddha. This mind is the mind that is no-mind, free from all marks. Between sentient beings and all Buddhas, there is no further distinction.
To be able to abide in no-mind is to be a practitioner who has reached the ultimate. If one does not directly attain this state of no-mind, then for kalpas on end—
If one practices in this way, one will ultimately not achieve the Way; one will be bound by the meritorious practices of the Three Vehicles and fail to attain liberation.
Nevertheless, there are differences in the speed with which one realizes this mind: some attain the state of no-mind upon hearing the Dharma for a single thought-moment;
some attain it only after reaching the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences; and some attain it only upon reaching the ten stages. Long...
When it is so brief that there is no thought, one abides; there is nothing further to be cultivated or realized, for truly there is nothing to be attained. This is the reality, not false.
Attained in a single thought-moment, it is exactly equal in its efficacy to what is attained through the ten stages (*bhūmi*); there is no difference in depth or shallowness.

It is merely that [those who follow gradual paths] have endured toil and hardship in vain over many kalpas. Whether creating evil or creating good, both are attachments to signs (*nimitta*). To create evil while attached to signs—

To undergo the cycle of saṃsāra in vain, or to perform acts of merit while clinging to appearances, is to undergo toil and suffering in vain. None of these compare to recognizing one’s own fundamental Dharma immediately upon hearing these words.

This Dharma is the mind; there is no dharma outside the mind. This mind is the Dharma; there is no mind outside the Dharma. The mind is itself without mind, yet there is also no one who is "without mind.
If you attempt to make the mind mindless, the mind instead becomes something existent. It is simply a matter of silent resonance; it is utterly beyond [conceptualization].
Beyond all conceptualization, it is therefore said that "the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.

A student of the Way merely identifies with seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, as well as with purposeful action and movement. If one empties out seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the path of the mind is severed and there is no place of entry.

Rather, one should recognize the original mind within the very state of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; yet the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor is it...
Be free from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; merely do not give rise to views or interpretations regarding seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and do not stir thoughts regarding them.
Nor should you seek the mind apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, nor should you abandon seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to grasp at dharmas.
Neither identical with nor separate from them, neither dwelling in nor clinging to them—transcending freely in all directions, there is nothing that is not the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Practitioners of the Way should have no doubts. The four great elements constitute the body; the four great elements are without self, and the self likewise has no master.

Therefore, know that this body is without self and without master. The five aggregates constitute the mind; the five aggregates are without self and without master. Therefore, know that this mind is without self and without master.
The six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses arise and perish through their conjunction; they are likewise thus.
Since the eighteen realms are empty, all things are entirely empty; there remains only the fundamental mind, vast and pure. There is the food of consciousness and the food of wisdom.
When the body of the four elements suffers from the affliction of hunger and disease, one provides nourishment accordingly without giving rise to greedy attachment—this is called the food of wisdom.

To indulge the senses in seeking flavors, to give rise to false discrimination, and to seek only what pleases the palate without generating a sense of weary detachment—this is called [the food of ignorance].
This is the food of consciousness. Ordinary people grasp at objects; practitioners of the Way grasp at the mind. When both mind and objects are forgotten, this is the true Dharma.
Forgetting objects is still easy; forgetting the mind is most difficult. People do not dare to forget the mind, fearing they will fall into emptiness where there is nothing to grasp.

They do not know that emptiness is fundamentally empty, being nothing other than the single True Dharma-realm. Because of the presence of greed, anger, and delusion, one establishes precepts and meditative concentration.
Wisdom is fundamentally free of afflictions; how then could there be bodhi? Thus the Patriarch said: "The Buddha taught all dharmas for the purpose of eliminating all mental states.
Since I have no mental states, what use have I for all dharmas? Ordinary people do not seek the Way, but instead indulge their six sense-faculties, thereby sustaining the cycle of the six realms.
When a person who has awakened to the Way calculates birth and death even for a single thought-moment, they immediately fall into the path of Māra. One.
To give rise to various views is to fall into the path of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). To perceive the arising of birth and its subsequent cessation is to fall into the path of the Śrāvakas.
Not seeing the arising of birth, but seeing only the cessation of existence, is to fall into the path of the Pratyekabuddhas. All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; even now, they do not cease.
Do not give rise to the two views; neither loathe nor rejoice. All dharmas are but the single mind; this is then the Buddha-vehicle.
Ordinary people all follow after objects and give rise to thoughts, whereby the mind subsequently experiences longing and aversion. If one wishes to eliminate objects, one must forget the mind.
When the mind is forgotten, objects become empty; when objects are empty, the mind ceases. If one does not forget the mind but merely attempts to remove [objects], [it will be of no avail].
Objects. Objects cannot be removed; they only increase confusion and turmoil. Therefore, the myriad dharmas are mind-only, yet even the mind cannot be apprehended.
What more, then, is there to seek? When an ordinary person approaches the end of life, they should simply contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty and the four elements are without self.
The true mind is without form; it neither departs nor arrives. At the time of birth, its nature does not come; at the time of death, its nature does not go.
It is profoundly still and perfectly quiescent; mind and object are one and the same.

If you can thus directly and suddenly realize this, you will not be bound by the three periods of time and will be a person who has transcended the world. You must not harbor even the slightest inclination toward anything. If you see what is good...
When various Buddhas appear to welcome one, or when all manner of phenomena manifest before one, there is no mind that follows them away.
Even if one sees various evil omens manifesting, there is likewise no mind of fear. Rather, by simply forgetting the mind and becoming one with the Dharma-realm, one attains mastery.
This is the essential point. To speak of *icchantika* means that faith is incomplete.

All sentient beings within the six realms of existence, even those of the One Vehicle, who do not believe in the fruit of Buddhahood—all such are called *icchantikas* who have severed their roots of goodness.

As for the Bodhisattva, they have deep faith in the Buddha-dharma; they perceive no distinction between the Great Vehicle and the Small Vehicle, nor between the Buddha and sentient beings, for all are of one and the same Dharma.
By nature, such people are called icchantikas or ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). They are mostly hindered by objects in their minds and by phenomena in their principles;

they constantly seek to escape from objects in order to settle the mind, and to eliminate phenomena so as to preserve the principle. Little do they realize that it is actually their own minds that obstruct the objects, and their principles that obstruct the phenomena.
Simply let the mind be empty and the objects will naturally be empty; simply let the principle be tranquil and the phenomena will naturally be tranquil. Do not apply the mind perversely.
Ordinary people for the most part are unwilling to let the mind be empty, fearing they will fall into nihilism; they do not realize that their own minds are fundamentally empty.
The foolish eliminate objects but do not eliminate the mind; the wise eliminate the mind but do not eliminate objects. The Bodhisattva’s mind is like space, relinquishing everything.
Whatever merit one has performed, one does not cling to it at all. Furthermore, there are three levels of relinquishment (*tyāga*).

To relinquish everything—internal and external, body and mind—just as empty space is free from any grasping or attachment, and thereafter to respond to things according to circumstances while forgetting both subject and object:

this is called "Great Relinquishment" (*mahā-tyāga*). If, on the one hand, one practices the Path and spreads virtue, yet on the other hand, one constantly relinquishes them with a mind free of expectation: this is [the second level].

Middle equanimity (*upekṣā*): If one extensively cultivates various virtues with some expectation of reward, yet upon hearing the Dharma and realizing emptiness, subsequently becomes unattached—this is called small equanimity.
Great equanimity is like a torch held before one; there is no longer any confusion between delusion and awakening. Middle equanimity is like a torch held at one's side;
it is sometimes bright and sometimes dim. Small equanimity is like a torch held behind one; one does not see the pits and traps ahead. Therefore, this is the Bodhisattva mind.
Like space, one relinquishes everything. The past mind is unattainable; this is the relinquishment of the past.
The present mind is unattainable; this is the relinquishment of the present. The future mind is unattainable; this is the relinquishment of the future.

This is what is meant by the relinquishment of all three times. The Buddha has three bodies (*kāya*). The *dharmakāya* teaches the Dharma of the self-nature of pervasive emptiness. The *saṃbhogakāya* teaches the One...
All dharmas are pure. The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) preaches the dharma of the six perfections and myriad practices; the dharma body (*dharmakāya*) preaches the dharma.

It cannot be sought through speech, sound, form, or written characters. There is nothing preached and nothing realized; it is simply the spontaneous penetration of intrinsic nature. Therefore it is said:

"There is no dharma that can be preached"—this is what is called preaching the dharma. Both the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body manifest according to the conditions and responses of sentient beings.
The Dharma that is taught also accords with specific matters and adapts to the faculties [of beings] in order to gather and transform them; none of these are the true Dharma. Therefore it is said:

"The Reward Body and Transformation Body are not the True Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma. As for the fruits of the śramaṇa, they are accomplished through the cessation of discursive thought (*śamatha*), not through learning.
You are now seeking the mind with the mind, wandering among the houses of others, intending only to learn and grasp—what is there in that?
Regarding the time of attainment: those of the ancients possessed sharp faculties; upon hearing but a single word, they immediately ceased their study.

This is why they were called "men of leisure who have transcended learning and attained non-action. People of the present day, however, merely desire to possess much knowledge and many interpretations, seeking extensively for literary meanings and calling this "cultivation.
They do not realize that such profusion of knowledge and interpretation instead results in obstruction; they know only how to give their children plenty of butter and milk.
"Eat. Whether it is digested or not, you know nothing at all. Those who practice the Way of the Three Vehicles are all like this;
they are all called 'those whose food is undigested. Question: "Delusion can obstruct one's own mind. I do not yet understand how to dispel delusion now. The Master said:
"To give rise to delusion and then seek to dispel delusion also constitutes delusion. Delusion originally has no root; it exists only because of discrimination. You should simply..."
Regarding both the ordinary and the sagely, do not harbor thoughts or calculations; naturally, there will be no delusion. What more need you propose to do to dispel it? Master Zhizang said:
"If one does not meet a world-transcending enlightened teacher, one will have served the Dharma-medicine of the Mahāyāna in vain.

At all times now—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—you should simply practice non-mind (*amanojña*). After a long time, you will surely attain it in reality. It is only because your capacity is small that [you have not yet realized it].
One can transcend [delusion] all at once, but this requires three, five, or even ten years; one must practice a point of entry so that understanding arises naturally.
Since you cannot do this, you insist on using the mind to study Chan and study the Way. What connection does this have with the Buddha-dharma?
The Patriarch directly pointed out that the original mind and original essence of all sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, requiring no external artifice.
Cultivation and realization do not belong to gradual succession; they are neither light nor darkness. Question: Does the Buddha exhaustively eliminate ignorance (*avidyā*)? The Master said:
Ignorance is precisely the place where all Buddhas attain the Way. Therefore, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Every speck of dust and every color that is perceived immediately accords with the boundless principle of nature. With every step raised and every step taken, one does not depart from the site of enlightenment. The Way...
The "site" (bodhimaṇḍa) is that which is without attainment. I tell you: precisely this non-attainment is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment.

On the eighth month of the Gengwu year of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, he passed away at his native mountain. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Duanjie, and his stupa was named Guangci.
Chan Master Changqing Lanyan Da'an of Fuzhou was the son of the Chen family of that prefecture.

He received his monastic training at Mount Huangbo, where he studied the Vinaya and the Mahayana teachings. He once reflected to himself, "Though I have practiced with diligent hardship, I have not yet heard the principle of the Ultimate Source.

Thereupon, he traveled alone with his staff to seek out teachers elsewhere, intending to go to Hongjing. On his way, he passed through Shangyuan and encountered an old man who said to him, "Master..."
"I am going to Nanchang; I shall surely gain something there. The Master then went to Baizhang, paid his respects, and asked:
"A student wishes to seek the realization of the Buddha. What is it that is the Buddha? Baizhang said, "It is very much like riding a cow while searching for the cow.

The Master asked, "Once it has been realized, what then? Baizhang said, "It is like a person riding a cow back home. The Master asked, "I do not yet understand how one maintains this from beginning to end. Baizhang—

He said, "It is like a cowherd who holds a staff and watches over his herd, not allowing them to trespass upon the crops. From this point on, the Master understood the essential meaning and no longer wandered in search of it elsewhere.

He joined with his fellow practitioner Daowu Yuanzhe, who had recently established his residence at Mount Guiyang. The Master personally engaged in farming to assist in the Way. When Yuanzhe passed away, the Master remained there.
At the request of the assembly, the successive incumbent ascended the hall and said: "All of you, you have all come here seeking peace; what is it that you seek?
If you wish to become a Buddha, you are already a Buddha yourself. Yet you carry the Buddha about with you as you run from house to house, like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage.
When will you ever attain accord? If you wish to become a Buddha, simply let go of these many inverted attachments,攀缘 (pānyuan), and delusions."
To perceive the minds of sentient beings as being defiled by the impurities of evil thoughts is itself the initial awakening of the right mind. What else would the Buddha seek elsewhere?
This is why he settled at Mount Mushi; for thirty years, he ate Mount Mushi’s rice and voided Mount Mushi’s excrement.
I do not study the Chan of Guishan; I simply watch a water buffalo. If it strays onto the path or enters the grass, I pull its nose back around.
As soon as it trespasses upon the crops, I whip it. Having been tamed for a long time, this pitiable creature now obeys my every word.
It has now transformed into a white ox in the open air, always standing before me, solitary and vast all day long.
It is far removed from the ground; even if you pursue it, you cannot catch it. You all possess within yourselves a priceless great treasure.

From the gateway of the eyes, it emits light that illuminates and perceives mountains, rivers, and the great earth. From the gateway of the ears, it emits light that receives and discerns all sounds, whether good or evil.
Thus, these six gateways constantly emit radiance day and night; this is also called the Samādhi of Emitting Light. Yet you yourselves do not recognize or grasp it.
The shadow resides within the body composed of the four great elements; it is supported from both within and without, never allowing it to lean or tilt.
It is like a person carrying a heavy burden across a single-plank bridge, yet never losing their footing. Tell me, what thing is it that sustains such a state?
There is not even a hair’s breadth to be seen. Have you not seen Master Zhigong say: "Search within and without"?
"First, there is nothing at all. Yet within the objective realm, the functioning of phenomena is vast and complete. Be careful! Question:

"When this aggregate has already passed away and the next aggregate has not yet arisen, what is it like? The Master said: "This aggregate has not yet passed away. Which one is the Venerable One? He said: "I do not understand. The Master said:
"If you understand this aggregate, you will clearly understand that aggregate. Question: "When the Great Function manifests before you and no fixed rules remain..."
"How is it? the Master asked. The monk said, "I can use it; I simply use it. Thereupon, the monk bared his shoulder and circumambulated the Master three times.
The Master said, "As for the matter beyond [the phenomenal], why do you not speak of it? As the monk prepared to open his mouth, the Master struck him and said, "You wild fox spirit, get out!
Later, a monk entered the Dharma Hall. Looking around east and west, he did not see the Master and said, "What a fine Dharma Hall! It is only..."
This was the monk Wuren. As the Master came out from inside the gate, he asked, "What is it? The monk had no reply.
Once, when Xuefeng entered the mountains, he found a piece of wood shaped like a snake. He inscribed upon its back: "Originally natural; no need for carving.
He sent it to the Master, who said, "A mountain dweller of true caliber would have left no marks of axe or knife. A monk asked: [The question follows].
"Where is the Buddha? he asked. The Master said, "Not apart from the mind. He asked, "Master Shuangfeng, what have you attained? The Master said, "Dharmas are unattainable.
Even if there were something attained, that attainment would be fundamentally non-attainment. He asked, "If Huang Chao’s army comes, where will you, the Master, go to avoid it?
The Master said, "Into the mountains of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). He asked, "What if you are suddenly captured by them? The Master said, "I shall become their commander-in-chief."
"What? the Master replied, "To trouble and disturb the General. The Master extensively transformed the city of Min.

On the twenty-second day of the tenth month of the *kaimao* year of Zhonghe during the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang dynasty, he manifested parinirvāṇa. Huangbo was interred at Mount Lengga, and by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Yuanzhi.
The Stupa of the Realization of Truth.
Chan Master Huánzhōng of Dàcí Mountain in Hángzhōu was a native of the Lú clan from Púsān. His cranial bone was rounded and prominent, and his voice resounded like a bell.

In his youth, he encountered the mourning for his mother; he lived in a grass hut at her grave site until the period of mourning had ended. Reflecting on how to repay her boundless kindness, he then went to Bìngzhōu.
He left home at Tongzi Temple and ascended Mount Song to receive the full precepts. There he studied the various Vinaya teachings. Later, he visited Bai Zhang to receive the mind-seal.
Taking his leave, he went to Changle on Mount Nanyue, where he thatched a hut atop Qianshan Peak. One day, Nanquan arrived and asked, "What is the master of this hermitage?
The Master replied, "The blue sky! The blue sky! Nanquan said, "Setting aside the blue sky for a moment, what is the master of this hermitage?"
The Master said, “If you understand, then understand; do not be so talkative. Baizhang Quan shook his sleeves and departed.

Later, while residing at Daci, he ascended the hall and said, “I, this mountain monk, cannot answer questions; I can only recognize illnesses. At that time, a monk stepped forward, and the Master immediately returned to his quarters.
Zhaozhou asked, “What is the essence of Prajñā? The Master replied, “What is the essence of Prajñā? Zhaozhou [remained silent].
He laughed loudly and went out. The next day, while Shouzhuo was sweeping the ground, the Master asked, "What is the essence of Prajñā?
Shouzhuo set down his broom, clapped his hands, and laughed loudly. The Master then returned to his quarters. A monk took his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going?
He replied, "To Jiangxi. The Master said, "May I trouble you with a matter? The monk asked, "What matter do you have, Preceptor?"
The Master said, "Can you take this old monk away? The monk replied, "Even those who surpass the Master could not take him away either.
The Master then ceased speaking. Later, the monk related this to Dongshan, who said, "Disciple, why did you speak in such a manner?"
[The monk] asked, "How about you, Preceptor? Sanshan said, "Attained. Sanshan then asked the monk, "What other sayings or phrases does Daci have?
The monk replied, "At times he addresses the assembly, saying: 'To speak a zhang is not as good as practicing a chi;
to speak a chi is not as good as practicing an cun. Sanshan said, "I do not speak in that way. The monk asked, "How then would you, Preceptor, speak?"

Shengshan said: "Preach that which cannot be attained through practice; practice that which cannot be attained through preaching. Later, during the reign of Emperor Wuzong, when the Buddhist teachings were suppressed, the Master lived in seclusion wearing coarse cloth garments.
In the *Ren-shen* year of the Dazhong era, he again received the tonsure and precepts and extensively propagated the fundamental tenets of the school.

On the fifteenth day of the second month of the *Ren-wu* year of the Xiantong era, he passed away without illness at the age of eighty-three and with forty-four years of seniority since his ordination. Emperor Xi...
His posthumous title was Great Master Xingkong (Nature-Emptiness). His stupa is named Dinghui (Concentration-Wisdom).

Chan Master Putian Puan of Tiantai was a native of Hongzhou. Having received the essential instruction under the guidance of Baizhang, he later heard of the magnificent scenery of Tiantai and the successive emergence of sages and worthies there.
Desiring to transcend the mundane world and follow in their distant footsteps, he then formed [a community].
He cleared away the weeds and grass and dwelt in tranquil seclusion beneath the trees. As the days passed and months rolled by, he became known to the fourfold assembly.
He established the Píngtián Chan Monastery and resided there. Ascending the hall, he said: "The divine light is never obscured; it is a magnificent legacy for all ages.

Those who enter this gate must not harbor intellectual understanding. He then descended from his seat. A monk approached to pay his respects. The Master struck him once with his staff. The monk stepped forward and seized the staff.
[The monk] held up his staff. The Master said, "I was a bit hasty just now. The monk struck the Master once with his staff.

The Master said, "An adept! An adept! The monk bowed. The Master grabbed him and said, "It was you, Ācārya, who were hasty. The monk laughed heartily. The Master said, "This monk has been thoroughly defeated today.
Later, when Linji visited the Master, he encountered an elder sister-in-law at the crossroads before reaching the Master's quarters.
While tending the oxen in the fields, Linji asked his sister-in-law, "Which way does the path to the level fields go? His sister-in-law struck the ox with a staff and said, "You beast!
You have wandered everywhere, yet you do not even know this road. Linji spoke again, saying, "I am asking you, sister-in-law, which way does the path to the level fields go?
His sister-in-law replied, "This beast! Even at five years old, it still cannot be used. At these words, Linji’s mind was opened.
The saying goes: "If you wish to examine the person before you, first examine what they employ. This carries the intent of extracting the nail and pulling out the wedge.
When Ji arrived, the Master asked, "Have you seen my sister-in-law yet? Ji replied, "I have already taken her in.
The Master then asked, "Where did you recently depart from? Ji said, "From Huangbo in Jiangxi. The Master remarked, "I knew well enough that you had come to see a master."
Ji said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master. The Master said, "We have already met.

Ji said, "According to the etiquette between guest and host, one ought to perform three prostrations. The Master said, "Since it is the etiquette between guest and host, then perform your prostrations.

He spoke a verse for the assembly, saying: "The Great Way is vast and empty; its constant essence is the true mind. Do not think of good or evil; let the spirit be clear beyond all things, following conditions as they arise."

He took his meals and lived there; what more was there to do? He passed away at this very monastery, and his stupa remains there to this day. During the Song dynasty, it was further renovated and he was posthumously granted the title Shouchang (Longevity Flourishing). A monk asked Chan Master Xingkong of Mount Shishuang in Tanzhou, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

The Master said, “Suppose there were a person in a thousand-foot-deep well; if you could get that person out without the aid of even a foot of rope, then I would answer you regarding the meaning of his coming from the West.

One should know that the boundless, immovable space of the ten directions, together with the shifting elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, are collectively termed the six great elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*).
Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing. A verse is shown to illustrate this: "Most profoundly deep."
"Most profound! The Dharma-realm and the human body are simply the mind. Those who are deluded take the mind to be the myriad forms;
when awakened, the lands and objects are the true mind. Body and realm—these two dusts have no real nature.
One who clearly realizes this is called a 'knower of the sound'. Yue asked again, "What is *dhāraṇī*? The Master pointed to the right side of his meditation seat and said, "This monk here..."
