The Master said, "Returning to the source through the faculty of the eye is named Mañjuśrī; returning to the source through the faculty of the ear is named Avalokiteśvara. From...
Returning the mind to its source is named Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s wondrous discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*);

Avalokiteśvara is the Buddha’s unconditioned great compassion; and Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s wondrous non-active practice (*asaṃskṛta-caryā*). These three sages are the Buddha’s wondrous functions, while the Buddha is the true essence of these three sages.
In terms of function, there are as many provisional names as there are sands in the Ganges; in terms of essence, they are collectively named as one Bhagavān.
Question: "Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. How is this principle to be understood? The Master said: "Listen to this old monk’s verse:
'Where there is obstruction, it is not a wall; where there is penetration, there is no void. If a person understands it thus, mind and form are fundamentally the same. He asked again:
"The Buddha-nature is majestically manifest, yet sentient beings dwelling within that nature find it difficult to see. If one awakens to the selflessness of sentient beings..."
"How does my face compare to the Buddha’s face? Regarding the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses, they ultimately lack any substantial entity.

How, then, can one speak of transforming the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom? The Master showed a verse, saying: "The seven arise dependent on the one; when the one ceases, [the seven] are extinguished."
One cessation sustains seven births; one cessation ceases that which has ceased. The six and the seventh never undergo transition. Question:
When an earthworm is cut into two segments, both ends move. I do not know in which part the Buddha-nature resides. The Master said: "Why do you harbor such deluded thoughts?
[The questioner] said: "But what of the movement? The Master said: "Do you not know that fire and wind have not yet dispersed? Question: How is this so?
[The monk] said, "I can transform mountains, rivers, and lands so that they return to myself. The Master asked, "How can you transform yourself into mountains, rivers, and lands?
[The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Under the city walls of Hunan, the people are well-nourished; rice is cheap and firewood is plentiful, sufficient for all four neighbors.

Perfect penetration has no two sides; the dharma-nature originally has no place of return. The Master of the Avataṃsaka asked:
"Is space definitely existent, or is it definitely non-existent? The Master said: "It may be called existent, and it may also be called non-existent. When space exists..."
"There is only provisional existence; empty space has no time. There is only the absence of provisional existence.
[The student] asked, "Regarding what the Master has said, what scriptural authority is there? The Master replied, "Virtuous One, have you not heard? The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says:

'The empty space of the ten directions arises within your mind, like a single cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the sky. Is this not to say that when empty space arises, it merely gives rise to a provisional name?"
He further said: "If even one among you were to give rise to the true and return to the source, the empty space of the ten directions would all vanish away.
Is this not proof that when empty space is extinguished, it is merely a conventional name that is extinguished? This is why I, the old monk, say: existence is conventional existence;

non-existence is conventional non-existence. A question was asked: "What is the sphere of activity for those of the highest rank? The Master said: "It is like the eyes of a dead man. [The questioner] said: "Superior..."

An asked, "What is the mind of a student? The Master said, "The entire world of the ten directions is your mind.

An asked, "What is the place where one rests the body? The Master said, "The great ocean is deep, and yet deeper. An said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The fish."
The dragon enters and exits, rising and sinking as it pleases. A question was asked: "When someone asks the Master, you answer according to the circumstances.
But when no one asks the Master, what then? The Master said: "When weary, I sleep; when vigorous, I rise. The questioner asked: "How should a student understand this?
The Master said: "In summer, one is bare-boned; in winter’s cold, one must have a robe. Question: "Regarding a deceased monk who has passed away..."
"Where are you going? The Master showed him a verse, saying: "Failing to recognize the adamantine essence, One instead calls it dependently arisen.
The ten directions are truly quiescent; Who is there, and who is traveling? The Master praised Nanquan Zhen, saying: "Majestic indeed is Nanquan!"
The source of the three periods of time is the eternally abiding Vajra; throughout the ten directions it is boundless, and the arising of Buddhas is inexhaustible.

Having manifested [this truth], he returns and offers this verse of exhortation to study: "Even atop a ten-thousand-foot pole, one must not yet rest; A grand path exists, yet few travel it. O Zen Master, you vow to reach Nanquan;
Before your eyes, green mountains stretch for ten thousand autumns. This is a verse on Linji’s "bare flesh ball."
Above is the True Person of No Rank, who says: "The myriad dharmas are of one suchness; there is no need for selection. In this one suchness, who selects and who does not select?
Right now, birth and death are fundamentally bodhi; the Tathāgatas of the three periods share the same eye.
A verse admonishing the cutting of pines and bamboos says: "A thousand-year bamboo, a ten-thousand-year pine— Branch by branch, leaf by leaf, they are all the same. I inform the four quarters:"

When the Monk of Mount Juyuyu in Ezhou first took up residence at Huguo Temple in Suizhou, he ascended the hall and held up a piece of bamboo, saying:

While the assembly of monks stood in attendance, the Master said, "Why do you all stand there so pale? There is no place to speak; it is quite stifling. A monk was about to ask a question.
The Master struck him and said, “Exert yourself for the sake of the assembly,” and then entered the Abbot’s quarters. A practitioner came to visit. The Master asked, “Have you been to see Zhaozhou?
The practitioner replied, “Does the Master dare to speak? The Master said, “Not only does Zhunü [Zhuoyu] say nothing can be said;
no one at all can say it. The practitioner said, “May the Master let me pass. The Master said, “From the beginning, this place has not permitted people to enter based on personal sentiment.”
"Ultimately, it is the compassionate heart that matters. The Master then struck him, saying, "I will deal with you after you have awakened.

A monk came to pay his respects and asked, "Do you come here, O *ācārya*, to sightsee and enjoy the scenery, or to seek the Way and practice Zen? The monk replied, "Venerable Sir, please judge for yourself.

The Master said, "Carving oysters and engraving clams—this is nothing but impervious mud. You have troubled yourself by coming from so far. The monk said, "My whole body is made of iron; yet I am still [struck]."
"A single blow. The Master said, "A surrendered general is not executed.
Chan Master Lizong of Zihu Cliff in Quzhou was a son of the Zhou family from Dancheng.
He left home at Kaiyuan Temple in Youzhou and received full ordination according to his age. Later, he entered the quarters of Nanquan and eventually arrived at Matishan in Quzhou.

He lived in seclusion in a thatched hut. In the fourth year of the Kāicheng era of the Tang Emperor Wenzong (the *ding-si* year), the local resident Weng Qianggui offered the Zi Lake below the mountain and established a monastery there.
The Master hung a plaque at the entrance for the assembly, stating: "Zihu has a dog;
it takes people's heads above, takes people's hearts from within, and takes people's feet below. To hesitate is to lose one's body and life."—The Linji Collection.

Two monks from the lower hall came to visit. Just as he was lifting the curtain, the Master shouted, "Watch out for the dog! The monks looked back, and the Master immediately returned to his quarters.

While working in the garden with Shengguang, the Master suddenly pressed down on his hoe and, looking back at Guang, said, "The matter itself is not non-existent, but to conceive a thought about it is already a deviation.
Guang then asked, "What is this matter? The Master kicked him in the chest, knocking him over. From that moment, Guang attained realization.
The nun arrived to pay her respects. The Master said, "Are you not Liu Tiemo? She replied, "I dare not. The Master said, "Turn left? Turn right?
She said, "Master, do not be perverse. The Master then struck her. One night, the Master stood before the Sangha Hall and shouted:
"There is a thief! The assembly was all startled and moved. A monk came out from inside the hall; the Master seized him and said, "Venerable Karmadāna!
I have caught him! I have caught him! The monk said, "It is not I. The Master said, "It is indeed you; it is simply that you are unwilling to take responsibility.
He spoke a verse to the assembly, saying: "For thirty years I have dwelt at Zihu; The scent of morning and evening gruel [pervades me]."

Lìcū was coarse and unrefined; he would climb a mountain and walk around it once for no apparent reason, asking passersby, "Does anyone understand? The Master resided at Zihu, preaching the Dharma for over forty years.
In the Gengzi year of the Guangming era, he passed away peacefully without illness. His stupa was erected at the mountain itself.
He was eighty-one years old and had been a monk for sixty-one years.
Chan Master Tanzhao of Baima in Jingnan used to say constantly, "How joyful! How joyful! Yet when the time of his death approached, he cried out, "Suffering!
Suffering! He further said, "King Yama has come to take me. The head monk asked, "Master, you usually spoke of joy; why are you now like this?
The Master raised his pillow and said, "You say that at that time it was so; what about now?"
The abbot was speechless. The Master threw down his pillow and passed away.
When National Teacher Zu of Yunji on Zhongnan Mountain first visited Nanquan, he asked: "People do not recognize the mani-jewel."
"It was personally received within the Tathāgatagarbha. "How is this 'garbha'? Jianquan said, "It is that which comes and goes with you. The Master asked, "What about that which does not come and go?
Jianquan said, "That too is it. [The Master] asked, "What is the pearl? Jianquan called out, "Master Zu! (The Master responded. Jianquan said, "There, you have found it."
The Master assented. Quan said, "Go; you do not understand my words. From this point on, the Master entered into faith.
Chan Master Yidu of Xiangyan in Dengzhou ascended the hall and said:
"Brothers, since we have not yet resolved our mutual matters, what is there to discuss together? In three or five days, I shall depart. Those who study now must reach a final resolution."
Set aside the present moment. Do not merely crave the "no-affairs" of those superior men above you, brothers.
Even if you manage to master various paths of differentiated meanings, it will never substitute for your own realization; you must ultimately exert effort to achieve it.
Merely memorizing others' clever phrases will only lead to increasing confusion. If you wish to attain correspondence with the truth, simply be as humble and reverent as possible.
Do not linger for even a hair’s breadth; only then will there be a small measure of true emptiness.
Because emptiness has no locks or bolts, no walls or enclosures, no physical form or segments, and no eyes or mind. At that time, a monk asked, "How was it when the ancients met one another?
The Master said, "I do not understand how the ancients saw. The monk asked, "In these times, where the life-lineage remains unbroken, how can one look up to them with admiration?"
The Master said, "What is there to admire? The questioner asked, "I am not asking about idle matters;
I ask the Master to provide an answer. The Master said, "What more do you seek from me? He replied, "It is not for idle matters. The Master said, "Then you are instructing me to speak."
He then said, "Brothers, the Buddha is a defilement; the Dharma is a defilement. Seeking throughout the day, what rest can there be?
At all times, do not let your emotions attach themselves. When emotion does not attach to things, there is no good to be grasped and no evil to be abandoned.
Do not allow yourself to be ensnared by them; only then is this the place of study. A question was asked: "I once took leave of an elder master. The master said:"
When one departs, one draws near to virtuous friends and attaches oneself to good companions. This monk now takes his leave of the Master; I do not know what instructions he may have for me.
The Master said, "Prostrate yourself. The monk prostrated. The Master said, "As for prostrating, you may prostrate as you wish, but you must not mistake a servant for a lord.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the direct source? The Master then threw down his staff and immediately [departed].
Returning to the Abbot’s quarters, he ascended the hall for discourse. "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Beyond speech and silence, there is a path. "The old monk’s mouth is too narrow;
I cannot explain it to you. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, a monk asked, "For what reason is the true cause nothing at all?
The Master said, "I do not linger. He then continued: "Even if one were to strip away everything layer by layer until reaching total purity..."
It is entirely without lingering; it is a temporary provision, a skillful means for guiding people. If it were a matter of "that side," such a thing would be impossible.
Chan Master Xian of Lingjiu in Chizhou ascended the hall and said: "This is the fundamental matter of you all. If I were to ask the old monk..."
"The Way is like drawing legs on a snake. At that time, a monk asked, "I do not ask about drawing legs on a snake;
what is the fundamental matter? The Master said, "Try saying it, Venerable Sir. As the monk prepared to ask again, the Master said, "Why draw legs on a snake?
A monk asked, "What is the sudden attainment of the Dharma-body? The Master said, "Once you have passed through the Dragon Gate, look toward the clouds beyond; do not—"
[He was] like a fish with its forehead marked by the Yellow River. Yangshan asked, "When there is silent stillness and no speech, how do you see and hear?
The Master said, "Before the seamless stupa, rainwater is abundant. [Yangshan] asked, "When both are without speech, what is it then? The Master said, "It is the eternal."
[The student] asked, "Is there anyone who surpasses the ordinary? The Master said, "There is. [The student] said, "I request that the Master initiate the song.
The Master said, "The Mysterious Pearl shines forth naturally; why seek light from outside the wall?"
A monk asked the Venerable Master of Mount Song at Luojing, “What is it like when the ancient road is level and smooth?
The Master said, “It does not go forward. The monk asked, “Why does it not go forward? The Master said, “Because there is no place for obstruction.

A monk asked, “What is the realm of Mount Song? The Master said, “The sun rises in the east; the moon sets in the west. The monk said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “East and west are also not [fixed].”
Huì asked, "When the six consciousnesses arise together, how is it? The Master said, "Different. [Huì] asked, "Why is it so?
The Master said, "The same.
One day, when the monk Rìzǐ came to pay his respects, the Master made a gesture of rising. Rìxī said, "This old mountain ghost still..."
Seeing that Xiangxi was present, the Master said, "A transgression! A transgression! Just now you failed to respond. As Xiangxi was about to speak, the Master gave a shout.
Xiangxi said, "When facing a great battle array, it is indeed difficult to withstand. The Master said, "Right! Right! Xiangxi said, "Not right! Not right!"
A monk asked the West Chan (Xichan) Abbot of Suzhou, "I do not ask about the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings;
what is the very intent of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master raised his whisk and showed it to him.

The monk did not prostrate himself and subsequently went to study under Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Zhejiang. Xuefeng asked, "Where were you this summer? He replied:
Xichan asked, "Master, how are you? The Master replied, "When I came, all was well. Xichan said, "Why did you not stay there at ease?
The Master said, "I have not yet clarified the Buddha-dharma. Xichan asked, "What is the matter? The monk recounted the previous conversation.
Xichan said, "Why do you refuse to accept him? The Master said, "Because he is an object. Xichan said, "Have you seen the men in the houses within the city of Suzhou?"
The woman said, "No. Feng said, "Do you see the trees and groves along the road, and the ponds? She said, "I see them.

Feng said, "All that you behold—the men and women of the houses, the great earth, the forests, and the ponds—is entirely the objective realm (viṣaya). Do you agree with this? She said, "I agree. Feng said:
"As for raising the whisk—why do you not accept it? The monk then prostrated and said, "I, your student, spoke thoughtlessly;
I beg the Master’s compassion. Feng said, "The entire universe is this single eye. Where will you sit and squat?
The monk was speechless.
Lu Xun, the Grand Master and Prefect of Xuánzhōu, asked Nánquán: "An ancient once raised a gander in a bottle.
As the gander grew larger, it could no longer get out of the bottle. Now, one must not break the bottle, nor may one harm the gander.
How, O Monk, can it be made to come out? Nánquán called out, "Grand Master! Lu responded, "Yes. Nánquán said, "It has come out. From this, Lu attained awakening. Immediately—
He offered his thanks and departed. Upon Nanquan’s passing, the Abbot of the monastery asked, "Why do you, Great Officer, not weep for our late Master?
Lu said, "If the Abbot can speak, then I shall weep. The Abbot was speechless. (Changqing spoke on his behalf: "Whether it is appropriate to weep or not.")

One day, the lay practitioner Gan-zhi of Chi-zhou entered Nan-chuan’s hall to provide a vegetarian feast. Huang-po was serving as the head seat (*shouzuo*). The practitioner requested that alms be distributed.
The head seat said, “The two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—are equal and without distinction.

Gan-zhi said, “If you speak thus, how can you deserve my offering? He then took [the offering] and went out. A short while later, he re-entered and said, “Please grant me material wealth. The head seat said, “Material wealth and the Dharma...”

The two acts of giving were equal and without distinction. Gan then performed the *dakṣiṇā* (offering). On another day, he entered the monastery to provide gruel and invited Nanquan to recite the scriptures.
Nanquan struck the gavel and said, "I request the assembly to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the sake of the wildcat and the white ox.
Gan brushed out his sleeves and departed. After the meal, Nanquan asked the steward, "Where has the Master been?"
Chushi said, "He left right then and there. Quan immediately smashed the cooking pot. Gan Chang received guests and travelers.
A monk asked him, "It is no easy matter for a lay attendant to receive guests. Gan said, "It is like feeding a donkey or feeding a horse. The monk then desisted.
There was a monk living in a hermitage who was soliciting alms for household goods. Gan said, "I have a question; if you can answer it, [I will give them to you]."

Gan made a donation and then wrote the character for "mind" (心), asking, "What word is this? The monk replied, "The character for 'mind'. Gan then asked his wife, "What word is this? His wife replied, "The character for 'mind'. Gan said, "My humble wife should also be fit to dwell in a hermitage. The monk was speechless, and Gan likewise gave no further gift. Shanshan asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? Guishan raised his whisk. The monk asked, "How do you understand Guishan’s meaning?
He replied, "To clarify the mind by means of phenomena, and to manifest the principle by relying on objects. Gān said, "It would be better for you to go back to Guishan."

National Teacher An of Yanguan was a successor of Chan Master Chang of Guannan in Xiangzhou. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master raised his staff and said, "Do you understand?
The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master then struck him. Whenever the Master saw a monk come to pay his respects, he would mostly [use] his staff...
He was driven away with blows from his staff. Some said, "He was a moment late. Others said, "He struck the drum of Guannan. Yet among his contemporaries, few responded with verses in kind.
When Chan Master Xuanzhen of Shuangling in Hongzhou first asked Dao Wu, "Why is it that the Bodhisattva without supernatural powers..."
"His traces are difficult to find," Mazu said. "Only those who walk the same path know him. The Master asked, "Does the Abbot know him?
Mazu replied, "I do not know. The Master asked, "Why do you not know? Mazu said, "Go away! You do not understand my words.
Later, the Master attained realization of the essential meaning under Yanguan.
Chan Master Jiǎnzōng of Jìngshān in Hángzhōu was the son of the Qián clan of Húzōu. He left home under Gāoxián at Kāiyuán Monastery in his native prefecture;
he mastered the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Sīmsī jīng) and was well-versed in the Pure Land teachings. Later, he went to Yànhuán to resolve his lingering doubts and obstructions.

During the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty, he resided at Jìngshān. He had a junior disciple named Hóngtīn (Tīn was the Great Master Fǎjì), who prided himself on his skill in debate. The Master said to him:
He said, "The true Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is direct and beyond verbal expression. Calculating the sands of the ocean—what benefit does this provide for the principle?
If you can simply not harbor cognitive views and extinguish external conditions, becoming detached from all mental activity, that is your own true nature. Yìn was left in a state of bewilderment;

he then took his leave and traveled to Mount Míu, where he finally realized the profound essence and became a successor of Mount Míu. This was during the intercalary month of the Bingxū year of the Xiántōng era.
On the fifth day of the third month, he demonstrated his passing. He was posthumously titled the Unsurpassed Great Master.
His stupa was erected beneath Daji Rock.
Chan Master Lingxun of Mount Fuyong in Fuzhou was a successor of Chan Master Guizong Chang. When he first visited Guizong, he asked, "What is the Buddha? Guizong replied:
"I have told you this; will you believe it? The Master said, "The Venerable One speaks the truth; how would I dare not believe it? Zhaozhou said, "You yourself are it.
The Master asked, "How does one maintain this? Zhaozhou said, "A single film over the eye, and empty flowers fall in confusion.
As the Master was taking his leave, Zhaozhou asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am going back to the Lingnan region. Zhaozhou said, "You have stayed here for a long time."
After a year had passed, he finished his preparations and came forward to have the Master preach the Dharma for him. The Master adjusted his robes and ascended the hall.
Yunmen said, "Come closer. The Master stepped forward. Yunmen said, "The weather is cold; take good care on your journey. Upon hearing these words, the Master was deeply moved.
He suddenly forgot his former understanding and returned to stillness. He was posthumously titled Great Master Hongzhao, and his stupa was named Yuanxiang (Perfect Phase).
A monk came from Jiaoshan to pay respects at Guting Heshang in Guocheng, Xiangyang. As soon as the monk arrived, the Master struck him.
The monk said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects; why do you strike me? The monk bowed again, but the Master struck him once more and drove him away. The monk returned.
He brought this up to Jia Shan. Jia Shan asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. Jia Shan said, "It is fortunate that you do not understand.
Had you understood, Jia Shan’s mouth would have been mute."
Master Daemao of Silla ascended the hall and said: "If you wish to recognize the Teacher of all Buddhas, recognize him within the mind of ignorance.
If you wish to recognize the eternally abiding, undecaying nature, recognize it in the midst of the shifting and changing of all things.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of Daemao? The Master said, "The blade is not revealed. The monk asked, "Why is the blade not revealed? The Master said, "Because there is no one to meet it."
When Chan Master Zhìtōng of Mount Wǔtái was initially in the assembly of Guīzōng, he suddenly cried out one night, "I have attained great enlightenment!
The assembly was startled by this. The next day, when the assembly had gathered for the hall discourse, Guīzōng said, "The monk who attained great enlightenment last night, come forward.
The Master stepped forward and said, "This humble one. Guīzōng asked, "What principle did you perceive that you say you have attained great enlightenment? Try..."

"Tell me," he said. The Master replied, "A nun was originally made of a woman. Zong was struck by this. The Master then took his leave. As Zong saw him off at the gate, he offered him a straw raincoat.
The Master took the raincoat, placed it on his head, and walked away without looking back. Later, he resided at Fahua Temple on Mount Tai.
At the time of his death, he spoke a verse: "Raising my hand, I grasp the Southern Dipper; Turning my body, I lean against the Northern Bushel."
The Dragon. Looking out beyond the heavens from the tip of its head, who is there like me?
Chan Master Gaji of Silla, a successor of Chan Master Chang of Daming, asked: "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master replied: "Wait until you are inside..."
[The Master] came forward and said, "I shall tell you right now. [A monk] asked, "What is the essential meaning of Damei? The Master said, "The curd and the cream are cast away at once.
When the Venerable Tiantong of Hangzhou ascended the hall, he addressed the assembly: "Do not wait for me; if you are to come, come now. If you are to go down..."
As you depart, you descend. Each possesses a Flower-Treasury Nature-Sea, complete with merit and unimpeded radiance;
each should take this up for themselves. Be careful. Question: How does one exit the triple world? The Master said: Where are you right now?

The Buddhist monk Fuguang was the Dharma heir of the Hangzhou Prefect, Bai Juyi, whose courtesy name was Le Tian. Having long studied under Fuguang, he attained the heart-dharma and simultaneously received the Mahayana Vajra Jewel Precepts.
During the Yuanhe era, he visited the Dharma Hall of Xingshan Monastery in Jingzhao and commissioned a four-bay [structure] (the wording is as seen in the source).

[Chapter on Promoting Goodness] In the fifteenth year [of his tenure], while serving as the governor of Hangzhou, he visited Master Niaoke. Their exchange of questions and answers is recorded (see the Chapter on Niaoke).

He once sent a letter to Dharma Master Ji, stating that since the Buddha’s unsurpassed great wisdom expounds the principles of the teachings, how could there be a yielding to the high or low capacities of beings and different responses for various ailments?
He argued that such views contradict the doctrine of the single flavor of equality, citing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in support.
Furthermore, he challenged [the opponent] by opening up two interpretations regarding the *Vajrasamādhi* and other six sutras.

He also established logical arguments to interrogate the inconsistencies between the earlier and later explanations of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) within the context of the five aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination. In doing so, he probed the profound and sought out the hidden, penetrating the obscure and illuminating the subtle.
Yet, he did not see the Dharma Master’s response, nor have there been many who have come forward to provide an answer in his stead. Furthermore, he received from the East...
Master Duning composed eight verses, each expanding upon one of the eight stages of gradual cultivation to explain their essential meaning.
From the shallow to the profound, they are like pearls strung together. Wherever he stayed, he frequently sought out the ancestral path, never adhering to a single teacher for his studies.

Later, serving as a guest official, he was assigned to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). He exhausted his own stipend to restore Longmen Xiangshan Temple; upon its completion, he composed a record for it himself.
All of his writings were invariably concerned with edification, and there was none that did not praise the Buddha-vehicle, as seen in his collected works.
The sequence of his official appointments and the details of his death and posthumous honors are preserved in the historical records.
Chan Master Zhengyuan of Guishan in Fuzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wuxie Mo.
He was the son of the Cai family of Xuanzhou. He once composed a verse to instruct his disciples, the first of which says:
How many times has the vast ocean turned to mulberry fields? Only empty space remains utterly serene. Those who have reached the shore need no longer cling to their raft;
those who have not yet crossed must surely rely on a boat. The second verse says: Having sought a teacher, one recognizes the source of the original mind.

Both banks are fundamentally one, neither being incomplete. If you are already a Buddha, there is no need to seek another Buddha; it is simply because of this that one forgets all conditions. Xiantong.

In the year Jichou (1049), he passed away at his native mountain. He was seventy-eight years old and had been a monk for fifty-four years. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Grand Master Xingkong, and his stupa was named Huiguan.
A monk asked Master Suxi, "What is the Buddha Dīpaṃkara? The Master said, "A duck swallows a field snail.
The monk asked, "May I turn myself around [attain realization], or not? The Master said, "The eyes pop out."
The Venerable Master Puhua of Zhenzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Panshan. His origins were unknown;

he served Panshan as his master and secretly received the true instructions, yet he feigned madness and spoke without restraint. Following Panshan’s passing, he went forth to propagate the Dharma in the northern regions. Sometimes...
In a city or amidst burial mounds, he shook a single bell and said: "If it comes from the bright side, strike from the bright side; if it comes from the dark side, strike from the dark side;
if it comes from the four quarters and eight directions, strike with a whirlwind; if it comes from empty space, strike with a continuous blow.
One day, Linji had a monk seize him and asked, "What if it does not come in any of these ways? The Master pushed him away and said, "Come tomorrow, Great Compassionate One."
There was a meal being held in the monastery. When the monk returned, he related this to Jie. Jie said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
Whenever he saw anyone, regardless of their status, he would ring his bell once; thus he was known at the time as Master Puhua.
Sometimes he would ring the bell right by a person’s ear, or place it against their back. If someone turned around, he would immediately open his hands and say, "Give me one!"
Qian would eat even food obtained at improper times. Once, he entered Linji’s monastery late in the evening and ate raw vegetables.
Linji said, "This fellow looks very much like a donkey. The Master then brayed like a donkey. Linji said to the steward, "Prepare some fine fodder for him.
The Master said, "The people of Shaoshi did not recognize me; now I have come again to Jinling. Linji’s single eye sees everywhere."
While acting as a guide for others, the Master encountered a cavalry officer who stepped forward and shouted, "Ho! The Master also shouted. The officer then assumed a wrestling stance.
The officer had his men strike the Master with five blows of the staff. The Master said, "It is similar, but it is not the same.
Once, while the Master was walking through the marketplace, he shook his bell and sang: "I seek a place to go, but it cannot be found. At that time, Daowu happened upon him.
Baizhang seized him and asked, "Where do you intend to go? The Master replied, "Where have you come from? Baizhang was speechless.
The Master pulled his hand away and departed. One day, Linji was sitting in the monks' hall with the Elder Mudata of Heyang.
They were discussing how the Master spent his days in the marketplace acting like a madman, and whether he was an ordinary person or not.
The Master [Shoushan Shengnian] suddenly entered. Linji asked, "Are you a commoner or a sage?
The Master said, "Now tell me, am I a commoner or a sage? Linji then gave a shout. The Master pointed his finger and said, "The bride of He'yang;
the grandmotherly Zen of the wooden pagoda; Linji the little fellow—yet he possesses one eye. Linji said, "You thief! The Master said, "Thief! Thief!"

He then went out. At the beginning of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, as he was about to manifest his passing, he entered the marketplace and said to the people, "I beg for a *zhidu* (monastic robe).
Some people gave him a padded jacket; others gave him a cloth cloak, but he accepted neither. He shook his staff and departed.
When Linji sent someone to deliver a coffin to him, the Master laughed and said, "That fellow Linji is too talkative. Thereupon, he accepted it.
He addressed the multitude, saying, "Puhua will pass away at the East Gate tomorrow. The people of the district led one another to escort him out of the city.

The Master spoke in a stern voice, "Today’s burial does not accord with the principles of the *qingwu* (the art of geomancy). He then said, "Tomorrow he will pass away at the South Gate. The people followed him accordingly.
Again he said, "Departing through the West Gate tomorrow would be auspicious. As the people departed, they gradually became sparse; once he had gone out, they returned. The people—
His resolve grew somewhat slack. On the fourth day, he personally carried the coffin out beyond the northern gate. Shaking his rattle-drum, he entered the coffin and passed away.
The people of the commandery rushed out of the city; they lifted the coffin to look at him, but he was already gone. They heard only the sound of the rattle-drum fading gradually into the air.
No one could fathom its source.
Chan Master Liangsui of Shouzhou, a successor of Chan Master Magu Cheshan, went to visit Magu.
When Magu saw him approaching, he immediately took up a hoe and went to weed the grass. The Master [observed this].
He went to where Gu was weeding, but Gu paid him no heed and returned directly to his quarters, closing the door behind him. The Master went again the following day, but Gu closed the door once more.
The Master then knocked on the door. Gu asked, "Who is it? The Master replied, "Liangsui.
As soon as he uttered his name, Gu suddenly attained realization and said, "Master, do not deceive Liangsui! Had Liangsui not come here to pay my respects to you, [I would have remained ignorant]."
By the time he had spent his entire life being led astray by the sutras and śāstras, Gu opened the door to meet him.
Upon returning to his lecture hall, Gu said to the assembly: "What all of you know, Liang-sui knows entirely; what Liang-sui knows, none of you know."
When Chan Master Hui-chao of Shu-shan in Ji-zhou, a successor of Chan Master Dong-shan of Dong-si, came to pay his respects, the Master said, "You have already established yourself in one place;
why have you come here again? Hui-chao replied, "I was unable to resolve my doubts, so I have come specifically to see the Master. The Master—
The Master summoned Liang-jia. Jia responded with an assent. The Master said, "What is this? Jia was speechless. The Master said, "A fine Buddha indeed, but he simply lacks radiance."
A monk asked Chan Master Chuwwei of Qianzhou, successor to Chan Master Xitang Zang:
"Regarding the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, one attains the subtle through the realization of their principle.

Are these the same as, or different from, the meaning of the Patriarchs? The Master said: "One must discern beyond the six phrases; one must not be turned by sounds or forms. The monk said: [The Master continued: "..."
"What are the six phrases? The Master said, "Speaking, silence, neither speaking nor silent, both together, neither together, and how would you do it?
The monk had no reply. He asked Yangshan, "What is your name? Yangshan said, "Huiji."
The Master asked, "Which one is wisdom? Which one is stillness? Sanshan said, "It is right before your eyes. The Master said, "There is still 'before' and 'after' present.
Sanshan said, "Setting aside 'before' and 'after' for a moment, what do you see, Preceptor? The Master said, "Go drink tea."
Chan Master Hongbian of Dajianfu Monastery in Jingzhao was a successor of Chan Master Zhangjing Hui.
Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty summoned him and asked, "Why does the Chan school have the designations 'Northern' and 'Southern'?
He replied, "The Chan gate originally has no north or south. In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa..."
Kāśyapa, through successive transmission, it reached the twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma, who came to this land as the First Patriarch.
Reaching the time of the Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren, while he was expounding the Dharma at Mount Dongshan in Qizhou, there were two disciples.
One was named Huineng, who received the robe and the Dharma and resided south of the Ling Mountains as the Sixth Patriarch; the other was named Shenxiu, who remained in—
The transformation was propagated northward. Subsequently, one of Shenxiu’s disciples, Pují, established Xiu as the Sixth Patriarch and proclaimed himself the Seventh Patriarch.
Although the Dharma they attained was one and the same, there were differences in their methods of guidance and awakening—namely, the sudden and the gradual.
Thus it is said, "The South is Sudden; the North is Gradual. It was not that the Chan school originally possessed the designations "North" and "South. The Emperor asked: "What is meant by 'name'?"
"Precepts," he replied, "are so called because they prevent wrongdoing and cease evil. The Emperor asked, "What is concentration?

He replied, "When the six sense faculties encounter objects, the mind does not follow after conditions; this is called concentration. The Emperor asked, "What is wisdom? He replied, "When both mind and objects are empty."

To perceive and examine without delusion is called wisdom (*prajñā*). The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'expedient means' (*upāya*)? He replied, "Expedient means refers to concealing reality and covering up appearances;
it is the gateway of skillful and provisional methods. To provide guidance for those of middling and inferior capacities through indirect application and instruction is called expedient means.
Even to say that for those of superior faculties one should abandon expedient means and speak only of the Unsurpassed Way—this too is a discourse of expedient means," and so forth.

The Patriarch’s original words state that he forgot his achievements and severed all designations; there were likewise no traces of expedient means employed. The Emperor asked, “What constitutes the Buddha-mind?

He replied, “‘Buddha’ is a term from the Western Heaven [India]; in the language of Tang, it means ‘Awakened. It refers to the fact that when a person possesses wisdom and illuminating awareness, this is called the Buddha-mind.
‘Mind’ is an alternative name for the Buddha, which has hundreds of thousands of different titles, yet its essence is but one. It has no form or shape.”

It is not characterized by blue, yellow, red, or white; nor by male or female, and so forth. Whether among devas or non-devas, humans or non-humans, it manifests as a deva or a human, and can appear as male or female.
It is neither beginning nor end, without birth and without extinction; therefore, it is called the nature of numinous awakening.

"Just as Your Majesty daily attends to ten thousand affairs of state, this is precisely Your Majesty’s Buddha-mind. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to transmit it together, it would not be something external or something else that could be attained.
The Emperor asked, "If there are people today who practice the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), how is that?

He replied, "When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he served as the Teacher of Gods and Humans and as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). He taught the Dharma according to their capacities; for those of superior faculties..."
The Supreme Vehicle was opened for those of superior capacity to realize the ultimate truth instantaneously.

As for those of middling and inferior capacities who were unable to attain such instantaneous realization, the Buddha, for the sake of Vaidehī, provisionally opened the sixteen gates of contemplation, enabling them to be reborn in Sukhāvatī through the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.

Thus, the Sūtra says: "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha. Outside of the mind there is no Buddha; outside of the Buddha there is no mind. The Emperor said: "If there are people who uphold this Sūtra..."

[The Emperor] asked, "Regarding the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name and holding mantras to seek the Buddha, how should one proceed? He replied, "The Tathāgata has praised various methods in all their forms, yet they are all for the sake of the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Just as the myriad rivers and streams do not fail to flow toward the ocean, so too these various distinct practices all return to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom).
The Emperor said, "Since the Patriarch has already attained the seal of mind-to-mind transmission (*citta-mudrā*), the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says 'there is nothing...'"
"How was the Dharma attained? He replied, "In the Buddha’s single transformation, there was truly not a single dharma given to others;
rather, he merely showed all people that their respective self-natures are identical to the Dharma-treasury. At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara simply certified Śākyamuni to his original nature."
Yet, by having nothing to attain, one finally accords with the original intent of Dīpaṃkara. Thus the Sūtra says: "There is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span;
this Dharma is equal. One cultivates all wholesome dharmas while not dwelling in signs.

The Emperor asked, "Since you, Master of Chan, have realized the meaning of the Patriarchs, do you still prostrate to the Buddha and recite the sūtras? He replied, "The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya family prostrate to the Buddha and recite the sūtras."
This is indeed the constant law for those who maintain the Dharma, and there are four types of retribution.

Nevertheless, one must cultivate the body according to the Buddha’s precepts, seek out wise teachers, gradually practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and tread upon the path traversed by the Tathāgata. The Emperor asked: "What is meant by 'sudden realization,' and what is meant by 'gradual cultivation'?
He replied: "To suddenly clarify one's own nature is to be of equal rank with the Buddhas. However, because of the defiled habits accumulated since beginningless time, one must rely on..."
He gradually cultivated remedies so that they accorded with his nature and functioned spontaneously. It was like a person eating a meal: one does not become full in a single mouthful.

On this day, the Master debated for seven *ke* (approx. forty-two minutes) and was granted a purple robe and the title Chan Master Yuanzhi. Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued to repair the ancestral pagodas throughout the realm, ordering that each be maintained and protected.
Chan Master Zhizhen of Guishan in Fuzhou was the son of the Liu family of Yangzhou. He first visited Zhangjing, who asked, "From where have you come?

The Master replied, "I have come to where there is nowhere to go; I have arrived from where there is nowhere to come. Although Zhangjing remained silent, the Master also attained realization for himself. Later, while presiding over the assembly in the Dharma hall, he said:
"A movement of the face, a blink of the eye—nothing emerges apart from the person themselves. A single thought of pure mind is the original source."

"This is the Buddha. He then spoke in verse: "The mind is fundamentally free from dust; what need is there to wash it? The body is without illness; why seek a physician? If you wish to know this Buddha, he does not reside in the body;
A bright mirror hangs high, yet has not yet reflected anything. Later, during the suppression of Buddhism under Emperor Wuzong, he addressed the assembly with a verse:
"An imperial edict falls like thunder upon the green peaks; Tears fall before the wind as I cast off my monastic robes."
In the clouds there is a temple where one cannot stay; amidst the dust there is no home, to where can one return?

The bright moon divides its form, ever new in every place; how could a layperson (baiyi) fall from being one who understands emptiness? Who says that living in the secular world hinders the cultivation of the Way?

Even the Golden Grain Buddha once had the body of a lay devotee (jushi). When the Bodhisattva of Endurance sat in meditation beneath the forest, he was once maimed by the King of Song; how much more so in our sagely dynasty!

This was not the case; even if he had merely been made to cease his practice of the Way, what cause for grief would there have been? Upon the restoration of the dynasty by Emperor Xuanzong, he no longer wore the black robes.
In the year of Yiyou during the Xiantong era, he passed away at his mountain monastery. He was eighty-four years of age and sixty years since his ordination.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Guiji, and his stupa was named Mizhen.
Chan Master Cao of Jinzhou in Lintao invited Master Mi for a meal. He did not arrange any seats. When Master Mi arrived, he spread his sitting cloth and prostrated;
Master Cao descended from his meditation seat. Master Mi then took the Master’s seat, while Master Cao sat on the floor instead.
When the meal was finished, Master Mi departed. An attendant said, "The Master is revered by all people; today your seat was taken [by another]."

Someone snatched it away. The Master said, "If he comes back after three days, I will accept him as my disciple. Three days later, the man indeed returned and said, "The other day I was robbed by bandits.

(A monk asked Jingqing, "What is the meaning of the ancient saying, 'The other day I was robbed by bandits'? Jingqing replied, "He only saw the sharpness of the awl-head; he did not see the squareness of the chisel-head.")
Whenever Master Gudī of Langzhou saw a monk coming, he would simply say, "Go! You have no Buddha-nature. The monks were unable to respond;
those who did respond failed to grasp his intent. When Yangshan arrived for an audience, the Master said, "Go! You have no Buddha-nature."
Dongshan joined his palms, stepped forward three paces, and responded with an assent. The Master smiled and said, "From where did you obtain this samādhi?
Dongshan replied, "I received my name from Danyuan; I obtained my ground from Guishan. The Master asked, "Are you not then a son of Guishan?
Dongshan said, "In terms of worldly truth, it is not that I am not; in terms of the Buddha-dharma, I do not presume to be so. Dongshan then asked in turn, "Master..."
"From where did you obtain this samādhi? The Master replied, "I obtained this samādhi from Zhangjing.
Baoshan sighed and said, "It is inconceivable; it is difficult for those who come here to find a place to settle."
A monk asked Master Gaoji of Hezhong Prefecture, “What is the Way? What is Chan? The Master showed him by means of a verse:
“That which has a name is not the Great Way; Right and wrong are both not Chan. If you wish to know the meaning within this, It is like yellow leaves used to stop a child’s crying.”
Chan Master Shanglin Jieling of Hunan was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yongtai Tuan.
When he first visited Mount Gui, the Master asked, "Virtuous One, what have you come to do?"
The Master said, "Your armor and helmet are fully equipped. Yangshan said, "Strip them all off before you may meet with the Virtuous One. The Master said, "I have stripped them off.
Yangshan scolded him, saying, "The thief has not yet been beaten; why are you stripping yourself? The Master had no reply. Yangshan spoke on his behalf, saying:
"Please, Preceptor, clear the area of attendants. Guishan gestured with his hand and said, "Yes, yes. Later, when the Master visited Yongtai, Yongtai finally explained its meaning to him.
The Master of Bimoyan on Mount Wutai always carried a wooden staff; whenever he saw a monk coming to prostrate, he would immediately [strike him] with the staff.
He tilted his neck and said, "Which demon-spirit taught you to leave the household life? Which demon-spirit taught you to travel as a pilgrim? If you can speak, you shall die beneath this cross;
if you cannot speak, you shall die beneath this cross. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Among the disciples, few were able to respond.
When Hetong came to visit the Master, as soon as he saw him, he did not prostrate but instead leaped into his arms. The Master pressed Hetong—
He struck him three times on the back. Then, rising together, he clapped his hands and said, "Elder brother, you have deceived me for three thousand li!
You have deceived me for three thousand li! and he immediately turned back.
Every day, Master Zhilin of Hunan would scold Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, calling them both malevolent spirits. Holding a wooden sword in his hand, he claimed to be subduing demons.
As soon as he saw a monk come to pay his respects, he would cry out, "A demon has come! A demon has come! and brandish the sword wildly before returning to his quarters.
He continued in this manner for twelve years. Later, he set aside the sword and remained silent. A monk asked, "Regarding those twelve years ago—"
"Why did he subdue the demons? The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor. [The monk] asked, "Why did he not subdue the demons twelve years later?
The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor."
Zen Master Qi’an of Huangzhou, successor to Zen Master Huayan Zang, ascended the hall and said:
"When words do not fall into fixed phrases, even the Buddhas have nothing left to bestow; when the profound resonance does not decline..."
"Who can know this? [A monk] asked. "How does one recognize one's own Buddha? The Master said:
"When a single leaf falls, it is not exhausted; when the pine wind ceases its melody, there is no one to lament. [The monk] asked: "What is one's own Buddha? The Master said:

"The spirited horse before the grass is truly difficult to fathom; to reach the ultimate subtlety, one must walk like a beast. [Another monk] asked: "How old are you, Master? The Master said: [He remained silent].
How could five, six, four, or three be comparable? It is truly difficult to fathom that they are not one or two. The Master had a verse which said:

Within the fiercely blazing flames, there is a path for people; atop the swirling wind, one dwells in steadfast stillness. Constantly and eternally throughout kalpas, who could ever deviate from this?
The radiant sun silently moves, its illumination reaching all equally.
Fourth generation descendant under Nanyue;
Dharma heir of Chan Master Huangbo Yun.
The Venerable Master of Muzhou, whose name was Daoming, was a descendant of the Chen clan of Jiangnan. At the time of his birth, a crimson light filled the room and auspicious clouds covered the sky;

these did not disperse for ten days. He had double pupils in his eyes and the Seven Stars were arrayed upon his face. His physical appearance was extraordinary, setting him apart from the common crowd.
Once, while visiting Kaiyuan Temple to pay respects to the Buddha, he recognized a monk as an old acquaintance. Upon returning home, he informed his father.
The Master’s mother wished for him to seek ordination; his parents granted their permission, and he entered the Sangha. He mastered the Tripitaka, and his realization accorded with that of Huangbo.

Later, he appeared in the world to reside at Guanyuan Monastery. When students questioned him, he would respond immediately and impulsively; his words were steep and perilous, as he did not follow conventional paths.
Consequently, those of shallow capacity often failed to fathom him, while only those among the seekers who possessed keen faculties felt profound reverence and submission. All...
They all turned toward him with devotion and honored him as a venerable elder. Later, he returned to Kaiyuan Temple and wove *púxié* (rush sandals) to support his mother;
thus he earned the title "The Rush Sandal Maker of Chen. When the Khitan rebels entered the territory, the Master hung a large straw sandal at the city gate.

The Khitans wished to discard it, but though they exerted all their strength, they could not lift it. They sighed, saying, "Muzhou has a great sage," and abandoned the city and departed, whereupon the region was spared.
In a state of commotion, during the evening *chan* (meditation) session, he addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, have you yet attained a point of entry?
If you have not yet attained a point of entry, you must seek one. If you have attained a point of entry, henceforth you must not bring shame upon this old monk.
At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "I, your disciple, shall never dare to bring shame upon the Master."
Shang said, "I have already been betrayed by you. I have told you clearly, yet you still do not understand;

how much less could you grasp it if it were covered over? Addressing the assembly, the Master said, "I, this old monk, have resided here as abbot, yet I have never seen a person who has attained the state of 'no-matter' (wu-shi) come before me.
Why do you not step forward? At that moment, a monk stepped forward, and the Master said, "Venerable Director of Affairs (Weina)."
"Not here. Take him away yourself; give him twenty blows outside the three gates.
The monk asked, "Where does this person's fault lie? The Master said, "Adding shackles upon a pillory. Whenever the Master saw a monk approach, he would immediately close the door.

However, if he saw a lecturer-monk, he would call out, "Lecturer! When the lecturer responded, the Master would say, "A fellow carrying only one shoulder of a wooden board. Or he would say, "Right here..."
There was a bucket. "Give me some water," [he said]. One day, while standing on the corridor steps, a monk asked, "Where is the room of the Venerable Master Chen?
The Master took off his straw sandals and struck him over the head with them. The monk then ran away. The Master called out, "Virtuous One! and the monk turned his head back.
The Master pointed and said, "Go that way instead. The envoy asked, "All three gates are open; through which one shall I enter? The Master called out, "Minister!
When the envoy responded, the Master said, "Enter through the Gate of Faith. The envoy then saw the murals on the wall and asked:
The Master asked, "What were the two venerable ones discussing? He pointed at a pillar and said, "Among the three bodies, which one does not preach the Dharma? Head Monk, investigate this!
The Master asked, "Are you not lecturing on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only)? He replied, "I dare not say so.

The Master said, "Leaving for India in the morning and returning to Tang China in the evening—do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Ho! Ho! You do not even observe the five precepts."
The Master asked an elder: "When one has realized that the tip of a single hair swallows the vast ocean, only then does one know that the great earth is but a single mote of dust.

Elder, what do you say to this? The elder replied, "To whom are you asking? The Master said, "I am asking you, elder. The elder said, "Why do you not acknowledge my words? The Master said, [silently].
"You do not understand my words. "Neither do I understand your words. He asked the presiding master, "What sutra are you lecturing on?
The master replied, "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The Master said, "May I ask about a certain passage of meaning? The master replied, "Yes. The Master kicked at the air and blew once, saying:
"What is the meaning of this? [The monk] said, "There is no such meaning in the sutras. The Master said, "You empty-talking, deceptive fellow!
You say there is no meaning to the story of the five hundred laborers lifting the stone! Seeing a monk, the Master said, "This is a ready-made case;
I grant you thirty blows. [The monk] said, "I am like this. The Master said, "Why does the Vajra-pāṇi at the triple gate raise his fist? [The monk] said, [silently].
"Even Vajra was like this," [the Master] said, and he struck him. [The student] asked, "What is the path that leads upward?
The Master said, "If you wish to speak, what difficulty is there? [The student] said, "Please, Master, speak. The Master said, "The first and third, the eleventh; the middle ninth, the lower seventh.
[The student] asked, "I do not ask about when one layer is removed by another layer. But when one layer is not removed by another layer, it is like..."
"What? the Master asked. "Yesterday morning I planted eggplants; today I am planting winter melons. A monk asked, "What is the true meaning of Caoxi?
The Master replied, "This old monk loves anger and does not love joy. The monk asked, "Why is it so? The Master said: [The text provided ends here.]
When meeting a swordsman on the road, you must present your sword; if you are not a poet, do not speak of poetry. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "Liu-yang.
The Master asked, "When that senior master there was questioned on the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, what did he say?
The monk said, "Nowhere on the ground is there a path to walk upon. The Master asked, "Did that senior master truly say those words? The monk said, "He truly did. The Master then took up his staff.
The Master struck him and said, "You talkative fellow! The Master asked an elder, "If a brother-monk were to come, how would you respond?
The elder replied, "I will wait for him to arrive. The Master said, "Why do you not speak? The elder asked, "What is lacking in the Master? The Master said, [nothing].
"Do not trouble yourself with such entanglements; come, monk. The monk replied, "I am a wandering monk (*paryaṭaka*). The Master said, "Have you yet paid homage to the Buddha?
He replied, "What would I do by paying homage to that mound of earth? The Master said, "Go out, and take this upon yourself. A monk asked, "I am both a lecturer and a wandering monk.
What is it like when one does not understand the meaning of the teachings? The Master said, "Truly, speak the truth as it is."
[The monk] repented and said, "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "If you had not asked, I, an old monk, would have kept my mouth shut and remained silent.
Since you have asked, I cannot remain silent. [The monk] said, "Please speak, Master. The Master said, "A heart that does not betray others; a face free of shame.
[Another] asked, "What is it like when a single phrase exhausts all expression? The Master said, "The meaning has fallen away."
[The monk] asked, "Where is the place where this student falls into error? The Master said, "Thirty blows—whom shall they be made to eat?
[The monk] asked, "When one bows high to Śākyamuni and does not bow to Maitreya, what then? The Master said, "Yesterday someone asked this; I have already driven him out.
[The monk] said, "Does the Master fear that I am not sincere? The Master said, "The staff is not here; it is the handle of a broom."
On the occasion of the thirtieth [anniversary], he ascended the hall. "I saw Baizhang; he did not know good from bad.
As soon as the assembly had gathered, he struck them all at once with his staff. He then called out to the assembly, and when they turned their heads, he said:
'What is this? What common ground is there for conversation? Huangbo was also like this: he called out to the assembly, and when they turned their heads, he said: 'The moon is like a bow...'"
The bow: little rain and much wind; it is still somewhat lacking. He asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk then shouted.
The Master said, "I, an old monk, have been shouted at by you. The monk shouted again. The Master said, "After three shouts or four shouts, what then?"

The monk remained silent. The Master struck him and said, "This fellow who plunders empty space! A scholar came to visit the Master and claimed he was versed in the calligraphic styles of twenty-four masters.
The Master pointed a dot in the air with his staff and asked, "Do you understand? The scholar was at a loss.
The Master said: "Furthermore, you say you understand the calligraphic works of the twenty-four masters, yet you do not even recognize the eight strokes of the character 'Yong' (永).
Ascending the hall, he said: "To unfold [the teaching] is up to me; to fold it back together is also up to me.
At that time, a monk asked: "What is unfolding? The Master said: "Three times nine is twenty-seven. Bodhi and Nirvana, True Suchness and Liberation, 'this very mind is Buddha'—I, for my part..."
[The student] said, "When you speak in this way, how do you yourself respond? He replied, "I do not speak in that way.
The Master said, "The cup falls to the ground; the saucer shatters into seven pieces. [The student] asked, "What is 'gathering together'? The Master then sat with his hands folded.

[The student] asked, "Are the meaning of the Teachings and the meaning of the Patriarchs the same or different? The Master said, "The green mountains are themselves green mountains; the white clouds are themselves white clouds."
Yun asked, "What is the green mountain? The Master said, "Give me back a drop of rain. Yun said, "I cannot say it; please speak for me.
The Master said, "The Lotus Sūtra is the vanguard; the Nirvāṇa Sūtra is the rear guard. He questioned a monk, "Where have you been this summer?
The monk said, "I will tell you when you, Reverend, have a dwelling place. The Master said, "A fox is not of the lion’s kind; a lamp is not..."
Riyue Ming asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk stared at him with wide eyes. The Master said, "A man who precedes the donkey and follows the horse.
The monk said, "Please, Master, examine me. The Master said, "A man who precedes the donkey and follows the horse. Bring me a phrase! The monk had no reply.

A monk asked, "What is the teaching of this one lifetime? The Master said, "The Great Man (Shang Daren) and Qiu Yiji. A monk asked, "What is Chan?

"Are you newly arrived? he asked. The monk replied, "I am. The Master said, "Set aside this entanglement for a moment. Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Carry your shackles and present your petition; go out and face it yourself. The monk then departed. The Master called out, "Come here!
I am truly asking you: where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Jiangxi. The Master said, "The Abbot of Letan is behind you, fearing that you might speak recklessly. Do you see him?"
The monk had no reply. [The Master] asked: "Regarding the *vajra* at the temple gate: if you expand it, it encompasses heaven, earth, and the great land;
if you do not expand it, not even a single hair is encountered. What do you say to this? The Master said: "Hūṃ! Hūṃ! I have never seen such a thing. The Master then asked:
"First leap three thousand feet, then retreat eight hundred. How will you manage this? The monk said: "Yes. The Master said: "First, I shall issue you a written reprimand."

The monk’s appearance was fine; as he was about to leave, the Master called out, “Come! I shall have some wordy entanglement with you. He spread his arms wide, saying, “This is the entire universe and the great earth.
Now tell me, how deep is the water of Lake Dongting? The monk replied, “I do not know how to measure it. The Master said, “And what of Lake Dongting itself?
The monk said, “It is simply because of the present age. The Master said, “If you cannot even understand this entanglement, then you truly do not understand.”

Yun [Zhaozhou] pointed to the clouds before him and said, "What kind of cloud is that over there?
Yun replied, "It is a black cloud to the south. The Master said, "It must rain today.

A monk asked, "That which is not formed by the character 'yi' (以) and is not the character 'ba' (八)—what chapter or verse is this? The Master snapped his fingers once and said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand."

The Master said: "In the boundless superior causes of the sermons and praises above, the toad leaps up into the sky; the earthworm passes straight across the Eastern Sea. He asked a monk: "Where have you recently come from?
The monk replied: "From north of the River. The Master said: "There is a person named Zhaozhou there; have you ever been to him? The monk replied:
"I have recently left from there. The Master said: "What words or phrases did Zhaozhou use to instruct his disciples?"
The monk brought up a story about drinking tea. The Master laughed heartily and said, "How shameful! He then asked, "What was Zhaozhou’s meaning?
The monk replied, "It was merely a provisional expedient for the occasion. The Master said, "Alas! You have just poured a bucket of filth over Zhaozhou," and he struck him.
The Master then asked the novice, "How do you understand this? The novice simply prostrated himself.
The Master also struck him. The monk went to the place where the śrāmaṇera was and asked, "The Master just now struck me;
what did you do? The śrāmaṇera said, "If it had not been for our Master, he would not have struck me. A newly arrived monk came to pay his respects.

[The master] said, "It is defiled by impurity. While he was pulling noodles, a monk visited him. The Master pulled out a noodle and showed it to him; the monk then departed.
At evening, the Master asked his junior attendant, "Where did that monk go just now? The junior attendant replied, "He left immediately.

As soon as the attendant opened the door, he went straight out. The monk entered, bowed, and asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "Just now..."
"Who is this person who comes and goes? As the monk attempted to step forward, the Master pushed him out and closed the door.
When Caoshan was traveling on pilgrimage, he asked, "What is the Dharmakāya Lord, the Vairocana Teacher?
The Master said, "If I were to tell you, it would be something else entirely. Caoshan related this to Dongshan, who said, "A fine koan; it simply lacks—"
Jin spoke. "Why do you not ask why he did not say anything? Cao then stepped forward and repeated Jin's words.

Chan Master Zongche of Luohan Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Wu family of Huzhou. He ascended the hall, and a monk asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said: "The bones are crushed. (In responding to the occasion, the Master frequently used this phrase; he was thus known at the time as "Master Bone-Crusher. [Another] asked:

[The student] asked, "When the nature-ground is mostly obscured by darkness, how does one attain awakening? The Master said, "When the clouds of affliction are swept away by the wind, the great void becomes vast and clear.
[The student] asked, "How does one attain clarity? The Master said, "A single orb is bright and pure; its light shines across ten thousand miles. Silence.
The stupa was later located in the northwest corner. In the Jǐmǎo year of the Zhēnmíng era of the Liáng dynasty, King Qián expanded the monastery and established it as Ānguó Temple;
he moved the master’s stupa to Dàcí Mountain. Today, both the temple and the stupa remain intact.
The layman Pei Xiu, styled Gongmei, was a native of Wenxi in Hedong.

While he was serving as the Prefect of Xin’an, it happened that Yunmen’s master had recently left the assembly at Huangbo Mountain in Lingnan and entered the Dà'ān Vihāra, mingling with the laborers to sweep and clean the halls.
When the Prefect entered the temple to burn incense, the administrative officials received him; while observing the murals on the walls, he asked: "What is this?"
[The Master] looked at the portrait. The attendant replied, "This is the true likeness of a high monk. The Master said, "The true likeness may indeed be observed;

where is the high monk? The attendant had no reply. The Master asked, "Is there any Chan practitioner here? [The attendant] said, "Recently there was a monk who came to this temple to take up service;
he bears a strong resemblance to a Chan practitioner. The Master said, "May he be invited here so that we may question him? Thereupon, Ba was immediately sought out and arrived.
When the Duke saw this, he said with delight, "I have just now had a question, but the various virtuous ones were stingy with their words. I now request the Master to provide a response in my stead.
Baizhang said, "I pray the Duke will pose his question. The Duke repeated his previous remark, and Baizhang called out in a loud voice, "Pei Xiu!"
The Duke assented. Huangbo asked, "Where is it? At that moment, the Duke understood the meaning, as if he had recovered the pearl from within his topknot.

He said, "My teacher is truly a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). How could such a direct pointing to people be found elsewhere? Why have I been mired in this place until now? The assembly of the monastery was astonished.

From then on, the Duke invited him into the government offices and treated him with the etiquette of a disciple. Although the Master repeatedly declined, the Duke would not stop and pressed his invitation firmly.
He resided at Huangbo Mountain to promote the ancestral Way. Whenever he had leisure, he would personally enter the mountains, or be invited into the prefectural seat;

his sole concern was the Dharma. Having thoroughly penetrated the intent of the patriarchs and being extensively versed in the characteristics of the teachings, all quarters agreed that he had not emerged from the gate of Huangbo in vain.
Upon his transfer to the governorship of Xuancheng, he longed to pay homage to the sacred site and consequently established a monastery there.

He was invited to reside there. Although Guifeng had long been held in high esteem by him, his devotion to Huangbo was even more profound, such that he followed his teachings with complete dedication.
Furthermore, in the inscription he composed for Guifeng’s stele, he wrote: "In the Dharma, I am your elder brother; in principle, I am your friend;
in gratitude, you are my spiritual benefactor; in the teaching, you are my internal and external protector. This is clearly evident. —Guifeng.

Feng authored the *Chan-yuan ch’üan* (Exposition of the Source of Chan), the *Yüan-jen lun* (Treatise on the Original Person), the *Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, and the *Notes on the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm*;

for all of these, he personally composed prefaces. Furthermore, he compiled the *Essential Sayings of Huangbo* and personally wrote a preface and introduction to be placed at the beginning of the collection, leaving it behind to serve as a permanent record for the mountain gate.

Furthermore, he personally transcribed five hundred fascicles of the Tripitaka, which have been treasured until the present day. The Duke was devoted to the inner scriptures and entered deeply into the assemblies of the Dharma;
his *Pranidhāna* (Vow Text) remains transmitted to the world.
Chan Master Fazu of Daisui in Yizhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Changqing An.
A native of the Wang family in Zizhou, he attained awakening at a young age and resolved to seek out a teacher.
He left the household life and received full ordination at Huiyi Temple; subsequently, he traveled south, where he first met Yaoshan, Daowu, and Yunyan.
Dongshan next went to the assembly of Daowei outside the passes, where he remained for several years. His food did not reach satiety, and he sought no warmth when lying down;
he refined his practice through austerity, and his conduct was beyond the common. Daowei held him in high esteem.
One day Daowei asked him, "Disciple, while you have been here with this old monk, you have never asked a single turning word. The Master replied, "Where would you have me apply my teeth?"
Guishan said, "Why do you not say, 'What is the Buddha? The Master then covered Guishan’s mouth with his hand. Guishan sighed and said, "You have truly attained the marrow.
From that time on, his fame spread throughout the four seas. Later, he returned to Shu and stayed at Huai Temple in Pengkou, Longshan, Tianpeng.

The monastery was named Dàsúi. Towering peaks rose in majestic beauty, and the mountain stream flowed with crystalline clarity. Within it stood a tree over forty feet in circumference, with a single opening facing south;
its interior was hollow and unobstructed, a natural hermitage formed without the aid of an axe.

At that time, it was called the "Wooden Chan Hermitage," and the Master took up residence there. For more than ten years he did not venture beyond the mountains, yet his reputation spread abroad, drawing students from all quarters.

From a thousand li away, people rushed to follow his teachings like the wind. The Ruler of Shu held him in high esteem and repeatedly sent envoys to summon him, but the Master declined each time on the grounds of old age and illness.
He was bestowed the title of Great Master Shenzhao. Ascending the hall, he said: "This nature is fundamentally pure and replete with myriad virtues.

It is only through the two conditions of defilement and purity that distinctions arise. Therefore, the sages, having awakened to it, employ it exclusively in its pure aspect and thereby achieve the path of enlightenment."
Ordinary people are deluded by this; they are consistently immersed in defiled activity and submerged in saṃsāra.

Since its essence is non-dual, it cannot be said that there are "no two, no division, no distinction, and no interruption. Question: When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, I wonder:
does this [essence] perish or not? The Master said: "It perishes. [The questioner] said: "If that is so, then it must follow along with it [the destruction]. The Master said: "It follows."

He said to the monk, "Return quickly and repent. When the monk returned to Daguī, the Master had already passed away.
The monk went back to Touzi again, but Touzi had also passed away. [The monk] asked, "What is the mark of a great man? The Master [responded].
[The Master] said: "There is no notice posted on one's belly. He asked a monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to live in a hermitage at West Mountain.

The Master said, "If I call for you from the top of East Mountain, would you be able to come immediately? The monk said, "No. The Master said, "Then you have not yet attained the ability to dwell in a hermitage.
He was asked: "When birth and death arrive, what then? The Master said, "When you meet tea, drink tea; when you meet rice, eat rice."
[The monk] offered him rice. [The monk] asked, "Who receives this offering? The Master said, "Close your bowl. Beside the hut was a tortoise.
A monk asked, "All other sentient beings have skin over their bones; why does this sentient being have bones over its skin? The Master picked up his straw sandals.
[The Master] covered it over the back of a tortoise. The monk remained silent. [The Master] asked: "What is the essential dharma of all Buddhas?
The Master raised his whisk and said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A fly-whisk. [Another monk] asked:

the Buddha-dharma pervades all places. Where would you have the student stand? The Master said:
"The great sea allows the fish to leap; the vast sky permits the birds to fly. [He] asked: "When father and son, who are most intimately related, part ways at a fork in the road..."
"How is it? The Master said, "Because there are father and son. The questioner asked, "What is the seamless stupa? The Master said, "Five feet high.
The student said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A solid brick. The questioner asked, "After the Master passes away, to whom shall the Dharma be entrusted?
The Master said, "The pillar and the brazier. The student asked, "Will they receive it? The Master said, "The brazier and the pillar."
The practitioner led the assembly to pay their respects. The Master asked, "When one who has attained realization is called 'East,' what is he?
The practitioner replied, "One cannot call him 'East. The Master rebuked him, saying, "You stinking donkey! If you do not call him 'East,' what do you call him? The practitioner was speechless.
The Master then asked, "What is the house style of this old monk? He replied, "Painting a winnowing basket with red earth. The practitioner said, "I do not yet understand this principle."
"How is it? The Master said, "A winnowing basket has lips; rice cannot leap out. He asked a monk, "What teaching do you lecture on?
The monk replied, "The Hundred Dharma-Wheel. The Master raised his staff and asked, "From what does it arise? The monk said, "It arises from conditions. The Master said, "Alas! Alas!
He asked another monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to Mount Wǔméi to pay homage to Samantabhadra. The Master raised his whisk.
He said, "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are both right here. The monk drew a circle, threw it behind him, and then prostrated.

The Master called to his attendant, "Give this monk a portion of tea. During the monks' period of inquiry, the Master made a gesture with his mouth as if suffering from a stroke and asked, "Is there anyone who can cure my mouth?
The monks vied with one another to bring medicine, and even laypeople did the same.
Hearing of this, many people sent him medicine, but the Master accepted none of it.

After seven days, the Master pinched his own mouth to straighten it and said, "For all this time, I have been beating these two pieces of skin, yet to this day no one has been able to cure them. He then sat upright and passed away.
