Chan Master Baizhang Shenzhao of Jingzhao was asked by a monk, "What is the Master’s profound place? The Master said:
A short man was crossing a deep stream. He asked, "What is it like when one is barefoot? The Master said, "Why not take off [your shoes]?

He asked, "What is it that is 'the non-arising of every dharma'? The Master said, "The myriad species and their thousand differences. He asked, "What is it that is 'the non-extinction of every dharma'?
The Master said, "Stretching out and crossing over, filling the eyes."
A monk asked the Second Chan Master of Fulong Mountain, "What is it like when one recognizes [the nature] in accordance with conditions?
The Master said, "Tell me, how high is the gate tower of Xingguo? A monk asked, "What is it like when the son does not speak of his father's virtue? The Master said:
"Preceptor, please lower your voice.
A monk asked Chan Master Longjun of Mount Shanjun in Shanfu: "What is the person who does not know good from evil? The Master said:
"Not even a thousand sages can approach them. The monk asked: "Does such a person still know of the matter that lies above? The Master said: "They do not know."

[A monk] asked, "Why do they not know? The Master said, "They do not recognize good and evil; how can you speak of matters that transcend [the ordinary]? [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what is it like?
The Master said, "Have you not heard it said: 'The wild dog's snarl'? [A monk] asked, "What is the person who transcends the Buddha? The Master said, "Without a trace.
[A monk] asked, "Whenever there is an expansion or manifestation, one invariably falls into the present moment. When there is no expansion or manifestation, what then?"
The Master said, “Not unfolding, not unfolding. [The monk] asked, “Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, “Not extending, not extending.
A monk asked the Third Generation Zen Master of Fulong Mountain: “Having traversed the thousand-fold mountain paths, what is the nature of the original mechanism?”

The Master said, "The path of birds has never been a place of rest. [The student] asked, "Since you are the Master, why is it that there is no rank or position? The Master said, "Ancients and moderns have failed to arrange it;
how could it be settled across the three periods of time? [The student] said, "If that is so, then I shall follow along with whatever comes my hand."
The Master said: "The spring breeze blows the willow catkins; when will their coming and going cease? Question: "What is the true limit (bhūtakoṭi)? The Master said:
"Throughout vast kalpas it has been no different; there exists no hierarchy."
A monk asked National Preceptor Seongna of Cheongnyeon Temple, successor to Chan Master Jiugeng Qian: "When racing horses compete for a ball, who is the winner? The Master said, "Who is the loser?
The monk said, "In that case, it is not a matter of competing. The Master said, "Even when one does not compete, there is still [a loser]."
[The student] said, "What is the fault? He asked, "How can one avoid this fault? The Master said, "In truth, it has never been lost.
He asked, "How does one refine that which is not lost? The Master said, "It cannot be lifted up with both hands."
A monk asked Zen Master Shendang of Letan in Hongzhou, "How does one discern the master within the four modes of deportment?
The Master said, "Just as I encountered Baofeng, I did not take off my shoes. The monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "An iron boat sails upon the void; waves surge over the mountain peaks."
Chan Master Xingxiu Huiquan (also known as Guangmu) of Nanyuan in Yuanzhou. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Nanyuan?
The Master said, "In many places, peaks and crags resound with the cries of monkeys and birds; across a stretch of level plains, travelers lose their way.
The monk asked, "What is the deepest place of Nanyuan? The Master said, "Everyone sees it. The monk said, "If that is so, then it must be shallow. The Master said, "It is."
This too is a case of swaying both ways. When asked, "How is it when there is no mind and one has not yet seen him?
the Master said: "In the ancient cavern, the dragon roars but does not emerge; before the cliff, the wooden horse neighs but has no form."
One day, Master Ming of Lestam in Nanchang went down to the guest quarters. The assembly requested that the Master return to the Abbot’s quarters.
The Master said, "If you can speak the Way, then I shall go. At that time, Preceptor Mou replied, "The assembly requests the Master. Thereupon, the Master ascended the Dharma Hall.
A monk asked, "When it is a state beyond thought and deliberation, such that consciousness and emotion are difficult to fathom—what then? The Master said, "I do not wish to contravene the ancients."
A person asked, "How is it not to go against the intention of the ancients? The Master said, "It is also fitting that you receive these three prostrations. Question:
"Regarding the pestle and the millstone—if one cannot grind them, one forgets them. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A live sparrow in the jaws of a tiger. Question:
"When concentration and wisdom do not arise, what is it like? The Master said, "An iron ox lies upon the grass, drowsy and unmoving."
[The Master] raised his head and asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Hairy and shaggy. [The student] asked, "What is the家风 (family style) of the one who has realized the Way?
The Master said, "Meeting the Venerable One before the Buddha Hall. [The student] asked, "What is the daily business of the Monk?
The Master said, "There are no chopsticks in the alms bowl. [The student] asked, "What is the daily activity of a śramaṇa? The Master said, "..."
A thunderous roar does not borrow the mechanism of ten thousand men.
A monk asked Chan Master Jishi of Mount Ji: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said: "A pine tree. [Another monk] asked: "With what does Mañjuśrī take his teacher? The Master said: "The lute has a melody truly worth listening to; having heard it..."
From the beginning, crookedness cannot be established.
Zen Master Letan Yanmao was asked by a monk, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas? The Master said, "I certainly do not say that earth, wood, tiles, or rubble are [the mind].
Question: "The sun has set behind the western mountain; what is the situation within the grove? The Master said: "In front of the courtyard."
Flowers bloom in profusion; inside the room, one knows not of spring. [The student] asked, "What is 'building a carriage while behind closed doors'?
The Master said, "One has lost the spotted cat. [The student] asked, "What is 'meeting the ruts upon going out the gate'?

The Master said, "Sitting on the ground, one reaches Chang'an. [The student] asked, "What is the Master’s true host? The Master said, "The painted drum resounds with repeated blows, yet no sound is heard by the ear."
A monk asked Chan Master Changcha of Tong’an Monastery in Fengxi, Hongzhou: “What is the house style of Fengxi?
The Master said, “Fengxi has no house style. The monk asked, “Since it is Fengxi, why is there no house style? The Master said:
He did not go out to meet guests, nor did he wait for visitors. A monk asked, "If that is so, then when one travels throughout the four seas in search of the Way, what should one do?
The Master said, "The food on the platter is provided by others. A monk asked, "What is the realm where the phoenix dwells?

The Master said, "A thousand peaks join the majesty of the mountains; ten thousand ridges know nothing of spring. The monk asked, "Who is the person within this realm? The Master said, "A solitary crag leaning against a rock."
Sitting. Without lowering the mind of white clouds, he asked: "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?
The Master said: "An iron dog barks at a stone ox; an illusory person gazes at the moonlight. He asked: "What is it to be a person with fur and horns? The Master said:
"Wearing a straw raincoat and a bamboo hat, one sells gold; how many who encounter such a person do not know how to call out? He asked: "A student has not yet..."
The monk understood the situation and requested the Master’s instruction. The Master said: "The pines and bamboos are uneven, shrouded in thin mist;

the layered peaks and ridges are slow to receive the rising moon. As the monk prepared to offer a word in response, the Master said: "Before the armor and weapons are deployed, the thief’s body has already been exposed.
The monk asked: "Why is that? The Master said: "A refined Yang bamboo is not pruned before the frost; ink and water vainly boast of the dragon of the sea. The monk circled the meditation seat.
[The Master] stepped out from behind the bed. The Master said: "Closing one's eyes while eating a snail—what a bitter and sour experience!
Question: "What is it like when one returns to the root and reverts to the source? The Master said: "Though the cicada has shed its shell, it cannot avoid clinging to a cold branch.
Question: "Who is the person of fierce and sharp capacity? The Master said: "The stone ox bellows with every step; the paper horse neighs within the flames."

The monk called out, "Newcomer! Holding his *khakkhara*, he circumambulated the Master three times, struck it once, and said, "Please speak, Master, regarding that place where neither ordinary beings nor sages reach.
The Master snapped his fingers three times. The monk said, "Today, Tongan has frightened me into forgetting what came before and losing track of what follows."
The Master asked, "Where did you set out from, Ācārya? The monk said, "I take my leave," and departed.

The Master said, "A patch-robed wanderer of the Five Lakes, a practitioner with a single staff—before you have even reached Tong’an, you will surely be left with doubts. The monk turned his head and said, "Hearing from afar is not as good as seeing nearby.
The Master said, "In greed for a single cup of wine, he lost the fish in the entire boat. [Question: What is the great non-existence?
[The monk] was a person of shame and remorse. The Master said, "I see this old monk committing such an act. [A monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The rhinoceros develops patterns on its horn because it gazes at the moon; the elephant has flowers enter its tusks because it is startled by thunder.

[A monk] asked, "What is the person heading toward [the goal]? The Master said, "A cold cicada clings to a withered tree; its weeping is exhausted, yet it does not turn its head back. The monk said, "..."

"What is it like for one who has returned? The Master said, "Reeds bloom beautifully within the fire; meeting spring, they seem just like autumn. The student asked, "What is it like for one who neither comes nor goes?
The Master said, "A stone ram encounters a stone tiger; looking at each other, they rest together from morning till evening.
The presiding lecturer asked, "I have a rough understanding of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. I do not know, however, what the Master’s teaching is."
"What Dharma do you teach people? The Master said, "I teach the Dharma of the One Vehicle. He asked, "What is the Dharma of the One Vehicle?
The Master said, "In how many hues do the clouds emerge from the mountain peak? In one uniform tone does the sound of the spring fall before the railing?
He asked, "I am not asking about this; what is the Dharma of the One Vehicle? The Master said, "You are remarkably sharp-witted. While admiring the moon, he said to a monk, "How extraordinary!"
"How marvelous! How marvelous! The stars are bright and the moon is clear; it is truly worthy of being beheld. Is this not the Way? The monk asked, "What is the Way?

The Master said, "Try to speak of it. The monk said, "He has no wound himself; do not inflict one upon him. The Master said, "One who carries a satchel and studies literature is unacquainted with the bow and arrow.
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Jiangxi. The Master said, "The Dharma of Jiangxi..."
"What is the Way like here? [The Master] said, "I am fortunate to have encountered you asking me this. Had someone else asked, disaster would have ensued.
The Master said, "I was a bit hasty just now. [The monk] said, "I am no infant; there is no need for those yellow leaves used merely to stop a child's crying.
The Master said, "To spare the turtle while harming the soft-shelled turtle—killing or giving life is up to me. He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? [The monk] said, "Wutai."
The Master asked, “Do you see Mañjuśrī? The monk spread out both hands. The Master said, “Hand-spreading is quite frequent; who beholds Mañjuśrī? He replied, “It would kill me with its urgency.

The Master said, “If you do not behold the wild geese in the clouds, how can you know the cold of the desert sands? A monk asked, “I have come from afar to your chamber; I beg for a word from the Master.

The Master said, “Under the gate of Sun Bin, they merely talk of drilling tortoise shells. The monk said, “My name is... [The Master continued: “...if you wish to be a man of the Way, you must first abandon your name.”
"Not obtained by chance. The Master said, "Go drink tea. The monk then said, "I take my leave" (*zhēnzhòng*). The Master said, "Though you have won one victory, you have lost both feet.
While the Master was reading a scripture, a monk came to pay his respects. The Master said, "The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present..."

[The monk] said, "There is no separate principle in either case. He asked, "What about the *ho-shang*? The Master struck him with his palm. The monk said, "So it is, so it is. The Master said, "This madman!
[The monk] said, "It has been thus from ancient times to the present. The Master said, "You intended to subdue a dragon, but instead encountered a dead tiger."
Tong’an said, “I am truly radiant. The Master said, “To wait by the stump and moor the ship—who else but you could do this?
Tong’an asked, “What about the Master? The Master said, “A Hu sheep going to Chu; it returns home feeling aggrieved. He questioned a monk: “When the realm of the eye has no light, how can one see?
The monk replied, “The Big Dipper turns east; the Southern Dipper shifts west. The Master said, “This is like Confucius entering the Grand Ancestral Temple and saying, ‘It is here!’”
"In that case, under Tong’an, the Way has been cut off and the path is desolate," [a student] said. The Master replied, "I carry an infant across my arms, intending to manifest the imperial decree.
Hearing the sound of magpies, the Master said to the assembly, "The joyful magpie cries in the cold cypresses; the Mind-Seal is transmitted by him."

A monk came forward and asked, "What is the difference? The Master said, "There is someone present among the assembly. The monk said, "Under Tong’an’s gate, the Way is cut off and the people are sparse.
The Master said, "A northern person drinking milk, yet instead blames the skilled physician. The monk said, "Enough, enough. The Master said, "An old crane enters a dried-up pond;

Below the entry for Wang Dao-wu: Zhou Jingang emerged [from him]. Although he scolded the wind and reviled the rain, even Buddhas and Patriarchs dared not encounter his sharp edge. I had long feared that the character "Huang" (皇) might be an error. Later, I obtained the two steles by Qiu Xuansu and Fu Zai and showed them everywhere, saying:

"I have always doubted why Deshan and Dongshan, though both descended from Shitou, differed so greatly in their 'reaching down with the hand'—one in life and one in death. Now, having verified this through the two steles of Qiu and Fu, it is perfectly clear.

Only then do I know that my own discernment of the Dharma and testing of men was not mistaken. This is a case of investigating directly from the point of expedient manifestation; a single word settles doubts for a thousand ages. It is like when a person’s lineage is in error: by examining the ancestral genealogy, one can certainly distinguish the truth. If it were but a single drop...

Thus, true and false are clearly distinguished; these inexhaustible words may truly be called "drops of blood" that allow one to attain the truth. According to what is recorded in the *Sankē* (Three Engravings), the evidence is precise and the discussion is meticulous; the doubtful cases of a thousand years are resolved all at once like melting ice.
The Third Generation of Nanyue:
Chan Master Longtan Chongxin of Lizhou, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Tianwang Daowu.
He was a native of Zhugong; his family sold cakes. The Master was brilliant from his youth.
They were different. Initially, Tianwang (Heaven-King) Wuzhuo had received the prediction and transmission from Mazu. Later, while residing at Tianwang Temple, no one could fathom his character.
The Master lived in a lane near the temple and would daily send him ten cakes. Wuzhuo accepted them;

each time he finished eating, he would invariably set aside one cake, saying, "I bestow this upon you so that it may provide shade for your descendants. One day, the Master thought to himself: "The cakes were brought away by me."
"Why have you returned these to me? Is there perhaps another meaning behind this? He then went to see him and asked about it. Huineng said, "It was you who brought them here;
returning them to you—what fault is there in that? Upon hearing this, the Master understood the fundamental principle somewhat and consequently entered the monastic life under him.
Huineng said, "In the past you revered blessings and goodness; now you believe my words. You may be named Chongxin (Devoted Faith). Thereafter, he served diligently at his side. One day...
A monk asked, "Since I arrived here, I have not received instruction on the essential point of the mind.

Baizhang Wu said, "From the moment you arrived, I have never failed to point out the essential point of your mind. The monk asked, "Where did you point it out? Wu said, "When you brought me tea, I accepted it for you;
when you brought me food, I received it for you; when you bowed in greeting, I lowered my head. Where else would I point it out?"
Baizhang did not point out the essential heart-mind. Master Wuzu lowered his head for a long time. Baizhang said, "If you see, see directly; if you deliberate, you are already mistaken.
At that moment, Baizhang attained realization. He asked again, "How should one maintain this? Wuzu said, "Roam freely according to your nature; be expansive and relaxed in accordance with conditions.
Simply exhaust the ordinary mind; there is no separate 'sage's understanding'. Later, Baizhang went to Longtan in Liyang to reside.

[He was] the Dharma heir of Chan Master Longtan Xian of the fourth generation under Nanyue.
Chan Master Xuanjian of Deshan in Dingzhou was the son of the Zhou family of Jianzhou. He left home at the age of seven and received full ordination according to his years.

He studied the Vinaya-piṭaka with great diligence and thoroughly mastered the essential meanings of the various sūtras on the nature and characteristics of phenomena. He once lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At that time, he was called Zhou Jingang. He once said to his fellow students, "A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean suffers no diminution;
a tiny speck is cast against a sharp blade, yet the edge remains unmoved. Whether one is a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), only I know this.

Later, hearing that the Zen seats in the South were flourishing, the Master’s spirit was unsettled, and he remarked, "For those who have left the household life, even if they study the Buddha’s deportment for a thousand kalpas and [the Dharma for] ten thousand kalpas..."

"By studying the minute details of Buddhist practice, one cannot attain Buddhahood. This 'son of Māra' from the south dares to say that one directly points to the human mind and sees one's nature to attain Buddhahood.
I shall tear open his den and exterminate his kind, thereby repaying the Buddha’s grace.
He then took up his *Qinglong shuchao* (Blue Dragon Commentary) and left Sichuan for Liyang. On the road, he saw an old woman selling cakes and stopped to rest his shoulder while buying some.

[The Master] was about to eat some refreshments. The old woman pointed to his carrying pole and asked, "What kind of text is this? The Master replied, "The *Commentary on the Blue Dragon* (*Qinglong shuchao*).

The woman asked, "Which sutra do you lecture upon? The Master said, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The woman said, "I have a question for you. If you can answer it, I will give you these refreshments;
if you cannot answer it, you had better go elsewhere. She continued, "The *Vajracchedikā* says: 'The past mind is unattainable...'"
"It is attained. The present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. I do not know which mind the Elder is pointing to. The Master remained silent.
He then went to Longtan and, upon reaching the Dharma Hall, said: "I have long heard of Longtan; now that I have arrived..."
The pond was no longer visible, nor did the dragon appear. The Pond Master extended his body and said, "You have personally arrived at the Dragon Pond.

The Master was speechless and subsequently took up residence there. One evening, while standing in attendance, the Pond Master said, "It is deep in the night; why do you not go out? The Master replied with a respectful farewell and departed.
He then returned and said, "It is dark outside. The Pond Master lit a paper candle and passed it to him. As the Master reached out to receive it, the Pond Master [snuffed it out].
[The candle] was blown out. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself. Longtan asked, "What have you seen?
The Master replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world.

On the following day, Longtan ascended the seat and said to the assembly, "In that group there is a fellow whose teeth are like a forest of swords and whose mouth is like a basin of blood; with a single blow of my staff..."
Without looking back, he said, "In time, I shall stand upon the peak of a solitary mountain and propagate my Way.

The Master took the commentaries and sub-commentaries, piled them before the Dharma Hall, and holding up a torch, said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the vast void;
to exhaust all worldly pivotal mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss. He then burned them. Thereupon, he paid his respects and took his leave, traveling directly to Mt. Mui.

Shanshan took his staff and ascended the Dharma Hall by way of the double staircase. Walking from west to east and from east to west, he looked toward the abbot’s quarters and asked, "Is there anyone?
Is there anyone? As Shanshan sat there, he did not look up at all. The Master said, "No, no," and then departed. Upon reaching the entrance of the gate, he turned back.
He said, "Even so, one must not act with such haste. He then prepared his formal robes and entered again for an audience.

As soon as he stepped across the threshold, he held up his sitting cloth (zuoju) and said, "Venerable Master! While Shanshan was about to take the whisk, the Master let out a shout; the guest then shook out his sleeves and departed.
That evening, Guishan asked the Head Seat, "Was the newcomer here today? The Head Seat replied, "At that moment, he turned his back on me."

In the Dharma Hall, he put on his straw sandals and went out. The Master said, "This man will hereafter settle a thatched hut atop a solitary peak and go about reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs.
The Master resided at Liyang for thirty years.

During the reign of Emperor Wuzong of the Tang dynasty, when the Buddhist teachings were suppressed, he took refuge in a stone chamber on Mount Dubu. At the beginning of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong, [the Prefect of] Wuling...
The Magistrate Xue Tingwang restored the hermitage on Mount Chongde, renaming it Gudé Chan Monastery.

Intending to seek out a wise master to serve as abbot, he heard of the Master’s virtuous conduct and repeatedly invited him to descend from the mountain. However, the Master declined each time. Thereupon, Tingwang devised a ruse, dispatching an official to falsely accuse him of violating laws regarding tea and salt, thereby taking the Master into the prefectural seat.
Upon meeting him, he paid his respects and earnestly requested that the Master reside there, whereupon the Master extensively propagated the Dharma.

The Master’s Teaching Style: Ascending the Hall. "If you have no concerns regarding yourself, do not seek falsely; even if you were to obtain something through false seeking, it would not be true attainment.
You need only be unconcerned with the mind and have no mind toward phenomena; then you will be spirit-like within emptiness and wondrous within voidness."
If you speak of the beginning and end of this [nature] even to the extent of a hair-tip, you are entirely deceiving yourself.

Why? A single thought tied to a hair’s breadth is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting stir of emotion results in shackles for ten thousand kalpas. Holy names and common titles are all but empty sounds;
extraordinary features and inferior forms are all but illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not be burdened? And when you grow weary of them, yet again—

The Master laughed heartily. Later, the monk went to Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Yantou. Xuefeng said:

A monk asked, "When two dragons contend for the pearl, who is the one that obtains it? The Master said, "Both are wrong. A monk asked Xuefeng, "It is said that when a Śrāvaka realizes their nature, it is like seeing the moon at night;
when a Bodhisattva realizes their nature, it is like seeing the sun by day. I wonder, how does the Master realize your nature?"
"How is it? Feng struck the staff three times. Later, the monk raised the previous dialogue and asked the Master.
The Master gave him three blows and asked, "How is it that you are the Lord of the Three Realms? The Master said, "Do you understand how to eat an iron staff?
One day Deshan said to the Master, "In my place, there are two monks who have been living in a mountain hermitage for a long time; go and see them."
"What do you say? The Master then took up an axe and saw two monks sitting inside the hermitage.
The Master raised the axe and said, "If you can speak, one stroke; if you cannot speak, one stroke. The two monks paid him no heed at all. The Master threw down the axe and said, "A master!
A master! Upon returning, he related this to Deshan. Deshan asked, "What did you say about them? The Master replied:
"It is not said that there is nothing at all under Dongshan’s gate; however, as for Deshan’s gate, you have not even dreamed of it.
A monk visited for an audience and drew a circle on the left side, another circle on the right side, and yet another circle in the center.
While he was about to complete [the pattern], the Master struck it with his hand once. The monk was speechless, and the Master then let out a shout.
A monk was about to step over the gate when the Master called him back and asked, "Did you come from Guanyin Temple in Hongzhou? The monk replied, "I did.
The Master said, "As for that circle on the left just now, what is it? The monk said, "It is the 'having words' (you-jù).
The Master said, "And the circle on the right? The monk said, "It is the 'no-words' (wu-jù). The Master said, "What about the circle in the center? The monk said—
“This is the phrase that is neither being nor non-being. The Master said, “But what about when I am like this? How would you respond?
He replied, “It is like drawing on water with a knife. The Master then struck him. Ruigan asked, “What is the Vairocana Teacher? The Master said, “Say something!”
Yan asked again. The Master said, "When you were seventeen or eighteen, you had not yet asked. What is it like when the bow snaps and the arrows are spent?
Yan said, "Go away. Yan asked, "What is the precise meaning within the crag? The Master said, "Thank you for pointing it out.
Yan said, "Please, Reverend, give me a direct answer. The Master said, "Take care. Yan asked, "When the three realms arise in competition, what then? The Master said, "Sit."
[The monk] put it on and asked, "I do not yet understand what you mean, Master. The Master said, "If Mount Lu were moved here, then I would tell you.
Question: "When arising and ceasing do not stop, how is it? The Master shouted and said, "Who is it that arises and ceases?
Question: "When one cannot turn within the wheel, how is it? The Master said, "Rough. Question: "When encountering a fierce tiger on the road, how is it? The Master said, "..."
Za asked, “What is the Way? The Master said, “Take your straw sandals and throw them into the lake.
A monk asked, “In a ten-thousand-fathom well, how can one reach the bottom? The Master said, “Hūṃ. When the monk asked again, the Master said, “It has already passed beneath your feet.
A monk asked, “How is it before the ancient sail is hoisted? The Master said, “The small fish swallows the large fish. Another monk asked as well.

Regarding a previous question, the Master said: "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass. Thereafter, whenever people asked about the Buddha, the Dharma, the Way, or Zen, the Master would simply make a sound of sighing.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "In the great comprehensive framework of the fundamental principles, one must certainly understand the critical phrases."
If one does not recognize the phrase, it is difficult to discuss and understand. What is this phrase? When there is no thought of anything at all, it is called the "correct phrase.
It is also called "dwelling on the summit," also called "attaining stability," also called "vivid clarity," also called "alert awareness," and also called "precise certainty."
It is also called "before the Buddha was born," it is also called "attaining the ground," and it is also called "at such a time.
By means of "at such a time," one shatters all that is right and wrong. As soon as it is "thus," it is no longer "thus"; it turns and rolls like a wheel.
If you cannot see through this, the moment you are pricked by another's words, you will stare blankly, like a sheep that cannot be killed. Thus spoke the ancients.

The Way is deep and obscure; it is not something one can simply like. One must be able to turn it before one attains it. As soon as you touch it, you must turn it. Just when it is so, it is no longer so.
Sentences are erased; non-sentences are also erased. Naturally it turns smoothly; naturally it is revealed nakedly before one’s eyes. It is full and snoring;
one does not understand, yet one does not cease to bite into it. Have you not heard it said: "To set aside things is supreme"? Do not pursue them.
Things are at the bottom. As soon as a subtle emotion flickers up, one has already fallen to the ground.

If one’s eyes are as red-hot as those of a pig or a dog that is gnawing on something, and someone asks, "What is Chan? you should tell him, "Shut your dung-hole! Only then will there be a modicum of life-breath.
Then you will know its depth and shallowness; it is solid and firm. You must recognize this face of the old cat.
At such a time, do not intentionally provoke it, nor attempt to weigh it. Among those people, there are some who, upon encountering an object, do not know how to turn away;
they are pierced and left in a state of utter confusion. To strike down ten thousand such as these would bring no fault whatsoever. If...
This is his true nature. As soon as he is touched, he leaps up and bites; he is like a fire-urgent hedgehog.
Before being touched, he preens his own bristles—how pitiable! But as soon as someone touches him, he immediately becomes enraged and snaps at them, leaving you no place to draw near.
If you have not yet attained such a state of total freedom, it is called "practicing according to the words. If there is [such a thing],...
One must break through them all equally. At such a time, not a single thing remains. One can truly know that all the phrases learned from the beginning have been cramped within the chest;
what use are they? Have you not seen it said: "Avoiding views and avoiding phrases—do not let them enter from without, do not let them go out from within.
Cut off both ends, and naturally there is a state of radiant clarity, not acting as a companion to a single thing."
Right. This is precisely the Samādhi of Non-contention. Brothers, if you wish to understand it easily, simply grasp it clearly at the root.
When you are about to emerge but do not yet emerge, you must immediately turn back and bite down. Once this is severed, there is no need to seek out the distance of its coming or going;
simply let go and leave it as it naturally is, bare and naked. There is no need for conceptual construction or attachment, which leaves one in a state of dull obscurity. As soon as there is...
Once that which is valued becomes a habitual trap, the ancients called it the "disease of the garment clinging to the body," which is the most difficult to cure.

When I was traveling on pilgrimage in the past, I studied under one or two venerable masters who merely instructed me to maintain constant vigilance and sit until my buttocks grew calluses and my mouth ran with saliva.
At first, I was in a state of utter darkness within the belly of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
"You say you sit in meditation to maintain control; yet at such a time, desire still remains. Have you not heard it said:

'To be without dependence and without desire is to be a Capable Man' (Nengren)? An ancient said: 'If poison is placed in milk, it will kill even when it has been refined into clarified butter (ghṛta).
This is not something you can acquire through study; this is not something you can take with you or leave behind; it is not."

You who dwell within form, do not mistake the gatekeeper’s words at the entrance for a deception that will lead you astray. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, when it is all in a state of bare agitation, it will be of no benefit.
You must not engage in artificiality or fabricate wonders; simply know how to put on clothes, eat food, defecate, and urinate.

When sending things out according to the occasion, do not disrupt the order by falsely claiming to be a "Way-man" (Daozhe). Not even a single piece of clothing is dared to be taken out to dry, for fear that others might see it;
one fears losing the reputation of a Way-man and seeks only the praise of others by acting in such a manner. This is not the practice of the central path, brothers.
Do not, under any circumstances, trust that old block on the rope bed who sits there dripping wet, pretending he is good at deceiving people and creating his own hells for you.
Know for certain that the ancient style is truly excellent. Have you not heard it said: "Existence is non-existence;
non-existence is existence"? When things are presented in this manner, one immediately knows their depth or shallowness. This is the ancient standard.
Among them, there is a certain type of person who spits out their convictions with colorful rhetoric. What inscriptions or records do they have?
They know only to call it "Chan" or "the Way," and they know only to call it "a single phrase. How soft and fragile they are! Truly, they are like iron hammers without holes;
even if you gather ten thousand such as these together, what use would they be? If one possesses true backbone and strength, there is no need for such abundance elsewhere.

When traveling on pilgrimage, you must bring your eyes with you; do not be deceived by others. Have you not heard it said: "To produce understanding based on the Dharma is still to fall into the realm of Māra"?
When preaching the teachings, you must be able to draw each word forth from within your own breast to serve as a model for others.
Is there anyone like this nowadays? First of all, you must recognize those who stand at your left and right.
This is the point of emergence. Recognize that which goes; recognize that which stays.

This is the sentence of the two extremes, the sentence of left and right, and it is also called the sentence of affirmation and negation. As soon as it arises, one bites through it; naturally, there is no more concern.
Brothers, seeing such talk as this, do you understand? Do not spend your whole days in a state of clamor and confusion; there will be no end to it.
If you wish to understand easily, simply know that before sounds and forms, you are not deluded by the myriad objects.
Then, naturally, you are bare and naked; naturally, you are without affairs. When sent before sounds and forms, you are vast and open, like a single mass of flames.
"It is as if touching it causes one to burn immediately. What else is there? Have you not heard it said: 'It is not that dust does not invade; it is simply that there is no self-mind'?
During a time of heat, [the Master] cautioned the assembly, saying: "When this old man departs, I shall go with a great roar.
Later, when bandits arose in the Central Plains and everyone fled their lands, the Master remained seated calmly and composedly. One day...
The bandits arrived in great numbers and, rebuking him for failing to provide provisions, proceeded to stab him with blades. The Master’s countenance remained composed;
he let out one great cry and passed away, the sound heard for several tens of *li*. This was the eighth day of the fourth month in the Dingwei year of the Guangqi era of the Tang Emperor Xizong.

His disciples later cremated his remains and obtained forty-nine *śarīra* relics. The assembly erected a stupa for them, and an imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of "Qing" (Pure).
Chan Master Yan’s stupa was named “Transcending the World.
Chan Master Yicun of Xuefeng in Fuzhou was the son of the Zeng family of Nanan County, Quanzhou. His family had served the Buddha for generations.

From birth, he loathed the consumption of pungent roots and meat. Even while still in his swaddling clothes, whenever he heard the sound of bells and Buddhist chants, or saw banners, flowers, or sacred images, he would invariably...
He was moved to change his countenance at this. At the age of twelve, he accompanied his father to visit Yujian Temple in Putian, where he met Vinaya Master Qingxuan;
he immediately prostrated himself and said, "This is my teacher. He subsequently remained there to serve him. At seventeen, he shaved his head and went to pay his respects to Changzhao of Fuyong.

He looked upon him with favor and regarded him as a vessel of great potential. Later, he went to Baocha Temple in Youzhou to receive the full precepts. After spending a long time in various Chan assemblies, his karmic affinity was established with Deshan.
During the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, he returned to Min Province, where he resided at Xuefeng and founded a monastery;

his disciples gathered there in great numbers. Emperor Yizong bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Zhenjue and granted him a purple *kāṣāya*. Initially, together with Yantou, he traveled to Aoshan in Lishu.
Zhizhuo Xue tou was constantly dozing off every day, while the Master (Dongshan) sat in meditation continuously.
One day, he called out, "Elder brother, elder brother, please get up. Tou asked, "For what purpose? The Master said, "This life will not yield its secrets to us.
We have been traveling together with this fellow Wensui, and everywhere we go, we are burdened by him. Today we have arrived here, and yet you simply keep on sleeping."
Deshan shouted, "You glutton! Go to sleep! Sitting on your bed every day, you are just like a local deity in a village of seven hamlets.
In days to come, you will go about bewitching the men and women of people's homes. The Master patted his own chest and said, "I am not yet settled here;
I do not dare to deceive myself. Deshan said, "I took you for someone who would one day settle upon the peak of a solitary mountain."
Caotang was spreading the Great Teaching, yet he still spoke in this manner. The Master said, "I am truly not yet at ease.
Caotang said, "If you are indeed as you say, then explain your realization point by point; I shall provide testimony for each of them."
"I will not let you dig it up in an improper place. The Master said, "When I first arrived at Yanguan, I saw him ascend the hall and cite the meaning of form and emptiness;
I attained a point of entry there. Baizhang said, "From now until thirty years hence, you must strictly avoid mentioning this.
Furthermore, he saw Dongshan’s verse on crossing the water: "Strictly avoid seeking from others; such a path is far removed from me. He is precisely I right now; I..."
"Now that is not it," Tou said. "If you act like this, you have not even reached the point of saving yourself.
The Master then said, "Later I asked Deshan, 'In the matter of the ancestral vehicle, does a student still have a share? Deshan struck me with a staff and said, 'Say something!
At that time, it was as if the bottom of my bucket had fallen out. Tou shouted, "Have you not heard it said?"
"What enters through the gate is not the family treasure. The Master asked, "How will it be after this?
Tou said, "If you wish to propagate the Great Teaching hereafter, let each and every thing flow forth from your own breast and bring it forward;
let it cover heaven and earth for me! At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. He immediately prostrated himself, then rose and called out repeatedly, "Brother Master!"
"Today at last the Tortoise Mountain has attained the Way.

When the Master was serving as the rice-preparer at Dongshan, while he was washing the rice, Dongshan asked, "Are you washing away the sand to keep the rice, or washing away the rice to keep the sand? The Master replied, "Sand and rice are removed all at once.
Dongshan asked, "What will the assembly eat then? The Master thereupon turned the rice basin upside down. Dongshan said, "By your karmic conditions, you belong with Deshan."
One day Dongshan asked the Master, "What have you been doing? The Master said, "I have been making a trough. Dongshan said, "How many blows of the axe did it take to complete it?
The Master said, "It was completed with a single blow of the axe. Dongshan said, "That is still a matter of this side. What about the matter of that side?
The Master said, "It is such that there is no place to apply the hand. Dongshan said, "That is still a matter of this side. What about the matter of that side?"
"How so? The Master ceased speaking. (Fenyang [Yixun] spoke on his behalf, saying: "I am already exhausted. The Master took his leave of Dongshan.
Dongshan asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "I am going back to the Ridge. Dongshan asked, "By which path did you come out originally?
The Master said, "I came out by the Feiyuan Ridge. Dongshan asked, "By which path will you go now? The Master said, "I shall go by the Feiyuan Ridge. Dongshan—
The Master said, "There is one person who does not go by way of Feiyuan Ridge; do you recognize him? The Master said, "I do not recognize him.
Shishan said, "Why do you not recognize him? The Master said, "He has no face. Shishan said, "Since you do not recognize him, how can you know he has no face?
The Master was speechless. Later, after he had taken up residence, a monk asked, "When you saw Deshan, what did you obtain?"
"Rest," he said. The Master replied, "I go empty-handed and return empty-handed. A monk asked, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?
The Master said, "The sound of thunder shakes the earth, yet it is not heard within the room. He added, "For what purpose do you, Venerable Sir, travel on pilgrimage?
A monk asked, "My eyes are originally upright; when they become crooked because of a teacher, what then? The Master said, "Meeting Bodhidharma while lost."

[The student] said, "Where is my eye? The Master said, "Obtaining [the Dharma] does not come from a teacher. [The student] asked, "Having shaved one's head and donned the dyed robes, one receives the Buddha’s protection;
why is it not permitted to recognize the Buddha? The Master said, "A good thing is not as good as having none at all. The Master asked the Dharma Master:
These two characters are entirely the topical outline (*ke-wen*). What, then, is the root text? The Master had no reply.
(Wuyun [Dongyu] supplemented this by saying: "Furthermore, divide it into three sections. Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "Why speak in your sleep? Question:
"What is the matter of direct encounter? The Master said: "A thousand miles is not yet far. Question: "What is the mark of a great man? The Master said: "Behold."
[The monk] looked up expectantly. Question: "What was the subject of the dialogue between Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti?
The Master said: "The meaning has fallen. Question: "When one is silent and without dependence, what then? The Master said: "This is still an illness. Question:

"After turning away from that, what then? The Master said: "The boatman goes down to Yangzhou. Question: "I have heard an ancient saying. The Master immediately assumed a reclining posture. After a long while, he rose.
The Master said, "What are you asking? The monk repeated his question. The Master said, "A fellow who lives in vain and dies in vain.

[The monk] asked, "When the tip of the arrow is exposed, what then? The Master said, "A master hand does not hit the mark. [The monk] asked, "When the eye is exhausted and there is no target, what then?
The Master said, "It is nonetheless a fine display of skill as it happens. [The monk] asked, "An ancient said: 'When meeting a man who has attained the Way on the road, do not use words.'"
[The Master] remained silent. [The monk] asked, "I do not understand what he was facing. The Master said, "Go drink tea. He asked a monk, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From Shenguang (Divine Light). The Master said, "By day it is called sunlight; by night it is called firelight.
What is this 'Divine Light'? The monk had no reply. The Master provided the answer on his behalf: "Sunlight, firelight. The kitchen supervisor Xi asked, "The ancients said..."
[The Master] said, "Only when one knows the matter that lies beyond the Buddha does one have a share in discourse.
What is this discourse? The Master seized him and said, "Speak! Speak! Xiqi had no reply. The Master then kicked him over, and Xiqi broke into a sweat at that very moment.

He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "I have recently left the region of Zhejiang. The Master said, "By boat or by land? The monk replied, "I have traveled neither path. The Master said, "..."
"How did you manage to get here? he asked. "What obstacle was there? The Master then struck him. After ten years had passed, the monk returned.
The Master asked again, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Hunan. The Master said, "How far apart are Hunan and this place? He replied, "They are not separated.
The Master held up his whisk and said, "Are they not separated by this? He replied, "If they were separated, how could I have arrived?"
At this point, the Master again struck him and drove him out. The monk refused to leave. Later, after he had settled in his own residence, whenever he saw anyone, he would revile Xuefeng.

One day, a fellow practitioner heard of this and went specifically to visit him to inquire about the reason. The monk recounted the two previous incidents in detail, explaining them thoroughly. The visitor then wept with grief.
He would often burn incense in the middle of the night, facing toward Xuefeng and prostrating himself in worship. Questioning the Ancients.
A person asked, "When one meets face-to-face with a human being, what then? The Master said, "Yes. The monk asked, "What is it to meet face-to-face? The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven!
The Master addressed the assembly, saying, "How many years old is this water buffalo? No one in the assembly could answer.
The Master provided the answer on their behalf, saying, "It is seventy-nine. A monk asked, "Why does the Master act as a water buffalo?"
The ox left. The Master said, "What offense has it committed? He asked a monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to pay my respects to the Abbot of Jingshan.
The Master said, "If Jingshan asks you how the Buddha-dharma stands here, how will you respond?
The monk said, "I will speak when he asks. The Master then struck him. Later, he raised this case and asked Jingqing, "Where does this monk’s fault lie?"
"Where? Qing said. "You have asked until Jingshan was utterly exhausted. The Master said, "Jingshan is in Zhejiang; why did you ask until he was exhausted?
Qing said, "Have you not heard it said that when asked about the distant, one answers with the near? The Master said, "Just so, just so.
One day, he said to Changqing, "I saw how Guishan questioned Yangshan: 'Where do all the sages of the past turn toward?'"
“Where has he gone? He replied, “Sometimes in the heavens, sometimes among humans. You say, “What was Yangshan’s intention?
Qing said, “If one asks about the place where the sages appear and disappear, it would be improper to speak in such a way. The Master said, “You flatly refuse to admit it.
If someone were to ask you suddenly, what would you say? Qing said, “I would simply say, ‘Wrong. The Master said, “That is you.”
"Quite so," he said. "How is this different from being wrong? He questioned a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Jiangxi.
The Master asked, "How far is it from here? The monk said, "Not far. The Master held up his whisk and asked, "Is it still separated by this?"
[The Master] said, "If you separate yourself from this, you are far away. The Master then struck him. A student asked, "I am a newcomer to the monastic community;
I beg the Master to point out a way of entry. The Master said, "I would rather let my own body shatter into fine dust than ever dare to blind the eyes of a single monk.
A student asked, "I do not ask about what happens after the forty-nine years; [what about] before the forty-nine years?"
"What do you think? The Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk. The monk took his leave and went to visit Lingyun.
He asked, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? Lingyun held up his whisk. [The monk asked,] "And how was it after he appeared in the world? Lingyun likewise held up his whisk.
The monk returned. The Master said, "Did you return too soon? The monk replied, "I went there to inquire about the Buddha-dharma;

as it did not accord with my understanding, I returned. The Master asked, "What was the matter you asked about? The monk recounted his previous conversation. The Master said, "Ask me, and I will tell you for you.
The monk then asked, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? The Master raised his whisk and said, "After he appeared in the world—"

"How is it? The Master dropped his whisk. The monk bowed. The Master then struck him. (Later, the monk raised this case to ask Xuansha. Xuansha said, "Do you wish to understand? I will give you a parable. Suppose a man sells a plot of land;

though the east, west, south, and north have all been settled by contract, the tree in the center still belongs to me. Chongshou Chou said, "Does he strike him because of his point of understanding, or is there another principle?

The Master cited the Sixth Patriarch’s words: "It is not the wind moving, nor the banner moving; it is the mind of the noble one that moves," and then said: (Note: The text provided ends with "乃曰" [and then said], indicating the Master was about to speak further, but the excerpt concludes there.)
"The great and small patriarchs have a dragon's head but a snake's tail; they deserve twenty blows of the staff.
At that time, Upāsaka Fu of Taiyuan was standing in attendance and unconsciously gnashed his teeth. The Master said, "I just said such things; I too deserve twenty blows of the staff.
When the Master was traveling on pilgrimage, he visited Wushi Guan. As soon as he knocked on the door, Wushi asked, "Who is it? The Master replied, "A phoenix."
The boy asked, "What is it that you have come for? The Master said, "I have come to devour Old Guan. Baizhang then opened the door, grabbed him, and said, "Speak!
Speak! The Master hesitated; Baizhang pushed him away and closed the door.

Later, after the Master had established his own monastery, he addressed the assembly, saying, "If I had been able to enter Old Guan’s gate at that time, where would you lot—this bunch of wine-dregs eaters—have gone to grope for the truth?"
The Master asked Huiquan, "How is it that you have attained entry? Quan said, "I have already discussed this with the Abbot.
The Master said, "Where did you discuss it? Quan said, "Where have you been coming from? The Master said, "And how is it that you have attained entry?
Quan had no reply, so the Master struck him. Quantan asked, "In the level fields and shallow grass, the deer gather in herds."
"How can one shoot and hit the leader among the deer? The Master called out, "Quanshan Tan! Tan responded. The Master said, "Go drink tea.
He then questioned a monk: "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Mount Gui. The Master asked, "What words or phrases did he say at Mount Gui?
The monk said, "I once asked him, 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? and Mount Gui simply sat there. The Master said, "Do you approve of him?"
[The monk] said, "I do not agree with him. The Master said, "Miaoyan was an ancient Buddha; you should go quickly and repent.
(Xuansha said, "That old fellow on the mountain has missed the mark regarding Miaoyan. The King of Min asked, "What would you say if I wished to build a Buddhist hall? The Master said:
"Great King, why not simply take one empty royal palace? The King said, "I request the Master's model. The Master extended both hands. (Yunmen said: "One move, forty-nine.
A student asked, "At the point where the Way cannot be spoken, I request the Master to speak it. The Master said, "I cherish people for the sake of the Dharma.
The Master raised his whisk to show it to a monk; the monk then departed. (Changqing later recounted this to the Grand Tutor Wang Yanbin.)

He then said, "This monk deserves to be called out and given another blow of the staff. The King asked, "What kind of mental state is this, Master? He replied, "How could I let him go? The Master then asked Changqing, "An ancient said:"
"Three before, three after; three times three. [The Master] asked, "What do you think? Qing then went out. He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Lantian.
The Master said, "Why did you not enter the grass? He ascended the hall and said, "On South Mountain there is a 'tortoise-nose' snake.
You all must watch it very carefully! Changqing came forward and said, "In the hall today, there are many people [who can see it]."
[The monk] was about to lose his life when Yunmen threw his staff before the Master and made a gesture of fear.
A monk reported this to Xuansha, who said, "Only Brother Leng could have done it. Nevertheless, I would not do it that way.
The monk asked, "How would you do it, Master? Xuansha replied, "Why use the Southern Mountain? One day, two monks arrived; the Master [acted as follows].
The Master pushed open the gate of the hermitage, stepped out, and asked, "What is this? The monk also said, "What is this? The Master lowered his head and returned to the hermitage.
As the monk was taking his leave, the Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "To Hunan. The Master said, "I have a fellow practitioner living at Yantou;
give him this letter for me. The letter read: "This letter is addressed to my elder brother. I, [Name], since the time I was a young man..."
After Shansheng attained enlightenment, he has remained without hunger until the present day. A letter was sent by a fellow practitioner.
When a monk arrived, Yantou asked him, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "I have come from Xuefeng; I have a letter for the Master. Yantou received it and then questioned the monk.
"What other words did he say? The monk then recounted the previous conversation. The Head asked, "What did he say?
[The monk replied,] "He remained silent and bowed his head as he returned to his hut. The Head said, "Alas! In the beginning, I regretted not having spoken the 'final word' to him.
Had I spoken it to him, no one in the world could have done anything with Old Xue. At the end of the summer retreat, the monk requested further instruction on this previous matter. The Head said:
