After he had left, [the monk] asked, "What is it like after departing? The Master said, "Reaching for the sky and groping on the ground.

[The monk] asked, "What is the point where the student is intimate? The Master said, "A compassionate mother cradling her infant. [The monk] asked, "What is the point where the student turns around? The Master said, "At every street corner and alleyway.
[The monk] asked, "What is the point where the student exerts effort? The Master said, "A thousand people scolding while the carrying pole rocks at both ends."
Question: "The ancient melodies have no fixed tones or rhythms; how can they be brought into harmony? The Master said: "Three times nine is twenty-seven;
at the fence-top, the double-reed pipe is blown. [The questioner] said: "The notes gong, shang, jue, and zhi are not what is wondrous; the stone man claps his hands and laughs heartily.
The Master said: "Only those on the same path understand."

Chan Master Fuyuan Yuanjian of Mount Fu in Shuzhou was a successor of Chan Master Xuecheng of Ye County. A native of the Wang family in Zhengzhou, he traveled to Bingzhou at the age of nineteen and entered the monastic order under Master Song of Sanjiao.
While still a śrāmaṇera, he saw a monk enter the room and ask about the courtyard cypress of Zhaozhou.

Regarding the circumstances: Song interrogated the monk, and as the Master stood by his side, he attained realization. After receiving full ordination, he visited Fenyang and Ye County, both of whom granted him their seal of approval.
Once, while traveling through Shu with Daguan Ying, Xue Datou, and several others—about seven or eight people in total—he nearly met with a violent disaster.
The Master liberated them through his wisdom. Because the assembly recognized that the Master was well-versed in administrative affairs, they titled him "Master Yuanlu" (Record-Keeping Master).
On the day he ascended the hall, a monk asked: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral style does he succeed? The Master replied: "An eighty-year-old old man rolls a brocade ball."
[The student] said: "If that is so, then one phrase transcends the lineage of the Patriarchs, and the trident-tipped weapons of the Three Ages shake the monastic forests.
The Master said: "Li Ling was originally a minister of the Han court. [The student] asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "The elder is like an elder brother;
the younger is like a younger brother. [The student] asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said: "A pile of bones rising from level ground."
Question: "Under the Gate of the Patriarchs, it stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; when the true command is exercised, the ten directions are cut off.
How will you, Reverend, indicate this? The Master said: "A cold cat does not catch mice. [The questioner] asked: "Is this not the very point of acting for others?"
The Master said, "A Persian does not tie a sash. [The monk] asked, "The New Year has already arrived; where has the Old Year gone?

The Master said, "There is nothing strange before one's eyes; there is no need to paste up a Zhong Kui. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "I thought there was nothing before one's eyes.
The monk drew a circle with his hand and said, "What can be done about this? The Master then struck him. The Master waited for Wang Zhi.
He established the discourse on the Way by drawing a single circle and saying: "First, one must not have a lone horse and a single spear; second, one must not return home wearing brocade.
The magpie shall not rejoice; the crow shall not suffer calamity. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The King was at a loss. The Master said, "I have seen through you.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Do not further discuss ancient tales; for now, rely solely on the matters before your eyes. I shall provide them to you all..."

The man [was] definitively distinguished. The monk then asked, "What is the matter of the present moment? The Master said, "The nostrils. [The monk] asked, "What is the matter that transcends [the present]? The Master said, "The eyes.
When Ou-yang Wen-chung Kung heard of the Master’s extraordinary brilliance, he visited his quarters;
however, he found nothing unusual about him. While the Master was sitting beside him as he played chess with a guest, Wen-chung suddenly called for the board to be cleared. He requested—

Using the game of Go as a means to expound the Dharma, the Master immediately ordered the drum to be beaten. Ascending the seat, he said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like two parties playing Go.
Why is this so? 'The opponent understands; when the opportunity arises, there is no yielding'—this is winning five points while conceding three."
Furthermore, one must first penetrate a single path before attaining it. There is a certain class of people who only know how to "make a living by closing the door";

they do not understand how to "seize the corner and charge through the pass. Their stubborn knots are level with the tiger’s mouth; once their narrow boundaries are shattered, their efforts at maneuvering are in vain.
Thus it is said: "The fat sides are easy to find, but the lean belly is hard to seek. If one thinks before acting, one often loses the connection; if the mind is coarse, one is constantly at a loss.
*Zhuang*: "Do not boast of being a national master, nor speak in vain of immortals. As for winning games and counting the pieces—that is not what I ask.
Tell me, before black and white have been distinguished, where does that first move fall? After a long silence, he said: "From of old there have been nineteen paths;
how many people have been deluded or awakened? Wen Zhong sighed with admiration and calmly said to his colleagues: "At first I suspected that the language of Chan was empty."

"Ah! Today, seeing this old fellow’s karmic conditions, what he has attained and created could never have been possible—how could such a wondrous principle exist unless it were realized within the ground of the mind?
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sovereign attains the One and brings order to the realm.
When the world's monks attain the One, calamity descends upon them. He struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they establish gates of transformation that do not depart from the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Their eye of wisdom is like the three eyes of Maheśvara: one eye is such that water cannot leak through; it is difficult for either the ordained or the laity to discern.

One eye is such that the great earth is fully opened; the ten directions are unobstructed. One eye is such that with a single glance, high and low, all myriad things gaze together. Although this is so,"
A monk of the fundamental division, meeting you on a crossroads, must possess the extraordinary, heaven-penetrating true eye before he can succeed.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know what exists; the cat and the white ox, however, do know. Now tell me, what is it that the cat and the white ox know?
Do you wish to understand? Deep autumn rain fills the curtains of a thousand homes; the setting sun rests upon the towers and pavilions.
Dichong retired to Huishengyan during his later years. There he expounded the profound meanings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and composed the Nine Baskets (*jiudai*), which are:

the Basket of the Buddha’s True Dharma Eye; the Basket of the Buddha’s Dharma Treasury; the Basket of the Pervasion of Principle; the Basket of the Pervasion of Phenomena; and the Basket of the Vertical and Horizontal Interpenetration of Principle and Phenomena.
The "Bent and Curved Sash," the "Exquisite Petals and Sash," the "Golden Needle Double-Lock Sash," and the "Level Mind Always Substantial Sash.

Once the students had transmitted and recited these, the Master said: "If one were to rely on the Dharma-gate of Perfect Fulfillment, there are originally ten such sashes; yet here we have only these nine."
I have already explained these for you all. There is yet one more "band" (dai). Do you see it?
If you can see it—vividly and clearly—then please come forth and explain it before the assembly. If you can explain it clearly, I shall grant you the preceding nine bands as well.
"If your vision of the perfectly luminous Eye of the Way is not intimate and direct, your explanations will be inconsistent with the truth.

To rely solely on my words and take them as your own understanding is called slandering the Dharma. When he asked, "What do you all say when you reach this point? the assembly remained silent. The Master rebuked them and departed.
A monk asked Chan Master Fayao of Baoying Monastery in汝州 (Ruzhou): "When a single word accords with the Way, what then? The Master said: "Seven topsy-turvy, eight upside-down.
The monk said: "I, this student, prostrate myself. The Master said: "Told to stop, he refuses to stop; he must wait until the rain drenches his head. [Another monk] asked:
"As for the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas—why did the Buddha-dharma not manifest before him?"
"One cannot attain the Buddha-way. "Why cannot one attain the Buddha-way? The Master said: "Barefoot, riding an iron donkey, one goes straight to dwell in Hainan.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, I allow you for a moment to cease all study. This is precisely what it means to study the Buddha-dharma.
Have you not seen how Ānanda, though foremost in much-hearing, was nevertheless expelled by Kāśyapa and was not permitted to participate in the compilation [of the scriptures]?"

Upon gathering [these reflections], one finally realizes that cleverness, broad learning, memory, retention, and conceptualization are all outward pursuits that have no further connection with the numinous, awakened mind.
One cannot break through the shell of the five aggregates; when circumstances accord with one's desires, joy arises, and when they oppose them, anger arises.

Thus, one is shrouded by deep and heavy obscurations, entangling and binding oneself until there is no liberation. One wanders through birth and death, with the six sense faculties acting as a source of affliction for the multitude.
Pressed by suffering and lacking any autonomy, one is nonetheless dominated within it by a deluded mind. A true man of great character should seize the opportunity early on!
[He lets out a shout] and says: "Investigate! Ascending the hall, he said: "The gate of Bao Ying is perilous;
those who enter lose their entire bodies. What is the phrase for emerging? If you cannot speak it, thirty years from now—"
A monk asked Chan Master Huiguo of Dacheng Mountain in Tangzhou, "What is the meaning transmitted from of old?
The Master said, "The golden platter is turned out for all to see. The monk asked, "When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then?
The Master said, "To brush away the dust is already deviant; to see the Buddha is already an error. The monk said, "If it is not like this at all, then what? The Master said, "An error."
Question: "What is the Way? The Master said: "It is wide where it is wide; it is narrow where it is narrow.

Question: "What is one who is on the Way? The Master said: "He suffers where there is suffering; he rejoices where there is joy. Question: "How far apart are the Way and the one on the Way? The Master said:
"One hundred and eight thousand [miles]. Question: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said: "A clear sky and the sun rising."
The monk said, "The student does not understand. The Master said, "When it rains, mud grows.
Chan Master Dingyin, a successor of Chan Master Baqing of Kaisheng Monastery in Jingnan Prefecture, asked: "What is the realm of Kaisheng? The Master said, "Three."
Wulu led the way. A monk asked, "What is it like to be a person within the realm? The Master said, "Two tigers patrol the mountain.
A monk asked Zen Master Guangyun of Miaozhi Temple on Mount Tiantai, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
The Master said, "Yellow chrysanthemums by the eastern fence. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning? The Master said, "The Double Ninth Festival.
Chan Master Daguang Tan-ying of Jinshan in Runzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Cong of Guyin.
He was the son of the Qiu family of Hangzhou. At the outset, he first visited Dayang Xuan.

The Master asked, "Dongshan specifically established the categories of partiality and correctness, ruler and subject; what matter does he intend to clarify? Yang said, "The state of affairs before one's parents were born.
The Master asked, "How do you realize this? Yang said, "Midnight is perfectly bright; at dawn, nothing is revealed. The Master was left speechless.
He then went to visit Guyin and recounted the previous conversation. Guyin said, "Daiyang did not say it was wrong; it is simply that his mouth is too narrow.
He could not finish speaking even with his mouth full. I, the old monk, am not like this. The Master asked, "What is the state of affairs before one's parents were born?
Guyin replied, "A brick from the latrine. The Master asked, "What is that which is revealed neither at midnight nor at dawn? Guyin replied: [The text ends here.]

He said, "A sleeping cat beneath a peony flower. Master [Yunmen] was increasingly perplexed and startled. One day, during a communal work assignment (*yunqing*), Yinyuan asked, "Are you carrying firewood today?
The Master replied, "Yes. Yinyuan said, "When Yunmen asked a monk, 'The person carries the firewood; the firewood carries the person,' how do you understand this? The Master had no reply.
Yinyuan said, "This matter is like a person learning to write: one who can accurately replicate the strokes and characters is skilled; otherwise, they are not."
“Crude! It is simply that you have not yet been able to forget the Dharma. You must reach the point where the brush forgets the hand, and the hand forgets the mind;
only then will it be possible. The Master then attained a silent realization. After a long while, he said, “As Shitou said: ‘To grasp at phenomena is fundamentally delusion;

to accord with principle is likewise not awakening. Yinyou asked, “Do you consider this to be medicine or a disease? The Master replied, “It is the language of medicine. Yinyou rebuked him, saying, “You take a disease as...”
"To serve as medicine—how could it be otherwise? The Master said, "The matter is like a box finding its lid; the principle is like an arrow with a straight shaft and point.

How could there be anything more wondrous than this? Yet you still regard it as a defect; truly, you have not yet grasped the essential meaning. Yinyue said, "Even such 'wonder' is merely a designation for principle and phenomenon (*li-shi*).
The intent of the Patriarchs cannot be reached by intellectual consciousness; how much less can it be exhausted by phenomena and principles? Therefore, the world..."
The Master said, “In principle, it obstructs right view; in fact, it continues the cycle of birth and death. The teacher was as if awakened from a dream and asked, “How do you make use of this?
Yinyuan replied, “If speech does not leave the nest, how can one escape the entanglements?

The Master sighed and said, “As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into the realm of conceptual thought; these are all dead ends and are by no means the living path. After he took up residence there, he addressed the assembly:
As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into the realm of conceptual thought; it is entirely a gate of death, none of which are living paths.
Even if one were to break through and escape, one would still remain mired in samsara. Do not let your lifelong efforts go to waste, nor let this life pass in vain.
If you wish not to let your life be in vain—look! [The Master] picks up his staff and strikes once, saying: "You must not be deceived by this staff! Look, look!
"The staff pierces through the skulls of you all and leaps into your nostrils! [With this, he strikes once.
A monk asked, "What is the first character of the sutra text? The Master said, "The character 'yi' (以)."

[The monk] asked, "What connection is there? The Master said, "Eight characters. [The monk] said, "How deceptive this is! The Master said, "Because of slandering this sutra, one incurs such retribution. A question was asked: "Who is to carry the iron cangue weighing one hundred and twenty catties? The Master said, "The old monk. [The monk] said, "One reaps what one sows. The Master said, "Bitter! Bitter! A question was asked: "Does the Master ever recite the Buddha's name? The Master said, "I do. The monk asked, "Why do you not recite it now? The Master said, "If I were to recite it now, I would be like a dog barking at a shadow. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I did not yet know how to recite it. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I had no time to recite it. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, my teeth have fallen out. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, my voice was not yet clear. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, my mind was distracted. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, my ears are deaf. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my studies. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with my duties. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I have no one to rely on. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with worldly affairs. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the Dharma. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the ghosts and spirits. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my parents. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with my wife and children. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with my disciples. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my own body. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with my mind. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with my breath. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my thoughts. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with my perceptions. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with my consciousness. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my desires. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with my attachments. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with my delusions. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my anger. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with my pride. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with my envy. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my greed. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with my ignorance. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with my suffering. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my birth. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with my aging. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with my sickness. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with my death. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the cycle of rebirth. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the path of liberation. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with the mundane world. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the supramundane. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the Middle Way. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with the provisional teachings. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the definitive teachings. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the unconditioned. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with the conditioned. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the unconditioned. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the non-dual. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with the dualistic. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the non-dualistic. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the ultimate truth. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with the relative truth. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the absolute truth. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the harmony of the two truths. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with the emptiness of phenomena. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the emptiness of the self. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the emptiness of both. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with the non-emptiness of phenomena. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the non-emptiness of the self. The monk asked, "What about now that you are old? The Master said, "Now that I am old, I am too busy with the non-emptiness of both. The monk asked, "What about when you were young? The Master said, "When I was young, I was too busy with the existence of things. The monk asked, "What about when you grew up? The Master said, "When I grew up, I was too busy with the non-existence of things."
The Master said, "I have never practiced the recitation of the Buddha's name. A monk asked, "Why do you not recite the Buddha's name? The Master said, "I fear it would defile people's mouths.
One day, as the assembly gathered, the Head Seat came forward to prostrate. The Master said, "Ask well.

As the Head Seat bowed his head to pose his question, the Master said, "Today I will not answer questions," and immediately returned to his quarters. On another occasion, he ascended the hall and said, "This mountain monk’s gate and courtyard..."
Having parted ways, he has changed the tracks of all directions. For Mañjuśrī, he pulls out the wedge from the eye; for Samantabhadra, he bids him cease chewing the iron in his mouth.

He exhorts people to loosen the hands that clutch the serpent at the waist, and he cuts away for you the hitching stake for the donkey. If you stop to dwell on this and attempt to deliberate, he shouts:
"Squeeze! Squeeze! Investigate! Ascending the hall, he said: "In my life, this mountain monk has always been fond of wrestling, yet I simply have none [to match me]."
"Matching pairs! Today, let us first match pairs with the Head Seat. He rolled up his *kāṣāya* and descended from the seat, challenging the Head Seat to a wrestling match.
As soon as the Head Seat stepped out, the Master said, "Tumbling on level ground! and immediately returned to the Abbot’s quarters.

Ascending the hall for a discourse, he said, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are but servants; the entire Tripitaka is but mucus and spittle. After a long silence, he asked, "Now tell me, what of the three periods of time?"
"Whose servants are all the Buddhas? He then took his whisk and drew a line, saying, "The Buddhas of the three periods are on this side.
Then he said, "Tell me, whose spittle is the entire Great Canon of Teachings? The Master then spat once himself. [This was] ascending the hall.
The scale-weights float up from the bottom of the well; the rat, after many years, has transformed into an ox. Hui-kong saw this and clapped his hands in laughter.
"A three-legged monkey—how different it is from an ordinary ape! [He then] ascended the hall and said: "The five thousand scriptures and teachings are the constant discourse of all Buddhas;
the eighty thousand afflictions are the wondrous functioning of sentient beings. Yet even these are not yet the Diamond Eye. What, then, is the Diamond [Eye]?"
[The Master] looked at his eyes for a long while and said, "Blind. He ascended the hall.

When the assembly had gathered and settled, a monk just as he stepped forward to prostrate, the Master said, "If you wish to recognize Buddha-nature, you must observe the conditions of time and season. The monk then asked, "What are the conditions of time and season?
The Master immediately descended from his seat. A monk asked, "What is one who is heading toward the future? The Master said, "Returning from here to the green mountains."
"From within the mountain crags, white clouds do not emerge. The questioner asked, "What is it like for the person who has returned?

The Master said, "Since wandering the purple avenues, who would be willing to hide away among the green mountains? The questioner asked, "What is 'taking the person but not taking the environment'? The Master said, "Within the home, there is no longer news of a return;
on the distant road, there is only an empty monument longing for one's hometown. The questioner asked, "What is 'taking the environment but not [taking] the person'?"

[The monk] asked, "What is 'seizing both the person and the environment'? The Master said, "The vast ocean is made to dry up to its very bottom; the green mountains are ground down until they become dust.

[The monk] asked, "What is 'seizing neither the person nor the environment'? The Master said, "Heaven and earth are yet empty of the sun and moon of Qin; the mountains and rivers do not see the sovereign and ministers of Han.

The Master said, "The feet are thin, but the straw sandals are wide. When the Master was over eighty years old, he passed away during the height of summer while sitting upright.
Seven days [passed]. His hands and feet were supple and smooth. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the east of the monastery.
A monk asked Chan Master Huineng of Huili in Linjiang Commandery: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind does he succeed? The Master said:
"The iron ox does not eat the grass by the fence; it climbs straight up to the summit of Mount Sumeru to sleep. [The monk] said: "In that case..."
"Thus, in the past at Ruyang you personally received the imperial decree; today at Linjiang you widely proclaim it. The Master said, "Having finished your prostrations, withdraw.
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Large head, small tail. The monk said, "I do not yet understand the original words; I beg the Master to point them out again.
The Master said, "The eyebrows are three feet two inches long. The monk said, "If that is so, then everyone wears him upon their heads. The Master said, "Those who see him..."
Everyone knit their brows. The Master let out a long sigh. A monk clapped his hands once and then prostrated. The Master said, "Feel free to leap about as you please."
A monk asked Chan Master Guanghui Dexuan of Ruizhou: "The patriarchs have transmitted one to another, passing down the seal of the patriarchs.
Whose Dharma heir are you, Master? The Master said: "When the younger brother blows the *xun* flute, the elder brother blows the *chi* flute.
The monk said: "In that case, you are the son of Guanghui and the direct grandson of Shoushan. The Master said: "I am sitting inside the rafters; I will not strike you, O *dashi* (monk)."

The layman Yang Yi, Duke Wen, whose courtesy name was Dainian, was designated a "Divine Infant" (*shenyin*) in his youth. By the time he reached adulthood, he was renowned for his talent and fame, yet he was unaware of the existence of the Buddha.
One day, while visiting a colleague, he saw him reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Laughing, he criticized it; however, the other continued to read as if nothing had happened.
The Duke, harboring doubts, asked, "Does this perhaps surpass the teachings of Confucius and Mencus? Why such extreme devotion? Thereupon, he examined several leaves of the text.
He was bewildered and had only begun to have a slight degree of respect and faith. Later, he met with Lord Li Wei of the Hanlin Academy, who encouraged him to seek instruction.

When he subsequently left his post as Director of the Imperial Library to serve as the regional governor of Ruzhou, he went first to visit Guanghui. Upon being received by Guanghui, the Lord immediately asked: "A cloth drum is being beaten at the front of the hall;
who is the one who knows this sound? Guanghui replied: "The wind that comes is clearly discerned. The Lord said: "If that is so, then the Chan guest..."
Upon meeting, [Zhaozhou] merely snapped his fingers. Huì said, "A gentleman may enter. The Official responded, "Yes, yes. Huì said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated.
During their conversation at night, Huì asked, "Director of the Secretariat, with whom have you ever discussed the Dharma? The Official replied, "I once asked the Monastery Attendant Liang of Yunyan:
'When two great tigers bite each other, what then? Liang said, 'A single unified form. I—[the Official].
[The Master] said, "I simply watch over it. I do not know if speaking in such a way is permissible. Huì said, "It is not so here.
The Master said, "Please, Reverend, offer another turn of phrase. Huì made a gesture with his hand as if pulling a nose and said, "This beast!"
Suddenly, he leaped up and stood there; under the Master’s words, he was liberated and free from doubt. He spoke a verse: "An eight-legged millstone runs through the empty sky;
A golden-maned lion transforms into a dog. If you wish to hide your body within the Big Dipper, You must join your palms behind the Southern Dipper.
He further set forth the details of his lineage and secret realization, sending them to Li, the Imperial Poet (Li Bai), saying: "I, the sick man, have long since..."

I, a person of stubborn ignorance, have been graced by your favor and attention, and have had the privilege of hearing the tenets of the Southern School. For a long time, I have accompanied you on your travels throughout the Central Kingdom.

Whether in matters of movement or stillness, I have sought your counsel; in every turn of affairs, I have relied upon your inspiration. That I may achieve a profound realization within my heart and remain free from shame like one facing a blank wall—this is truly due to your guidance beneath your seat and at your side.
Moreover, the Great Master, the late Master An, constantly bestowed upon me inducements toward the Way, ever since we were together at Shuang... [text continues].

When Linmiexing departed for the West in his single sandal, his inner mind was vast and boundless, and he knew not where he would rest. For years he suffered from chronic illness, his spirit and thoughts wandering in a state of confusion.
When he finally found a brief interval of recovery, he once again sought to clarify the direction of his path. Furthermore, he received the visit of the Great Being Master Liang of Yunmen.
Liang’s fundamental purpose was identical to that of Master Dao’an; both returned from Mount Lu to Yunju.

They have all come from the lineage of Fayan. Last year, while serving as the acting governor of this prefecture, I happened to meet the Chan master Guanghui, who truly inherited the dharma from Nan’uan Nian.
Nian succeeded Fengxue; Fengxue succeeded the former Nan’uan; Nan’uan succeeded Xinghua;
Xinghua succeeded Linji; Linji succeeded Huangbo; Huangbo succeeded Baizhang; and Baizhang succeeded Mazu.
The Patriarch [Huiming]. The Patriarch succeeded Master Ruang (Rang). Ruang was the primary legitimate heir of Caoxi.

With his monastic duties being few, during the leisure of his post-meal time, he would sometimes sit waiting for [the Patriarch] to arrive, or at other times order his carriage to follow him. He requested instruction without fixed method, and his obscurities and stagnations were instantly resolved.
After half a year, he became vast and free from doubt; it was as if having forgotten something and suddenly remembering it, or as if falling asleep and suddenly waking up.
The burden that had long constrained his chest fell away with a sudden crash, and matters that had remained unclarified for kalpas appeared before him in their full clarity.

Thus, his discernment was thoroughly penetrating and his engagement with the world was unhindered. Reflecting further on the former masters, he saw that they mostly engaged in extensive inquiry, such as Xuefeng.
Jiushang went to Dongshan; San arrived at Touzi and subsequently succeeded Deshan. Linji received the Dharma from Dayu, yet ultimately inherited Huangbo’s lineage.
Yunyan received much instruction and guidance from Daowu, and thus became a son of Yaoshan.
Danxia personally received the seal of approval from Mazu, yet in the end became a descendant of Shitou. In antiquity, there were many such cases, and in principle, they are not to be questioned.
The present opportunity for this sick man to succeed to [the lineage] truly rests with Guanghui (Guanghui), yet the inspiration to urge him forward has personally emerged from Aofeng (Aofeng).

Joy, joy! The Master asked Guanghui: "I have heard the Venerable’s words that all sinful karma arises from wealth and treasures, and you advise people to distance themselves from profit and gain; how much more so for the multitude of Jambudvīpa?"
[The Master] said, "Life depends on wealth; states and nations gather people through wealth. Within the teachings, there are two kinds of giving: that of material wealth and that of the Dharma.
How can you urge people to distance themselves from wealth? Hui said, "The iron cage atop the flagpole. The Official said, "The horses of Haitan are as large as donkeys.
Hui said, "A chicken of Chu is not a phoenix of Mount Dan. The Official said, "Two thousand years have passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa."
Master Qiu felt somewhat ashamed. The Duke set forth one hundred questions and requested that Master Guanghui provide answers.

As Guanghui answered each one in turn, the Duke asked Officer Li, "What did Śākyamuni achieve after six years of ascetic practice? The officer replied, "One knows the weight of the firewood only when the shoulder is strained.
Later, while suffering from a slight illness, the Duke asked Grand Master Huan, "I have suddenly fallen ill today. Grand Master," he said.
The Master asked, "How can your compassion provide medical treatment? Huian replied, "A bowl of clove decoction. The Master immediately made a gesture of vomiting.
Huian said, "Affection and love result in affliction. While Huian was preparing the medicine, the Master cried out, "Thief!

Huian placed the medicine before him and stood to one side with his hands folded. The Master stared at him with wide eyes and said, "You young monk from the forest retreats! Thereupon, Huian shook his sleeves and departed.
[He] went out. On another day, he asked, "My four great elements are about to disperse; Great Master, how will you save me? Huán then struck his chest three times.
The official said, "Fortunately, I have encountered a master craftsman. Huán said, "How many years have you studied the Buddha-dharma? The vulgar air has still not been removed.
The official said, "Calamities do not come alone. Huán made a sighing sound. The official wrote a verse and left it for Li Dushi.

The Commandant said, "The arising of foam and the extinguishing of foam—these two dharmas are fundamentally equal. If you wish to know the place of true return, it is east of Zhaozhou’s East Courtyard.
When the Commandant saw this, he remarked, "Selling paper money in the Temple of Mount Tai. By the time the Commandant arrived, the Master had already passed away.

Shanshi was a summer retreat attendant for Ciming. Shanshi was a high-ranking disciple of Ciming; Daowu Zhen and Qiye Hui both submitted to his brilliance.

The Master (Ciming) was personally confident that since he had met Ciming, there was no one in the world who could satisfy him. When he spoke with Shanshi, however, he realized the latter had not yet reached full penetration and laughed at him.
One day, while walking in the mountains, as they engaged in a sharp exchange of debate, Shanshi picked up a piece of tile or rubble and placed it upon a flat rock.
The Master said, "If you can utter a turning word right here, I will grant that you have personally seen Ciming. The teacher looked left and right, intending to respond.
Shanshan scolded him, saying, "To pause in thought and halt the faculty of discernment means your emotional consciousness has not yet penetrated it; how could you have even dreamed of it?
The teacher was filled with shame and returned to Shishuang. When Ciming saw him coming, he scolded him, saying, "A true traveler on the path must surely know [the truth]."

It was the season when there was a matter of great urgency; though summer had not yet ended, he had already arrived here. The Master wept and said, "My elder brother Shan possessed a poisonous heart that ultimately obstructed others;
therefore, I have come to see the Venerable. Ming asked him abruptly, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?"
The Master said, "Cloudless sky arises above the peaks; the moon exists within the heart of the waves.
Ming glared at him with wide-open eyes and shouted, "With hair as white as snow and teeth falling out, you still harbor such a view! How will you ever escape birth and death?

The Master was struck with awe and sought instruction. Ming said, "Ask me. The Master repeated his previous statement and questioned him. Ming roared, "Cloudless sky arises above the peaks! and then [the text ends].

"The moon has fallen into the heart of the waves. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. His spirit was fresh and transcendent, and his wit and eloquence were swift and sharp; the monastic communities stood in awe of him.
He left [his previous residence] to dwell at Cuoyan. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "In the same pit, there is no different soil.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Deep plowing with shallow sowing. A monk asked, "If..."
"What is the place where a student of the Way transforms his body? The Master said, "When one wall is repaired, a hundred walls are harmonized. "How is it that a student exerts effort?
The Master said, "A thousand days of gathering firewood, burned in a single day. "What is the place where a student attains intimacy?
The Master said, "The whole family is sent off by the boat at the river's edge. [The student] asked for a phrase to benefit others; he requested the Master to grant one.
He pointed [at something]. The Master said, "A three-legged frog flies up into the sky. [Another] asked, "In the frost and snow of the village ahead, last night a single branch blossomed.
The Master said, "When hungry, one encounters a royal feast but cannot eat it. [Someone] asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "As soon as you step out the door, you see it.
[The questioner] asked, "What is one who is on the Way? The Master said, "Carrying a cangue and passing through the legal proceedings. Ascending the hall, the Master said, "The former sages..."
The Way. This matter is like the pattern on a tortoise shell that has been cracked; once it cracks, a sign is formed. If it does not crack, it remains dull.

Whether it cracks or does not crack, you must grasp it directly right now. Shanglan, however, is not like this: there is no cause and no necessity—riding a horse through empty space, sailing a boat on dry land.
"Clouds rise on the Southern Mountain; rain falls on the Northern Mountain. He then took up his staff and said, "O staff!

Transform yourself into a Heavenly Great General and patrol the four continents. Report at once to Śakra, Lord of Devas, whether there are those who maintain their integrity or fail to do so, whether there are those with virtuous conduct or lack thereof.
He then gave a shout and said, "A man of spirit possesses a will that pierces the heavens; do not—!"
“The Tathāgata walks where he walks. *He strikes the meditation seat once.* He then ascends the hall and cites a verse by Longya:
“Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: When smoke appears, do not yet stop. Only when the golden star manifests Will you have reached home at last.

Shendeng said: “Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: When smoke appears, you should stop at once. Do not wait for the golden star to manifest; It will only scorch your feet and burn your head. The Master [concludes].
He said: "If we speak of the sudden (sudden enlightenment), Longya is still only halfway there. If we speak of the gradual, Shending still lacks full awakening.
As for this matter, what do you say? You worthy ones, this year there are many fallen leaves; where have you gathered them to take home? [The Master] ascended the hall.
"One who faces the enemy on the battlefield without fear of life or death possesses the courage of a general. To enter the mountains..."
Those who fear tigers and rhinoceroses possess the courage of a hunter; those who enter the water without fearing crocodiles and dragons possess the courage of a fisherman.
But what is the courage of a monk? Taking up his staff, he said: "This is a staff.
If you can pick it up, grasp it, and move it, the three thousand great thousandfold worlds will all shake at once. If you cannot pick it up or grasp it..."
It cannot be attained; it cannot be moved. Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī himself; liberation is liberation itself. [End of] the inquiry.
Ascending the hall for the formal discourse, he raised the following cases: A monk asked Baling, “What is the Way? Baling said, “A clear-eyed person falls into a well.
Again, a monk asked Baoying, “What is the Way? Baoying said, “In front of the Five Phoenix Pavilion. Again, a monk asked Shoushan, “What is the Way? Shoushan said, “The feet.”
The depth below is three feet. These are the three turning words: one phrase stands like a wall a thousand fathoms high; one phrase is a boat traveling on dry land;
one phrase is the mutual interpenetration of guest and host. Is there anyone among you who can discern them? Come forward and speak! If there is none, [then listen].
Furthermore, he practices the compassion of an Arhat because he has destroyed the thieves of the fetters; he practices the compassion of a Bodhisattva because he brings peace to sentient beings;

he practices the compassion of a Tathāgata because he has attained the mark of suchness. Question: What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said: "The worthy sages of the five supernatural powers."

The student said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "My tongue reaches up to the Brahma Heaven. As the Master was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, he manifested an illness that was extremely arduous.

He spread straw mats upon the ground and rolled about, never resting for even a moment. Attendant Zhe wept as he watched and said, "Throughout your life you reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs;
why are you now acting like this? The Master gazed at him intently and rebuked him, saying, "Do you also hold such a view? Thereupon—
He sat up in the full lotus posture, called for his attendant to burn incense, and as the smoke rose, he passed into *parinirvāṇa*.
Chan Master Juehai Zanyuan of Jiangshan was the son of the Fu family of Yiwu in Wuzhou; he was a descendant of the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara).

Having cultivated the wisdom of the seeds (*bīja-jñāna*) from past lives, he manifested birth in accordance with his vows. His parents were moved by auspicious signs, and the village praised him as extraordinary. At the age of three, he left home...
He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and traveled to seek teachers at fifteen. He journeyed far to visit Shishuang and ascended into the Master’s chamber.
Upon seeing him, Ciming said, "Work well in the fodder shed. The Master then brayed like a donkey. Ciming remarked, "Truly a vessel for the Dharma," and appointed him as his attendant.
For twenty years, he personally performed all tasks—carrying water and hauling firewood—undeterred by cold or heat, seeking the Way through every act.

Later, he appeared in the world at Mount Sutai, Tianfeng, and Longhua. The Regional Commander of Baibyun invited him to reside at the Dharma-seat of Master Zhi, where he upheld the essential tenets of the school.
His spiritual acuity was swift and sharp, and his realization was in accord with his practice; thus, he was esteemed and served by all quarters.

Prime Minister Wang Anshi, deeply honoring his virtue and reputation, specifically submitted a memorial for the bestowal of ceremonial robes and a posthumous title, which the Master firmly declined. He then retired to a thatched hut at Dinglin.
In a mountain forest, he spent the entire day in leisurely conversation with the Master beneath the trees. He presented a verse to the Master, saying: "Not opposing things, the True Way is vast;
Following conditions as they arise, one's own meditation is deep. The faculty of the tongue is already pure—who could destroy it?
Its traces are like space; I have found them. A monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Striking the east wall."
On the west wall [was inscribed]: "When a guest arrives, how do you attend to them? The Master said: "Firewood on the mountain; water in the well. Question:
"What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? The Master said: "In the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse. Question: "What is the meaning of Lu Zu’s facing the wall?
The Master said: "The affairs of abbotship are many. Question: "What is a great *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend)? The Master said: [Silence].
A butcher was skinning a sheep. [The Master] asked, "Why is it like this? The butcher replied, "Karma lies within. Ascending the hall for formal instruction, the Master said:
"If this is so, it is like a tiger wearing horns. If this is not so, what would you call it? After a long silence, he said, "To feed the donkeys and the horses. Take care!
In the *Wuyou* year of the *Bingyin* cycle during the reign of Emperor Zhezong of the Song dynasty, the Master passed away. Prime Minister Wang...
The Duke wailed in grief at the stupa and praised the Master’s portrait, saying: "How virtuous was this man! His conduct was rigorous yet his countenance was tranquil;

he understood speech yet was able to remain silent. He did not rejoice in praise or honor, nor did he grieve over disgrace or defamation. He was neither arrogant nor self-aggrandizing, even when others extolled his virtue.

Whether they were monastics or laypeople, coming from the south or the north, he showed no favor to some and no resistance to others; he did not oppose them nor suppress them. He did not look for outward splendor, but only [sought the truth]."
The meal is finished; who will truly succeed to it? I have bequeathed these rules.
A monk asked Chan Master Zheng of Mount Wushan in Ruizhou, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Cloth makes the person;
water makes the field. He ascended the hall and said, "At the seat of Huangmei, among a sea-like assembly of a thousand people, the Dharma was transmitted and the robe was bestowed."
"Whether it be a practitioner at a mill, the red sun rising in the west, or the lunar disc ascending in the east—*can*.
Master Xinghui of Shuangfeng Temple on Mount Nanyue ascends the hall and says: 'A man from Nanfan sails his boat;
a man from the north of Sai shakes the oars; a Persian enters the Great Tang; Mount Sumeru performs a dance. What kind of talk is this? The Master [spoke] during the Song dynasty.
On the seventeenth day of the ninth month in the Guihai year of the Yuanfeng era during the reign of Emperor Shenzong, he shaved his head and bathed, then took leave of the assembly with this verse:
"Ninety-two years of passing time, I have clearly explained before the assembly. The distant caves disperse the cold clouds; Through the secluded window passes the waning moon.
Having finished speaking, he passed away while seated. Upon cremation, his teeth and crown protrusion remained unharmed, and above them appeared a wondrous light of five colors.
A monk asked Chan Master Daoning Daokuan of Hongzhou, "When Kāśyapa had the correct view, why did he see the Buddha pick up a flower and then smile?
The Master said, "Unable to restrain one's impatience. A monk asked, "When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the temple steward’s eyebrows and beard fall off?
The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor. A monk asked, "Since it is the One True Dharma..."
[The monk asked about] the *dhātu*. "Why is it that there are nevertheless a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions? The Master said, "The roots are deep and the leaves are lush.
The monk drew a circle and said, "Can one even transcend this? The Master said, "Seeking cleverness leads to clumsiness.

[The monk] asked, "What is the 'three before three and three after three'? The Master said, "Counting to nine, yet not reaching nine. [The monk] asked, "What is the Great Dharma of the Buddha? The Master said, [silence].

The student asked, "Master, when brewing tea, one must use water that has boiled a hundred times. The Master asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Drink it all up; leave no dregs behind.
A student asked, "What is the white ox on the open ground? The Master stuck a fire-tongs into the brazier and said, "[Look at this]."
"Do you understand? [The monk] said, "I do not. The Master said, "The head is not lacking; the tail is not redundant.

While the Master was at Tong'an, a monk asked, "Since this is Tong'an, why is there still a sick monk passing away? The Master said, "Giving alms is not as good as repaying one's debts. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The subtle secret of Shaolin, the family style of the ancient Buddhas—its application is according to the occasion. Roll it up..."
Relaxed and self-possessed. Like a fist becoming an open palm, opening and closing occur at their proper time; like water forming bubbles, arising and ceasing have no fixed duration.
Motion and stillness are both manifest; speech and silence are fully revealed. All functions are spontaneous; here, one reaches this state without exerting mental or physical effort.
This is called "letting a boat drift with the current. But tell me: who is the masterful hand when rowing against the wind? After a long silence, he said: "To play in the tide, one must..."
This is one who plays with the tide. (He lets out a shout. Entering the hall:

Taking non-thought as the school, taking non-abiding as the root, taking true emptiness as the essence, and taking wondrous existence as the function. Therefore it is said: "The entire earth is true emptiness; throughout the dharma-realm is wondrous existence.

in the bustling marketplace there are many people. Everyone, tell me: right now, as the vegetable stew is being served, how many people are receiving it?"

While the common people were being taxed, a monk came out and paid his respects. The Master said, "In the North Chan Temple, there is a monk who asks about that which does not fall into the second or third [categories].
I pray you, Master, speak quickly. The Master said, "The three dots before, the three dots after.

Heng. With what will you determine the weight? Having set aside the bowl, spoon, and chopsticks, with what will you eat your gruel and rice?

He said: "The wind scatters the clouds; the long sky is still. Deep in the night, the bright moon shines before the window.
Ascending the hall, he called for the Rector and ordered him to receive the greetings of the four newly arrived monks from yesterday. As soon as the newcomers had stepped forward, the Master said:

"With one shout and one strike, the eyes grow eight-cornered, the nostrils flare wide, and the eyebrows stand tall. If you can understand this—"
The moon sets behind the western mountains. If you do not understand this, it is like a sesame cake or noodles. [The student] asked: "What is the first phrase? The Master said:

The monk said, "I certainly have strength. The Master said, "If you truly had strength, you would not be here asking me about the sky. The monk said, "I am not asking about the sky. The Master said, "Then what are you asking about? The monk said, "I am asking about the earth. The Master
"What is it that cannot be carried? The Master said, "The Great Way. He ascended the hall for the discourse: "If one discusses this matter, do not speak of it at all;
if you speak of it, horns will grow. A monk asked, "Horns have grown. The Master said, "A calamity! The monk said, "It is my fault.
The Master said, "A dragon's head with a snake's tail. "I pray you, take care. [The Master was under] Emperor Zongyuan of the Song dynasty.
On the evening of the twelfth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Feng era (1247), he suddenly wrote this verse:

With snow-white hair and frosty whiskers for ninety-nine years, I have worn a patchwork robe over one shoulder, exhausting all worldly conditions. Suddenly, with a vast laugh, I point to the dispersing floating clouds; The jade hare pours forth its light, illuminating the great thousandfold world.
He cast aside his brush and passed into stillness.
Chan Master Dezhang of Lingyin first resided at the West Sutra Repository Hall of the Great Xiangguo Monastery.

On the first day of the ninth month of the Wuzi year of the Qingli era (1048), Emperor Renzong summoned the Master to the Yanchun Pavilion for a meal. He proclaimed the name Puzhao and questioned him.
"What is the single phrase that meets the occasion? The Master said, "A single word transcends the azure heavens; one walks on the precipice before a ten-thousand-fathom peak.
[The monk] asked, "How does one walk on the precipice? The Master then gave a shout. [The monk] said, "How can you act like this before the Emperor? The Master said, "I cannot let this pass either.
The following year, he was again summoned to the inner palace for a vegetarian feast, and was further summoned for a general assembly.
Zhao asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'? The Master said, "The thunder startles the fine grasses as their sprouts emerge;
advance upon the high mountain, do not delay. Zhao asked, "What is 'taking away the environment but not taking away the person'?

The Master said, "Wearing horns and shrouded in fur, one moves back and forth with total freedom. Zhao asked, "What is 'taking away both person and environment'? The Master said, "Stepping out the door..."
"Beyond the heavens, far and distant; flowing light and shadows are not real. He asked, "What is meant by 'when both the person and the environment are not wrested away'?

The Master said, "In the cold forest there are no overnight guests; in the great ocean one hears the dragon's roar. He was subsequently summoned to the Huicheng Hall for a meal offering. Xuanshou Xian questioned him.
The vegetarian feast was grandly opened. [A monk] asked, "How can one repay the Sage Ruler? The Master said, "Seeking bird tracks in the sky. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Seeking fish traces in the water. The Master then offered the *Xin zhu ge* (Song of the Heart-Bead):
"The mind is as it wishes; the mind is as it wishes. Spontaneously following conditions, they do not part. Know only this: do not seek outside. Seeking outside, one will ultimately find nothing."
This is so. To labor in vain is to obscure the True Principle. The pearl of the awakened mind shines like the sun; its secret treasury is profound and dense, devoid of form or substance.
When brought forth within the palm, all people are struck with wonder. How could those of the Two Vehicles, despite their diligence, ever hope to fathom it?

The blue-eyed barbarian need not point at the mountain; his wondrous functioning in response to the occasion has never faltered. In ordinary life, one must strictly avoid showing it to others; the mountains and rivers of the great earth tremble.

In the *Yiyi* [Record], it is stated that in the Gengyin year of the Huangyu era, the Master requested to retire to the mountain forests to spend his final years. By imperial decree, he was appointed as the abbot of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou and granted the honorary title Mingjue (Illuminating Enlightenment).
Chan Master Jinyuan Shàn of Jingzhou was a native of Gutian, Fuzhou. He served as an attendant to Címíng. Together with Cuìyán Zhēn, he spent the summer retreat at Jinyuan.
Zhēn prided himself on his personal acquaintance with Címíng and believed there was no one in the world who could satisfy him. When the Master spoke with him, [Zhēn was moved].

Realizing that [Xuefeng] had not yet attained thorough penetration, the Master raised a discourse while walking in the mountains. Because Xuefeng’s response involved slight deliberation, the Master rebuked him directly.
Feeling truly ashamed and terrified, Xuefeng immediately returned to Shishuang. When the Master arrived at Dayu, he entered the room; Dayu kicked out a single sandal and showed it to him.

The Master stepped back and stood; the Fool bent down to pick up his sandals, but the Master immediately tripped him over. The Fool rose and faced the wall, pointing at the Master with his hand and drawing three lines across the wall.
The Master stood staring behind him. The Fool spun around and struck the Master with his shoulder.

When they reached the Dharma Hall, the Master said, "To teach people in this way is to blind the eyes of an entire city. He first entered the world [as a teacher], and subsequently occupied the seat at Jinluan.
Later, he returned to Min from Fenglin and moved to Zifu; his final whereabouts are unknown.
Chaoxin Haoyin Chan Master of Dinghui Monastery in Suzhou was a successor of Chan Master Langye Huijue and a native of Kuifeng. A monk asked: "What is the Buddha?"
[The questioner asked about] the general meaning of the Dharma. The Master said, "A spotted bamboo staff from Xiangyuan.

[The questioner] asked, "What is the essential meaning? The Master said, "Every branch bears traces of tears. [The questioner] asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "Nanda the Asura in a fit of rage.
[The questioner] asked, "What is the second phrase? The Master said, "The patch-robed monk is at a loss. [The questioner] asked, "What is the third phrase? The Master said, [silence].
In the West and in this land, he ascended the hall: “A clay snake bites a stone turtle; the pillar chirps and squeaks.
Strike Mount Sumeru with a staff; Old Yama laughs heartily. *Cen* (Investigate). He ascended the hall: “If you recognize Prajñā, you are bound by Prajñā.”
If you do not recognize Prajñā, you will likewise be bound by Prajñā. Setting aside both recognition and non-recognition to one side, I ask you all:
what is the essence of Prajñā? Go to the hall for study. The voice of the oriole has ceased; the sound of the cicadas is urgent.
Entering the water, the turtle’s head remains dry; the heron flies into the reeds. Neither the snow nor the moon can rival their combined radiance.

"The finger points at the moon. [The student] asked, "I do not yet understand: what does the finger point to? The Master said, "Please look with wide-open eyes.
[The student] said, "When the dawn light has not yet parted, everyone gazes; once daybreak comes, it is as usual. The Master said, "In declining years, ghosts play tricks on people."
A monk asked Chan Master Fang of Jiangshan in Yuezhou, "What is the Venerable One of Immovability?
The Master said, "Wearing only his cotton robe, he passes through the marketplace. The monk said, "I do not yet understand. The Master said, "Riding a donkey, he tramples the waves of Lake Dongting.

The monk said, "Having passed through the three tiers of waves, he waits intently for the single roll of thunder. The Master said, "Reaching out his hand, he cannot see his own palm. The monk said, "Do you still permit me, your student..."

[The monk] said, "There is no one who can advance toward it. The Master said, "Treading upon the earth, you cry out to empty space. [The monk] said, "Under the Gate of Thunder, a cloth drum is difficult to sound.
The Master said, "Upon the eight-petaled flower ball, there is no need to embroider a red banner. [The monk] said, "Thirty years from now, this talk will spread widely. The Master then struck him.

The Master said, "Small eyes. [The monk] asked, "What is it like after emerging from the water? The Master said, "Throughout the day, one spreads a frown of worry.
[The monk] asked, "What is 'one mote of dust entering into right concentration'? The Master said, "A snake bites the tail of a rat.

[The monk] asked, "What is 'all motes of dust arising from samādhi'? The Master said, "A turtle bites a fishing rod. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then east and west cannot be distinguished, nor can north and south be told apart."
[The monk] departs. The Master says: "A bowl of bright lamp before the hall; several stalks of green, slender bamboo outside the curtain.

The Master said: "The sky is cold, the days are short, and the nights grow longer. He replied: "An embroidered brocade curtain with mandarin ducks."

"A traveler is difficult to encounter. The Master said, "The breath from within the skull gushes toward heaven. The monk called out, "Master! The Master said, "The head of a rooster and the tail of a phoenix.
The monk said, "Everywhere else they wash in the mud; Jiangshan has brought it forth in a painting.
The Master said, "Jiangshan is acting as a guest today, so I hope you, Reverend, will transmit it well. Even so, I cannot let this pass," and he struck him.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "To pierce the clouds but not cross the waters; to cross the waters but not pierce the clouds. Heaven and earth are held fast, yet not held fast; empty space is let loose, yet not let loose.
Transverse and vertical, three and four; now parting, now uniting; using the long to compensate for the short—this I do not ask of you.
You people, the sentence 'rice is made from grain'—it is indeed difficult to speak of. After a long silence, he said: "Private matters are not discussed in public."

A monk asked Chan Master Xian-duan of Mount Bailu in Fuzhou, “What is the Way? The Master said, “The nine provinces and the hundred Yue tribes.
The monk asked, “What is one who walks the Way? The Master said, “Riding in fatness and wearing brocade. The monk asked, “What is a great spiritual friend (mahākalyāṇamitra)?
The Master said, “Holding a blade and pressing a sword. The monk asked, “Why is it so? The Master said, “To maintain the decorum due to a sovereign.”
A disciple asked, "What is meant by 'different species'? The Master said, "A phoenix hatches from a crow's nest. He ascended the hall and said:

"Kāśyapa Matanga entering the Han was like carving a sore upon flesh; Saṃghavarman coming to Wu was like adding grit to the eyes. Bodhidharma sitting in face-to-wall meditation for nine years was the origin of a demonic apparition;
the Second Patriarch standing in the snow seeking his mind ended up becoming undutiful. You all, having reached this point—"
"How do you express it? If you can speak it, you shall roam freely across the sea. If you cannot speak it, you shall lie alone amidst the forest.
With this, he struck the meditation seat once with his staff. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha without marks?

The Master said, "A stone lion at the riverbank. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "With heart, one dwells by the river; one does not fear the waves washing away the sand."

[The monk asked about] the meaning of the Patriarch. The Master said: "Before Mount Xiong'er. [The monk asked: "What is the difference between the meaning of the Patriarch and the meaning of the Teachings?
The Master said: "Cold pines join with green bamboo; autumn waters face red lotuses."
A monk asked Zen Master Zhiquan of Langya Mountain in Chuzhou, "What is the realm of Langya? The Master said, "The pines are sparse and withered because they have limits;
the flowers bloom at random because they are insentient. The monk asked, "What is it like for one within the realm?"
The Master said, "The hair is long and the monk’s appearance is ugly. [The student] asked, "What is the Master’s phrase for guiding people?
The Master said, "Three feet of snow before one's eyes. [The student] asked, "Is that not it? The Master said, "A single flower behind the head."
A monk asked Zen Master Yuan of Liangfeng Cave in Quanzhou, "What is nirvana? The Master said, "Chopped by knives and split by axes.
The monk asked, "What is liberation? The Master said, "The shirt is long and the trousers are short. [The monk] asked about the place where all sages do not arrive.
The Master replied, "Do you know it or not? The Master said, "In my old age, I lack the strength to descend from the meditation seat. Question:
"What is it like when one is free from the four propositions and transcends the hundred negations? The Master said, "The thatched gate is overgrown with weeds.
Question: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master said, "Pines are straight; brambles are crooked. Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A reflection in the golden sand."
[The monk] asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "A jade maiden throws the shuttle. [The monk] asked, "How far apart are the Buddha and the Way?
The Master said, "Turtle hair is twenty feet long; rabbit horns are eight feet long."

Chan Master Tan of Xingjiao Monastery in Xuancheng was the son of the Niu family of Yongjia; his trade was silver-smithing.

While sharpening and polishing a vessel, he attained realization and immediately left the household life to study under Langye. His words and insights were suddenly in accord with the master’s. Later, he relied upon Tiānyī Huái at Xingjiao.
He was appointed as the First Seat (Dìyīzuò). When Foyin accepted an invitation from another state, he wished for Master Tan to succeed him.
At that time, the scholar Diāo Jǐngchún was serving as Governor of Wānlíng. Fearing that Diāo might be influenced by external opinions, Foyin made a vow before Guanyin, saying:
"If the Dharma-eye of Head Seat Tan is clear and he is fit to serve as abbot, I pray you grant a dream-sign to Scholar Diāo. That night, Diāo...
In a dream, he saw a cow on the seat where the Dharma was being expounded. The next morning, Yunyan took his leave of the Prefect. When the Prefect mentioned his dream, Yunyan laughed loudly.

The Prefect asked for the reason, and Yunyan said, "The Head Seat Tan is surnamed Niu (Cow), and his birth year also falls under the Ox. The Prefect then issued an invitation from his seat, requesting him to come.
The Master accepted the invitation and ascended the seat. Xuedou’s attendant, Shengzong, stepped forward and asked: "Before all Buddhas appeared in the world..."
"Everyone's nostrils reach up to the heavens. After leaving the world, why is there no news at all?
The Master said, "Before Mount Jizu, the wind is still. Yunmen said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "Great snow fills Chang'an. Yunmen said, "..."
"Who would have known this intention? It makes me remember Nanquan. With this, he brushed out his sleeves and returned to the assembly, refusing to prostrate himself further.
The Master said, "Xinxing, you have lost ground today. He then returned to his quarters and sent someone to invite Zong to see him.

The Master said, "Just now, you gave a wrong response to a single phrase before the assembly of devas and humans. Why did you not prostrate yourself? You should have covered it over. Zong said, "Great..."
"Sir," [Zhaozhou] said, "there is gold beneath your knees. How could you be willing to prostrate before an old man who has no eyes? The Master replied, "I have another saying.
Zong then proceeded to explain his previous words until he reached the point where Zhaozhou had said, "Wait until later, then speak again. The Master said, "I have thirty blows to spare;
I entrust them to you to strike Xuedou. Zong then prostrated.
Chan Master Guizong Ke Xuan of Jiangzhou was a native of Hanzhou. In his youth he became a monk;

immediately upon crossing the gorges, he relied upon Langye Huijue, and upon hearing a single word from him, his myriad doubts were instantly stilled. Langye approved of him, and before long, he was ordered to share the teaching seat with the master.

When Guo Gongfu visited his door to inquire about the Way, they became close friends. By the time the master took charge of Guizong, Gongfu was serving as the Magistrate of Nanchang. Shortly thereafter, the Prefectural Governor...
The Master was resentful that he had not been accorded the proper rites, and his indignation was extreme; he subsequently wrote a letter to Gongfu, saying:

"My worldly karmic ties still have six years remaining, yet I am oppressed by the Prefectural Governor. I must cast off my remaining breaths and take rebirth in your household; I pray you do not obstruct me.

When Gongfu read the letter, he was both surprised and delighted, and nodded his head in agreement. In the middle of the night, his wife saw the Master enter her bedchamber in a dream, and she cried out in alarm.
Xuan said, "This is not where the Master came from. Gongfu shook him and questioned him; his wife then related the matter in detail.

She called for a lamp, took out the letter, and showed it to him. They laughed together incessantly. Subsequently, she conceived. When the child was born, they named him Xuānlǎo. By the end of his first year, his memory and questioning were as they had been before.
When he reached the age of three, Băizhūn Yuándù arrived at their home. Upon seeing him for the first time, he said, "My nephew has come!"—Yuán.
Xuan asked, "How many years has it been since you parted from the Upādhyāya? He counted back on his fingers and said, "Four years. (This was because he had died one year after they parted.
Yun asked, "Where did you part? He replied, "At Bailian Village. Yun asked, "What is the proof? He said, "Father and mother;
tomorrow, please invite the Upādhyāya for a meal. Suddenly, the sound of a cart being pushed was heard. Yun asked, "What is that sound outside the gate?"
Xuān made the gesture of pushing a handcart with his hands. Yún asked, "What about after it has passed? Xuān replied, "Two ruts on level ground.
Indeed, after six circumambulations, he passed away without illness.
Lecturer Zixuan of Changshui in Xiu Prefecture was a native of Jiaxing County. Since his tonsure, he had recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* without ceasing.

Following the lectures of Hongmin, when he reached the passage, "The two aspects of movement and stillness are clearly seen as not arising," he attained a realization. He said to Min: "Even 'knocking on emptiness' and 'striking wood' still fall within the realm of the trap and the snare;
raising an eye or lifting a brow has already become a matter of deliberation. Only by departing from these two paths..."
He understood this principle and Min patted him in confirmation. Nevertheless, wishing to explore the source of Chan, he knew not where to turn.

Hearing that Langye was esteemed for his Way in the world, he immediately hurried to his seat. Just as the Master was ascending the hall, he stepped forward and asked: "The essence is pure and still from the beginning;
why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Langye replied with a haughty air: "The essence is pure and still from the beginning; why do mountains..."
Hebei Dadi attained realization under Master [Yun]yan. He prostrated in gratitude and said, "I wish to serve you with the ritual cloth and water jar.
Yunyan said to him, "The tradition of your school has not flourished for a long time. You should rouse your resolve to support it and repay the Buddha’s kindness;

do not let differences between schools be a hindrance. Thereupon, as instructed, Hebei bowed twice and took his leave. Later, while residing at Changshui, he addressed the assembly daily, saying, "The Way is beyond words and forms. Upon attaining [realization],...

Chan is not to be grasped through deliberation; it is known when the meaning is intuitively realized. The essence of the school has never had any distinct artifice, and for this reason both schools look up to it.
He once composed commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and other scriptures, which have circulated widely throughout the world.
Chan Master Wenyue of Yunfeng on Mount Nanyue was a dharma heir of Chan Master Dayu Zhi.

In the *Renxu* year of the Yuanfeng era of Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty, he resided at Huayan. On the tenth day of the fourth month of the *Yichou* year, he responded to the imperial summons.

On the fourteenth day, after returning from preaching the Dharma within the imperial palace, he ordered the drums to be beaten and ascended the seat; there, he took leave of the assembly and passed away.
A monk asked Chan Master Weishi of Qingyin Monastery in Nankang Commandery, "What is the Way?
The Master said, "Slanting streets and winding alleys. The monk asked, "What is one who walks the Way? The Master said, "A hundred arts, a hundred failures."
Chan Master Fenneng ascended the hall at Hengyue Temple in Tanzhou. As soon as the wind of the school was raised, ten-thousand-mile clouds were swept away;

when the law of the Dharma was put into practice, a thousand peaks took on a cold hue. Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, white waves overflowed to the heavens; amidst the billows of the great ocean, red dust filled the earth.
One should reflect upon the days of Huangmei in the past and Shaoshi in former times: unable to retreat or yield to others, he [the Master] thus...
To have one grind chaff to fulfill a vow or sever an arm to repay a heart—how does that compare to here at Mount Heng? We eat millet from the mountain fields with a bucket of unsalted soup;
we dwell together in shared hardship and joy, following the high and adapting to the low. This is not like buying something expensive at the southern market.
At the northern end, the price is sold low; it simply causes Mañjuśrī to bow his head and Kāśyapa to knit his brows. Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa swallow their voices and suppress their breath;
Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra cannot even manage it. Why is this so? Observe carefully the Dharma of the Dharma-King:
such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King.

Chan Master Fang Rui of Langye in Chuzhou, ascended the hall and said: "The Creator has no intention to produce things, yet every single thing..."

It is spontaneously accomplished. Dew and rain do not possess the intention to moisten things, yet the numinous sprouts flourish of their own accord. Thus, medicinal compounds need not be ingested for the illness to subside;
a skilled teacher need not be encountered personally for the mind to become clear. Therefore, know that wondrous wisdom and numinous light are not obtained through conditions.
Only when you reach this point may you be permitted to advance. Langye meets you in a different manner—do you understand?
"Is there such a thing? If not, one must not force a noble person into servitude.
A monk asked Master Xiyin of Mount Xingyang in Yingzhou, "What is the phrase for letting go over a precipice?"
The Master said, "The bright moon illuminates the deep valley. [The monk] asked, "What is the phrase for passing away and being revived?
The Master said, "White clouds arise in the great void. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then the woodcutter leaves the forested hills, singing of the spring colors everywhere. The Master said, "..."
This person has attained the Way and ascended the hall. To see or not to see—having seen it, is it yet understood?

The traveler on the road; the birds nesting in the forest. The pagoda within the moon rises twelve stories high; the constellations beyond the heavens number five hundred points. Do you wish to understand?
Holding the talisman of night-brightness in hand, how many know the dawn?
Chan Master Zhicaī of Ruiyan in Mingzhou, successor to Chan Master Jin of Shimen, was asked by a monk: "What is the phrase that cuts off all streams? The Master said:

"Excellent. [The student] asked, "What is the phrase of 'following the waves and drifting with the current'? The Master said, "To follow. [The student] asked, "What is the phrase of 'the casket covering heaven and earth'? The Master said, "To join.
