West Wall. In the early years of the Daguang era of the Song dynasty, Li Xiaoshou, the Governor of Kaifeng, memorialized that the Master’s spiritual practice was preeminent among the monastic community and that he should be granted official recognition.
Accordingly, the Master was bestowed with a purple robe and the title of Chan Master Dingzhao.

When the eunuch arrived bearing the imperial decree, the Master, after expressing his gratitude, declared his own resolve: at the time of his renunciation, he had made a solemn vow not to... [serve the state].

He sought profit and fame, vowing to devote himself single-mindedly to the study of the Way to benefit his nine generations of kin. He declared that if he were to violate this vow, he would rather cast away his life.

His parents granted him permission based on these words. Now, if he does not uphold his original resolve and instead surreptitiously accepts this imperial favor, he would be betraying the sacred pledge made before the Buddha.
Thereupon, he composed a formal petition to explain his position and again sent a memorial to the Capital Governor, firmly refusing to accept it. The Master remained steadfast in his refusal.

He returned and was imprisoned for refusing the order. By imperial decree, he was sent to the Jikisi (the Court of Judicial Review). When the officials heard this, they discussed transferring him to Zizhou.
Knowing the Master’s loyalty and sincerity, they wished to show him leniency and asked, "Elder, you appear haggard;
are you ill? The Master replied, "I am not ill. [The official] asked, "Then why are there scars from moxibustion? The Master said, "I was ill in the past; today I have recovered."
The official ordered him to reconsider. The Master said, "I am fully aware of your kind intentions, but what is delusory is not where I find peace.

He then proceeded calmly toward the place of execution, and those who followed him were as numerous as a crowd returning from the market. Upon arriving in Zichuan, he rented a dwelling, and his students became even more devoted to him. In the winter of the following year, by imperial decree, he was permitted to live as he pleased;
he then built a hermitage in the center of the Fuyong Lake. Monastics and laypeople gathered there like a river. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Now, to go forth..."

As for "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*): it is because one grows weary of worldly toil, seeks liberation from birth and death, quiets the mind and halts discursive thoughts, and severs all attachments to external conditions that one is said to have "left home.
How could one allow the trivial pursuit of profit and sustenance to bury one's entire life? One must simply cast everything open at both ends and let go in the middle.
When encountering sounds or forms, it should be like planting flowers upon a stone; when encountering profit or fame, it should be like placing dust in one's eyes.
How could this be possible? Moreover, from time immemorial, there is nothing we have not already experienced, nor is there anything whose sequence we do not know.
It is merely a matter of turning the head into a tail, coming to no more than this. Why must you persist in such bitter attachment? If you do not cease now, [the cycle will continue].
When else would you wait? Therefore, when the ancient sages taught people, they simply wanted them to exhaust this very moment. If one can exhaust this moment, what further matter could there be?
If one attains a mind free from affairs, even Buddhas and Patriarchs are but enemies; so too are all worldly matters.
Only when one is naturally detached and indifferent will one finally correspond with that state. Have you not seen how Yinyangshan refused to see anyone until his death?
Zhaozhou refused to speak of it until his death. Biandan gathered acorns and chestnuts for food; Damei used lotus leaves as clothing;
the "Paper-Robed Wayfarer" wore nothing but paper; and the Venerable Xuantai wore nothing but cloth. Shishuang established...
In the Kūmoku-dō (Hall of the Withered Tree), when sitting or sleeping with others, the sole purpose is to cause you to die to your own mind.
Tōji sent someone to prepare rice so that we might cook and eat together; this was intended to save you from worldly affairs. Furthermore, the various sages of the past have set such precedents.
If you possess no such excellence, how can you bear it? O virtuous ones, if you investigate this matter thoroughly, you will certainly not fail anyone.

If you are unwilling to accept this responsibility, I fear that in the future you will find it exceedingly difficult. This mountain monk’s own practice is without merit, yet I have the honor of presiding over this mountain gate.
How could I sit idly while consuming the monastery’s resources and utterly forget the entrustment of the former sages?

Therefore, following the example of the ancients, I shall establish the protocols for a resident abbot and settle them with you all: from now on, I shall no longer descend the mountain, attend formal meals, or go out to solicit offerings.
Master, we shall take only the annual yield from the monastery’s estates and divide it into three hundred and sixty equal parts, using one part per day.
We shall not increase or decrease this amount according to the number of people. If it is sufficient for rice, we shall prepare rice; if insufficient for rice, we shall prepare porridge;
if insufficient for porridge, we shall prepare rice soup. For those who newly arrive and meet us, there shall be only tea and soup.

No longer shall there be the boiling or serving of tea; instead, a single tea hall shall be established where you may take and use it yourself. Your primary aim must be to minimize external conditions and focus exclusively on practicing the Way.

Furthermore, all necessities are provided and the scenery is never lacking: the flowers know how to smile, the birds know how to sing, the wooden horse neighs eternally, and the stone ox runs with ease.
Beyond the heavens, the green mountains possess no color; beside one’s ear, the murmuring spring has no sound. On the ridge—
Above, the macaque cries; dew wets the moon at midnight. Between the trees, the crane calls; the wind turns back through the pines at the clear dawn.
When the spring breeze arises, the dragon roars from the withered wood. The autumn leaves fall and the flowers scatter from the cold forest.
Moss patterns spread across the jade steps; human faces bear the hue of mist and clouds. Sounds and traces are silent; all news is utterly still. A single flavor of desolation.
There is nothing here to pursue. Today, as this mountain monk speaks of our family tradition before you all, it is already an impropriety;

how could I go further to ascend the hall, enter the room, brandish the mallet, raise the whisk, shout to the east and strike with the staff to the west, or knit my brows and glare with eyes wide open like one suffering a seizure?
Not only would this humiliate the Venerable One, but it would also be a betrayal of the former sages.
Do you not see? When Bodhidharma came from the West, beneath the mountain of Shaoshi, he sat facing a wall for nine years.
The Second Patriarch went so far as to stand in the snow and sever his own arm; one could say he underwent the utmost hardships.
Yet, Bodhidharma never uttered a single word, and the Second Patriarch never asked a single question. Can you still call Bodhidharma "one who did not act for others"? As for the Second Patriarch...
Is it not possible to attain this without seeking a teacher? Whenever I speak of the deeds of the ancient sages, I feel as though there is no place left for me to stand;

I am filled with shame that later generations have become so weak. Furthermore, when people offer the finest delicacies one after another, saying, "Only when our four requisites are fully provided can you resolve to practice," I fear that by the time one attempts to act, it will already be too late—effectively a lifetime or even several lifetimes away.
It is gone. Time passes like an arrow; it is truly a great pity. Even so, it still depends on others to deliberate upon it at length.
I, this mountain monk, cannot force you to understand. O virtuous ones, do you see the verse of the ancients? "Rice from the mountain fields, coarse and unhusked;
wild vegetables with plain yellow pickles. Eat them if you wish to eat; if you do not, go as you please. Prostrate.
May we follow the same path. Each of you must strive diligently. Farewell. In the *Zhenghe* era, the year *Dingyou*, Emperor Huizong bestowed the plaque naming this place “Huayan Chan Temple.
On the fourteenth day of the fifth month of the following year, *Chonghe* era, the year *Wuxu*, he took up his brush and wrote this verse, entrusting it to his attendant monk, saying:
"I am seventy-six years old; my worldly ties are now exhausted. In life I do not crave heaven, and in death I have no fear."
As for the hells: casting off one's hands and laying down the body beyond the three realms, one drifts freely and spontaneously—what constraints could there be? He passed away some time later.
Chan Master Ba’en of Da’hong Mountain in Suizhou was surnamed Wei and was a native of Liyang; his family had been eminent scholars for generations.

Before his capping ceremony, the Master displayed strategic brilliance and was ranked first in the imperial examinations. Later, weary of the mundane world, he petitioned the court to resign his official robes and become a monk.
The Emperor granted his request, whereupon the Master devoted himself to the Way of the Patriarchs. Upon reaching Touzi, he realized the essential point of the mind before long.

The Master said, "You are truly insatiable. The monk said, "An adept master. The Master said, "Nor is that so."

He was in a deep sleep and spoke much in delirium, saying: "If you had not come up here to pose this question, how could you have encountered the pivot of Shaolin?

Furthermore, one cannot depart with the bow broken and the arrows exhausted. Moreover, the practitioners of the Zen school can illuminate the distant and clarify the near.
Then, picking up his staff, he said: "It pierces the nostrils of Deshan and replaces the eyes of Linji;
it overturns the great ocean and shifts the void of space. Tell me, three thousand miles away, who is the one who knows? At this point, be clear.
"Attained! It is much like the bright sun shining across the sky. Should it not yet be clear, one cannot avoid the rising clouds and falling rain.
[The Master] struck once and asked: "The Patriarch came from the West; for nine years he faced the wall. What is the final word? I pray you, Master, proclaim it. The Master said:
The Master Heizei (Hei-moku Byaku), who once established one hundred questions to interrogate his disciples, stated briefly:

"Even if one does not forget the karma created throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, why is it that by reciting 'Namu Butsu' but once, sins are extinguished for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges?
Furthermore, he drew this [circle] symbol and said: "The myriad phenomena of the forested world are all contained within it. Let those Zen practitioners with true eyes try [to explain it]."
Please discern this. Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Look, look! The great earth is covered in deep snow; though spring has arrived, it is especially cold.

Lingfeng and Shaoshi—how could they possibly have anything to do with one another? Do not discuss the meaning of the Buddhas or the patriarchs; do not vainly claim that every word and phrase is perfect.
When the iron ox is let loose, there is no trace left behind; the bright moon amidst the reeds—you must see this for yourself. He struck the ground once with the staff.
Zhang Xiazuo: The Master had long been on friendly terms with the layman Wujin (Wujin Jushi), Zhang Gong Shangying.

Wujin once sent a letter inquiring about the essential tenets of the Three Teachings, stating: "In the third fascicle of the *Śubhākarasiṃha-ṭīkā*, it is said that the heterodox views of the Western Regions do not exceed four types of views.
The Confucianism and Daoism of this land likewise do not exceed these four views. For instance, the calculations of Zhuangzi and Laozi take 'spontaneity' (*ziran*) as the cause."

To claim that [the *tathāgatagarbha*] can give rise to the myriad things is a false cause (*mithyā-hetu*). The *Yi Jing* says, "The Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*) gives rise to the two polarities (*liangyi*). To take the Supreme Ultimate as the cause is likewise a false cause.
If one were to say that "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way (*dao*)" and that it can give rise to the myriad things, this too is a false cause.
If one calculates that the One is empty and non-existent, then it would be without cause. Now, I have a doubt:

Laozi’s concept of spontaneity (*ziran*) is not the same as the spontaneity of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Heavens. Why is this so? Laozi said: "Always be without desire to observe its subtlety;
always have desire to observe its periphery. When there is no desire, there is constant being; when one observes the periphery, one has already entered the Way. This is what he meant.

How could there be any talk of "false causes"? The *I Ching* says: "The alternation of one Yin and one Yang is called the Way (*dharma*); that Yin and Yang are unfathomable is called the Spirit (*śūnyatā*).
As for this Spirit, it is spoken of as that which wondrously permeates all things; it is quiescent and unmoving, yet when stirred, it immediately penetrates the affairs of the world.
Now, you instead destroy the Way of the transformation of Yin and Yang as being false causes, and cast away the unfathomable.

"O Master, how could there be anything to say? I hope you will grant me an instruction after reading this paper, so that I may sever the net of doubt. The Master replied: "The schools of the non-Buddhist outsiders in the Western Regions have many paths;

yet, when their essential convergence is examined, they do not go beyond the four views of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence. These are:

the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of both existence and non-existence, and the view of neither existence nor non-existence. This is because they do not realize that [all things] are none other than the One Mind."

If one speaks of "the Way," then the Way is not my own; therefore, it is called an external way (*bāhyamārga*). If one does not realize that all phenomena are the mind, then phenomena will vary according to one's views;

therefore, this is called false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). For instance, if one says they exist, existence implies non-existence; if one says they do not exist, non-existence implies the absence of existence.

Where there is both existence and non-existence, views of existence arise in competition; where there is neither existence nor non-existence, views of non-existence arise. This is also true if one says they both exist and do not exist.
The view of neither existence nor non-existence is likewise so. Indeed, if one cannot free oneself from various views, there is no means to clarify one’s own mind;

and if there is no means to clarify one’s own mind, one cannot know the Right Path. Therefore, a sutra says: "Regarding the teachings expressed through words and phrases, those of small intelligence falsely discriminate.
Unable to comprehend their own minds, how can they know the Right Path? It further says: "There is..."
To "see" is itself a defilement; this is not yet true seeing. To remain far removed from all views—in this way one sees the Buddha.

Judging by this, the heterodox and the orthodox follow different paths, precisely because their realizations regarding "seeing" differ. Thus, Qingliang [Zongmi] held that according to the calculations of Zhuangzi and Laozi, the Way and its Law are spontaneous (*ziran*) and can give birth to the myriad things;
while the *Yi* states that the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) gives birth to the two polarities, and one Yin and one Yang...

To speak of "Yang" as the Way (*dào*)—taking the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*) of spontaneity as its cause, and asserting that the alternation of Yin and Yang constitutes the Way capable of generating the myriad things—is a false cause.
To calculate "One" as non-existence (*śūnyatā*) is to posit no cause at all. Allow me to examine this: Now, the three realms are but mind;
the myriad conditions are of one principle. Because the mind arises, phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, phenomena cease. Let us extend this reasoning further.
It encompasses all phenomena yet is not existence; it unifies and synthesizes them, reaching the ultimate state of quiescent extinction, yet is not non-existence.
It is neither non-existence nor not non-existence; it is neither existence nor not existence. Once these four attachments have vanished, the hundred negations are thereby dispelled.
Then, natural causality is seen to be mere conceptual play, and both emptiness and reality are equally provisional names. As for what is said...
The Great Ultimate (Tàijí) and Yin-Yang can give birth to the myriad things; they are both eternally non-existent and eternally existent, serving as the gateway to all wonders.

That Yin and Yang cannot be fathomed is what is called the "boundless spirit. Although the Sage establishes teachings to provide instruction and awakening through manifold means, since these differ from the One Mind, how could they not be the four views?
How is this made clear? It is because emptiness and non-being constitute the Way (Dào), and the Way is thus non-being. If...
It is spontaneous. Whether it be the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*) or the alternation of Yin and Yang as the Way (*dào*), the Way is existence;
yet, as "constant non-existence" and "constant existence," it is both non-existent and existent. As the unfathomable interplay of Yin and Yang, it is neither existent nor non-existent.

Some former scholars have said that that which wondrously orchestrates all things is called the "Spirit" (*shén*); thus it is not merely one among things. Since things themselves are also non-existent, the various great [masters] of India...

The masters of the treatises all regard the existence of dharmas external to the mind as the view of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), while taking the principle that "the myriad dharmas are mind-only" as the orthodox tradition.

This is because when the mind is taken as the fundamental principle, all [erroneous] views naturally vanish; thus, although their words may differ, they are not sufficient to constitute a true difference.

When there are dharmas external to the mind, however, various views compete to arise; thus, although their words may be identical, they are not sufficient to constitute a true identity. Nevertheless, the Confucians...

The Way of the Sage certainly does not stem from ignorance; rather, it is that he maintains [the truth] without engaging in discourse. This is because he did not immediately and explicitly designate the one mind as the source of all phenomena.
Even if he occasionally spoke of it, he still did not engage in such discourse, much like the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Heavens.

All these are the manifestations and activities displayed by the Great Power Bodhisattva. By generating various views and exhaustively exploring diverse heterodoxies, he clarifies that the Buddha-dharma is the true path;
this is why it constitutes the Way of the Sage, wherein both the conforming and the contrary take it as their ultimate source.

It is not something that can be known through mere intellectual speculation. Thus, an ancient said: "In the past, before the True Doctrine had arrived, Confucius merely took it as a point of mental focus.
Now that we know where the ultimate principle resides, we ought not to continue clinging to provisional teachings.

However, to know that a provisional teaching is provisional does not necessarily mean one knows the provisional; to know that the provisional is itself the real—that is what constitutes knowing the provisional. This is also [the teaching of] the Zhou.
The fundamental intent behind the teachings and the establishment of the words by Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi is that which constitutes the beginning and the end of the Great Matter (mahā-kārya).
Thus, the three teachings share a single mind; though their paths differ, they follow the same course. As for the ultimate source of the Way, it is fundamentally beyond words and speech.
Were it not for the Great Being Vimalakīrti, who else could understand this meaning?
Chan Master Yun of Dongshan in Yizhou ascended the hall and said: "The autumn wind rolls across the earth; the night rain overturns the void.
Within this, there is something distinctively cool and refreshing; herein, there is no further feverish affliction. What is this livelihood? Only those who arrive know it.
As soon as one falls into seeing and hearing, one remains on the road. But tell me, what is it like after arriving home? One wanders alone at will, without companion."
Abiding in the central position, one does not abide in the partial.
Chan Master Chang'an Fuyingwen ascended the hall and said: "Clearly manifest at the tip of every blade of grass—clearly manifest is the meaning of the Patriarchs.
To accept this directly is to mistake the bow for the arrow. Those who are alert and discerning run into obstacles; those who are dull-witted..."
Mud mixed with water; tortoise-hair whisks filling the void of space; rabbit-horn staffs propping up heaven and supporting the earth.
When the sun strikes the coral grove, how many can truly know this? [The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
A monk asked Chan Master Tanguang of Shengshou at Longpan in Chuzhou: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind do you succeed? The Master said:
"Clouds billow atop Mount Yangguang; cypresses grow green beside Moonlight Hermitage. The monk said:

Chan Master Danxia Zichun of Dengzhou was the son of the Jia family of Jianzhou. He became a monk at the age of twenty and attained thorough realization in the presence of Fuyong.
He ascended the hall and said: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a single treasure hidden within the mountain of form.
Dharma Master Zhao spoke thus, but he only knew how to point to tracks and discuss traces; he was simply unable to pick it up and show it."
People! Today Danxia tears asunder the universe and shatters the mountain of form; he brings it forth for all of you—let those with eyes discern it.
He strikes once with his staff and says: "Do you see? The egret standing in the snow is not the same color."
The bright moon and reeds amidst the flowers are not like others. [Ascending the hall: He cites Deshan’s address to the assembly, saying:

"In my school there are no words or phrases; truly, there is not a single dharma to give to anyone. Deshan speaking in such a manner may be said to know only how to enter the grass to seek people, yet he fails to realize that his entire body is covered in mud and water.
Upon careful observation, it appears he possesses but a single eye. If one were a person of Danxia...
Xia said: "It is not so. In our school there is a saying: 'The golden scissors cannot cut it open; the profound, original, and wondrous intent is the jade maiden conceiving in the night.
Ascending the hall, he said: "At noon, the sun stands tall yet is still half-hidden; at the third watch, all is silent yet the moon is not yet full.
The six gates have never known the warmth of spring; coming and going, one always remains before the bright moon. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Precious Moon..."
Radiant light flows; reflections spread across the clear pool. The water has no intention of soaking the moon; the moon has no intention of dividing its light.
When both water and moon are forgotten, only then can one be called "severed. Therefore it is said: "The matter of ascending to heaven must be cast away;
the matter of reaching perfection must be discarded. When a coin lands with a golden sound, there is no need to look back. If you can act thus, only then will you understand how to proceed.
"Moving among those of different kinds. When people arrive here, do they still understand? After a long silence, he said: "Constantly walking without lifting his feet from the human path;
clad in fur and wearing horns, he mingles with the dust and mud. A monk asked, "What was it like before Ox-head saw the Fourth Patriarch?
The Master said, "The golden chrysanthemums have just begun to bloom, and the bees compete to gather them. The monk asked, "What was it like after he saw him? The Master said, "The sprouts."
The withered flowers have fallen, leaving nothing to rely upon. In the spring of the Jihai year of the Xuande era of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty, he passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the south of Mount Hong.
Chan Master Mudu Facheng of Jingyin Monastery in Dongjing was a native of Chongde, Jiaxing. He ascended the hall and said: "Suddenly, the lantern..."
"You laugh heartily. How is it that even a pillar conceives? At dawn she gives birth to a white-haired girl, who wanders about to this day and has not yet returned.
This wretched creature—how good it would be if she returned! For whom were the yellow chrysanthemums and green bamboos planted so long ago? Ascending the hall, he said:
"Only those who know the matter of the Buddhas and Patriarchs that transcends [the ordinary] have the right to speak. All you practitioners of Zen, for now—"
The Way. What is that which transcends the Buddhas and Patriarchs? There was once a man’s son whose six sense-faculties were incomplete and whose seven consciousnesses were not whole;
he was a great icchantika, devoid of the Buddha-nature. Meeting a Buddha, he killed the Buddha; meeting a Patriarch, he killed the Patriarch.
Neither heaven could contain him, nor did hell have a door to receive him. "Do you all recognize this person? After a long silence, he said: "Facing [him]."

His face was not that of a celestial being; he slept much and spoke in his sleep. Ascending the hall, he said: "The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet the expedient means have many gates.
If you only understand the nature of returning to the source, what need is there to worry about the gates of expedient means? Do you all wish to understand the nature of returning to the source?"
To take a pillar and make it into a wooden ladle—those bystanders will not consent to follow him. Do you wish to understand the gate of skillful means?
To take a wooden ladle and make it into a pillar is equally suitable for propping up heaven and supporting the earth. But tell me:
how would you express that single phrase which does not fall into the gate of skillful means? After thirty years have passed, do not let it be cited erroneously.

"What is it like for the sovereign to look upon his minister? The Master said, "The phoenix carriage departs from the celestial palace to visit Zi Ling with earnest courtesy.

[The questioner] asked, "What is it like for the way of sovereign and minister to be in harmony? The Master said, "Myriad songs praise the sage's virtue; for a thousand years, their names are engraved upon the Lingyan Gallery.

Since the Master took up residence as abbot, he received offerings without greed and gave alms without satiety. When the harvest failed and food was scarce, he exhausted his own resources to provide for the assembly.
Of those [who were saved], several tens of thousands relied upon him for their survival. Daily, he would not eat past noon.

In the ninth month of the *dingchou* year of the Shaoxing era during the reign of Emperor Gaozong, he visited his fellow officials and donors; subsequently, he called upon Zhao Gong Lingcong, the Regional Commander of Yue, with whom he took his leave.
On the seventh day of the tenth month, he returned to the mountain. On the following day, during the hours of Chén and Sì, he bathed and changed his robes.

Sitting upright, he addressed the assembly, looked toward his attendant monk, and requested a brush to write a letter. He entrusted the matter of future affairs to Yùwáng Gǎo, requesting him to preside over the funeral rites.

He then wrote a verse, saying: "Like a dream, an illusion, or a flower in the air; Sixty-seven years have passed. The white bird vanishes into the mist; The autumn waters join the sky. Having cast down the brush, he passed away. His remains were left in the funerary shrine.
After seven days, his countenance remained as if alive. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Donggok; he was posthumously titled Hongji, and the stupa was named Myogwang.
He lived to the age of sixty-seven and had been a monk for fifty-three years.

Chan Master Huizhao Qingyu of Dahuang Monastery in Suizhou was the son of the Hu family in Yingzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "To take one step forward is to tread upon the water and grass of the king; to take one step back is to trample upon the ancestral fields and gardens. To neither advance nor retreat is to remain right within the waters of death. Is there any path for emerging from this? The evening breeze rustles through the pines, their needles short.
The spring breeze ripples; the willow threads are long. [He] ascends the hall. He cites the story of Chuangzi instructing Jia Shan, saying:
"You must ensure there are no traces where you hide your body; do not hide your body where there are no traces. For thirty years I was at Yaoshan, and I clarified only this matter.
Why is it that people of the present day act so hastily? The Cinnabar Mountain has no multicolored phoenixes; the precious palace does not retain them.
Guān was sometimes blunt and sometimes foolish; who could have known him while he was still on the road? Later, he moved to Xíngguó on the south side of the river.
Following his local governor, he became renowned for his practice of the Way. Emperor Gāozōng bestowed upon him the title Huìzhào. During the Shàoxīng era, he retired to seclusion at Xuěfēng.
As he approached the time of his passing, he wrote a verse: "The final phrase is most difficult to clarify; To turn back and look again requires thousands of miles of effort.
Aside from my own true and legitimate son, Who else would dare to tread within? Having cast down his brush, he passed away with a smile upon his face.
Master Wuyin of Chuzhou ascends the hall: Strolling at ease within the wondrously luminous home of ultimate reality, he shifts his step and turns his body to point toward the setting clouds.
Though boundless white clouds remain unseen, he rides the bright moon through the reeds at night.
Chan Master Zigui of Tianfeng on Mount Tai, a successor of Chan Master Jingyin Cheng, ascended the hall. He struck his staff once and called to the assembly, saying:
"The eighty-four thousand Dharma gates have been flung wide open with these eight characters. Do you see them? The golden phoenix roosts at night where there is no shadow."
The trees; the peaks and ridges have just appeared, yet they are shrouded by sea clouds.
A monk asked Chan Master Fashuan of Jixiang in Taiping Prefecture, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "A long drought has brought no sweet rain; the rice stalks in the fields are withered. The monk asked, "What is the underlying intent? The Master said, "This year..."
The price of rice is high; when things are simple, do not disdain the coarse.
Master Shouchang of Huguo Monastery in Taizhou ascended the hall, held up his staff, and struck it, saying: "The beginning of the thirty-six decades;
the source of the seventy-two seasonal signs; the time when the myriad realms welcome the harmonious breath; the Eastern Emperor spreads forth life."

By imperial decree, Heaven spontaneously bestowed auspicious radiance and the Earth gathered signs of integrity and blessing. A faint, fine rain washed the cold sky; a light spring glow enveloped the wild landscapes.
This may truly be called receiving grace in accordance with the season; every celebration was appropriate. All people throughout the world have added a year to their lives.
I dare ask you all: tell me, how old is that one person? After a long silence, he said: [The text ends here.]
The thousand-year-old man’s countenance is like jade; the ten-thousand-year-old boy’s topknot is like silk.
Master Dharma Teacher Danxia Puyue of Dengzhou ascended the hall and said: "Before Vipaśyin Buddha, who could discern this? After Dīpaṃkara Buddha, who was truly a connoisseur?
Even if one were to take it up on the other side, one would still not avoid being split into two pieces. Even if one were to..."
Even this current practice of ours has likely not yet attained perfection. This is because when [Vimalakīrti] sealed his mouth at Vaiśālī, the celestial mechanism was already leaked;
even if one were to remain in seclusion at Mahādeva’s cave, the seams and gaps would ultimately be torn asunder. Do not say that the true permanence is manifest in its essence.
This is simply pure clarity, utterly free of a single speck. What need is there to speak of shedding one's skin? It naturally functions alone as solitary luminosity.
Although it may seem fresh in this way, it does not yet accord with the spirit of a monk. Only when the five eyes are opened together and the three lights are fully revealed can it be so.
From this point on, with the thread upon the fishing pole, one naturally avoids disturbing the waves. One must clearly understand the shifting of positions and the turning back of the faculty;
only then can one enter the marketplace and extend the hand. Therefore it is said: "Even if the teeth grow hair, do not let the eyes look back.
To recognize [it] is like a confusion of empty flowers; to speak of it is to have divergent paths of language. Since this is so, I venture to ask you all: [The text ends here.]
"A person does not violate a single sharp edge of a word. How do you say it? After a long silence, he said: "At midnight, the tortoise’s eyes open wide;
when dawn breaks, all phenomena are of one color."
Master Huiguang Jingzhi of Tōkyō Myōe-ji ascended the hall and, citing the story of Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman, said:
"Zhaozhou’s tongue reaches to the heavens; the old woman’s brow-light covers the earth. Having clearly seen through her upon his return, countless ordinary people fall into a deep slumber."
Chan Master Qinggu Zhenji Dezhi of Yuantong Temple in Jiangzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Baofeng Zhao.
He was the younger son of Xu Hongzhong, who held the rank of Jinzi. His family had resided in Liyang for generations.
The Master’s eyes were a deep azure-blue, and his spiritual radiance struck those around him. At the age of ten, he did not yet know how to read or write. He was often...

He was fond of sleep, so his father called him the "Dullard. By the time he reached the age of maturity, his retentive memory surpassed that of others, and his literary compositions were marked by extraordinary phrasing.

In his early twenties, he dreamed of a strange monk who bestowed upon him a four-line verse. Shortly thereafter, someone presented him with a statue of the Master of Nanyue (Nan’an Yanzhu), which bore inscribed upon it the very same "Verse of Intelligence" (*cóngmíng jì*).
From then on, he recited and held it in his mind without forgetting. Five years later, he followed the Jin...

Zi was transporting grain to Western Luo when, one night, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He composed several gāthās in succession; one said: "Not because of words or phrases, nor because of another person;
Not because of objects or colors, nor because of sound. At midnight, I blew out the lamp and drew back the pillow; Suddenly, here, it was already daybreak.
He continued to chant and sing as usual, leaving the assembly unable to fathom him. He then earnestly sought to leave the household life, but his father would not permit it.
[The Emperor] granted his request and intended to bestow an official rank upon him. The Master said, "I am about to cast off the worldly net and shall not dwell within the three realms;
how could I again thrust my head into the midst of profit and fame? I beg that you instead confer this upon my cousin, Jue. Thereupon, he shaved his hair and received full ordination.

Within a few years, his reputation resounded throughout the capital. In the spring of the second year of the Xuande era, Emperor Huizong bestowed upon him the title Zhenji (True Limit) and commanded him to reside [at the monastery].
Yuantong ascends the hall for formal instruction. Twenty years ago, this mountain monk was blind in both eyes and could see nothing at all;
I only heard people say that above the blue sky there is a great sun-disk that illumines the three thousandfold world system.
There was no place where it did not pervade. Though he devised myriad schemes, he could never see it. Twenty years later, his eyesight gradually opened;
yet he encountered continuous overcast weather with thick clouds surging in all directions. He observed the four quarters and scrutinized everything above and below.
When seeing clouds moving, one immediately makes calculations regarding their movement; when seeing clouds staying still, one immediately establishes a fixed nest within that stillness.
It is just like this: suddenly encountering a man of much learning who asks, "Do you wish to see the solar disc?
Why not go to the summit of a high mountain? The mountain monk then challenges him, saying, "Where is [the summit]?"
"Atop the peak of a high mountain," he said, "it is where the dust of the mundane world does not reach. O virtuous ones, what a wonderful, authentic message!
Do you understand? On the long couch, it is *Buddha-tāya*. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Last night, the Yellow-Faced Gautama..."
He brought forth the three thousandfold world system and swallowed it all in a single mouth, leaving no trace behind—just as a person drinking hot water, which dissolves instantly.

At that moment, all the great bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, arhats, and the entire multitude of living beings were entirely unaware and unknowing; only Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra caught a fleeting glimpse of it, even so.
He was seen. Vast and boundless, it was as if he were rising and submerging his head within the great ocean.
Everyone, tell me: what is this news? If you can discern it through investigation, I grant that you possess the single eye atop your crown.
He passed into nirvana. Wherever the smoke from his cremation reached, everything became śarīra (relics). His remains were enshrined in a stupa at Sīkōng Mountain, and [the relics] were distributed.
At the Fengdie Stone Slope, Zen Master Zhēnrú Dàohuì of Tāizhōu ascended the hall and said: "The matters of the empty kalpa are spontaneously acknowledged when one is willing to take them up;
they are fully manifest in daily life—what leakage could there be? It is precisely right to return home and sit securely, letting the snow cover the green mountains, leaving nothing behind."

The Primordial Character. Whose heart is burdened? Waves overturning upon the surface of the water. But tell me: how shall one present this single phrase—“In the absolute, no primordial character is established;
in the relative, nothing is attached to objects”? When the shuttle-head is free from the hanging thread, the patterns unfold freely and the meaning is naturally distinct.
Chan Master Zhìtōng of Xīngguó Army, whose secular surname was Wáng and who hailed from Tāizhōu, was known as the "Greatly Deceased Old Man" (Dàsǐwēng).
From childhood, he was unlike his peers. At the age of eighteen, he received the tonsure under Guǎngdù Zhī. He first visited Jìngcí Xiàng, and one day he heard Xiàng say:
To know through reflection and to understand through deliberation are both the livelihood of ghosts; my enthusiasm could not be restrained, so I went to Baofeng to seek entry into his room.

Baofeng said, "You must sever the thoughts of arising and ceasing, sweep away the paths of mystery prior to the empty kalpa, avoid the deviations of the orthodox and the biased, exhaust the present moment, and let go of yourself entirely.
Let go until you have let go completely, and only then will you have a share of true freedom."
Upon hearing this, the Master immediately grasped its essential meaning. Feng struck the drum and addressed the assembly, saying, "I have deeply realized the Way of the Great Death of the Icchantika;
those who study hereafter should rely upon it. Consequently, he was titled the "Old Man of Great Death" (Dasiweng). In the first year of the Jianyan era, he ascended the hall at Fazhitong to preach.
"Coming, one does not enter the gate; going, one does not leave the door. With no trace of coming or going, how can one proclaim the Dharma? It must be such that even the ancients..."
Moss seals the paths; the antelope has left no tracks. The moon locks the azure mists of Cangwu; the vermilion phoenix does not alight. Thus it is said:

"Where one hides the body, there is no trace; where there is no trace, do not hide the body. If you can act thus, then going and staying are without dependence, and there is ultimately no turning toward or away.
Do you understand this? Now we are scattered like clouds and cranes; you and I have forgotten each other, and wherever we touch upon things, [we find only the Way].
Original Text: A monk asked, "What is 'the biased within the central'? The Master said, "An old woman with a black face pulls out white threads.
The monk asked, "What is 'the central within the biased'? The Master said, "A white-haired old man wears a black robe.

The monk asked, "What is 'coming from the central'? The Master said, "Performing somersaults in excrement. The monk asked, "What is 'arriving at the simultaneous'? The Master said, "A sharp-edged blade is sheathed."

He did not injure himself. [The student] asked, "What is 'arriving within the integration'? The Master said, "Kunlun walks through the night. [The student] asked, "Is there anything further beyond this?
The Master said, "To catch a turtle and call it a soft-shelled turtle. [The student] asked, "I beg the Master to grant me further expedient means.
The Master said, "Entering the mountains, one encounters a tiger; leaving the valley, a ghost comes to pull one along. [The student] asked, "How can there be such conflict of arms?"
[The Master] waited. The Master said: "Three or two strands [make] one pound of hemp. At the beginning of the Shaoxing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty, he returned to reside at Baocangyan.
He lived among the common people, adopting their dress. In the second month of the *renshen* year, he manifested a slight illness and said, "My worldly ties have come to an end.

On the thirteenth day of the third month, he gave a small-scale sermon (*xiaochan*) for the assembly, and further spoke this verse: "No need to shave the head; What need is there to bathe? A single heap..."
"Red flames! A thousand feet, ten thousand feet! Although it is thus, tell me: is there still something further above?
Thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away.
Chan Master Zhipeng of Huayao in Hengzhou was the son of the Huang family of Siming. He relied upon Baofeng for many years without attaining realization.
Consequently, he served as the bowl-bearer for the assembly. Baofeng personally inscribed his own portrait, saying: "The rain washes the pale red peach buds tender;
The wind shakes the light green willow filaments light. Within the shadows of white clouds, strange rocks are revealed; Amidst the luster of green waters, ancient trees are clear. Alas!"
When you arrived at Jiaoshan, Gucheng saw you and sighed, saying, "Only today do I know that this old man has truly met his former teacher.

The Master then requested an explanation of the eulogy. Cheng said, "Have you not seen how Fayan took up the story of Jianshan’s 'scenery' and said, 'For twenty years I have only understood it as scenery'?
At these words, the Master attained awakening. (The *Luohu Yalu* states: "Cheng pointed with his finger.")

He asked the Master, "Do you understand? The Master said, "I do not. Cheng said, "Can you recite the *Fazheng* [verse] that imitates Hanshan? The Master then recited it. When he reached the line, "Who knows this meaning? It makes me recall Nanquan," at the word "recall" (*yi*), Cheng suddenly covered the Master's mouth with his hand and said, "Stop!
Stop! At that moment, the Master had a sudden realization and exclaimed, "So this is how it is! Cheng asked, "How do you understand it?"
The Master said, “In spring they grow, in summer they mature; in autumn they harvest, in winter they store. Cheng said, “One must simply maintain this. The Master responded with an affirmative grunt.
At the beginning of the Xiangxing era, he went forth to reside at Tianning in Hua, Yao, and Wuzhou, and later moved to Qingliang. He ascended the hall and said: “The sea wind blows through my dreams;
the mountain monkeys cry out under the moon. I dare ask you all: what season is this? If you understand it thus, you will see the shadowless tree.”
"Go below and wander at leisure. If this is not yet so, you must strike through to the bottom beneath the three rafter-ends. Later, he retired to Ruiyan in Mingzhou.
Jiankang again sent Qingliang to entice him back, and the Governor of Ming also urged him to go.
The Master did not comply; he composed a verse to send off the messenger, saying: "I trouble you, special envoy, to enter the mists and clouds; The ashes are cold, there is no hot water to brew tea."
Cha. He sent word to the worthy Governor of Yongdong: "It is difficult to make withered wood bloom again. Not long after, he passed away.
Zen Master Qiyuan Qi of Qingyuan in Jixian was a successor of Zen Master Yizhen of Shimen;
he was the son of the Chen family of Fuzhou. At the age of twenty-eight, he took leave of his father and elder brother to follow Yun...

Gai Zhi left the household life and served as the administrative head monk (*śrāmaṇera*). One day, after the head monk had finished presiding over the *fubi* (the incense-burning sermon), the Master asked him, "I have heard what the Head Monk has said, yet I do not understand its meaning.
I humbly hope for your compassionate instruction. The Head Monk exhorted him earnestly, leading him to investigate this Dharma through the teachings of Wuzhuo.
After two days had passed, he attained realization and presented his understanding in verse, saying: "In expounding the Dharma, nothing compares to this..."

This very person: throughout the ocean of lands in the ten directions, there is but a single mote of dust. If one can clearly realize the True Principle herein, has a single person ever been seen upon this great earth?
The assembly was struck with awe. Having attained liberation through the words of his teacher, he traveled extensively, visiting masters in all quarters.

Later, he arrived at Shimen (Stone Gate), where he was deeply honored and accepted as a worthy vessel. He went on to reside at Qingyuan for barely twelve years. On the day of his passing, he spoke a verse to the assembly, saying: "Yesterday..."
Past the third watch of the night, crossing a swift rapid; at the head of the rapids, clouds and mist stretch vast and black.
With a single staff as one's true companion, one shatters a thousand barriers and ten thousand gates.
Chan Master Tianyi Facong of Yuezhou ascended the hall and said: "The cold lamp in the dark chamber needs no lighting; the bright moon in the void pierces the clouds and sky.
If you wish to know that daily life is always uninterrupted, a strange sprout emerges from within the blazing flames.

At that time, while preparing to paint the Great Being Samantabhadra and opening his eyes with light, the Master climbed the ladder, took up his brush, and looked at the assembly, saying: "If you can speak [the truth], then..."
He was about to apply the brush when the assembly had no reply. The Master called to his attendant, saying, "Help this old monk firmly hold the ladder," and then he pointed at it.
Chan Master Fotong of Xiangshan Nunnery in Suining Prefecture attained realization while reciting the Lotus Sutra. She went to see Shimen.
He then said, "One cannot eat it in Chengdu; one cannot eat it in Suining. He then took up his staff and struck him out.

The Master suddenly attained enlightenment and said, "Those who flourish do so of their own accord; those who decline do so of their own accord. Autumn dew and spring wind—how could they not find their place?"

He shook out his sleeves at the gate and returned to the abbot’s quarters; the Master likewise turned away and departed. From this point on, both clergy and laity followed him in admiration, and many attained the Dharma.
He was a successor of Chan Master Jue of Jingyin.
Chan Master Hui-lan of Huayan in Tokyo ascended the hall and said: "The Great Master Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years;

even before he had opened his mouth, he was enough to leave people in doubt. Yet, as soon as he was glanced at by the Dharma Master Chan-guang, his hands and feet fell into a frantic flurry, and he immediately declared:
'I have come to this land from the West / To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings / One flower opens into five petals.'"

The result was naturally accomplished. At that time, had there been a man who possessed in the back of his head the eye that illuminates past and present, and held in his hand the tongs and hammer that cut through space, as soon as he heard such a statement, he would have grabbed him by the chest and asked:
"He said 'one flower and five petals'—set that aside for a moment; what is it that you transmit?"
This is the fundamental Dharma. Waiting for him to open his mouth, [Huayan] immediately overturned the meditation seat.

Even if it were Bodhidharma with his full capacity, he would have been forced to retreat three thousand miles, lest he be seen as burdening his descendants for a thousand ages. How could Huayan today allow this to be in vain?
Not only will he restore the collapsed纲 (gāng), but he must also clear the wrongs of all people. He then took up his staff and held it across [his body].
He called to the great assembly, saying, "Where has Master Bodhidharma gone? He threw down his staff, descended from his seat, and ascended the hall.
Taking up his staff again, he said: "At the assembly on Vulture Peak, it was called 'Plucking the Flower'; before the peak of Shaoshi, it was named 'Obtaining the Marrow.
The ancient worthies of old could only look on from the sidelines; the masters of this final age all simply fold their hands in submission. [He spoke of] the Avataṃsaka.
Today, one must not follow the waves or drift with the current. One intends to point out the spring colors of the entire world before the Ten-Thousand-Fathom Peak.
Do you understand? The skull has no joyful consciousness; the withered tree resounds with dragon-songs.
Zen Master Ci of Xijing Xiongeri, successor to Zen Master Tianning Hu, ascended the hall and said: "Prajñā is without cognition; it reflects in response to conditions.
Today this mountain monk is urinating and defecating; he releases here and voids there. The eastern mountains and western ridges laugh heartily. Fortunately..."
A single expanse of cool clarity was just defiled by Xiong-feng. Do not murmur about his defiling it; the clay ox and wooden horse all rebuke him.
Let us not discuss his transgressions that fill the heavens; when shall we see such purity again? Do you understand?
Next year there will be new branches once more, yet the spring wind that causes such disturbance will never cease.
Chan Master Da-hong Qing-xian of Suizhou was a successor of Chan Master Da-hong Sui.
He was the son of the Yang family from Guang’an in Shu. While reciting Baozhi’s Twelve Songs, he attained a realization.

Subsequently, he studied under Fo-xing and Hong-zhi, both of whom provided him with inspiration and guidance. The military governor of the Western Capital listed the Master’s spiritual conduct [among the eminent monks].
In the morning, an imperial decree was issued appointing Jixi as the Abbot of Dahong, and he was granted the title "Great Master Juezhao Huikong Fozhi Mingwu.
A monk asked: "When Subhūti sat in meditative seclusion within his cave, Śakra rained down flowers; now that you, O Master, newly occupy the peak of Hong, [how do you respond?]"
"What auspicious signs are there? The Master said: "An iron ox plows through the land of Fusang; a golden crow leaps forth, illuminating the sea gate. [The monk] asked:
"I do not yet understand what the essential principle of this is. The Master said: "A hot-iron cauldron for boiling tea is not the same as a tea kettle."

Chan Master Shu of Tianzhang in Yuezhou, a Dharma successor of Chan Master Datong Zhi, ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "Spring is about to arrive and the year is already drawing to a close.
Reflecting upon the past and the present, it is nothing but this same pattern. Cast your gaze upon the customs of old; set foot upon the ways of yore."

Old Wang of the eastern village laughs heartily; nowadays, people discard this Way like common dirt.

Master Xingyu of Baoning in Jiankang ascended the hall. Entering the Way-place, his reflection was contained within the mirror of the school, radiantly brilliant.
Stars are scattered across a clear night; flowers bloom brilliantly in the springtime. The wooden man secretly operates the mechanism of transformation without the slightest error;

Zen Master Fatang of Beishan in Zhenzhou ascended the hall and said: "Why can one who has swallowed up the three periods of time not open their mouth?

Chan Master De-peng of Chongxian Bamboo Tube in Gaoting, Hangzhou, was the son of the Gu family of Yanguan.
He was a disciple of the renowned local monk Shou-zhang. In the Wuchen year of the Shaoxing era, he went to Jing Mountain to attend upon Zhenxie.

While staying overnight at the foot of the mountain, Zhenxie dreamed that two moons entered the monastery; when the Master arrived the following morning, Zhenxie marveled at this omen. He investigated the teachings for four years. One day...
Hearing the sound of water dripping from a bamboo pipe, he attained great enlightenment. Xie approved of this and consequently named him Zhutong (Bamboo Pipe).

When Xie received the imperial decree to reside at Chongxian Monastery, the Master accompanied him. After Xie passed away, the Master succeeded him in accordance with the imperial decree during the Guiyou year of the Shaoxing era.
On two occasions, imperial edicts summoned him to the Cining Palace to preach the Dharma. Because Zhao Zhang was advanced in years, he declined the post and returned home to visit his parents.
Two years later, by imperial decree, he was again appointed to reside at Chongxian. In the Dinghai year of Emperor Xiaozong’s Qiandao era, he passed away without illness.

Chan Master Wen’an Sizong of Xuedou in Mingzhou was a successor of Chan Master Tiantong Jue. He was born into the Chen family of Huizhou. In his youth, he studied the sutras and received full ordination.

Relying on his wondrous, profound wisdom, he questioned [Hui]mi in succession until he attained a clear and complete realization. Hui nodded in approval. Later, he went to visit Hongzhi and received his seal of certification;
his Way became even more honored. He left to reside at Puzhao, Shanquan, Cuiyan, and Xuedou.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Every person has a nostril. Only Shanquan has no nostrils. Why does he have none? Twenty years ago, I broke..."
People have already been pulled out of the Luo River. Every person has two eyes, yet only Shanquan has no eyes. Why does he have none?
Because they were exchanged for a wooden prayer-bead rosary by others. Every person has a skull, yet only Shanquan has no skull. Why does he have none?
Because it was borrowed from someone to serve as a dung-scoop. He then called to the assembly, saying:
No nostrils, no eyes, and no skull. Do you all still recognize this skillful means (*upāya*)?
If you do not recognize it, you are burying this skillful means. If this is not yet so, listen further to this verse: "The mud ox at the bottom of the ravine has its face gilded with gold;

the pillar is originally but wood; the weight is merely cast iron. If you go to other places, do not say that this mountain monk is loquacious. A monk asked:

The Master said, "The play before the act of biting the arrowhead. [The student] asked, "What is 'reaching through the integration'? The Master said, "The ten directions..."

**Not Passing Through Depletion** Question: "What is 'turning function to accord with the position'? The Master said: "Letting go of all support, the whole body is manifest; a lone boat and a fisherman sleep amidst the reeds. Question:

an old monkey cries out once from a high tree. Question: "What is 'function and position both fully revealed'? The Master said: "The autumn river flows clear and deep; the bright moon shines over the vast expanse."
The Master said: "Once you have left the gate, you do not tread the path by which you came; before one's eyes, flying dust fills the view, yet there is not a single speck of dust.

[The questioner] asked: "What is it to have both function and rank concealed? The Master said: "The clay ox drinks the moonlight from the clear pool; the stone horse, spurred on, does not turn its head. The Master passed away at his own mountain seat.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa in the southwest corner of the temple.
Chan Master Fazhi of Shanguan in Changzhou was the son of the Bai family of Shanfu. In his youth, he received the tonsure at Sengguo Temple in the Western Capital and studied the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Later, he left to visit Nan yang Jin, and subsequently attended Da Hongzhi. For over ten years he attained no realization; however, later, beneath the words of Hongzhi, he experienced a sudden awakening.

the guests have dispersed, and the wine cups on the cloud-palace are empty. Entering the hall: In the Three Realms there is no dharma;

where can one seek the mind? A startled snake enters the grass; a flying bird leaves the forest. After the rain, the mountain hall is still in the autumn night; the clamor of the marketplace never reaches this solitary place.
Cen was the Chan Master Zide Huihui of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, born into the Zhang family of Kuaiji.

In his youth, he relied upon Dao Ning of Chengzhao Monastery, where he received the tonsure and full ordination. At the age of twenty, he visited Zhenxie at Changlu, where he attained some degree of realization before returning to his hometown.
He went to visit Hongzhi. Hongzhi asked him, "When there is light within the dark, do not meet it with darkness; when there is darkness within the light, do not gaze at it with light.
Chuyuan’s words did not accord with the Master's. At the first watch of the night, he rose from his seat and went before the sacred statue of the Buddha to burn incense.
At that moment, Hongzhi arrived. Upon seeing him, the Master suddenly understood the previous dialogue. The following day, when entering the room for instruction, Hongzhi cited the saying:

"Alas, on the day he departed his countenance was like jade; yet when he returned, one sighed that his hair was like frost. When questioned about this, the Master replied: "His entry was distinct from his exit; it is subtle.

Dingsi year: He opened the Dharma at Putuo, moved to Wanshou, and then to Jixiang Xuedou. During the Bingshen year of Emperor Xiaozong’s Chunxi era, he was by imperial decree appointed to Jingci.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The piercing cold wind sweeps through the withered forest; Leaves fall back to their root, revealing the bare heartwood. Myriad streams flow toward the source as the boat reaches the shore;
The six windows are empty and bright, like a mustard seed meeting a needle. This is the original manifestation—do not look elsewhere."
Investigation: The nature-ground is vast and serene, shining through ancient and modern times. Outside the door, the frost has melted and the spring colors stir;
the four mountains resound as one with the cry of the wooden dragon. [Ascending the hall: Śākyamuni Buddha exhausted all principles and fully realized the nature;

With white hair, he left the mountain crags and valleys. At midnight, piercing the clouds, he entered the marketplace.
Entering the hall, he cited the Dharma-body verse of Master Fu: "Holding a hoe in empty hands, Walking while riding a water buffalo.
A person passes over the bridge; The bridge flows, but the water does not flow. Master Yunmen said: "Whether you come from the east, the west, the south, or the north, each of you..."
"Each of you comes riding upon a water buffalo. Although it is thus, even if there are a thousand or ten thousand heads, one must simply recognize this one head.
The Master said, "Yunmen is usually dry and parched; the awl cannot penetrate him. Yet, when he reaches this point—"
"I also understand how to drag through the mud and carry water. You people, do you wish to see this one head right now? The weather is somewhat cold; each of you return to the hall.
Ascending the hall, he raised the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner. The Master said:

"If you can apply an eye where the wind and banner move, it is indeed the Upādhyāya. If you lose that eye where the wind and banner move, then it is simply the wind and banner. If this is not yet so..."
"Indeed. It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind. Monks merely force themselves with needles and awls. After the rain has passed over the mountain retreat, the misty smoke is still;
lying down, I listen as the cool breeze arises from the bamboo grove. In the autumn of the *gengzi* year, he retired to Xuedou.
On the twenty-ninth day of the second month of winter in the *jimao* year, at midnight, he bathed and passed away. His entire body was interred to the right of the Mingjue Pagoda.
Chan Master Fagong of Shichuang at Ruiyan in Mingzhou was the son of the Lin family from Fenghua in the commandery.

He received the tonsure and full ordination at Qizhen Temple. Later, he went to Yanqing Temple to study the lectures on the sutras. One night, while reciting the *Lotus Sutra*, he reached the passage:

"The eyes born of one's parents can see the three thousandfold world-system. At that moment, he heard the sound of wind rustling through the leaves of a *tāla* tree; he suddenly attained awakening and abandoned his formal studies.

At Tiandong, he first clarified the great principles. All those propagating the Dharma in his time went to him for consultation and resolution. He left [Tiandong] to take up residence at Nengren, Guangxiao, and Ruiyan.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring wind and willow brows; the spring birds warble with a hundred tongues.
A single piece of the Patriarch’s mind—leaks out in both places. Without moving a step, one returns home; habitual outflows are instantly extinguished. Casting a jewel into the darkness..."
The awns of the grain pierce through the golden needle-holes at dawn; deep, firm, and profoundly remote—who, being no one, could discern them? How shameful for these pitiable beings!
At every turn they follow the same track, yet they do not contemplate Amitābha; "Namu to the dry dung-stick. Before those who lack wisdom and are deluded, one must never speak [of this].
Entering the hall: When you see through to the bottom, its function is intimate; wherever you meet, it is all this.
One who is among those within [the Way]: Looking at the sky, one rains down jewels—do not boast of wealth. Having no place to stick even a锥 (a small awl)—is this not poverty?

Treading upon a scale-weight as hard as iron: Eight *liang* has always been but half a *jin*. Ascending the hall, he raised the koan of the World-Honored One pointing to heaven and pointing to earth after his birth.
He offered this verse: "A single arrow of thistle and mugwort from the Five Indias, Stirring up a million soldiers in China."

The soldier failed to carry out Yunmen’s true command; he nearly mistook the weight of the scale. In the eighth month of the *xinchou* year of the Chongxi era of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song, [Yunmen] manifested slight illness.
He sent a letter summoning Zizide to come; when they met, it was as if nothing were amiss. He entrusted him with his final affairs.
At dawn the following day, he ascended the seat, recited a verse, and passed away. His age was eighty, and his years since ordination were fifty-nine.
Chan Master Fazhen of Qingliang at Shimen in Xiangzhou was a native of Jianmen. He ascended the hall and said: "The willow color holds mist;
the spring light is exquisitely beautiful. A single peak rises solitary and steep; ten thousand plants vie for their fragrance. The white clouds are limpid and already without mind;
the green mountains before one’s eyes have never moved. The old fisherman casts his line; a stream of cold snow has not yet melted. At the wild crossing, there is no one."
For ten thousand ages, the azure pool is as clear as a mirror—this is the guest within the host. Holding a staff that spans the wheel of the sun and moon—this is the host within the guest.

Treading through grass shoes until they are worn away, walking barefoot—thus it is that guest and host manifest each other, killing and giving life with freedom, principle and phenomena are fused, and the orthodox and the deviant are no longer obstructed.
Entering a desolate field, one does not discriminate; one simply picks up whatever grass comes to hand. But tell me, what is it like?
What is the full detail? Although there may be arts of invisibility within the dust, how can they compare to entering the Imperial Capital with one’s whole body?
Chan Master Liaotang Sicheng of Kuangxiao Temple in Mingzhou ascended the hall and said: "A sheep-headed cart pushes the bright moon; A bottomless boat carries the morning breeze.
One phrase instantly transcends the realm of sentiment and measure; The Way has no north, south, east, or west."
Therefore, the news prior to the kalpa cannot be transmitted by mouth or ear; how could the true rule beyond the category be understood through deliberation?
You must know that from Buddha to Buddha and Patriarch to Patriarch, not a single dharma was ever given to others.

From generation to generation, one must directly and completely shoulder this entire body. Since the myriad functions have already been stilled and eliminated, naturally not even a grain of dust remains. It is the profoundly still wave.
Clear waters coldly reflect the autumnal colors; the numinous illumination shines forth. A clear sky washes the icy orb clean;

winding and interlacing, they harmonize and encompass one another. With dream-like hands, one pushes open the jade doors; with a turn of the body, one sets the mechanism’s wheel in motion. As the true command is just enacted, one sees the first yang begin to sprout.
The workings of the Great Artificer move in secret; suddenly, one is startled by the transformations of the three periods of time. Although this is so...
Silent and speechless, how can one resist the constant, blazing discourse that never shifts or changes? Today, let it be set aside for a moment.
Whether old or new, tell me: how shall you explain this? Do you all understand? When the various aggregates have been entirely stripped away, tomorrow is the day of "Writing the Clouds."
Chan Master Dahong Fawei of Suizhou was the son of the Bao family of Tiantai. He ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma-body is formless;

it cannot be sought through sound or voice. The wondrous Way is beyond words; how could it be understood through written characters? Even if one transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs, one still falls within the rungs of a ladder.
Even if one speaks of the wondrous and discourses on the ultimate source, one will ultimately remain caught between the lips and teeth. One must [realize that] merit and achievement..."
Transgressions leave no trace; withered trees and cold crags no longer receive a drop of moisture.

When the illusory person and the wooden horse are both empty of emotion and consciousness, one can finally extend a hand to enter the marketplace and turn the body into other species. It is said: "In the realm of non-outflows, one cannot remain;
one returns instead to lie upon the cold sands in the misty ravines."
Chan Master Daolin of Changlu in Zhenzhou ascended the hall and, holding up his staff, said: "As for its fundamental principle, it is beyond mind, intellect, and consciousness.

As for its essential purport, it transcends the past, present, and future. Because it is beyond mind, intellect, and consciousness, it classifies the myriad phenomena without perceiving any distinction between them."
Transcending the past, future, and present, it pervades the ten directions without further leakage; it does not offend at the very head and is utterly without dependence.
Awakening occurs prior to the arising of any signs; its function lies in the realm where merit and achievement cannot reach. This is the ordinary livelihood.
Do not hesitate; in the mere interval of deliberation, you are already cut off from the matter.

Master Wù, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Yù of Dahóng, ascended the hall at Huílì Monastery in Línjiāng Commandery and said: "All sounds are the Buddha's voice—the dripping of rain before the eaves."
The resonance rings out clearly and coldly. All forms are the Buddha’s form; face-to-face, they are presented, impossible to avoid. If one simply proceeds in this way, how can it be clarified?

Hearing this, Dahong remarked, "Brother Shen’s discourse on Chan is like this; it is a pity that his karmic fortune was not sufficient. One day, he gave a general sermon.

Master Tianfeng Gui, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Master Tongli of Donglin in Jiangzhou, ascended the hall and said: "A metal boat is steered atop a mountain peak; at the third watch, the sun’s disc blazes bright."

The mind is at ease, yet it does not manifest itself; one knows only when the fallen leaves have been swept. Carelessly plucking a pear from Zhengzhou, let go of the hand and it is found to be a jujube from Qingzhou.
[This was said by] Chan Master Tiantai Cong, a Dharma heir.
Chan Master Huiji Fa’an of Suzhou was a native of that prefecture. A monk asked, "What is the one phrase by which you, the Master, benefit others?
The Master said, "When a dog runs, it shakes its mouth. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "When a monkey worries, it scratches its head."
Chan Master Hugu Qin of Wenzhou ascended the hall and said: "A phrase, no phrase; light comes, darkness departs.
A living capture, a swift seizure; a dispatch, a proclamation. Like a vine leaning against a tree—things gather according to their kind.
Ginseng from overseas, cotton from Shu. When the tree falls, the vine withers; one must strictly avoid following patterns. Where do these phrases return? *Sulū sulū*. Hehe! Great!"
A laugh! The broken mirror does not reflect; the great earth is vast and boundless—let it be as it is, leaping and bounding at will.
Chan Master Ji-xiang Yuan-shi of Wu-wei Army was a native of Gao-you. Since arriving at Tian-yi, he has applied himself with diligent effort day and night.
His elbows did not even touch the seat. One day, he happened to laugh out loud and disturb the assembly; Yunyan banished him, and he stayed overnight in a village field.

There, beholding the brilliant stars and moon, he attained a realization. At dawn, he returned to the abbot’s quarters. Upon seeing him, Yunyan asked, "How do you explain the Five Ranks of Lord and臣 (Minister) of Dongshan?
The Master replied, "In my place, there is not even a single rank. Yunyan ordered him to attend the hall, and then addressed his attendant.

Thereupon, the Master secretly realized the profound meaning and uttered this verse: "The single rank is just revealed, and the five ranks are distinguished; When ruler and subject are in harmony, purple clouds gather."
The night-bright curtain is rolled up, shining impartially; the layered golden halls reveal the Most Honored One. His robes were fitting for his virtue. Later, he resided at Jixiang.
Chan Master Daoyuan of Touzi in Shuzhou had long served Tianyi without attaining realization. Tianyi rebuked him; the Master forgot [his pride].
He remained in seclusion for over a month. One night, hearing the sound of the watchman’s bell, he was suddenly struck by a profound realization and exclaimed: "Stop! Stop!
A single sound pierces straight through the path to the azure heavens; who knows of the bright moon in the cold pond? The mud ox butts the coral tree.
Subsequently, when he was appointed to the position of Abbot of the Treasury (Cangsi), whenever anyone questioned him, he would brandish his whisk in the manner of shaking a bell.
Chan Master Xuedou Zhijian of Mount Xuedou in Mingzhou was a descendant of the fifteenth generation under Chan Master Tiantong Ju.
He was the son of the Wu family in Chuzhou. When he was a child, his mother washed a sore on his hand for him.
The Master asked, "What is this? He replied, "My hand is like the Buddha’s hand. Having long lost his parents' protection, he relied upon Zhenxie at Changlu.
Zhenxie took him as a worthy vessel and appointed him as the head of the assembly. Later, he withdrew to Mount Xiangshan, where no hundred strange apparitions could distract him.
In the deep of night, he attained awakening and sought confirmation from Yanshou Ran, who said, "These days my belly has grown large, yet there is nothing to eat; the hermitage is small and lacks—"
"The bed may be used for lying down. If you can provide food and set up a thatched hut, then I shall stay; otherwise, I shall depart. He added, "This fellow, from where have you seen gods or ghosts?

Finally, he said, "Master Jian is a man of thorough realization. He then went to see Daixiu at Yuelin, whose skillful discernment was such that—
He escaped. Xiu said, "From now on, neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs can do anything with you. Consequently, he ordered him to go begging for the sake of the assembly.

The Master carried two bags and accepted whatever he obtained immediately; he underwent many hardships and labors. At Mount Cui, Zongbai called out to the Master, saying, "You have exerted yourself to the utmost for the sake of the assembly;
are you not weary? The Master replied, "One must know that there is a state where there is no weariness. Zongbai asked, "In the position of the Honored and Noble One..."
"When it cannot be grasped, what then? The Master said, "Meeting everywhere, yet not recognizing one another.

The Master said, "Do not forget, but do not remember either. If you remember, you bind yourself; if you forget, you lose the Way. Hold fast to the Middle Way, and you will naturally accord with the Dharma. The student bowed and withdrew. The Master remained silent. After a long pause, he spoke again: "The Dharma is like the moon reflected in water; it appears clearly yet leaves no trace. If you seek it in words and phrases, you will miss it entirely. If you can look directly into your own mind, you will see that it is originally bright and pure, unconditioned and unchanging. This is the true essence of the Buddha-Dharma. The student bowed once more and departed. The Master closed the door and sat in meditation. That night, he dreamed of a golden light filling the room. Upon waking, he felt a profound sense of clarity and peace. He recorded these exchanges as the "Recorded Sayings" to transmit the Dharma to future generations. Thus ends the first chapter of the *Linji Lu*.

The Master said: "It is not a mere coincidence. He ascended the hall and said: "Śakra, Lord of Devas, and Śākyamuni Buddha are both here in the midst [of this assembly]."

"What is the matter? The Master said, "If you cannot decide, then speak. [The monk] asked, "When humans and devas meet, what is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Presenting one's faculty before the assembly. He ascended the hall and said, "You sons of the Buddha, you must first clearly grasp the nostrils of a patch-robed monk.

"Please," [the monk] said, and he descended from his seat. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of coming from the West? The Master said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
The monk asked, "Is there anything further above this? The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is the matter further above this? The Master said, "Śākyamuni Buddha is in the Western Heaven;
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva dwells in these Eastern Lands. The monk asked, "When both parents have passed away..."
"What? The Master said, "Both are lost; let us set that aside for now. Which one is your father and mother? [The student] said, "It is a matter of profound suffering.
The Master said, "Truly so! Truly so! [Student] asked, "What is the great donor? The Master said, "To encounter the situation without discernment.
[Student] asked, "When someone comes who is utterly shrouded in darkness, how do you rescue them? The Master said, "A double case; receive it on a single document."
Guo asked, "For whom should one explain the teachings? The Master said, "Come closer. Guo asked in a loud voice. The monk came forward and asked. The Master then struck him.
A monk asked, "How old are you, Master? The Master said, "Seven times nine is sixty-eight.

What will you do? Each of you should find a place for rebirth; do not wander aimlessly from state to state.
These fellows merely wish to twist and wring out some idle talk; they wait for the old monk’s mouth to move, then immediately ask about Chan, the Way, the "upward" and "downward," or "how" and "what.
